en: Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, whose body is consciousness. Now begins the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī*.
That which, from the beginningless, manifests as "I" from the luminous plenitude that is free of appearances...

I bow to that non-dual reality which consists of the supreme Śiva and Śakti, the entirety of existence, which, while possessing the states of opening, expansion, closing, and persistence from its own nature, subsequently desires to divide itself into two branches in order to manifest its own power. 1.
This is the reflection of the consciousness of Śrī Somānandanātha, who resides within the pearl-like center of the lineage of Śrī Tryambaka. //2//
He proclaimed the stainless treatise known as the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, which is the supreme and peerless means for attaining the goal of human life witnessed by no other. 3.
Having learned this from the venerable Lakṣmaṇagupta, I, Abhinavagupta, the disciple of his disciple, compose this brief commentary on that Sūtra. 4.
The intended meaning [of the Sūtras] has been established by the author through the Vṛtti, and their investigation through the Ṭīkā;
therefore, for the sake of those of dull intellect, I shall provide a correct exposition of the meaning of these Sūtras in this manner, for the purpose of discerning Pratyabhijñā. (5)

Whether toward one of limited intellect everywhere, or toward someone of very great intelligence in some particular case, or even toward anyone else, this [instruction] will be beneficial only to oneself. //6//

The author of the work, desiring to transmit to others that state of identity with the Supreme Lord—a power he has directly perceived within himself—and considering that its attainment will occur without obstacle provided it is preceded by the surrender of his own identity, sets forth the purpose of the work as follows, with the intent of establishing the fitness for identity with the Supreme Lord through a reflection on total devotion to the excellence of the Supreme Lord: [The text continues with the first sūtra: *śrīmataṅge tathā coktaṃ śivena paramarṣiṇā | anuttaravibhūtiryā parāṃ kāṣṭhāmupāśritā ||* Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmataṅga* by Śiva, the supreme seer: "That which is the sovereignty of the Absolute (Anuttara), having reached the highest pinnacle... [and so forth].
Having somehow attained the state of servitude to Maheśvara and desiring to benefit all people,
I shall establish that recognition (pratyabhijñā) which is the cause for the attainment of all perfections.
In this context, the meaning of salutation is this humility— characterized by the application of body, speech, and mind toward the Supreme Lord as their sole object—
and it is appropriate for an authoritative person to perform it in such a manner only if they perceive the excellence of the one worthy of universal salutation.

Otherwise, for one who does not reflect upon the underlying reasoning and who exerts himself in paying homage even to that which is not the ultimate reality, there is only the state of being cast among worldly people. As it has been said:
"Stained by attachment to [mundane] knowledge, they do not find the Supreme God.
For as long as one is being driven by the impure *vidyā*, *rāga*, and *kalā* belonging to *māyā*, one remains nothing but a bound soul (*paśu*).
However, in comparison with others, there may also be excellence due to having transcended several temporal paths. As it has been said:

"O Lord, for one who beholds Your unimpaired glory through Your natural instruments [the senses], how could even an inferior person, out of delusion, desire to praise another deity while setting You aside?"
Thus it was said by the illustrious Vidyādhipati;
and we shall establish this in the section on scripture (āgamakāṇḍa).
Therefore, even the contemplation of all excellence must be accepted therein.
Although this entire ground of Supreme Śiva comes to the range of one's own heart by itself for one upon whom the firm descent of the Lord’s power has occurred,
no personal human effort whatsoever can be effective here;
for all such effort consists of *māyā* and is like blinding darkness, serving as a means only toward its own opposite— the non-*māyic*, pure light.
Because it is not logically tenable [otherwise],

the object of reflection must be understood through the interpenetration of words such as "victory" (jayati) and so forth— which express every particular excellence in their entirety— with the desire to go [to that state];
thus, this is what is implied by the act of salutation.

Even when the word "Victory" (*jaya*) is uttered— which possesses such an excellence that one who does not humble themselves before it remains a mere bystander, yet is supremely beneficial to the non-Self— it follows by this very logic that the act of salutation (*namaskāra*), though implied by that specific excellence, must necessarily be included within the context. Therefore, when either "Victory" or "Salutation" is employed as the introductory practice, the other must necessarily be admitted as being implied by the sense.
Since even acts such as salutation, bowing, recollection, and profound meditation have as their ultimate reality nothing more than the sense of homage and victory, this alone is the path.
In this regard, however, the author of the treatise has adopted such a method that both of these [aspects] are explicitly grasped by their own words.

And this will become manifest precisely at the occasion of explaining the meaning of the words. Furthermore, the reference by its own term (*svaśabda*) is logically appropriate because it is beneficial for all people; for that [term] is immediately understood by everyone's heart.

However, only a few [meanings] are implied by implication (*arthākṣipta*), because it is impossible for there to be a reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of the reality of speech (*vāktattva*) arising from one's own intuition (*pratibhā*) with respect to each [meaning];
and because a manifestation (*prakāśa*) devoid of the reflective awareness of the reality of speech is virtually non-manifestation.
This will become clear later.
With this intention, the author followed this path by avoiding the deceptive application of words such as "well-known victory" (*prasiddhajaya*) and so forth;
for whatever appears here, that is merely the manifestation of one's own self in the form of the Lord (*īśvara*) which is about to be described.
In that regard, however, the relationship of cause and effect— beginning with the relationship between means and end— is indeed ultimately real, just as it appears,
because the manifestation [of consciousness] (*prakāśa*) is undeniable. As Bhaṭṭa Tivākaravatsa said in the *Vivekāñjana*:
"Light indeed [is the nature] of all things...
and so forth,
up to "...it is not dissolved by the utterance of a curse."

Thus far. However, even within that causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), in certain cases there shines forth an uninterrupted manifestation of a distinct state of being, embraced by the inseparable nature of the sovereignty characterized by absolute freedom (*paripūrṇasvātantrya*) and touched by the infinite wheel of powers (*anantaśakticakra*). That [causal relationship], however, will be established as belonging to the sphere of Māyā (*māyīya*).
And this [reality] is divided into hundreds of internal distinctions such as the insentient and the sentient;
and from that arises this entire manifestation of the relationship between the produced and the producer, and the known and the knower, which takes the form of worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*).

However, where the cause is the unimpeded self-luminosity of one's own nature—which possesses the unsurpassed power consisting of the manifestation of the pure form of one's own Self and is devoid of the intervention of any other illusory manifestation—[therein lies the true ground].
In this regard, that very Blessed One is the cause.
And this final, fifth supreme activity of the Lord, characterized by grace, brings about the highest human goal,
because the ultimate liberation is dependent upon it.
For liberation (*apavarga*) consisting in release from something specific, rather than from everything, is a mere semblance of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasābhāsa*), as we shall explain later.

Furthermore, this second type of causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is distinct from the well-known causal relationships established through worldly positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).

How can that which is not perceived as a distinct form, whose ultimate reality is inferred from the occasional existence of things, whose wondrous nature is brought forth by the manifestation of sovereignty characterized by the performance of the most difficult tasks, and which is difficult to attain even through hundreds of desires to remove the veil over its own self-luminosity— being devoid of any temporal form at the very first stage of conceptualization— be described by the word "somehow" (*kathaṃcit*), accompanied by an adverbial particle indicating "how"?
And by some means—namely, through the propitiation of the feet of the Guru, who is non-different from the Supreme Lord, and which is itself fashioned by the Supreme Lord—as it has been said:
"The connection is exceedingly difficult to establish...
[and so forth]. Regarding the word "āsādya" (having attained): it means having fully established [the state] in its entirely complete form on all sides.
Having rendered his own capacity for enjoyment unimpeded;
by this much, having known all that is to be known, his qualification for composing a treatise for the sake of others is demonstrated;
otherwise, it would be nothing more than mere deception.
Here, immediate succession is intended by way of priority;
otherwise, if there were a sequence of attainment, how could instruction by another be possible once the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the mass of *māyic* impurities have been destroyed?
For Viṣṇu, Viriñca, and others are indeed possible as presiding deities within *māyā*.
Even those who have transcended that [level] are presided over by Mahāmāyā; they consist of the Mantras, their Lords (Mantramaheśvaras), and the Great Lords (Maheśvaras), being both pure and impure.

Even the pure ones, such as Śrī Sadāśiva and others, have become lords through the drops of sovereignty belonging to Him. That Blessed One is Maheśvara, whose ultimate reality is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), the nature of which is uninterrupted light and bliss.
By the word "servitude" (*adāsya*), he indicates that the establishment of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of that [Lord] yields a great fruit.
A *dāsa* is one to whom everything desired is given by the master.
By the phrase "the state of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*), the capacity for the sovereignty that constitutes the nature of the Supreme Lord is expressed.
Regarding the word "of the person" (*janasya*): it refers to anyone who is being born.
By this, he shows that there is no restriction whatsoever regarding the qualified recipient here;
for whoever experiences this manifestation of one's true nature (svarūpa), for that person alone is there the great fruit,
because manifestation itself is the ultimate fruit.

And because that [knowledge] cannot be obstructed by those things generally considered to be obstacles— according to the maxim that "what is well-established is not [subject to] non-establishment"— it has been said:
"In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor is there any falling back."
"Even a very small portion of this dharma protects one from great fear.
Thus [it is said]. And by the venerable Paramaguru himself in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"Once, by means of valid cognition, from the scripture, or from the word of the Guru..."
When Śiva-nature, which resides in all things, is known through a firm-minded realization, [one attains liberation].
There is no purpose whatsoever for an instrument or even for meditation once [reality] has been known all at once;
what need is there for instruments and the like to establish the reality of gold once it has been recognized?
"Truth consists in a firmness equal at all times to that toward one's father, mother, and so forth.

By the phrase "of people who are incessantly tormented by birth and death," he indicates that they are objects of compassion and thus worthy of being benefited. The word *api* (even/also), revealing his non-differentiation from them, excludes any possibility of another purpose for himself beyond the accomplishment of the welfare of others through his own perfection.
Moreover, the welfare of others (*parārtha*) is indeed a purpose (*prayojana*), because it possesses that very definition;
for this is not a divine curse that the purpose must be solely one's own interest and not the interest of others,
since even that [self-interest] would lack the status of a purpose if it did not possess that definition.
That which is intended as the primary object to be accomplished is the *prayojana* (purpose), for it alone is the motivator for actions.

For this very reason, in order to demonstrate that even though God is distinct [from sentient beings], His purpose in performing the creation and so forth is solely for the sake of others (*parārtha*), the Creator of the System of Logic (*Nyāya-nirmāṇa-vedhas*) has defined it:
"That object aiming at which a person acts is the *prayojana*."

Thus: by the word *icchan* ("desiring"), [the author] shows, through the use of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), that the fruit which has been made the object of desire is the cause of the activity.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that the power of desire, through its progressively swelling nature, culminates in the power of action.
The prefix *upa-* signifies proximity.
Therefore, the fruit here is the bringing of people into the proximity of the Supreme Lord and His Dharma.
For this very reason, he says "entire" (samasta); for when the state of being the Supreme Lord is attained, all prosperities—which are the outflow of that state—become truly accomplished.
Just as when one finds a mountain of jewels, there is no need for other riches;
for one who has lost sight of the ultimate reality of the self, what is gained by anything else?
And even for one who has attained that ultimate reality, there is nothing else remaining to be desired.
As it was said by the author himself:
"For those enriched with the fortune of devotion, what else remains to be prayed for?
Or for those impoverished of it, what else remains to be prayed for?"
Thus, the purpose has been stated by means of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*);
however, by means of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the means (*upāya*) is indicated.

The "perfection" (*saṃpat*), that is, the attainment or realization, of the totality—whether positive or negative, external or internal, such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—is the manifestation of its true nature (*tathātva*).
The correct attainment of that [recognition] is its establishment through reflective inquiry (vimarśa);
that very inquiry is the cause of that recognition,
for it is taught here that the attainment of the ultimate subject occurs precisely by means of seeking out cognitions such as blue or pleasure, which possess a most vivid manifestation.
As it is said elsewhere:
"The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of 'this' as something distinct is that repose in one's own essential nature; that reflective awareness is 'I am this.'"
Thus, in that very same place:
"The resting of the Light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of 'I-ness' (ahaṃbhāva);
and that very resting is said to arise from the cessation of all dependence."
"Autonomy, as well as agency and primary lordship," thus [it is said].
By this much, the doubt regarding the extreme difficulty of the means (*upāya*) has been refuted; as he will demonstrate at the end:
"This path is easy to traverse and new" (IPV 4.1.16).
Regarding that Maheśvara, *pratyabhijñā* is the recognition (*pratīpa*)—that is, knowledge directed toward one's own self (*ātmābhimukhyena*), which is the light (*prakāśa*).
As for "toward oneself" (*pratīpam*): indeed, the manifestation of one's own self has never been previously unexperienced, because its light is uninterrupted.
But that [object] appears as if interrupted or as if conceptualized solely by that [power of consciousness]—this will be explained later.
Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) consists in the synthesis of a previously perceived form with a presently appearing form;
it is the cognition directed toward an object present before one through the synthesis [expressed as]: "This is that very Caitra."

In common worldly usage as well, when someone who has been known— whether by such qualities, such a form, or even merely in a general sense— is encountered again, the knowledge that is animated by reconnection (*pratisaṃdhi*) is designated as "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*),
as in expressions such as, "This person has been recognized by the king."

In this case as well, when the Lord—whose nature is one of perfect power known through established Purāṇas, Siddhāntas, Āgamas, inference, and so forth—is present within one's own self and becomes manifest, knowledge arises through the recognition of Him: "Surely, I am that very Lord. I shall now demonstrate this.
"Arising" (upapatti) means occurrence;
I bring about that occurring [arising] through the performance of the necessary actions, which is the operation of the instigator.
For instance: first of all, he indeed arises.
Because its manifestation is uninterrupted;
rather, the only proof required there is the mere removal of the power of Māyā, which is considered to be the cause of obstruction.

Since the distinction between self and other does not exist when the realization of Pratyabhijñā (recognition) is established, such things as the intention of an agent—which depend upon that distinction—are impossible; thus, the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) occurs [in the scriptures].
And thus, the construction of this verse is as follows:
having somehow attained service to Maheśvara, which is the cause for obtaining all prosperity,
and having somehow caused even ordinary people to attain— that is, to reach— recognition of Him (tat-pratyabhijñām).
Desiring that service which consists in being a servant of Maheśvara— the cause for obtaining all prosperity—
I shall establish that very recognition of Him (tat-pratyabhijñā), which is the cause for the attainment of all prosperity.
In the phrase "having attained" (āsādya), there are two causative suffixes (*ṇic*) when applied through repetition.
And in this much of the commentary, the author of the *Vṛtti* has not placed a heavy burden [on himself],
because he is engaged solely in the task of expanding upon the concise indications of the Sūtra, as it was said:
"In [this work] whose function consists merely in the expansion of the concise indications of the Sūtra..."
Thus, even the author of the *Ṭīkā*, being intent on explaining only the *vṛtti*, did not touch upon this;
however, our effort is directed solely toward the explanation of the *sūtras*—thus [the commentary] has been explained by making such a distinction.
This applies everywhere.
Thus, by this verse, the subject matter, the purpose,
and the purpose of that [purpose] are established.
The purpose of that [work],
the definition of the qualified practitioner, the succession of gurus, and the relationship— these have been shown.

For instance—that very object which was previously explained as characterized by all forms of perfection (*saṃpat*) and as the cause in merit, demerit, and so forth, which are the root causes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), is recognized by this [means]. Thus, through the etymological derivation from the sense of "instrument" (*karaṇa*), it is determined here as the means (*upāya*) toward the supramundane path;
such is sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) characterized by the power to accomplish the most difficult tasks.

By indicating that which will be defined at the end of the branch with the words "the path is ninefold" (Ipv 4.1.16), the means [of attainment] is shown as the subject matter. For this very reason, it is said:
"For thus, for those who have become insentient... (Ipv 1.1.4).
Following this introduction, there will be another verse.
The purpose [of the treatise] is the knowledge of the means for recognition (pratyabhijñā),
and the purpose of that [knowledge] is recognition itself.
The purpose of that [liberation] as well is the attainment of the singular form of supreme sovereignty characterized by all forms of perfection;
beyond that, there is indeed nothing else,
because it is the ultimate fruit of all, even in its most minute aspects.
As I myself have stated in my hymn:
"O Lord, the ultimate fruit of ritual actions or injunctions is indeed nothing other than being identical with You;
however, for those who still desire something else in this regard, their state is that of the deluded, characterized by endless instability."
Thus [it is said]. This will be stated by the two quarters [of the verse]: "Placing his foot here... (IPV 4.1.16).
By the word "of people" (janasya), the qualified candidate is indicated;
he will conclude with the words:
"Thus... By the phrase "in some way" (kathaṃcit), the succession of the lineage of gurus is indicated; he will state: "Thus..."
As it was said by the Great Teachers in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise:
(Ipv 4.1.16). Thus, by means of this summary of all things to be recognized, this sentence constitutes a formal enunciation (*uddeśa*), being essentially a condensed thesis (*pratijñā*).
The middle portion of the work, however, is that which establishes the reasons (*hetu*) and so forth.

The final verse, "Thus [this] has been revealed by me," constitutes the concluding section (*nigamana*). In this way, this treatise consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*) and results in the instruction of others. The author’s intention is that the very sequence of the Naiyāyikas possesses ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) even within the realm of *māyā*.

This will become manifest in the subsequent sections (uddeśas). Such is, for now, the intended meaning of the text: a virtuous person, being well-acquainted with worldly lords, reveals a lord who is endowed with the qualities of a servant, and regarding a subject, he reveals a lord who is endowed with qualities such as being approachable (abhigāmika) and so forth.
This much meaning has been shown in general by the genitive compound *tasya pratyabhijñā* ("the recognition of that").

And at the time of hearing this verse, for the disciples, through the process of the transmission of this meaning, there arises an identity with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-tādātmya*) itself. To explain: from hearing the word "of people" (*janasya*), [they realize], "We are those afflicted by birth and death, and our activities are unsteady."
Desiring to do us a favor,
he has attained the state of servitude to Maheśvara and establishes that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) which is the cause for the attainment of all prosperity.
And therefore, we have indeed attained such a recognition of that [Self];

for in this very way, the transfer of the meaning of the scripture to the qualified person— like the reflection of an image into a mirror— becomes the object of the imperative (*loṭ*) and optative (*liṅ*) moods, whereby the sense of the third person is transformed into the sense of the first person, and not through mere externality.
Because otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of no distinction between the qualified and the unqualified in their understanding [of the injunction].

When the meaning of the sentence— such as "those desiring health should serve Śivā" or "you all should serve"— is transferred to the qualified person in the form "we shall perform the service," then, even though the fulfillment of human goals (puruṣārtha) belongs to the third stage which falls within the realm of objective reality, the [practitioner] conceives of it as having been assimilated into his own self by entering into his own nature, which is untouched by time.
Precisely because of that, one who possesses a beautiful reflective awareness of expanded consciousness attains the sense of fullness;
however, for another, due to the very absence of such a nature, there is a lack of qualification, as they are characterized by a life-force centered on neutrality.
Let this intermediate point rest, for it is exceedingly profound—thus it is established.
By this verse, the propitious presence of the Lord (*īśvara-sāṃmukhya*) and the presentation of the purpose and so forth for those to be trained (*vineya*) are accomplished—thus:
"We praise that Śiva forever, in whom the supreme vibration (*spandana*), which illuminates the infinite mass of existents (*ananta-bhāva-saṃbhāra*), serves as the introduction (*upoddhāta*). (1)
Now, it might be argued that the proof of God must indeed be established.
But what is this "proof"?
It cannot be origination, because He is eternal.
Nor do the authors of the *Īśvarasiddhi* and other such works establish its logical proof (*upapatti*).

If it is argued that "proof" (*siddhi*) means "cognition" (*jñapti*), then for that which is of an uninterrupted nature of light (*anavacchinnaprakāśa*), there is no utility whatsoever in a proof consisting of a light produced by the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But surely, how can it be said that "His light is unconditioned"?
For when there is the manifestation of blue, pleasure, and so forth, from where does that [universal] manifestation come?
And even when those are not manifesting—as in deep sleep, fainting, and the like—it is all the more so.

Anticipating the objection—"Even if the Lord is self-luminous, what has happened to the cognizers such that the operation of their means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be of no use?"—he says: "In the Great Lord, who is the agent, the knower, one's own Self, and established from the very beginning—who, being non-inert, could effect either a negation or an establishment [of Him]? (IPK 1.1.2)

In this context, who is it that would establish— by means of what kind of proof— the existence characterized by the cognition "God exists," or who would effect the negation characterized by the cognition "He does not exist"?
If you say "the knower" (pramātā), then who exactly is he?
Is the body and so forth insentient, or is there something else denoted by terms such as "Self" (ātman) and so on?
Furthermore, is that [Self] of the nature of self-luminosity or not?
If it is argued that the body and so forth are insentient, [then...]
If that very [self] is unestablished in its own nature, what establishment could it effect in another?
Furthermore, if the self were not self-luminous, it would be merely insentient (*jaḍa*), sharing the same fate as those [objects].
If it is argued that its nature is indeed self-luminous, [then...]
In what kind of own-form does it shine? If it shines in the form of established pure consciousness alone, then there would be a differentiation of cognitions.
Furthermore, for those things that have been differentiated, there could be no non-differentiation through internal synthesis;
therefore, it first appears as having the nature of being independent and self-luminous.
For those things that have been differentiated, there could be no non-differentiation through internal synthesis.
To that extent, it appears as having the nature of being independent and self-luminous; and appearing in such a manner, what kind of Lord (*īśvara*) could it possibly establish or negate?
If you say its nature is that of an agent and a knower (*kartṛ-jñātṛ-svabhāva*), then surely that is the subject (*pramātṛ*) himself in that state—so who else could he be?
Now, it might be argued that omniscience and omnipotence do not belong to the knower;
for indeed, the meaning of the word "all" does not differentiate between the essential natures of knowing and acting.
Even when a distinction is observed, this is because the eternal knowledge, volition, and effort of the Lord cannot have their excellence augmented by an object that is not its cause.
If it is argued that being an object (*viṣayatva*) consists simply in being brought to manifestation, we reply:
it is improper for that which is by nature unmanifest to possess such a status—this we shall explain later.

Furthermore, if the object were of a manifesting nature, it would be entirely submerged within manifestation itself; thus, if the ultimate reality were merely that "manifestation manifests," what distinction could there be between the omniscient and the non-omniscient?
In this way, even the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is to be questioned in terms of its being established or unestablished;
the same applies to its establishment as well.
Therefore, having taken the object intended as the domain as its very body, it is the Self alone that shines forth, appearing without any separation.
It is indeed manifest even with respect to deep sleep,
otherwise recollection would be impossible;
and because manifestation is eternal, there is an absence of any cause for its interruption.
Furthermore, because it manifests in dependence upon another subject,
and because the distinction between self and other subjects— which is created by that [consciousness]— will be described as being of the nature of *māyā*,
this [consciousness] is autonomous (*svatantra*).
And we shall explain in many ways that its sovereignty consists in differentiating what is non-different, and in unifying what has been differentiated through internal synthesis;
this very thing is its supreme lordship, its primary form consisting of bliss— this is what was previously referred to by the term "in the agent."

However, that very sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is analyzed and stated by means of the subsequent designation "in the knower" (*jñātari*). For it will be said that action has the nature of being a mere offshoot of knowledge.
Therefore, as much as is meant by "in the independent one who possesses all powers regarding all actions," so much is meant by "in the agent who is the knower."
And this very [state] is the nature of consciousness (*saṃvitsvabhāvatā*).

However, when it is called "consciousness" (*saṃvid*), because it touches upon the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) through its capacity for conceptualization (*vikalpyatva*), it is not ultimate consciousness (*paramārthasaṃvit*)—as we shall explain later.
Even when he is designated as "the Great Lord, the agent and the knower," that same [conceptual] mode would necessarily follow.

Thus, one must strive as far as possible to avoid the stain of disparaging the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameya*) by establishing it upon its proper ground; this is why the instruction is given using the past tense (*bhūtavibhakti*). For at the time of the teaching, it is impossible to entirely eliminate that very status of being an object of knowledge for it.

Regarding the phrase "in one's own self" (*svātmani*): by this expression, "in one's own nature which is non-departing," the doctrine of an insentient self (*jaḍātman*) as maintained by the Vaiśeṣikas and others is refuted.
"In the eternally established" means in that which is of uninterrupted manifestation;
"in the Great Lord" (maheśvara).
This alone is the sovereignty of Maheśvara: the ascent onto the throne of being the knower and the agent by virtue of having uninterrupted light.
As for the "non-inert self"—let those, such as the Vaiśeṣikas, for whom the self is inert, attempt to establish the existence of God.
But another [opponent] refutes the Sāṃkhya and others;

for even the Sāṃkhya, who maintains that cognition—which consists in the manifestation of objects—is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), arrives at the conclusion that the Self is in reality insentient (*jaḍa*).
And an insentient Self, in which even a slight trace of the sovereignty of self-luminosity is impossible, is like a stone: it is incapable of accomplishing or negating anything.
Nor is this appropriate even for one who is not insentient;
for instance, he would have to effect his own establishment in this way only if that which appears to him as something new had not appeared previously;
yet if there is no such appearance, that is precisely insentience.
And one should formulate the refutation in this way: if that [object] were not manifest, it would be insentient;
yet it has been stated that this [manifestation] is not possible for the insentient, nor is it possible for the non-insentient.
Therefore, the manifestation of the jar and so forth is nothing other than the manifestation of consciousness;
it is not some independent, real entity.
Furthermore, consciousness alone is the Self.

Therefore, in that case, there is no operation of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) either, just as there is no operation of an agent (kāraka), because self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva), like eternality, is present therein. //2//

Now, one might object: "If the activity of an agent (*kāraka*) and the activity of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are not possible in the case of God, then what kind of activity is this that was mentioned—namely, 'I cause [him] to recognize'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
However, because this [Self] is not recognized even when seen due to the power of delusion,
it is demonstrated through this *pratyabhijñā* (recognition) by means of the manifestation of its inherent power.
That Self, whose nature is the Lord, shines forth;
and since He possesses absolute freedom therein, there is no form whatsoever in which He does not shine.
Thus, He shines even as that which is non-luminous by nature, and likewise as that which is luminous by nature.

In that case as well, within the nature of light, there must be illumination either entirely through its nature as light, or partially; and if it is partial illumination, it must occur either by way of distinction or non-distinction from the whole,
or by way of distinction or non-distinction from a certain portion.
Or [it may be understood] by way of the completeness of the aforementioned modes;
thus, there are these seven modes.
Among them, the first mode is the manifestation of the insentient (*jaḍollāsa*).
The final [state] is the essence of Paramaśiva; the intermediate [states] are the manifestations of individual souls (jīva),
which are indeed the Lord’s power known as Māyā, the deluder.

Although the Self is constantly manifesting as the nature of light by virtue of that [consciousness], it remains unperceived because it is not manifested in its entirety; consequently, it does not reach a state of being fully assimilated into the heart, and thus fails to perform the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) that is accomplished through the manifestation of fullness. Therefore, [this effort is undertaken] for the sake of achieving a specific form of self-identification (*abhimāna*) consisting in the manifestation of that fullness.
Recognition, which has been explained previously, is now demonstrated; how so?
By means of the manifestation—that is, the disclosure—of power (*śakti*), which is well known as residing in the Lord (*īśvara*) and consisting of vision and action.
Because purposeful actions accomplished through conceit cannot be established without the establishment of that very conceit;
and thus he shows an example: "By those various prayers [offered by them]... (Ipv 4.1.17).
Thus it is said: this means that there is no activity of an agent (*kāraka*) in the Blessed One, nor is this an activity of a communicator (*jñāpaka*);
rather, it is merely the removal of delusion (*moha*).

For the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish worldly transactional usage (*vyavahāra*) find their rest in that very [immediate awareness]. Indeed, by the statement "this jar is present because it is perceptible," the jar is not being made known; rather, it is already manifest through perception itself.
Otherwise, the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*).
Only delusion alone is removed;
and both this delusion and its removal are merely the manifestation of the Blessed One himself.
But there is nothing further—this has been stated and will be stated again. //3//
Now, one might ask: within this mass of manifest phenomena, whose power is being manifested, and toward what?

First of all, insentient things possess no power consisting of consciousness; nor can their power consist of action, for since that would require independence, and such independence is absent, it remains a ground of impossibility.
And likewise, regarding such expressions as "the chariot goes," some have accepted this as a metaphorical usage;

yet it is not appropriate to employ such a means of conventional discourse for those who are insentient. Therefore, both [the literal and the metaphorical] are intended with reference to the community of sentient beings.
In that case, the hope that the Great Lord (maheśvara) is the self of everyone is extremely remote; having raised this doubt, he explains as follows:
"For thus, the foundation of insentient things rests upon the living being."
Knowledge and action are considered the life-force for living beings who possess life.
The phrase "tathā hi" indicates the commencement of a logical argument; its meaning is "let it be seen, indeed.
By the word "tathā," the probandum (sādhya) is indicated.
Others say that "hinā" means "by the reason";
the meaning is that the subject under discussion, the probandum (*sādhya*), is undertaken as being dependent upon the establishment of the reason (*hetu*).
By the word "tena" (by that), it refers to that which resides in the intellect.
Or rather, the meaning of the word "tathā hi" (for thus) is that all this is logical because of the text already mentioned and the manner about to be described;
for instance, in this context, the mass of existing things exists insofar as it is investigated in such a way,
since it arises by relying on that which is essentially animated by light, taking refuge in the manifestation of existence.
For if an object were not examined, one could not say whether it is blue or yellow, existent or non-existent; what answer would there be to such an inquiry?
Therefore, whatever is examined in a certain way and to a certain extent, and remains uncontradicted, exists in that way and to that extent.
Thus, it will be explained that substance, action, relation, and so forth—even though their natures are extended across space, time, and form—exist as ultimate reality (paramārthasat) in their unity.

By such statements as these, it follows that although this universe is vast, when it ascends to the state of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in its contracted form, it exists in only two forms: the insentient and the sentient. Among these, the insentient, when being reflected upon, do not possess autonomy;
for their state of being reflected upon is not some property inherent within their own nature, as that would entail the consequence of them ceasing to be insentient.
"Blue appears to me" and "blue is known by me"—
for those [objects] which, though consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), have been rendered inert by the power of the Lord called *māyā*,
their "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) consists in abiding in a state of orientation toward that cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*) by depending upon a living subject.
Therefore, so-called insentient things do not exist apart [from consciousness];
as the author himself has stated:
"In this way, these [objects], which are like non-existent fictions in relation to the self, exist only as manifestations of light."
"The insentient [is non-existent]; light alone exists, by its own self and by itself and others.
For that alone can be said to exist by its own self whose form shines unconditioned by anything else;
and there is no such thing as an insentient entity that is not conditioned by the nature of light.
"By that, power is indeed manifested for the sake of the insentient"—this much is simply untenable.

As for those others who are known by the name "living beings," distinct from the insentient—even their bodies, vital breaths, subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and forms of emptiness are indeed insentient; what, then, can be said of them?
For this very reason, [the same applies to] a jar, a body, the vital breath, pleasure, and its [objects].
That which appears as the fixed form (lagna) is itself the true nature of the individual soul (jīva);
and although multiplicity appears at first glance, that [multiplicity] belongs to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body, which are insentient objects of knowledge.
Therefore, that [multiplicity] is ultimately unreal due to mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).
For living beings (jīvas) partake in duality due to their distinction from the insentient (jaḍa), and the insentient likewise partake in duality due to their distinction from living beings;
thus they arrive at such distinctions as "this is his body" and "this is what he perceives.
However, the distinctions between states such as blue, yellow, and so forth, being attached to the subject (pramātṛ), have ascended even further to the very ground of duality itself.
What follows from that?
Thus, since non-difference alone has been established for all living beings, it results that the cognizer is "living.
And "living" consists in being the agent of life, which is essentially composed of knowledge and action.
For he who both knows and acts is said to "live.

Therefore, this cognizer (pramātṛ), by virtue of possessing the powers of knowledge and action, is to be designated as "Lord" (īśvara), just like the Lord well-known in the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other traditions.

Even if that [specific deity] is not established, lordship—consisting in the very nature of possessing the power of knowledge and action regarding all objects—is established simply because it is invariably concomitant with those [powers].
Moreover, because such pervasion is grasped in the case of an imagined Lord, such as a king, [in the form]:
"Whoever is a knower and an agent to a certain extent is a Lord to that extent, like a king," since both knowing and acting are contrary to the nature of one who is not a Lord.
And since the Self is everywhere the knower and the agent, the *Pratyabhijñā* (Recognition) is established.
The powers of knowledge and action are indeed innate; when the emergence of differentiation has not yet unfolded, they constitute Sadāśiva and Īśvara;
when differentiation has generally unfolded, they become Vidyā and Kalā.
Upon drying up, they will sprout again, like the group of organs of intellect and action;

"insentient" (jaḍāḥ) means non-living, while others are living—this is what appears at first glance, but it does not appear upon the arrival of true consciousness. Thus, by the word "living," these [beings] are indicated as being exclusively mobile (jaṅgamāḥ). //4//
Now, one might raise the objection: "How can knowledge and action themselves be established, such that the manifestation of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) can be proven? To quell this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, knowledge is self-established; action, being dependent on the body, may be perceived by others as well. Through that [action], the other's knowledge is inferred. (5)
"I know," "it has been known by me," and "it will be known"— in this way, that which is called knowledge is established solely as the self-luminous reflective awareness of the "I" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*);
what else is there to be deliberated upon therein?

For if that were not manifest, the entire universe would be plunged into blinding darkness, or perhaps it would not exist at all; for even a child experiences only a state of rest within that manifestation. As it has been said:
"By what means, my dear, would one know the knower?
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14). For if that [knower] were denied, what question could there be, and what answer could there be?

And therein, even the application of internal impetus (*saṃrambhayoga*) shines forth as "I know," by which the body— through the quality of white and so forth, which is utterly insentient— attains the nature of consciousness; and that impetus is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which constitutes the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
As it was stated by our supreme preceptor, the venerable Śrī Rāmānanda Pāda:
"Even at the time of perceiving a jar or other objects, one knows the jar; that is the action.
Therefore, the internal power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), like knowledge itself, is self-established and self-luminous.
But that very [power], by its own capacity,

moving through the body via the sequence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), being of the nature of vibration and consisting of activity, is the object of the means of knowledge— such as perception— even in the state of dreaming.
And when that [power] is perceived in conjunction with another body and so forth, it makes known its own nature, which is essentially consciousness.
Furthermore, knowledge does not appear as "this-ness," for "this-ness" is indeed ignorance;
nor can one object appear as having the form of another object while appearing as such.
That supreme knowledge indeed shines;
and that which shines is itself the very body of "I"—thus even supreme knowledge is one's own self.
Its "supremacy" consists solely in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body and so forth.

And when that [universe] is investigated, it is found that there is no other; thus, the entire multitude of subjects (*pramātṛvarga*) is, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), a single subject, and he alone exists. As it has been said:
"The Light alone exists through its own self and through the natures of both itself and others.
Consequently, from the Lord Sadāśiva who knows down to even a worm that knows, there is only one single subject; thus, as a result, the subject possesses omniscience.
The same should be said regarding agency as well.
As was stated by our supreme preceptor in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"The jar perceives through my self, and I perceive through the self of the jar."
I know through the self that is Sadāśiva, or he knows through my own self.

"Śiva himself remains knowing his own self through various states," and so forth. By the word "is inferred" (*ūhyate*), he demonstrates that the status of knowledge as an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is not tenable;
otherwise, he would have said "it is inferred" (*anumīyate*).
Thus, for those who have not been rendered grey by the falling dust of the disputations of logicians on this path of direct experience (*saṃvedana*),

they— knowing themselves to be the Lord by means of just this [realization]— submerge the jar, the body, the vital breath, pleasure, and its absence right there [in that consciousness], and thereby become truly possessed by the Lord.
This, then, is the introductory summary (*upoddhāta*).

The prefix *upa* signifies that near to oneself (*ātmanaḥ samīpe*), by means of which excellence—characterized by the recognition of the Lord (*īśvarapratyabhijñāna*)—is struck, that is, brought to rest like a chisel;
and this alone is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of this work.
Furthermore, this constitutes the introduction (*upoddhāta*).

Having made it subtle and uninterrupted (*upāṃśu avitatam*), [the term] "ud" [indicates that] according to the scripture, the delusion regarding the object of cognition (*prameya-viṣaya*) is indeed struck away or removed by it—this is the meaning.
Alternatively, because the root *han* has the sense of "going," its meaning here is "knowing";
thus, it means that by which the object of cognition is known.
Some, however, say that the meaning of the root *han* (to kill) refers specifically to this context: "he goes to a woman who is his destination.
Thus, through the firm cultivation of the meaning of these four verses, the Supreme Śiva is attained. May there be auspiciousness! //5//

Thus ends the Introduction to the Chapter on Knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*) in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāvimarśinī*, composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, who received instruction from the venerable teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta, the disciple of the illustrious teacher Utpaladeva.
This concludes the First Daily Lesson (*āhnika*).
Now begins the second chapter:

We praise that Śiva, by whom the universe, having been manifested through differentiation as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), is led to the conclusion of the final position of non-differentiation (*abhedottarapakṣa*).
In this context, that which is the nature of ultimate reality becomes most excellently clarified when it is defined by means of the refutation of the counter-positions being suspected.
As Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa said:
"Salutations to you, who, having brought forth the delusion of those bewildered by worldly existence, shatters it."
And having chosen the bliss of knowledge, which is free from duality, O Lord, they reveal it.

Herein, desiring to explain the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) by first dispelling the delusions of those who propound a non-self and a non-Lord, he first sets forth their [position] with eleven verses: "Now, that which appears as a specific characteristic... and so on.
By these [verses],

ending with "Therefore, even the agent is imagined," the non-existence of the permanent self is stated through the non-perception of the visible for those who maintain that the self is perceptible, using two verses therein.

In that regard, it has been stated against those who maintain that the self is inferable—that the connection with memory established from mental formations (*saṃskāra*) is not sufficient for the inference of a self because it is not established in others;
thus, by one verse, the inference that "the substratum possessing qualities is apprehended through its qualities such as cognition" has been refuted.
Having thus rejected the self, [the author proceeds].

Then, in two verses, it was demonstrated that the sovereignty consisting of the relationship between the powers of knowledge and action— which is asserted by other schools as being either the very nature of knowledge or something distinct from it— is untenable according to both the Sāṃkhya school and [the Buddhist view].
Subsequently, with one verse, it was stated that there is no such thing as "action" anywhere at all.
In that regard, having rejected the proof and set forth the sublation,

he then establishes the non-existence of the relationship by means of a verse, stating the absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Having stated the subverting proof for that very point in the verse itself, [he proceeds].

"The self is not stable, nor does it possess sovereignty characterized by being a knower and an agent"—thus is the conclusion of our own position; this is the summary meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Now, the meaning of the text itself is explained:
"But surely, one [cognition] has the appearance of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while another..."
Nor are those two—the one associated with verbal expression and the one called conceptual construction—many.
Since no eternal perceiver whatsoever appears here [in this cognition],
even this perception of "I" terminates in the body and so forth.
The word "nanu" is used in the sense of an objection:
here, first of all, it is untenable that the self is stable and has consciousness as its intrinsic nature,
because even that which is stable and self-luminous would not be manifest.

For instance—cognition manifests itself solely in such forms as the manifestation of a jar, the conceptualization of a jar, the recognition of a jar, the recollection of a jar, and the imaginative construction of a jar; these cognitions appear as distinct in their temporal duration, distinct in their objects, and distinct in their modes. Among these, the manifestation of blue is a cognition in which the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) appears, which is unique to itself, not following after anything else, and which partakes in a contraction of its own nature.

The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) consists of place, time, form, and appearance; that cognition in which there is an internal manifestation—that is, illumination—while it assumes an externalized nature, is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). Even when there is a difference of objects, it is of a single genus because there is no cause for diversity in its own nature.
For in conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the cause of diversity is verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).
And that [blue] does not exist as such;
for verbal expression is not a property of blue,
nor is it perceivable by the eye.
Therefore, that former [experience] must be remembered;

yet there is no memory as long as the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has not been awakened, and its awakening arises from the perception of an object. Thus, at the time of perceiving the object, there is no recollection of the verbal expression.
Beyond that is conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-jñāna*),
because every conceptualization is rooted either directly or indirectly in non-conceptual [perception] (*nirvikalpaka*).
Furthermore, the term "beyond" (*param*) indicates that its object is a different form, namely the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Because it is impossible to establish a convention— whether based on worldly usage by elders or based on instruction— that is to be accomplished through extensive conceptualization upon a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is so extremely restricted;
and because even if such a convention were established, it would be useless.
Therefore, there is no further conventional usage for that which does not follow [the object].
And that [conventional usage] is of many varieties, because it exists together with expression— that is, with verbal discourse in the form of sound.
And this verbal designation is:
"this is that," "that is this," and "this is that very thing."
"This might be so"— or "this indeed is that," and so forth— it is divided in many ways;
yet that does not fall within the category of an object.
Rather, it is that very nature of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which appears as it makes itself variegated; thus, conceptual construction possesses many divisions.
In this way, the succession of experience and conceptual construction shines forth by virtue of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).
It might be argued: "That upon which this succession is fixed also shines forth. To this, [we reply]:
Since both of these— the conceptualized and the non-conceptualized forms— do not belong to any other seer or experiencer distinct from them,
whereas they may indeed belong to the object of vision according to the doctrine of external objects; the reason for this is that [they belong] to that seer.
Precisely because it is accepted as having the nature of consciousness, and because it is capable of self-luminosity, it has attained the conditions for being perceived;
therefore, between these two cognitions, there is no manifestation.
[Objection: But surely there *is* a manifestation—thus, the non-perception of the perceptible remains unestablished.

For instance: in the manifestation that persists as "I," which is distinct from the knowledge, memory, and so forth that constitute the meaning of verbal roots such as *vid* (to know) in expressions like "I know," "I ascertain," or "I remember this," and also distinct from the object in the form of "this" that serves as the grammatical object (*karman*).
The form appears as something following after [it].
Who says that it "appears"?
For appearance is indeed free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka).
The conceptual cognition "I" is permeated by the word [“I”].
But even so, what is it that is conceptualized by this?
Is it the continuum of the body, because of cognitions such as "I am thin"?

Or is it the continuum of cognition (*jñānasantāna*) that is the "I," because of the cognition "I am happy"? Furthermore, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) refers only to the continuum itself, not to something distinct from it. This has been stated: "The cognition 'I' also [refers to] the body..."
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it is understood that [the mind] necessarily knows, ascertains, and conceptualizes by way of its nature as a continuum.
"Because it is permeated by a latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting in the capacity to grasp the distinction from another similar state"—
this [impression] has not been denied by us,
since it is included by the phrase "that which is called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), accompanied by verbal expression."
This is what is meant: first of all, the cognition of "I" is not the self, because that too is of the nature of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and is unstable.
Nor is there any other basis for this cognition apart from the body and so forth.
Or else, even if it exists, it would fall on the side of the object of cognition (*vedya*).
Nevertheless, the proof of a self (*ātman*) distinct from consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the object of cognition is not established—this is what is indicated by the word "even" (*api*).
Thus, there is no self distinct from consciousness and the object of cognition, because such a visible entity is not perceived. //1// //2//
In this regard, the proponent of the self (ātmavādin) sets forth an inference:
"Now, if memory follows upon the destruction of experience, how could it occur? If the experiencer were not eternal, the self would have to be non-eternal. (IPK 1.2.3)
In this case, regarding the time of recollection, let the object intended to be remembered either persist or perish— what does that matter?
For there is no dispute among anyone that the experience itself has already perished.
And memory arises following that very [perception];
for thus, in memory there is neither the manifestation of the object nor its conceptual determination.
Nor is it like two fingers [in relation to each other] for the experience and the object;
nor is it like a staff [qualifying a person] for the object as qualified by the experience, because in all those cases there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "this is that."
However, in recollection, it is the manifestation of the experience itself that is primary;
since an experience consists in the manifestation of an object, the appearance of the object is inseparable from the manifestation of the experience.
Thus, if the experience has entirely perished, [the object cannot appear].
In that case, how could memory—whose nature is the manifestation of that [object]—be directed toward the object by means of it?

Furthermore, since all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is seen to be performed by means of it, this [memory], being undeniable in its own form, indicates that something remains unperished even when the experience has perished.
And that very thing is the agent of the experience—the nature of the experiencer.

"The self is the experiencer and is eternal"—this much alone constitutes the lifeblood of the proof of the self. And this very point has been clearly elucidated here by the Teacher; nothing more than this is required.
With the intention that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) should not be concluded for the time being, because there is a remainder of what remains to be said, [the author asks]:
"How could it be?
For its purpose (*artha*), at least, is ineffective in that regard.
Furthermore, since experience has perished, memory could not arise in any manner whatsoever;
and in the absence of that [memory], all conceptual constructions—which depend upon the recollection of conventional words—would also vanish.
Since non-conceptual [cognition] is, for all intents and purposes, like being blind, deaf, and mute, alas, the entire universe would perish without anyone to cry out! //3//
In this case, one must postulate something beyond the effect itself that is sufficient for the accomplishment of that effect;
however, the self is not such [a thing],
for it is the object that is remembered.
And it has been stated that this [object] is known through the medium of the manifestation of experience, while the experience itself has perished;
if there were some self (ātman), what would be the use of it?
For this too must be stated: "Space also exists.
Now, if it is argued that this is not established by the self alone, but rather that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of experience is also necessary here—
"In that case, let it be just that; what is the use of this [other theory]?"—this he demonstrates as follows:
"Even though the self exists, because of the destruction of vision, [there is no perception] of perceived objects by means of that [vision]."
Now, by what means does memory arise? It occurs at the very same locus where the original experience took place.

Regarding the memory of objects that have been seen and experienced, within that memory, the experience whose nature is perception (*dṛk*) serves as the gateway for the contact with the aspect of the object.
And even though the Self exists, that experience has perished;
for if it were not destroyed, this very [perception] would be an uninterrupted manifestation—so what would memory be?
"What could the experiencer of that [object] do for the memory?"—
in whatever object the experience occurred, that very thing is the locus (*pada*) of that memory, namely the object being remembered.
The term *tatpadā* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
"That" refers to memory. //4//
Now, one might object: "How can there be the conceit of being a subject (*viṣayin*) for that [consciousness] when its object is another cognition? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"For since the arising of memory occurs from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience, if this is so, what purpose would there be for a permanent self (*ātman*), which is like a useless internal goitre (*antargaḍu*)? (IPK 1.2.5)
For by experience, an impression (saṃskāra) appropriate to itself is produced;
and that impression establishes a state of existence in its former form,
as in the case of birch-bark or similar materials that have been bent for a long time and are now being straightened, such as branches that were once drawn out.

Therefore, even in this case, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produces that memory which conforms to the prior experience; thus, the object of the memory is indeed the object of that [prior experience]. If this is so, then the self (*ātman*) is like a useless goitre, serving only for excessive exertion; just as that [goitre] is, so too the postulation of a permanent self results merely in the labor of conceptual construction—what is the use of it?
For the entire world of worldly affairs and households is indeed supported by conditioned activity, holding on with hands that have been fashioned [by it]. — 5/5 —

Now, one might object: "The substratum for that very *saṃskāra* must be stated, for since it is a quality (*guṇa*), it requires a substratum; and that which is the substratum would be the Self (*ātman*). Anticipating this objection, he says:

Therefore, when phenomena have ceased, since their specific nature remains unchanged, memory is established through mental conditioning; thus, the rememberer is merely a conceptual construct, just like the seer.
In this case, when a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) arises,
if it were a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) of the self, then, being non-different [from it], that self would not be eternal.
If there is no distinction for it whatsoever, then what is the point? Or, if its very distinction consists in its being a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra), [then...]
In that case, since this [impression] is not distinct [from the cognition], it follows once again that the impression resides in a non-eternal cognition.

A cognition that produces an effect called "distinct recollection," being distinguished from the original experience, arises through a causal chain; such is the extent of the purpose of an impression (*saṃskāra*).
Now, if the specific quality consisting of the impression were something distinct [from the cognition],...
In that case, what is this [inherence]? Furthermore, that relation will be refuted as being distinct [from its relata].
In the same way, knowledge, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, and demerit are also to be analyzed.

This is what he says: "Therefore"—that is, even if one accepts that there are qualities distinct from the self, and even while those exist, because there is no difference in the self's own nature (*svarūpa*), that self would not be active in memory; for its form would remain as it was previously, unconditioned by the forms of "I" and so forth.
Because there is no lapse [of memory], the establishment of memory occurs from the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) alone— thus it is said.
Furthermore, he who thinks "I remember" and is the rememberer is determined to be merely a continuum of bodies and a continuum of cognitions,
just like the seer.
For it was stated previously:
"This very cognition of 'I' also terminates in the body and so forth" (ĪPV 1.2.2).
Thus, both perception and inference as means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing the self have been refuted.
And a subverting argument has been indicated: if there is connection with a property (dharma), there is a loss of eternality;
otherwise, what is the use of it? As it has been said:
"If it were like a hide, it would be non-eternal; if it were like space, it would be equivalent to a non-entity."
What do rain and sun have to do with space? For it is upon the skin that their effects are found. //6//
Having thus refuted the self, he speaks in order to refute its sovereignty as well, specifically to examine the power of knowledge:
"And if knowledge is of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), then why is it not impermanent like the self?"
Moreover, since this [consciousness] is insentient, how can it have the nature of illuminating objects?

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) employs this reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) by relying on the opponent's own admission, thinking: "I shall obtain the reversal of the reductio.

In that regard, the proponent of the self (*ātmavādī*) asserts the eternity of the self as follows: "In this context, what is called 'time'—by assuming the role of a qualifier for that which is characterized by 'this-ness' (*idaṃbhāva*), and thereby qualifying it—renders it non-eternal through its limitation."
Furthermore, because the Self has the nature of consciousness (*citsvabhāva*), it lacks the status of being a substantive (*viśeṣya*) due to the absence of the manifestation "this is...";
for the relationship between qualifier and qualified depends upon a unifier,
and there is no other unifier in that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).
Being addressed in this manner, he is questioned: "In that case, cognition (*jñāna*) is also self-luminous; the same principle applies there as well. Why, then, is it not eternal?
Furthermore, no relationship can exist between two things that are both eternal, for such a relationship is nothing other than the relation of cause and effect."
Consequently, the notion that knowledge is a power belonging to the self is undermined.
Now, if knowledge were not self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), then it would not be manifest even to another;
for it is only by imparting its own self-luminous nature to another that cognition becomes manifest to that other as well.
Therefore, being devoid of self-luminosity, this manifestation of the object would not be a manifestation at all, just like any other entity. //7//
"Even though it is insentient (*jaḍa*), this [intellect] will thus become the manifestation of the object"—anticipating this Sāṃkhya position, [the author] says:
"Now, just as the intellect assumes the form of the object, so too does it [assume] the consciousness of the Self... (IPK 1.2.8)
In this world, there is indeed the common usage: "I know the object. In that case, the ultimate reality is merely this: the manifestation of the object.
That [manifestation] is not the object's own intrinsic nature.
Otherwise, it would follow that everything is such [as it appears] for everyone, or else that nothing is such for anyone; thus the world would be either omniscient or ignorant.
Nor has this form fallen upon the object from something else.
For this very same fault would apply.
Therefore, surely this property [of manifestation] must reside in something else, in another reality;
and even there, how could the object be manifested? Surely, in that other reality, that object enters as a reflection.
That other principle (tattvāntara), due to the predominance of *sattva*, is capable of receiving reflections; yet, because it is veiled by *tamas*, it is turned away from reflecting everything.
Since *rajas* partially removes that *tamas*, it receives only a slight reflection;
that very thing is called the *buddhi*-principle (*buddhitattva*).

And cognition is the apprehension of the reflection of an object; its nature as a function consists of a specific transformation distinct from transformations such as [the change of milk into] curd, which conceal its prior designation.
In this way, the intellect (buddhi) maintains the form of the object.

And because it is an object of enjoyment through the states of pleasure, pain, and delusion inherent in the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, it is insentient (*jaḍa*) and, like a mirror, lacks self-luminosity (*aprakāśa*).

Furthermore, it is not logically tenable for that which is an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*)—being unmanifest—to possess a nature consisting of manifestation in the form of subjectivity (*bhoktṛtā*), which is its opposite; therefore, there must be an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) distinct from it.
And that manifestation has only this much as its nature:
for otherwise, how could an object of enjoyment, whose nature is non-manifestation, be conceived as being the very nature of the enjoyer?
If that manifestation of the universe were [the light] solely by virtue of having the nature of pure light,
then it would manifest all at once; the manifestation of a jar would be the manifestation of a cloth, and thus the universe would become confounded.

And how could that [object] be the manifestation of the object— since it is distinct from the object itself, from the reflection of the object, and from the intellect-principle (*buddhitattva*) which is their substratum—
given the lack of connection? Therefore,
it is the intellect alone that, due to its transparency, receives even the reflection of the light.

Then, because the light [of consciousness] has entered the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) through the power of grasping the reflection of that light, there occurs a transfer extending as far as the objects such as blue and so forth, which are reflected therein; thus, the object shines by means of the entry of the light, and the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is established.

Therefore, in this way, although cognition is insentient due to its non-difference from the insentient *buddhi-tattva*, it becomes the illumination of the object through its union with the reflection of consciousness.

This much, at least, is improper: that the person, whose nature is light, should cast a reflection into the intellect; for we observe the transfer of a reflection only into a clear medium possessing similar qualities, in dependence upon an original object, just as the reflection of the form of a jar appears in a mirror that possesses color.
Furthermore, there is an extreme disparity between the self and the intellect;
moreover, the intellect is not as pure as the self—this much may be granted. With the word "atha" (now), he indicates this.
However, he shows that even by means of the theory of reflection (*pratibimba-vāda*), nothing at all would be resolved.
Thus, that [consciousness] alone is non-inert; for in the state of inertia, there is no manifestation of objects.
If, upon the occurrence of the reflection of consciousness, that reflection itself were not primarily of the nature of light,
then nothing would be accomplished by it; for a mirror, being a mere reflection of a mass of fire, could not burn what is to be burned.

If that reflection were indeed of the nature of the primary light itself, then it would be non-different from the intellect; thus, the intellect would have become the very nature of the primary light.
For this [distinction] has been postulated by those who are afraid of the superimposition of contradictory attributes.
Furthermore, that very [intellect] itself expands its own blazing vital energy;
consequently, that intellect alone would be composed of consciousness— what need is there for a Puruṣa?
Thus, by way of the reflection of the object, [the cognition] consists of the object—so too has the Vijñānavāda doctrine arrived at.
To the question, "How does this [cognition] possess that form?
the answer must be stated: "From a succession of prior causes."
If that very [nature] were of the form of consciousness (cidrūpā),
then, as before, the consequence of its being eternal would follow;
nor, if it were not of the form of consciousness, could there be eternality even for that which is of the form of consciousness.
In that case, there is no eternal self whatsoever that could possess the power called "knowledge"; rather, there exists only knowledge itself.

Since the practical engagement with objects is established by that much—namely, by the cognition whose nature is the manifestation of an object and by that which consists of conceptual construction, memory, and so forth—it follows by the method of reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga-viparyaya) that if knowledge is of the nature of consciousness (cit), [then it is not dependent on a separate self].
This is the intended meaning of the two verses beginning with "ityādi. //8//

Having thus examined cognition, one examines action: Action, too, consists in the arising of an object such as the body in this or that particular place and so forth; it does not [arise] from anything other than what is perceived. (IPK 1.2.9)
In this context, first of all, that which has the nature of vibration—
such as "it goes," "it moves," "it falls," and so forth— is within the range of phenomenal appearance.
In that case, what is perceived is merely the nature of Devadatta as situated in the interior of the house immediately followed by his nature as existing in the external space;
we do not perceive any other action whatsoever distinct from that nature.

However, in the expression "Devadatta stands for a day," there appears the nature of Devadatta characterized by the time of dawn, followed by that nature embraced by the time of the first watch, and so forth.
In the case of the statement "milk transforms," there are forms such as sweet substances, sour substances, liquid forms, solid forms, and so forth.
Likewise, recognition occurs there due to similarity even when the body, hair, nails, taste, and so on have changed;
for even when there is a change in place and form, a change in time is necessarily present, despite that change in place and time.
Since space is nothing other than the very nature of the object itself,
and since there is a difference in nature when there is a difference in time— even though place, time, and form ultimately resolve into form alone—
Nevertheless, from a coarse perspective there is a distinction; for they are spoken of as distinct by the Buddhists—this is the intended meaning.
Thus, action is not perceived anywhere through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and because of its absence, it cannot be [established] by inference (*anumāna*) preceded by that [perception].

Furthermore, since the effect—consisting of the subsequent moment such as reaching the village, as well as the form and other qualities of the object in that location—is not otherwise possible [without a cause], that [unseen force] cannot be postulated even on the grounds of the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of the effect.
Thus, its non-perception through both perception and inference has been stated as the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhakapramāṇa*).
He now states the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) as well:
Nor is that [succession] possible for a single [entity] that is itself successive.
In that regard, the state of being prior and posterior belongs to moments through the synthesis performed by conceptual cognition;
however, within its own nature, there is nothing prior or posterior,
for it is merely the bare thing-in-itself.
Therefore, that which is sustained by conceptual construction—the state of being prior and posterior, the sequential nature of action—does not touch a real entity for even a single moment;
for those moments do not enter into one another's essential nature. How, then, can there be a single action?
For sequence is pervaded by difference, and since that [difference] is absent in what is non-distinct, [there can be no sequence].
Since unity is the opposite of difference, how could it be that [the cognition] is both successive and one?
If it is argued that it is "one" because it abides in a single substratum,
even in that case no substratum other than those very moments is experienced.
For it is only moments that appear as occurring in a continuous stream.
Furthermore, how could a substratum permeated by such momentary acts—which possess distinct locations, times, and forms—be a single entity?
For this very reason, [one says] "this is Devadatta."
The recognition that arises due to similarity, such as "he himself has reached the village," is not capable of establishing actual identity. //9//

Having thus examined both knowledge and action, [the author] first states the absence of any means of valid cognition regarding that relationship which, when present, connects those two and enables them to establish the sovereignty consisting of omniscience and omnipotence; he does so in order to destroy that very relationship.
It is observed that when this or that [cause] is present, this or that [effect] comes to be;
there is no other relation than that of cause and effect.
When there is a lump of clay, there is a stūpaka;
when that exists, there is a śivika, and so on up to a jar. Thus, only the moments of becoming are perceived;
nothing further appears to direct perception.

Nor can it be established by inference—as one might say in the case of an action—for this very same path applies everywhere, including in cases such as the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*): namely, that immediately after the perception of a jar and a plum as having separate forms, there arises the perception of a specific jar and plum in a state of immediate contact.

And this very phenomenon, when designated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as having a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority in relation to another phenomenon, is called "the causal relation" (*kāryakāraṇa-bhāva*).

Furthermore, there is no causal relationship between the self and knowledge or action, because the self is not the effect of those two; knowledge is the effect of its own specific causal complex (sāmagrī), and action is non-existent [in the self]. Thus, there is no connection with knowledge or action from which the states of being a knower (jñātṛtva) and an agent (kartṛtva) could arise. //10//
Having thus refuted the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he examines the sublation of the relation by way of both the general and the particular:
