"Because that which resides in two [relata] possesses multiple forms, and because that which is already established is independent of anything else."
And because dependence on another and so forth would be untenable, by that [reasoning] even the agent is merely imagined.
First, regarding connection (*saṃbandha*): its general definition is that, between two things possessing connection, there exists a single [entity] consisting of their mutual reaching.
And how is that?
For it is not possible for that which has rested the entire essence of its body in one place to rest in another, because that would entail a difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*).
By this, conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and other relations based upon them, which have been assigned the burden of being immune to sublation, should be understood [as refuted].

Even that relation characterized by dependence (*pāratantrya*) which is conventionally employed—whether among sentient beings through the conceptualization of that [dependence] or among insentient things—is not applicable to an established entity, precisely because it is already established.
An established thing possesses no dependence.
It is all the more impossible for that which is unestablished and devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvarūpa) to possess those properties, because of the impossibility of such a connection.
The same should be said regarding dependence (apekṣā).
Furthermore, how could two forms be joined together?
Because the identity of the two is untenable; or, if they were one, what would their conjunction be?

Therefore, just as the object "knower" is a conceptual construction arising from the relation to knowledge and is not a real entity, so too the agent "doer" is merely a mental construct arising from the relation to action—such is the prima facie argument.
This is the summary. Thus all is auspicious. (11) [Total from the beginning: 16]

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Prima Facie View," in the *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*, composed by the illustrious teacher Abhinavagupta, within the section on Knowledge (*Jñānādhikāra*).
Now begins the third chapter:
We praise that Śiva, whose nature is unceasing awakening, without whom not even all philosophical views could exist.

Regarding this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), that which was stated—that the accomplishment [of memory] arises from mental impression (saṃskāra) alone—precisely that is to be refuted: "True... [and so forth].
This group of seven verses, beginning with "ityādi" and ending with "{jñānasmṛtyapohanaśaktimān}," [is as follows].
Regarding the action (*kriyā*) and its relation (*saṃbandha*), the refutation [of objections] will occur in the second section on action (*kriyādhikāra*).

As for that which was rejected by others—such as the followers of Kaśa, the Sāṃkhya, and so forth—in their view, namely that cognition is distinct [from the object], that is precisely what the author of the treatise accepts; therefore, that [objection] is merely another point of refutation.

In this regard, by means of two verses, it is shown that because cognition has the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), experience does not manifest within memory, even though memory is produced from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

Then, having refuted the possibility that memory is an error by means of two verses following an objection, the suspicion that all determinations (*adhyavasāya*) are likewise erroneous was dispelled incidentally by the third verse.

Subsequently, it was stated in one verse that if memory were impossible even when latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) exist, there would be a cessation of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); and in another verse, its feasibility within our own position was explained—this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Now, the actual subject matter of the text is being analyzed.
It is true; however, memory-cognition, though produced from the latent impressions of a prior experience and residing within the self, does not perceive that original experience.
By the words "this is true," it is shown that much from the opponent's position must first be accepted by me;
however, that which cannot be accepted is refuted by the specific term "but" (*kiṃ tu*).
Here, in this Smṛti, there is no need to establish the mere manifestation of the object, as that is already established through mental impression (*saṃskāra*) alone.
But how could there be a memory of the form "that [object]" without the manifestation of the experience?
And how, without that memory, could there be practical activity (vyavahāra) through desire?
For it is by means of experience that its status as a means to pleasure is determined.
From that arises appropriation (*upādāna*);
in this regard, this much has arisen from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experience.
Even though that cognition was not produced by an object, [it nevertheless occurs].
Nevertheless, it has that as its object—so [it is argued].
But this does not amount to anything, because within self-abiding, self-luminous knowledge, the prior experience, just like the object, would remain unmanifest. //1//
One might object: "Since it is produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), why should memory not take even the prior experience as its object? Anticipating this, he says:
"The vision [of consciousness] is self-luminous and cannot be known by another, just as the vision of form [is not known by taste].
Although memory is produced by an impression, it is merely similar to that [prior experience]; it does not grasp that [original experience] itself. (IPK 1.3.2)
Vision is knowledge, and it is distinguished from the insentient by its nature as a single, self-luminous form;
for the insentient must be described as being separate from light,
whereas vision is self-manifesting.
Appearance (*ābhāsa*) is the state of being manifest; it is that whose own form is inseparable [from manifestation], and whose very nature is the manifestation of itself.
Even if an external object exists, the manifestation transferred to its body cannot constitute the true nature of cognition.
Indeed, the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition is said to be precisely the manifestation of its own nature, which consists in the illumination of another.
[Objection: But surely that cognition of experience will appear in memory as being self-manifesting itself.
[Reply: No—thus he says: "it is not to be known by another."
If cognition were to appear in another [object], then it would not be self-manifesting;

for this indeed is the definition of that which is self-luminous: if it were to manifest by itself, then, because there would be no connection with another, how could the locative case "in another" (*paratra*)—which has connection as its very life-force—be logically consistent?
Thus, by means of a cognition of color, the cognition whose object is taste is not perceived in the taste.
In this way, the taste would indeed be apprehended by the eye alone as a result.
Now, if the experience does not appear in the memory, what then has been accomplished by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*)?
For the cognition of form is not produced from the latent impression born of the cognition of taste.
How, then, can this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) arise? Therefore, it is the mental formation (saṃskāra) alone that is capable of dispelling the faults you have imputed.
This is not so, because this awakening of memory has arisen from an immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) that has been conditioned by that very formation.
Therefore, let it be that this subsequent configuration is similar to the former configuration, like the arrangement of a house being equal to its previous arrangement;

however, it is not logical to say that whatever is produced from a certain conditioning factor (saṃskāra) must possess the same nature of sensation as that [factor]. How, then, is the understanding or comprehension of this similarity possible?
For the cognition of direct experience does not convey similarity,
nor does the cognition of memory; because the two are not mutually perceived, it is impossible to determine a similarity that resides in both.

And because that which consists of the nature of the cognition of both [the object and its prior experience] is absent upon repeated practice, it is established that memory, following the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), possesses only a subjective object;

however, it does not possess the status of being an object of direct experience (*anubhava*), nor does this object possess the quality of having been made an object of a previous experience—this is the certain conclusion. //2//
Now, if in the cognition of memory there were a real manifestation of the experience,
and through that, of its object,
then there would be room for what you have said.
Since memory, being of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), merely determines the experience and its object as something appearing solely as other [than itself],
it is by nature erroneous; so why this insistence?
This very point he demonstrates by way of what is being suspected:
"Even though memory does not have that [external object] as its domain, because it is determined as such, it has a perceived object through delusion... (IPK 1.3.3)
Neither that perception nor its object is the actual object of memory;
nevertheless, both are determined by memory through its erroneous nature.
He refutes this:
"This is inconsistent. (Ipk 1.3.3)
Regarding this, he states the logical justification in a verse:

"How can it be memory at all? And how can there be the persistence of an object through an error? Furthermore, why is dependence upon the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience required? (IPK 1.3.4)

The non-deprivation—that is, the non-removal—of an experienced object, which has been manifested by that experience, and its manifestation in that very same way, is the essential nature of memory; this would utterly collapse in the absence of such a manifestation.

Furthermore, in error, either a non-existent thing or the form of the self appears, but the object is not appropriated by that [error], because it is not manifested; thus, the object is not established by that [error] at all.
For establishment (*vyavasthāpanā*) consists essentially in manifestation;

therefore, how could there be linguistic usage regarding an object through desire based on memory? Moreover, if that [object] were not manifested, nothing would be achieved by its being produced from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
For that similarity is relied upon in order to be apprehended;

and there is not even the slightest similarity between experience—which consists in the manifestation of an object—and the error called memory, since the latter does not touch the object in any way whatsoever. //4//
Now, it may be argued that since the experience and its object are determined by that [cognition],
there is a similarity between the experience and the memory from that perspective;
and for the sake of establishing that, the inclusion of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is necessary.
What is meant by "it is determined"?
If it means "it is manifested," then there is no error;
if it means "it is not manifested," then the object has not been touched by this [cognition] at all, and thus "similarity" is merely a verbal赘 (redundancy).
To demonstrate this, he says:
"If the determination were an error, the object would not be established by means of something insentient;
therefore, since it is not insentient, it must rest upon its own internal reflection, and thus the object is not established from that [reflection]. (IPK 1.3.5)
In this context, whether it be memory or another type of erroneous cognition, there is no error regarding the aspect of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),

because in that regard there is an absence of discrepancy; however, the internal form (*svākāra*) which is determined therein is erroneous in that specific respect, because it is perceived erroneously as being an external object (*artha*) when it is not its own form.

And since that aspect characterized by the object is not touched by memory or by any other error, it follows by necessity that this [memory] is silent with respect to that aspect, just as the cognition of a jar is silent regarding a cloth;
and nothing whatsoever can be accomplished for an object by means of what is insentient.
Consequently, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) regarding external objects would be lost.

If, however, its non-inertness is maintained by relying upon that aspect of self-awareness which consists of the determination (*avasāya*), or upon its own form (*svākāra*), even so, in this state of non-inertness, it is established as being limited to these three: its own self-awareness, its manifestation (*ullekha*), and its own form.

Since one who is unable to even grasp the name of the object cannot, through that determination by memory (*smṛty-adhyavasāya*), establish the object or possess the capacity to bring it into the sphere of linguistic convention (*vyavahāryatva*)? //5//
Even if a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) exists, memory is not possible in any way;
consequently, all cognitions would be devoid of mutual connection—this which was stated in the five preceding verses is now applied to the present context:
"Thus, for those [cognitions] which are mutually distinct and do not know one another..."
The worldly condition of living beings would perish, born as it is from the continuous succession of cognitions.

Whatever state or worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) belongs to people—that is, to the world—is dependent upon that synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of all cognitions which consists in the attainment of memory established through the state of having a single object. For instance: all worldly transactions are based upon memory.

For even the first moment of perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*) is not possible without being sustained by memory, which involves the synthesis of preceding and succeeding forms such as "I"; for if it did not find its rest in the subject (*pramātṛ*), it would follow that it is not perception at all.
The same should be understood regarding pleasure and other such experiences.
Because of the acceptance of the impelling of rejection and acquisition, worldly transactions consist of nothing but memory;
thus, when the opponent’s position is accepted— that the stability of people arises from the synthesis of cognitions—
it is possible that [the world] would perish, and indeed it does perish.
If it is asked "Why?",
he states the reason by means of a qualification:
first of all, cognitions are mutually distinct— namely, one is the cognition of experience, and...
Now, present cognition—which is considered conceptual—is one thing, while cognition accepted as memory is another.
These [cognitions] consist merely in the illumination of their own respective objects; with respect to other objects, they are like the dull, blind, mute, and speechless.
Nor are they of the nature of mutual illumination. //6//
Thus, there is no synthesis consisting of a unification either in terms of their own nature or of the two objects of cognition;
nor is there a mutual relationship of object and subject.
Furthermore, it is not possible to conceive of a fourth state that, being based on what is known, could provide the support for synthesis; consequently, all worldly transactions would perish.

Nor do they perish merely by the force of your desired curse, "May they perish," for they continue to manifest; therefore, this [objection] follows: you must strive to justify this very point. And that justification is impossible even for an ordainer (*vidhi*) unless it is done in the manner we have proposed—this he demonstrates: @----- [The original Sanskrit text continues: na hi vayaṃ brūmaḥ — śāpamātrād eva teṣāṃ nāśaḥ syāt — iti, kiṃ tarhi? yadi śāpo dīyate, tadā sa eva śāpaḥ svaviṣayasya vastunaḥ svarūpaviparyāsaṃ kuryāt, na tu tasya sattām evocchindyāt | yasmāt teṣāṃ svarūpaṃ prakāśate, tasmād etad āpatitam — etad eva samarthanīyam — iti | tac ca samarthanam asmābhir abhipretena mārgeṇa vinā vidhātur api kartum aśakyam — iti darśayati | [Translation of the continuation: For we do not say that their destruction occurs from the curse alone; rather, if a curse is pronounced, then that very curse would effect a transformation of the nature of the object within its scope, but it would not annihilate its existence itself. Since their nature continues to manifest, this consequence follows: this very point must be justified. And that justification cannot be accomplished even by an ordainer without the method we have favored—thus he shows.

If the Great Lord were not one whose infinite universal form is contained within himself, he could not be the singular embodiment of consciousness possessing the powers of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance].
No one denies that consciousness first of all shines forth;
however, if that consciousness were to rest solely within itself, how could it be the manifestation of an object?
For that [manifestation] would have to be a property of the object itself.
Consequently, since the manifestation of the object terminates at that very point, the relationship between the grasped and the grasper has dissolved.
Therefore, by one who maintains that consciousness is of the nature of the manifestation of the object, the object itself must necessarily be admitted as being included within that very nature;
and if that manifestation of the object were distinct in each case, [the aforementioned consequence would follow].
Therefore, since remembrance is not logically possible [otherwise], this [consciousness] must be one alone;
and because of its unity, the entire mass of objects of knowledge is embraced by it—this too must be accepted even by one who does not wish it.
Even so, the universe would manifest at all times, whether emerging or submerging, as the very self of consciousness.
Because it would [otherwise] possess such a nature;

yet this is not the case. Therefore, it follows that while grasping within itself another mass of objects submerged in its own nature as having a distinct form, it manifests only a certain object as emerging from its own nature.
This very [consciousness] is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
And the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), when differentiated by emergent manifestations due to its extroversion and through the coloring of their reflections, is called "ever-new knowledge.
Even so, since these ever-new manifestations undergo arising and passing away at every moment, that same [power] results in the cessation of the flow of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Therefore, regarding that consciousness which was previously directed outward toward some previously perceived manifestation, its inward-turned nature—which is the essence of consciousness—persists even at a later time; it reflects upon its own state of being directed outward toward that specific object. This is the power of memory.

And as for that which it manifests anew or remembers, in reality, it functions through identity with consciousness, which consists of the universe; thus, it is entirely full and universal. Consequently, nothing new has been manifested or remembered.
Or it may be so;
this too must be accepted as following from the current of the argument: namely, that whatever is manifested is separated from consciousness, and consciousness is likewise separated from that.
And consciousness is not distinct from another consciousness,
nor is the object of cognition distinct from another object of cognition;
for in reality, no such separation is possible.
Thus, it is said that there is merely the appearance of a separation;
yet this does not constitute ultimate reality by that much alone,
for this very [appearance] is the ultimate reality of everything that is being manifested.
For this very [consciousness] is called "delimitation" (*pariccheda*) because it delimits [objects] all around; its capacity to manifest those [objects] is the power of exclusion (*apohana*).
Through these three powers, all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are carried out.

And that very triad of powers belongs to the Blessed One alone— that which manifests as Caitra, Maitra, and others, whose natures consist of being an experiencer, a rememberer, and a conceptualizer of such things.
For he alone knows, remembers, and conceptualizes by means of those various bodies.
As has been stated by the Teacher himself:

"Even though the stability of objects is restricted to the individual soul (jīva), which is constrained by the vital breath and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), it nevertheless rests within the Supreme Self."
And so forth. Regarding these powers of knowledge and the rest, there is an incalculable variety of conceptual diversities;

their capacity is autonomy (*svātantrya*), which is independent of anything else, full, and a great sovereignty (*mahadaiśvarya*)—so called in comparison with the sovereignties of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others created by that [autonomy].
Thus, taking "the one whose body is consciousness" (*cidvapuḥ*) as a single unit, this much has been established: "He whose form is the universe" (*viśvarūpaḥ*).

And precisely because it is distinct from insentient entities—which are established as having a single, fixed form—he has attained the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consisting in the possession of powers such as knowledge. [Otherwise,] there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that nothing at all would appear; however, things do appear. Therefore, this must necessarily be accepted—this is the reversal of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*).
"The human condition would perish if it were not so"—this is the connection with the preceding verse.
By the word "cet" (if), its opposite is indicated. //7//
Thus all is auspicious. From the beginning, [chapter] 23.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Impossibility of Other Philosophical Systems," in the *Vimarśinī* on the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtra*, composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, within the section on Knowledge. 3.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
We praise Śiva, who weaves together the collection of jewels of categories (padārtha) gathered in the treasury of his own heart, by means of the very thread of memory within [his] continuum. (1)

Thus, it has been demonstrated according to the sequence of the actual entities involved that memory is preceded by knowledge, and that there is a power of exclusion (*apohana-śakti*) which supports both of them.
Now, following the initial approach, memory itself must be examined from the perspective of establishing the reversal of the contingency that was indicated.
"True, but as for the cognition of memory..."— thus it was introduced. In that regard,
let us first grant that memory might indeed arise from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone.

However, this must be stated: in order to dispel the doubt—"How could even one who possesses the power of the Blessed One as accepted by you and others produce such [memory]?"—there follows the determination of the true nature of memory, beginning with: "For he [is the perceiver of an object previously experienced]...
and so forth.
The eight verses ending with "{...the two objects appear to the knower}" state that, according to his own position,
memory is logically established. Among those, it is stated in one verse that memory is consistent within his own system.
By the second [verse], it is stated that memory possesses the capacity to manifest the particular (svalakṣaṇa) that was made the object of a prior experience.
By the third, it is stated that memory’s immersion reaches the point of complete identity with both the experience and its object.
By the fourth, it is established that the experience is not manifested by memory as an object.
By the fifth [verse], it is shown that even the yogi’s cognition does not objectify experience as something separate—thus the meaning of the fourth verse is further strengthened.
By the sixth, the apprehension of experience by memory as a separate object, which might otherwise be suspected, is dismissed as a mere verbal quibble (*kākanītika*) and rendered unreal.
By the seventh, through the context of memory, it is demonstrated that even in conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), there is an immersion into the identity with the prior experience.
By the eighth [verse], the resting of the object to be remembered, the act of remembering, and the rememberer within the single state of consciousness was stated;
and by way of a supplementary discussion, that of the visible, the seeing, and the seer. This is the intended meaning.
Now, the meaning of the verse is explained in sequence.
For he, being one who perceives objects previously experienced, even while existing at a later time, reflects "this is it"; thus, being independent, he is designated as "one who remembers."
The internal awareness that perceives an object previously experienced still exists even at a later time, such as during recollection;
for that which is of the nature of pure consciousness cannot be subject to limitations consisting of specific contractions produced by time.
Furthermore, it is established without effort that the object also resides within the experience in a state of non-separation.

This much, however, must be considered: if there is a reflective awareness of the nature of consciousness within that which is not limited by time, and within the entire multitude of entities existing therein, then it must necessarily consist of the full reflective awareness "I" alone;
or else, it would have to occur through the manifestation of entities as separate, characterized by "this-ness" (idantā).
Nevertheless, in this regard there are two possible courses:
if the "this-ness" (idantā) comes to rest within the aspect of "I" (aham), then the state of Sadāśiva and so forth, characterized by the formula "I am this," must result.

Now, if [the object] does not arise [as a new experience], then it must appear as "this is that very thing"; and because of the appearance of novelty, that would be a direct experience (*anubhavana*) itself and not a memory—anticipating this objection, he says: "one who is independent" (*svairī*).
He impels his own personal instruments toward their respective functions and is necessarily of that disposition;
he impels himself as well and does not, moreover, depend upon an external instigator for his own duties—thus he is "svairī," meaning independent.
Because of this independence, he reflects: "I am [the agent]."

The nature of this "it" (*sa*) as an act of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) is as follows: it is neither exclusively a reflective awareness of a nature that is entirely untouched by time, nor is it a reflective awareness characterized by absolute difference. Rather, it is that very entity which, at the time of its prior experience, was set apart through the assistance of its own place, time, and other subjects, yet was not dissolved into the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*).
That entity, having been shrouded as if by darkness and left in such a state, is what is designated by the term "residual trace" (*saṃskāra*).
It casts aside that which was concealing it;
once that has been cast aside, it appears as distinct just as before. [Objection: But would it not appear as "this" (idantā) just as it did previously? [Response: It is not so.
For the manifestation of that [object] occurs precisely without disregarding its connection to the body and so forth as they appeared at that time;
and consequently, even the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the time of the present manifestation and recollection does not close up.

Thus, because the reflective awareness of the prior time is predominant upon the foundation of that [present] reflective awareness, it is called "reflective awareness" (*parāmarśa*) precisely because its nature consists in a reflective awareness of the preceding and succeeding moments that appear to be contradictory.

And thus, that very Supreme Lord remembers. For this indeed is His state of being a rememberer (*smartṛtva*): namely, the assumption of the state of a subject of *māyā*, which is capable of enduring the touch of the divisions of time and so forth appropriate for such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Therefore, consisting of both *māyā* and *vidyā*, as well as their non-duality, and for that very reason resembling a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) skilled in bestowing all supernatural powers (*siddhi*), those versed in the scriptures consider remembrance itself—when animated by mantras and the like—to be [the source of power]. And so it is said: [The verse follows: ...@-----
"Having attained the state of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth through mindfulness alone, the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) manifests Your glory.
Enough with this for now.

By means of this compound ending in the suffix *tṛn*, [the author] demonstrates, through the medium of the object of experience, the contact with time, the resting in the object, and the establishment of both [object and subject] within the cognizer (*pramātṛ*)—whether by way of difference or non-difference—through deliberate effort.
It is established through the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*);
and we shall explain later that this [compound] consists of both difference and non-difference. //1//
The following verses are intended to establish this very principle of the nature of memory (*smṛti-tattva*).
In this regard, if someone were to say: "In this context, memory is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and by it no object is revealed,"
For conceptual constructions do not touch upon the actual object;
and that experience by which the object was brought to manifestation has now become a mere form of renown,
and even that is not manifested by memory— because one cognition cannot be cognized by another cognition, and because [the original experience] no longer exists.
If it is argued that because there is no manifestation of the object, the cognition "I remember this" is merely an error— and thus the same problem arises once again—
then it is said in response to that:
"And it manifests [the object] at its own time, while reflecting upon what was previously manifested by the object."
The specific characteristic [of the object] exists either as a mere appearance of a jar or in its entirety.
In this case, first of all, in the conceptualization of memory (*smṛti-vikalpa*), the object is determined;
otherwise, one would fall into the state of being like one who is asleep or unconscious.
And thus, as long as there is a determination of the object, it follows by implication that the object must be admitted to exist to that extent—that the object is manifest.
If that which is to be determined were not manifest, the act of determination would be like that of a blind man;
and manifestation occurs neither by the abandonment of the present time nor by its doubling.

Because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of its appearing merely as "this," the time of the past experience must be required in the objective aspect (*vedyabhāga*) by way of projecting the specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*) of the previously experienced entity, through its being identified with the manifestation consisting of light (*prakāśa*);

and the time of the manifestation of the body, vital breath, and so forth of the rememberer must be taken as the support in the subjective aspect (*vedakabhāga*), through its being identified with the element of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
For the essential nature of an entity is indeed nothing but its manifestation,
since the operation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) extends to each individual manifestation.
That very nature becomes clearly manifest through the intermingling with other manifestations, like the blending of the light of a thousand lamps.

However, even in the absence of any admixture with other appearances, it is precisely through its intermingling with the appearance of time that the particularity (*svālakṣaṇya*) of that appearance is established;
for it will be stated later that the power of time alone is the differentiator.

Thus, first of all, the state of being a particular characteristic belongs to the appearance of a jar by means of the appearance of time, which has arisen through the assistance of the previous appearance of the body.
Or rather, memory itself is exceedingly clear even when mixed with other appearances.
Even when it reaches a state of extreme clarity, its occurrence at that very moment does not break away from the present, because there is no manifestation of commonality with anything else.
However, when such a manifestation occurs for a yogi, it is merely his own creative emanation.
In the case of what was spoken by Brahmā and so forth, however, there is only a fresh manifestation.
Here, however, the means is a succession of recollections of the true nature of Brahmā and others, experienced through other means of knowledge such as scripture (*āgama*).
The word "bhāsayet" (should cause to manifest) indicates a restriction (*niyama*) by way of an injunction (*niyoga*) in the form of a mandate.
"It does not illuminate"—this is not so; rather, it certainly does illuminate.
"At its own time" means at the time of recollection.
"Touching" refers to the present time as it enters into the subjective portion of the knower;

"the previously manifested particular characteristic" refers to the past time as it touches the objective portion, and it is shown that even for the mere manifestation of a jar, this is the cause for its attainment of particularity.
This much alone is the unfailing nature of memory.
The word "atha" (then) indicates that clarity arises from the intensity of the seeker's longing;
he expresses this very point by saying "asvilātmanā" (with a non-dull nature), which means with a body mixed with all appearances. //2//
Now, one might object: "If the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is thus manifested, it would appear externally as something distinct;
for this alone is what constitutes external manifestation—namely, the manifestation of the particular characteristic. To dispel this doubt, he explains:
"And it is not logical that the object being remembered should appear as distinct [from the memory] within the memory itself."
Therefore, he is the knower of cognitions occurring at different times, by virtue of which their unity is established.

If that object were to appear as distinct from the cognition of recollection and as having an external form, then the very appearance of the remembered object would not occur; it would not be "remembered" at all, but rather it would be "experienced"—that is to say, it would be a present perception.
[Objection: But if this is so, how can it be said that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is manifested?
This is not a manifestation occurring now, but rather at a previous time;
and at that time, it indeed appeared externally.
But if that is so, what happens now?
We say it is "reflective awareness" (*vimarśana*).
But surely, it follows that manifestation and reflective awareness would occur at different times.
What of it? Neither of the two would exist at all.
Because this [consciousness] is the life-force of one another;
do not say so, for this objection is indeed irremediable for one for whom the very nature of reality consists of distinct cognitions alone.

In our system, however, even cognitions belonging to different times are manifested as one by the free Knower through the non-abandonment of their own respective times; to the extent that he reflects upon them through inwardness, there is, for the light of consciousness, the appearance of being external at those respective times, while for reflective awareness, there is a state of being inwardly directed at the present moment.

This very state of being the knower (*veditṛtva*), which exceeds mere sensation, is defined as the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) consisting in the ability to perform the joining or disjoining of sensations according to one’s will;

this alone is called agency (*kartṛtva*). To demonstrate that the synthesis—whether expressed as "I experienced the jar" or "that is the jar"—is non-different from the synthesizer, it is shown through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that the identity itself is the knower.
It has been shown;
by saying "this is that," the true nature of the subject, which was as if concealed, has been made to appear clearly—
namely, "this."
By this statement, pregnant with wonder, recognition itself is indicated;
as the author himself has said:
"That which has been defiled by those who, while denying their own self-awareness, speak in such a manner—"
Having silenced those who are mute [in their opposition] through clear arguments, that reality of the knower has been made manifest.

Now, if the very prior experience itself is the manifestation in the form of the external appearance of that which is being remembered, then let this much be said: "That experience is now made an object by memory.
What is the point of this extraordinary [claim] regarding their identity? In order to dispel such delusion, he says:
For the prior experience does not appear in memory as something separate from the object, like the object itself,
because it appears as having ascended upon the self in the form "I experienced this previously."

The former object, such as a jar, appeared as "this" with a sense of distinctness; however, at the time of recollection, it does not appear as distinct from the knowledge of memory in the form "this was my previous experience.

And just as at the time of recollection that object does not appear as distinct from that knowledge of memory in its prior nature as "having existed before"—because at the time of recollection there is no external manifestation—by that very same reason, the previous experience also does not appear as distinct [from the memory].
How, then, do both appear? It is in the form "I experienced.
If it is asked, "What is this saying?"—

The Self, whose nature is "I"— which is inward-turned in its consciousness of both the preceding and succeeding [moments]— is that in which there is an ascent, that is, repose; by reason of that, because the nature of the preceding consciousness, which is self-luminous, shines forth, even a jar that has merged therein shines as if belonging to the sphere of self-luminosity.

And because of the maxim that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together with the self [of the word],"— whether it be the sense of the base (the number) implied by the suffix, or the substrate possessing that [number] which serves as the agent, within this referent of the word *asmad* ("I"), the experience (*anubhava*) is submerged, and through that, the object (*artha*) as well.
But this [object] does not exist independently;
for that very reason, the object (karman) was not mentioned separately.
Furthermore, at the time of experience, an object such as a jar does not ascend to the status of the "I" (asmadartha).

For indeed, because the prior experience does not appear as something separate from that which was stated in the latter half [of the verse] due to the reason mentioned there, therefore "there is oneness of consciousness"— this is the connection with what precedes.
Since the past tense is indicated by the *luṅ* suffix, the word "prāk" (previously) is placed out of its logical order.

By the Supreme Person, there is the "mounting" (ārohaṇa) of our own self, even that which is expressed as "I"; thus, the root *ruh* is used both in its non-causative form (*aṇijanta*) and its causative form (*ṇijanta*). //4//
Now, who has said that experience does not appear separately?
If you say it does not appear like a jar, what of it?
For even a jar does not appear as a companion to experience; does it therefore not appear?
However, the fact that [an object] appears by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*) is common to both cases.
For instance, it is accepted that past, future, and subtle objects become objects of a yogi’s cognition; likewise, the mind of another (*paracitta*) does so as well.

Regarding the statement, "{the knowledge of another's mind is [attained] through mastery over the mental modification}" (Yoga Sūtra 3.19), and so forth: in that context, it is *sattva* itself, as transformed into the activity of cognition (*jñāna-vṛtti*), that is denoted by the word "mind" (*citta*).
Otherwise, how could it be said that the mental modification (*pratyaya*) is the object of *saṃyama*?
And how could one suspect that there is both a connection with an object and yet no object?

Therefore, having raised the objection that "one's own [consciousness] should be made an object just like another's experience," [the author] shows by the words ending in "bhānti" that the example itself is unestablished; or, even if it were established through concession, he shows by the remainder of the passage that it is dissimilar to the point at issue.
Even for yogins, these [perceptions] do not appear as objects of sight within another system of vision;
they appear either as having self-awareness alone as their sole means of knowledge, or even when situated in the domain of the object of knowledge.

Regarding that specific type of knowledge concerning the minds of others which arises for yogins through meditation and other means— this being a distinct form of perception— within it, "visions" (dṛśaḥ), meaning apprehensions, do not appear as [external] objects.
For instance, according to the Buddhists, knowledge is of a single nature consisting solely of self-luminosity.
If that [consciousness] were to be known by another cognition, then its own essential nature— which consists in its manifestation as being unknowable by anything else— would not be manifested.
Even for the Sāṃkhyas, perception is merely the reflection of the Puruṣa; and since the Puruṣa is itself unperceivable by nature, how could it be an object of perception?
For the Vaiśeṣikas as well, how could consciousness—which inheres non-differently in the self and resides in another—be grasped by the mind, which functions only within the body?
But if there were entry into another body, the distinction of the self would dissolve, because that very [self] would be made into a "possessor of a body" by the manifestation of "I-ness.

Furthermore, it is not tenable for the self to be eternally inferable; and it has already been stated that if one cognition were cognizable by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress and other such faults.
Therefore, at the time when a yogi perceives another's mind, there is this much manifestation: "The manifestation of the jar, pleasure, and so forth, which accompanies the manifestation of this body.
In that context, the jar, pleasure, and so forth appear as "this" (idantayā), whereas the manifestation inherent in them appears as "I"—thus manifesting through its own self-luminosity.

However, because of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the manifestation of the body, vital breath, and so forth of another's body—which has been made into an object of cognition—the yogi, whose distinction between self and other has not yet dissolved, conceives of that [other] as "this" even within the sphere of light, and thus thinks, "This is the knowledge of another.

But the yogi who has attained excellence, seeing everything as his own self, considers the distinction between self and other to be merely his own creation; therefore, [ordinary] knowledge is not something to be illuminated by the knowledge of a yogi.
Or, even if that were so, it would still not be equal to the subject at hand.
For instance, the manifestation of the yogi regarding the experience "this one experiences" is established solely in another;
it does not occur by way of superimposition upon the self in the form "I am experiencing."

But here, in the expression "I experienced," the resting upon the "I" aspect of the experience occurs without even being touched by the state of "this-ness"; thus it was rightly said: "Since the experience does not appear as separate [from the self], therefore the knower is the unity of cognitions occurring at different times. //5//
If it is argued that, due to the repose in non-existence (*abhāva*), the experience does not appear separately in memory, then [the opponent's position is as follows]:

either another reflective awareness (*parāmarśāntara*) is directly perceived as reflecting the experience through the "this-ness" (*idantā*), or else the experience is perceived as manifesting its repose in objects such as jars which are appropriate to the state of "this-ness.
Therefore, why is it not treated accordingly? Thus he refutes the intention of the opponent.

When one remembers, "That very same perception which was mine [in the past] is this," even though there is a distinction, that is merely the verbal determination (*vyākaraṇa*) of this memory, based on the recollection: "I have seen this."
For the world at large, there is no such awareness;
indeed, it does not conceive of the act of seeing as something distinct, thinking, "That seeing was mine.
Nevertheless, even though it is of this nature, there is a certain recollection that occurs to someone who considers himself discerning.

That is the analysis of memory; it is merely a conceptual differentiation and presentation to others, like the determination of the meanings of bases and suffixes in a word, which is nothing more than a formal exposition.
Even that, if it causes one to experience the fundamental cognition according to the previously described sequence, [is valid].
At that time, one does not perceive experience as something separate,

because one regards the distinction as merely conceptual, like the expression "the head of Rāhu. Otherwise, just as in the case of "that jar," even in the phrase "that vision" (sā dṛk), one would have to depend upon a prior, distinct vision.
For by the word "that" (tat), it is stated that either the jar or the vision has become an object of a previous experience;
otherwise, it would simply be "vision.
Consequently, it would follow that "the vision was experienced by me through another vision."
Even in that case, if it were so, there would be an infinite regress.
Now, what is the fundamental nature of memory?
It is said: "I have seen [it]."

But surely, here it is stated that the vision rests upon the lotus-face of the beloved and so forth, and not that it is mounted upon the self, because the *niṣṭhā* suffix arises in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Thus, he does not even perceive his own words.
For an object is that which is to be attained through the action of the agent; thus, the action of seeing resides solely in the agent.
Accordingly, they describe the action of seeing as residing in the agent in such cases as "the king causes his servants to see" (*darśayate bhṛtyān rājā*).
Even by the followers of Jaimini, seeing—which consists of cognition—is said to be of the nature of a productive impulse (*bhāvanā*) that rests entirely within the cognizer.
Manifestness is merely a property of the object called "perceived-ness," or else it is another consciousness that is not independent; this is a different matter.
I have said "by me" only to express the state of resting within the subject.
"By him I experienced," or "I experienced"— this is merely a variety of verbal expression,
but there is no difference in meaning.
Others, however, apply the words by shifting the order as follows: "That vision was mine," and "It was seen by me"—this recollection is its grammatical analysis (*vyākaraṇa*).
This refers to the recollection that has been appropriately pointed out immediately prior, namely, "I experienced [her].
The particle *api* is used in the sense of "and. //6//

Now, it may be argued that even that which has been seen by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is not remembered as long as it has not been grasped through a resting in a specific reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), just like grass, leaves, and so forth seen on a path are not remembered in their specific forms;
therefore, this very point must be investigated: at the time of the immediately following conceptualization (*vikalpa*), did that seeing appear as "this" (*idantayā*) or not?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"And that cognition by which I perceive 'this is a jar,' or whatever determination [arises], that perception also resides in the cognizer as something inherent. (IPK 1.4.7)
In this context, whatever kind of vision there is, it must always manifest through that very same [vision] as its own body;
and that, at its own time, is appropriately luminous in the form of "I" alone, not being illuminated by anything else,
while the investigation of the portions of conceptualization therein is not a factor anywhere at all.
Or let it be that [the object] is a mere word;
however, he indicates by means of the word "also" (*api*) that the determinative cognition (*avasāya*) is likewise of such a nature.

In that regard, the object, being grasped by the immediately subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is grasped either through the medium of the reflection upon experience, as in "I see this," by way of its presentness; or...
By the word "this" (*imam*), its status as an object of direct perception is shown through its being perceived as such.
Or rather, it is referred to in this very way—as "this jar.
Here, by the word "this," its state of being perceived directly is expressed.

In that regard, since in the final type of conceptual construction there is no reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the perception as something separate, what room is there for the suspicion of "this-ness" (*idantā*)? Consequently, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), its reflective awareness here must exist as "I-ness" (*ahantā*);

for if that were absent, then since conceptual construction occurs even when the eyes are closed, how could there be a determinative ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*)—which, while clearly touching the object itself, culminates in the non-object [the subject]—if it were not grounded in "I-ness"?

In the first case, however, although perception (*darśana*) is referred to, it is included within our own self; it rests in the subject who is the locus of the "I-sense" (*ahambhāva*), and thus it is perceived as being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) itself. Therefore, even this conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not indicate that consciousness is an object of another consciousness. [The term] *avasāya* means determination (*avasā*).
The term *samaveta* expresses non-separation (*apṛthagbhāva*).
The term *avasātari* means in the independent, introverted self whose nature is consciousness and which is the locus of the "I-sense" (*ahantā*).
"Perception" (darśana) refers to non-conceptual experience;
this is also an elliptical expression that includes conceptualization, memory, and so forth,
for this same principle applies when one cognition is reflected upon by another cognition.
"I conceptualize," "I remember," "it has been conceptualized by me."
The thought "it was remembered by me" arises because conceptualization and the like manifest precisely through the ascent of the ego-sense (*ahantā*).

For this very reason, it has been shown in the passage "possessing the powers of knowledge, memory, and exclusion" that these [powers] such as conceptualization are specific powers of the Self, since their very body rests within it. //7//
Thus, in order to summarize the result of this much that is to be known, he says:
"I see this," "that has been seen"—even while reflecting thus, the two objects, non-different from the states of grasped and grasper, appear within the cognizer. (IPK 1.4.8)
The word "tat" (that) signifies the sense of "therefore," indicating here that the previously mentioned object of knowledge (*prameya*) is being relied upon as a logical reason (*hetu*).
Since it has been stated thus— "Because memory does not appear as distinct from the experience itself, and the power of memory belongs to the Supreme Lord alone"—
therefore, this is the established reality (*pariniṣṭhita-tattva*) in this context.
It has been stated here that memory encompasses experience (*anubhava*).

Experience, moreover, is of two kinds due to the distinction in reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*): sometimes, preceded by a reflective awareness of its own self, it reflects upon the object of experience where intentionality (*abhisaṃdhi*) predominates, such as "I see this."
Sometimes one primarily perceives only that which is to be experienced, where there is a sudden encounter with an object without any prior intention,
or a particular insistence toward a specific purposeful action;
even in such cases, there is indeed a perception of manifestation.
Otherwise, manifestation would be impossible.

Thus, when there is experience in both ways, a memory for each [object] also arises consisting of the reflective awareness of both; this constitutes four varieties of memory and two varieties of experience.
Synthetic recollection (*anusandhāna*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), which consist of the union of these two, are also included herein.
That [recollection] is eightfold due to its divisions, and sixteenfold because each of those is further divided into two by way of resting upon either the preceding or the succeeding [moment].
Thus, these are the twenty-two varieties of cognition. Among them, the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is first of all not external to the manifestation (*prakāśa*),
because otherwise its manifestation would be impossible.
And that [object] is external,
because it is impossible for it to have any other nature,
nor is it [produced] from that very [consciousness].
At that very moment,
that which is non-different becomes differentiated here; therefore, there must certainly be some other object here whose nature is imagined light (*kalpitaprakāśa*),
by virtue of which this mass of objects, becoming differentiated, would also attain mutual distinctness.
Otherwise, how could there be any mutual distinctness among things that are non-different from the Light?
This [object] is merely a single portion of the cognizable,
and is indeed fragmented.

Precisely while the state of being the object of consciousness (*vedyabhāva*) has not been abandoned, that which is reflected upon by a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) appropriate to a light devoid of the separation [of subject and object] as "I" will be called the *māyā*-subject, as stated in the passage: "[In the body, in the intellect...]". (IPV 1.6.4)
And that is called the "grasper" (grāhaka).

Thus, it is precisely in this way that the Supreme Lord, within His own self which is like a stainless mirror, manifests a pair that is non-different from His own nature as light; this very [manifestation] constitutes the Blessed One’s agency of knowing and agency of remembering, consisting of the power of knowledge and the power of memory.
This is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
As for the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*): when the cognizer, whose nature is light, reflects "this" and "it is seen by me," that by which he experiences is called [the means of knowledge].
From that act of reflective awareness (*āmarśana*), this is perceived:

the two objects—the jar and so forth, and the body and so forth—which possess the natures of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), and which are conjoined, appear and shine forth within the subject whose nature is pure light (*viśuddhaprakāśa*).
Thus, it is the subject, whose nature is light, who reflects upon them as "this has been seen" and "that."

Since he is designated as "one who remembers," it is therefore indicated by this very fact that his dependence on the nature of prior experience— previously mentioned— is being reaffirmed; thus, in this context, the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*) has also been brought to light as a necessary consequence.
The suffix *śatṛ* is substituted [for the present participle] in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The word "also" (*api*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*).
The word "object" (*artha*) denotes that which is to be known as distinct [from the subject].
The grasper is illusory and imagined; it is the cognizer whose nature is impure light. May there be auspiciousness! (Śivaṃ). From the beginning, verse 31.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Power of Memory," in the first section on Knowledge of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the fifth chapter. We perpetually praise that Śiva, who, by means of the lamp of the power of knowledge, illuminates the multitude of existents submerged within the great cave.
Thus, the nature of the power of memory has first been established;
now, having at length determined the ultimate reality of the power of knowledge upon which that [memory] depends,
[the author proceeds] with the verse beginning "vartamānāvabhāsinām" (of those things appearing as present).
He explains this through a sequence of twenty-one verses, ending with [the verse beginning] "it appears sequentially.
Therein, with the very first verse, he makes the formal proposition (*pratijñā*) regarding the subject matter: "The power of cognition is of such a nature.
Then, with two verses, he states that light (*prakāśa*) alone is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of objects.

Then, having raised the concern that the proponent of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) has reinforced the existence of external objects through the two preceding [verses] by refuting the [theory of] latent impressions (*vāsanā*),

the author shows with the third [verse] that even if that [existence] is not accepted, nothing at all is undermined. Then, with the [fourth] verse, while demonstrating the reality of the object according to his own system, he refutes perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence of external objects.
Then, with two [verses], he refutes the inferability of the external object as well;

immediately thereafter, with one verse, he demonstrates that objects necessarily exist within the conscious self by virtue of being of the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Following that, with four verses, through the examination of the nature of experience, scripture, and reasoning, he declares that the very life of the light which is the subject consists precisely in reflective awareness.

Immediately thereafter, he states the logical justification in three verses for the primacy of that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which alone consumes the object of knowledge—rendering it pure and not abandoning its nature as the subject.
He states in one verse that when the sole nature is Light (*prakāśa*), the distinction between knowledge, the knower, and so forth vanishes.

Then, in two verses, he states that just as in the case of the knower, even in the pure knowledge consisting of both non-conceptual and conceptual forms, reflective awareness alone is the vital principle.
Therefore, having refuted the opponent's position regarding the knower and knowledge,
the author supports their distinctness by means of a verse through the method of conclusion; such is the purport of this chapter.
The meaning of the verse is now being examined.
Now, it may be argued that memory, conceptual construction, and so forth have experience alone as their life-force;
therefore, if objects appear within them as distinct [from one another], it would be logical for them to appear in that same way within those [experiences] as well.
If it were not otherwise, then the very experience of those entities appearing as present must first be investigated as being of the nature of cognitive power; with this intention, he says:
"The manifestation of entities appearing as present..."
It is only for those who exist within that it is possible [to appear] by means of an external self.
For those for whom there is an appearance as "this" in the form of a clear manifestation characterized by presentness—

[an appearance] which occurs because of the state of being separate from the subject (pramātṛ), whose body ranges from the imagined void (śūnya) up to the illusory (māyīya) [body], conceived as having an external nature—

that appearance of things distinct from and severed from that illusory subject occurs only for those who remain within the ultimate subject, who consists of pure consciousness, and who have not abandoned their identity with Him.
It is logically consistent and established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

therefore, it is said that the Lord’s power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*) is the manifestation of an entity—which is not abandoned by its non-difference from consciousness—as distinct [from it] with respect to the imagined subject (*kalpitapramātṛ*). //1//
It has been stated that [the self] is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); he now demonstrates that valid cognition:
"Without having the nature of light (*prakāśa*), the object would be as unmanifest as before;
nor could the light of the object be distinct from the self, for the object's luminosity is its very being as light. (IPK 1.5.2)
The object is blue and so forth;

if its manifestation consists precisely in that very nature of being blue and so forth, and not some other manifestation-essence transcending the body of the object, then— just as it is called "blue" for everyone because of the possibility of that [blue]— it would be the same here.
It is not blue with respect to anything whatsoever, nor is it blue in reality within its own self, because it is impossible for that which belongs to another to be established in another;
nor is it non-blue within its own self, because without the favor of manifestation, no determination is possible.

Likewise, its manifestation is not toward all [subjects], nor toward none at all, but rather only within itself; or else, even within itself, it might not exist—thus there would be blindness for the world.
Now, if this blue-characterized [object] has arisen as something distinct, possessing the nature of light, from the collection of moments such as the sense organs and illumination;
Even so, that same consequence remains;
this very same defect applies even to the theory of manifestness (*prakaṭatāvāda*).

If manifestation were to rest entirely within the body of the object, then the state of manifestation as "this light appears to me" could not be established, since it must be grounded in the subject (*pramātṛ*). Thus, the persistence of manifestation as being attached to the subject is difficult to justify.
For at that time, the cognizer—consisting of the sense organs and so forth—would be the cause of the manifestation of the object’s form, just as a seed is the cause of a sprout.
Yet, the sprout is not of the nature of the sprout while depending on the seed;
therefore, if it were not of the nature of manifestation, it would remain unmanifest even upon the arising of cognition, just as it was before the arising of cognition.
But surely, cognition is of the very nature of the manifestation of an object;
how then could there be equality of the object regardless of whether cognition arises or does not arise? This might be so, if it were logically possible.
To what extent can that cognition which is distinct from the object and consists of the nature of illumination be related as a property of the object?
If the very nature of cognition is such that "the object is illuminated," then identity alone results between the object and the cognition.

Since it has been stated that the nature of the object consists in its being cognition, and since illumination, while possessing the nature of the object, would entail that the object is identical with itself— a fault already mentioned—
if you instead claim that the intrinsic nature of cognition is "to illuminate the object," [then...]
In that case, since it would follow that cognition produces the object as it is being manifested, the same fault arises once again.

Furthermore, this distinction between the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*ṇya*) has already been elaborated by me in the *Bhedavidāraṇa*; therefore, it should be sought from that very source.
Consequently, there is not even the possibility that a distinct manifestation could belong to the object.
And this follows by logical necessity: the very nature of an object consists in its being manifest, which is its non-difference from manifestation (*prakāśa*).

Now, if the manifestation were one in the case of a jar and another in the case of a cloth, then unification (*anusaṃdhāna*) would be impossible, because two manifestations would each terminate in their own self alone; this has been demonstrated at length in the passage beginning with "the world-order would perish."
Therefore, there is only one light;
this very point has been shown through repetition: "and the light would not be divided. //2//

Even while accepting that cognition, though distinct [from the object], has the nature of illuminating the object, he states another refutation: "If the illumination were distinct [from the object] yet non-different [in its essence], there would be a confusion of objects;
for the object to be illuminated must have the nature of illumination, and that which is not illumination cannot be established. (IPK 1.5.3)

If the luminosity that is the nature of cognition were indeed something other than the object— and for that very reason distinct from the object— then within its own self, because it consists solely of luminosity, there would be non-difference alone. For instance, in the case of "the manifestation of blue" and "the manifestation of yellow," whatever constitutes the blue portion and the yellow portion [is essentially the same].
That [difference] cannot first of all be the nature of cognition itself, for that would entail the abandonment of the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*).
If, on the other hand, it is the object, then this very point is being deliberated: here, by the power of manifestation, a difference between blue and yellow must be admitted.
And by that very same manifestation through which blue is apprehended as "blue indeed," how could yellow be coherently apprehended as "yellow" by that same manifestation?
For [the latter] would have been produced by the blue.

Whatever is asserted— such as that [the cognition] is produced by the yellow [color], or that it possesses the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*) as that [yellow color], and so forth— could only be established if a difference between blue and yellow were already proven;
that very difference is what remains to be investigated.
Now, if this [cognition] has a blue form, it is untenable if that is due to the power of a reflection, because of the non-appearance of a second object.
If, on the other hand, there is non-difference, then the doctrine of difference is abandoned.

Likewise, in the theory that [cognition] is an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, how can there be a distinction—such as knowledge of something on a mountain peak being produced by many blue objects and the like, being intense in one case and dull in another—given that the body of illumination (*prakāśa-śarīra*) is non-different?

And if such were the case, even when a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced by the perception of only one [of those objects], it would follow by force of logic that there must be remembrance of all of them; thus, there is great confusion.
It might be argued: "Let it be the object itself [that is diverse]."
"What is the use of this manifestation that brings about such a defect?
To this he replies: "There is no establishment whatsoever of that which is non-manifest;
for if blue were not manifest within itself, it would be nothing at all."
How could that be faulty?
For this very reason, it has been stated elsewhere by the author himself:
"In this way, these [objects], though appearing as if non-existent in the Self, are in reality nothing but the Light itself."
"Inert things exist only as manifestation, through their own and other natures.
If that is so, then if it is manifestation, it must be an object;
and how can that [inert thing] be manifestation?
If luminosity itself is the body of the jar, and that same [luminosity] is the body of the cloth, and so forth, then light as the body of the entire universe is established. //3//

One must conclude that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consists in the capacity of the single Light (*prakāśa*) alone to manifest such a manifold diversity of forms— including sequences, non-sequences, causal relations, and so forth—
and this conclusion holds provided that any other cause for this manifold state of the Light has been refuted.

In that regard, the cause of the sequential manifestation of diversity within the non-differentiated light is that which consists of a reflection, being of the same nature as that reflection; that very thing is the external form such as blue.

And although that is inferable, nevertheless, because it is determined by the perception "this is blue," and because the establishment of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is sustained by such determination, it will be designated as "perceptual."
The statement "it is what has been taught by the proponents of external objects" indicates that another reason is being inferred, showing that the external form is being considered as a possibility.

"If that which appears adventitiously as this or that were to cause the inference of an external [object], it would not be possible for a non-differentiated consciousness to be the cause of such variegated appearances. (IPK 1.5.4)
Nor can a diverse awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) serve as the cause here;
for what would be the basis for the diversity of that very awakening?
In this context, consciousness is indeed non-different;
for its ultimate reality is nothing but pure luminosity.
If there were a nature of the blue object that exceeded this luminosity, [it would not be consciousness].
In that case, if its nature were non-luminous, it would not shine;
yet, if its very nature were such that it shines in that way, how could there be a yellow appearance?
Moreover, if its essential nature were merely the manifestation of successive forms such as blue, yellow, and so on,
then the manifestation "I am devoid of the appearance of blue and the like" would not occur in states such as deep sleep;
therefore, manifestation is simply manifestation.
Since there is not even an atom’s worth of another form within it, cognition is non-different;

and since that non-different [cognition] cannot logically be the cause of those various appearances— such that at one time there is the appearance of blue and at another time the appearance of yellow— because a difference in effects is impossible when the cause is non-different.

Therefore, the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādī) maintains that each particular form—such as variegated blue, yellow, and so forth—which is adventitious and whose cause is established through unperceived direct perception, necessarily leads one to infer, by virtue of logical fitness, an external object that produces its own nature as a reflection within consciousness; this external object is similar to its own form, consists of a multiplicity of distinct aspects arising in succession, and is in every respect entirely separate from the cognition itself. //4//
And this is not merely a matter of conjecture for him;
rather, it culminates in certainty.
For instance, the reason stated by the Vijñānavādin—that the cause of diversity consists in the awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)—is not tenable.
It is well known that a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which produces memory is called a *vāsanā*;
however, in this context, what must be sought is that which is the cause of the diversity of experience.
Or, let it be that the *vāsanā* is a capacity consisting of a fitness (*yogyatā*) of cognition, whose nature is the power to bring about the appearance of blue and so forth.
And its "awakening" (prabodha) is its orientation toward the accomplishment of its own effects; from that awakening comes the variety of manifestations (ābhāsa-vaicitrya) among the cognitions.
To this we reply: even if it were said here that the manifestations existing within cognition are non-ultimate and possess only conventional existence (saṃvṛti-sattva), [the objection remains].

Nevertheless, that which belongs to these [impressions] must be accepted as being truly real (*vastusat*), because it is impossible for that which is non-real— characterized by a total absence of capacity— to possess a nature whose essence is the power of producing effects, which is the very lifeblood of causal efficiency. This being the case, if these impressions, which are desired as the causes of manifestation, have a form distinct from consciousness, [then...]
And if that [consciousness] exists as ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*),
then this is merely a variety of the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*) disguised by different terminology.
Or, if it exists as conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*), [then...]
In that case, causality would be untenable in that form.

Likewise, if causality exists in the same form by which these [appearances] possess ultimate reality, then that [form] is merely consciousness and is non-different; consequently, the differentiation of effects—such as the appearance of blue and so forth—would be unestablished.

Thus, if the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are not diverse, what hope can there be for their awakening to be diverse? Or, even if the latent impressions were distinct, since there is no cause for the awakening—such as space, time, or objects—that is intended to be diverse and exists apart from mere consciousness, the awakening would be non-diverse; thus, there would be only a single awakening.
The diversity of blue and other colors would appear all at once.
If it is argued that other cognitions existing within one's own continuum are the causes for awakening this diversity, that is incorrect.

If the distinctions of pleasure, pain, cold, heat, and so forth, as well as the differences of space and time such as "prior" and "subsequent," were merely of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and if consciousness were established solely on the basis of its being pure luminosity (*prakāśa*), then—since no difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*) would be possible—such a distinction between cognitions would be untenable.

This same mode of non-distinction applies equally to other internal cognitions that take the form of another subject (*parapramātṛ*), which are designated by the term "other mental continuum" (*saṃtānāntara*).
There too, the same applies to the body intended by others, characterized as thin, stout, and so on.

If there is no difference from the nature of pure consciousness as conceived by the [Advaitins]— who hold that the vital breath (prāṇa), such as inhalation and exhalation, and the qualities of the intellect (dhīguṇa), such as pleasure and pain, are all one— then we do not know to what "otherness" (paratva) could belong.
If it is argued that this [existence] belongs to consciousness (*bodha*) which is established therein,
even that [consciousness], if not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is simply non-existent; and if it is established,
yet as an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), then it is indeed insentient (*jaḍa*).

Nevertheless, like the body and so forth, [the mind] has the nature of mere cognition, because its form as mere self-awareness (*svasaṃvinmātra*) is not established for another. Now, it is observed that actions such as speech are pervaded by their cause—the desire in one's own person in the form "I shall speak"—and therefore, such [speech] must also exist in Caitra’s body, being caused by that [desire]. Yet, it is certain through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) that no such volition belonging to my own continuum exists there.
And from that, the effort of another is established, which is precisely what constitutes a different mental continuum (*saṃtānāntara*).

To this, it is replied: here, for the inferrer, the appearance of speech occurs in two ways: at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is the form "I speak," which has its life-force in non-interruption; [and so on].

And at the occasion of inference, [the opponent] says: "This person speaks" and "he whose life consists of separation"—if pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped with respect to one thing, while the appearance (*ābhāsa*) is another, how could that now be the logical reason (*hetu*)? Since he says "this person speaks," the reason for the appearance would be entirely unknown; how then could the effort (*samīhā*) be inferred from that reason?

Furthermore, as for this appearance of speaking that manifests as something separate in another subject who is accepted as an inferrer, how could it be the effect of the supreme effort which is the object of inference?
For that [consciousness], the effect which is the appearance of "I speak" must be one whose life is uninterrupted.

And it is not logical for something consisting of non-interruption to have as its effect something consisting of interruption, because there is no means of apprehending such a relationship between cause and effect;

indeed, it is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that this appearance of non-interruption within itself produces an appearance of the nature "the other speaks" which is interrupted in another.
Because this matter is preceded by the establishment of another,
and because the established other cognizer depends upon such a thing [as this], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Furthermore, there is no necessary rule that what is uninterrupted must necessarily be followed by what is interrupted, for there is deviation from such a rule.

Nor can it be said that the production of a [subsequent] appearance is certain because of its connection with a preceding one, even though that preceding appearance has ceased, for even when that [preceding appearance] exists, this [subsequent one] may not arise, and when it is absent, this may arise.

Furthermore, regarding the desire "let a severed appearance arise elsewhere," the very apprehension of a causal relationship between a previously arisen severed appearance and that [desire] is impossible if the other [term] is unestablished;
thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself remains unproven.

Furthermore, if other subjects were distinct [from one another], then the appearances residing within them would necessarily be distinct as well, according to the principle that "what is not separate from cognition is itself cognition.

Consequently, because there would be an absence of resting upon a single appearance, there could be no collective worldly transaction among subjects based on a single appearance; thus, the impossibility of anything else follows—namely, that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) would be distinct from consciousness (*bodha*).
