Since the argument based on the necessity of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) and so forth is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), what harm has been done by the mass of objects of cognition such as blue and yellow, such that their resting within their own nature cannot be tolerated? Therefore, other subjects (*pramātṛ*) are likewise unestablished.

Or, even if [the manifestation] were established, the manifestations contained within all subjects would produce a variety of awakenings of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as the cause for the variety of manifestations in each subsequent [moment], because there is no other cause for such restriction;
yet even so, the establishment of the variety of blue and so forth is not achieved.
Thus, there is simply the impossibility of the various latent impressions and their causes, which are the factors that awaken them.
And thus, this remains established:

if the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) should say that "cognition is non-different [from its object], because it is impossible for it to be the cause of a sudden difference in manifestation; therefore, an external object is inferred," then this is the meaning of the two verses. The word *cet* ("if") indicates the doubt regarding the meaning of the sentences in those two verses.
Thus, by means of being suspected in this way, the firm conviction of others has been demonstrated. //5//
Now, however, in order to weaken this presumption, he says:
"Let it be so; since all worldly transaction is concluded within those very appearances themselves, what is the use of another external object that is logically untenable? (IPK 1.5.6)

This may be so: when the phrase *syādetat* is explained as an acceptance of the aforementioned possibility, then it should be interpreted that the remainder of the verse demonstrates another possibility regarding its weakness by means of the supplementary clause *kiṃ tu*. However, if the insertion [of such a clause] is not tolerated, then *syādetat* itself would constitute yet another possibility.
What is stated by this verse should be construed as forming a single syntactical unit.
Even with this difficult hypothesis, you— who seek to establish external objects— have nothing whatsoever to achieve through them,
since practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is accomplished by those mere appearances (*ābhāsa*) which you yourself have accepted.
For there is no practical activity whatsoever with that which is eternally inferable; so what is the use of an external object?
Moreover, there is no proof for its existence, and as for a refutation, the primary one is this: if it were distinct from manifestation, it could not be manifested even as something to be inferred.
The refutations based on additional arguments against the whole (avayavin) are: the impossibility of its subsistence [in its parts], the non-establishment of inherence (samavāya),

and the conjunction of contradictory properties such as motion and lack of motion, concealment and non-concealment, being colored and not colored, and the distinction between different spatial directions.

Even in the doctrine that external objects are an accumulation of atoms (*aṇu*), since there is no accumulation other than the atoms themselves, if those atoms are joined together without any interval, there must necessarily be a distinction of spatial directions (*digbhāgabhedah*). Thus, when six atoms are accumulated around a central atom in the six directions, if another atom were to adhere at the very same point where one is attached, it would result in the central atom being no more than the size of a single atom.
Now, if one [part] is in one place and the other part is elsewhere, there necessarily follows a division of parts;
thus, being merely a part itself,
this same reasoning applies to it as well, so that nothing remains externally in reality.
Nor should it be argued that because corporeal things cannot occupy the same location,

conjunction does not eliminate their being in different locations; therefore, the effect-substance called a dyad (dvyaṇuka) residing in those [atoms] possesses atomic dimension, whereas from those three [dyads], a larger effect is produced.
For this is the doctrine of the whole (avayavin), and that has already been refuted.
Furthermore, as for the claim that conjunction is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), how could that be consistent with [the view of] partless [atoms]?

For if this [universal] inheres in its own substratum, what else remains for it that it would not pervade? Furthermore, this is a refutation by means of an over-extension (abhyucaya-bādhaka), and thus we have not exerted ourselves here;
it has been demonstrated in detail by the teacher Śaṅkaranandana in the *Prajñālaṅkāra*. //6//

Now, one might object: "A sublation (*bādhaka*) is truly incapable of doing anything to an entity established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that very firm *pramāṇa* brings about the invalidity (*apramāṇatva*) of that which is intended as the sublation and has been sublated. Furthermore, the proving *pramāṇa* for this [position]—namely, the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) appearing as various accidental occurrences (*ākasmika*)—has already been demonstrated here in the verse. Anticipating this objection, he says:
For the Lord, who is the very self of consciousness, manifests the entire range of objects externally from within by the power of His will, without any material cause, just as a yogi does.

In this regard, although it is indeed possible that in dreams, recollections, mental constructions, volitions, and the like, the manifold appearance of blue and other objects manifests even in the absence of any external cause that could provide them,

nevertheless, that manifold appearance might be suspected of being unreal because of its instability, because it is not common to all subjects, and because it is conceivable that it arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous experiences.
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of the diversity of cities, armies, and so forth, which is seen by yogins through mere will (*icchāmātra*),
no material cause (*upādāna*) consisting of the well-known diversity of clay, wood, semen, blood, and so on, is possible there. Indeed,
it cannot be argued that omnipresent atoms, suddenly assembled by the will of the yogin, would initiate the effect.
This is being examined in order to establish that [the theory] does not deviate from what is well-known in the world as the nature of causes;
for it is not commonly accepted that gross objects such as jars arise directly from atoms alone,
but rather through the intervention of potsherds and so forth.
Nevertheless, even when one relies upon fixed auxiliary causes, there is the application of specific place, time, and dominant factors (adhipatya), as well as the excellence of training and practice;

yet, if this much were required, a yogi fashioning a jar would simply be a potter, since he would be producing a jar preceded by the production of a complete set of materials already established for a potter.
Therefore, when transcending well-known causes, what is the point of speculating about other material causes such as imperceptible atoms?
In this regard, that very consciousness of the yogin possesses such a power— that it manifests the multitude of objects in the form of a variety of appearances.
It is possible that consciousness itself, having accepted sovereignty and by virtue of a specific will characterized by non-obstruction,

[manifests] this entire collection of entities existing within itself as "this," without losing its nature as the inexhaustible self of consciousness, [projecting it] through the vital breath, the intellect, the body, and so forth.
Why is autonomy (*svātantrya*) not accepted as being established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which consists of a consciousness that has transcended [the limitations of] mere limited objects?
Why is one distressed by the exertion of seeking other reasons?

By the word "only" (*eva*), he says this: first of all, for every proponent, the establishment of objects must necessarily be admitted as having the nature of consciousness; for it has been stated that this is primordially established.
And since his very sovereignty—designated by the word "God" (deva)—is his nature as consciousness (cidrūpatva), what is the use of this obsession with searching for another cause?
For it is precisely because he manifests in this way that he is conceived of as "God";
therefore, what is the point of an external [cause] which is logically untenable? This is the connection with the preceding [verse]. //7//
Surely, in this way, an inference based on possibility (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*) arises in both cases;

therein, should we, by means of the example of a jar reflected in a mirror, postulate a cause for the diversity of appearances as reflections in cognition that is distinct from the mirror of consciousness— that is, something considered "external"— or rather, should we state that the very sovereignty of consciousness (*saṃvitsvātantrya*) is the cause, using the example of a yogi?
Anticipating the doubt that "this [external object] remains a matter of uncertainty," he speaks the following two verses in order to dispel the possibility of inferring external objects:
"Inference is not accepted regarding what has never appeared before; the sense organ [is required for] that which has already appeared.
[Inference proceeds] from the appearance of a causal entity, such as a seed and so forth. (IPK 1.5.8)
Furthermore, how could an appearance ever belong to an external object? Therefore, its existence is established neither through perception nor through inference.
Not only does the external object not appear through direct perception—
given that this much alone constitutes perception, namely "this blue appears," which is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness and nothing more—
but even by means of inference there is no establishment of this external [object]; such is the intended meaning of the word "also" (api).

In this regard, it is shown by these two sūtras that inference is not able to function at all here; even if it were to function, it would not achieve the proof of the subject under discussion. In this context, inference is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
It is well known that all this conceptual construction (vikalpa) is rooted in experience.

Therefore, regarding that which has never appeared before in any way and has never been experienced, no proponent whatsoever accepts that inference—the operation of inference consisting of conceptual construction—can occur there.
Now, one might object: let this discussion apply to inference based on what has been perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa).

But regarding the *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* [type of inference], what will you say concerning the inference of the sense-faculties from the apprehension of objects? It is replied: even in that case, the established position is that the object is inferred in the manner that it is touched by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
And conceptual construction does not touch the object—such as a sense-faculty—in any specific form, such as through a particular configuration (*saṃniveśaviśeṣa*) or the like.

Rather, [it is said] that "there is some cause for perception" by virtue of this very nature; and that nature, characterized as causality, is indeed apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Thus, in cases such as "from a seed, a sprout [arises]" or "from threads, a cloth [arises]," the relationship between cause and effect is first determined by the force of direct perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*).

And in that regard, each individual manifestation possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*), because the cognitive operation characterized by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) proceeds toward an object denoted by each single word, and because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) follows that [operation]; as it will be stated:
"The uncontradicted cognition regarding an object has a single denotation as its domain."
Thus, it is established that the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely an appearance (*ābhāsa-mātra*).

Non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as well, which consists in the apprehension of something else, rests solely within mere appearance; therefore, in the cognition "the sprout [arises] from the seed," the causal appearance is indeed grasped as devoid of particularity (*viśeṣa-śūnya*).

For whatever follows the necessity of another without deviation is its effect, because in every jar, there is the appearance of the mere cause and its possessor in the form of clay and so forth. //8//
Furthermore, that which is external to the manifestation cannot itself be of the nature of a manifestation;
for it is a contradiction to say that it manifests while being external.
Moreover, in the absence of manifestation, there is no operation of inference, which consists of conceptual construction.

That which is external to a village, house, or the like is not called "non-village" and so forth, because otherwise it would follow that individual items such as fences, marshes, walls, or scales would also be non-villages; rather, it is that which is in close proximity to them.
Therefore, the expressions "external to the village" and "external to the appearance" are merely a similarity of words, not a similarity of reality.

Thus, for those who maintain that an object does not appear within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), even their own inferential conceptualization would not be applicable to an external object. However, we have already established—in the Sūtra—that even determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) has as its object that which appears, and that this determination is erroneous.
Therefore, if an object such as "blue" were not permeated by manifestation in the form of inferential conceptualization, it would not be inferred at all.

If, on the other hand, it is indeed permeated [by consciousness], then by the logical principle that "the object would be unmanifest, just as before," it must have the nature of manifestation alone and not be external.
Therefore, whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is brought forward to establish the existence of an external object, [is rendered futile].
On the contrary, this rather proves its non-extrinsic nature; thus, it is indeed contradictory.
For this very reason, he says "in any way whatsoever" (*kathaṃcana*):
in no manner whatsoever—whether as direct perception (*pratyakṣātmanā*) or as inference (*anumeyātmanā*)—has there ever been an appearance (*ābhāsa*) of that which is external and non-apparent.
Therefore, it is established that the Lord is indeed the conscious self alone. //9//
Now, one might object: "It was stated that what resides within must be manifested externally; therefore, that state of residing within must be established. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"The manifestation of the multitude of objects residing within the Self of the Lord certainly exists; for without that [manifestation], the reflective awareness of will (*icchāmarśa*) does not proceed. (IPK 1.5.10)
Even when appearing as external form, the nature of the "I" (ahantā) does not break;
for it will be stated that "interiority is identity with the subject."
And that [consciousness] is always so,
because the subject is manifestation itself;
for without having that as its essence, that which does not manifest would lack reality.
However, in that context, where the appropriate reflective awareness is "I," this very reflective awareness as "this-ness" (idantā) is precisely what constitutes externality;
whereas here, it is the reflective awareness itself in its form appropriate to consciousness— namely, "I"— which constitutes internality,
and this indeed exists for blue and other objects here.
But it is not that [the object] does not exist;

for if it were not so, then that reflective awareness—which is denoted by the word "desire" (icchā) and depends upon a future action, such as a potter's thought "I shall make a jar"—would be unrestricted with respect to the object of desire. If that were the case, why would the desire for a cloth not also arise? Thus, all worldly transactions would become confused.

Now, if even in that case, the object to be sought were produced at that very moment and thus come into existence, then that creation would not be possible within the conscious self (*cidātman*) without a desire; therefore, it will be explained here that for one who wishes to remain [in this state], desire alone is the cause.
Furthermore, regarding the alternative as to whether that desire is itself restricted by an object or not, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If [the desire] were constrained by the object, then self-hood itself would have arisen;
otherwise, there could be no desire for a cloth in a jar.
If one were to argue that it occurs there at that very same moment, it would lead to an infinite regress.

Therefore, this entire mass of existing things, whose form is eternally radiant as "I" within the conscious Self, is projected outward by consciousness through its sovereign nature characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*); that is, through its state of being the Master, it manifests this [world] externally in diverse forms such as succession and non-succession, preceded by the manifestation of the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Even there, in certain appearances, [the subject] unifies the perceivers, as spectators are unified in the sight of a woman’s dance;
for their unity exists only so far as that appearance is concerned.
However, regarding the aspects of the appearances of the body, vital breath, intellect, pleasure, and so forth, because the sense of difference has not dissolved, there is no unity in every respect.
For this very reason, by means of the diversity of uniting and separating the subjects at every moment, the Supreme Lord unfolds the universe through emanation, withdrawal, and so forth.
As it was said by the Teacher:
"Always delighting in emanation, always seated in the bliss of maintenance..."
"Salutations to You, who are ever satiated by devouring the three worlds," and so forth. Śrī Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa also [said]:
"Unceasingly, again and again, [You consume] the triple world with hundreds of mental constructions..."

"Even while conceptualizing, a certain unique one remains free from conceptualization; he is unborn. Therefore, it is established that the multitude of objects exists within [him], because without him, there could be no reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) regarding those objects. //10//
Now, one might object: "Reflection (*parāmarśa*) is indeed conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
how then could it exist in the Blessed Lord, whose nature is non-conceptual pure consciousness? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Otherwise, they know reflection to be the very essence of manifestation."
Even though light is colored by objects, it remains like an insentient substance such as a crystal.

In this context, if manifestation (*avabhāsa*)— which is light— and non-manifestation (*anavabhāsa*)— which is non-light, such as a jar and so forth— were to be established within their own selves by mutually excluding one another,
then their distinction, namely "this is conscious" and "this is insentient," would be as difficult to establish as it is between a jar and a cloth.
Now, if it is argued that because illumination is related to the object,
it is therefore not insentient,
then even a dead body would be non-insentient simply by virtue of having a relation to a jar.
Now, if it is not merely its own relation [to the object], but rather that the manifestation (*avabhāsa*) is the illumination (*prakāśa*) of the object,
then it follows that this illumination has the very nature of the object.
And it is not logically tenable for one thing to be illuminated by means of the nature of another.

Now, if the jar, though possessing a different nature, is the cause of the manifestation, then the manifestation must also be the cause of the jar; consequently, the jar would also be non-inert (ajaḍa). Or, if it is argued that even though the jar exists as something other [than the manifestation], it has imparted a shadow in the form of a reflection to the manifestation;
Because it bears that [reflection], it is said to be "possessing a jar," and consequently, it is non-inert (*ajaḍa*).
If that were so, then even crystal, water, a mirror, and the like would be of such a nature, and thus they too would have to be non-inert.
Now, even though it is of such a nature, the crystal and other such things are incapable of apprehending that Self and the jar or other objects; thus they are inert (*jada*).

This very non-apprehension is what constitutes the life of non-inertness (*ajāḍya*): it is the natural state of the manifestation, characterized by resting within its own self, consisting of the sovereignty of the internal and external organs, and termed "not looking toward another" (*ananyamukhaprekṣitva*).

For when the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) arises—"I am this luminous Self, shining"—one's own consciousness alone considers the subject, object, means of knowledge, and so forth to have achieved their purpose, and does not desire anything separate from itself.

For a crystal and the like, even when they have grasped a reflection, require another cognizer for that [reflection] to be established as such; thus, because they lack self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), they are insentient (*jaḍa*). In reality, however, because there is everywhere a resting in the *ahaṃ-parāmarśa* (the reflective awareness of "I"), which is identical with the nature of the cognizer whose essence is self-reflective awareness, there is indeed non-insentience at both the prior and subsequent limits. As it has been said:
"The fulfillment of this 'this'—of the fragmented reflective awareness—"
"That which is repose in one's own essential nature is this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*): 'I am [this]'.

Thus, it is established that the intermediate state itself—when the "this-ness" (*idantā*), which constitutes the prior and posterior limits, is being reflected upon—is the sphere of *māyā*, the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) for the deluded; therefore, reflective awareness alone is the primary essence of the Lord. //11//

He shows that it is not only we who have stated the primacy of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) regarding the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), but that this has also been taught by other scriptures: "Therefore, the Self is indeed consciousness, the activity of consciousness, and the agency of consciousness; for that reason, He is declared to be essentially distinct from the insentient. (IPK 1.5.12)

Since reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is the primary nature of the Self, it is with reference to this very cause— which functions as its purpose— that the Self, though being the subject (*dharmin*) and possessing the nature of a substance (*dravya*),
is spoken of and described by means of the word "consciousness" (*caitanyam*), a term denoting an attribute (*dharma*), through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
thus it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Śivasūtras*.
Thus it is recited.
For "consciousness" (*caitanya*) is an indicative term denoting a quality;
[it refers to] the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), which is unchanging.
"...for one who sees thus, there is isolation" (Yoga Sūtra 2.25);
"the seer is consciousness alone" (Yoga Sūtra 2.20).
In such passages as well, the teacher Ananta has shown that the self stands in grammatical apposition with the word *dharma*.
For that is called a substance (*dravya*) wherein the entire range of categories of objects finds its rest, shines forth, and is sought for the sake of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
If this entire collection of principles, beings, and worlds were not thus resting within consciousness, it would not exist in such a manner;

therefore, that very [consciousness], which is the nature of other categories of objects serving as the substrata for attributes such as qualities and actions, is the primary essence of substance itself.

That which is the substratum is itself the substance (*dravya*). Since that [substance] serves as the foundational wall for the repose of the multitude of infinite attributes (*anantadharman*), that very attribute— consciousness (*caitanya*)— is shown primarily by means of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) derived from a word ending in an agentive *kṛt* suffix, even though that suffix denotes a relationship.

For it is thus: since the cognition [of the agent] rests upon the relation, and since the substance-form of the relatum is already expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*), the suffix *ṣyañ*—by making known the property (*dharma*) in the form of the act of consciousness as being related [to that substance]—conveys the extracted portion [of the agent].
And the act of consciousness is the state of being an agent (*kartṛtā*) with respect to consciousness.

Sovereignty (*svātantrya*)—consisting of the forms of conjunction, disjunction, succession, and so forth—is, within the state of pure selfhood alone, the lack of repose like an insentient object, having as its essence an undivided light, and not looking toward another.
It is precisely this [sovereignty] that brings about the distinction from the insentient non-self, which lacks the sovereignty of conjunction, disjunction, and so forth.

Thus, intending to emphasize it as supreme and primary, when one ought to say "the Self is consciousness" (*cetana*), one says "the Self is consciousness" (*caitanya*) in order to subordinate other attributes and to elevate the attribute of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Thus it has been said.

The compound is to be analyzed as "the state of being the agent of the activity of consciousness" (*cit-kriyā-citi-kartṛ-tva*). For in poetry, the convention is that there should be a pause at the half-verse, but this is not the case in a scientific treatise (*śāstra*).
Or if it is argued that consciousness (cit) is the self and the agency of consciousness (citikartṛtā) is something distinct, this has not been stated anywhere [in the scriptures]. //12//

Now, an objection might be raised: just as both "light" and "non-light" reside within their own self, so too, when "light" is mentioned, its distinction from the insentient (jaḍa) would not have been expressed;
likewise, both "reflective awareness" (vimarśa) and "non-reflective awareness" (avimarśa) reside within their own self.
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how is there a difference between the insentient and the sentient? he says:
"Consciousness (citi) has the nature of self-reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa); it is the supreme speech (parā-vāk), arisen by its own inherent force.
This is the primary freedom (svātantrya), which is the sovereignty (aiśvarya) of the Supreme Self. (IPK 1.5.13)

In the phrase "he intends" (*cetayati*), that which is the act of intending (*citi*)— its reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), characterized by the wonder (*camatkāra*) of one's own self, is its essence (*ātman*) or nature (*svabhāva*).
For instance, a jar does not produce wonder within itself,
nor is its own self reflected upon.
It is not manifested within itself by that [consciousness],
nor is it perceived as something undifferentiated;
therefore, it is said to be "cognized" (cetyate).
But Caitra, through the union with the splendor of the outpouring of the surge of the "I" within his own self, experiences wonder;
he cognizes his own self and manifests it within his very own self.

That which is determined as "this" is manifested through its specific form and by way of its differentiation from others, appearing in an infinite variety of ways such as blue, yellow, pleasure, pain, or their emptiness;
therefore, it is said that "it is cognized by Caitra.
And thus, the claim that "reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is not reflective awareness within itself" is unproven.
For reflective awareness (vimarśa), being all-enduring, assimilates even that which is other, makes itself other,
and unifies both.
Its nature is such that it subordinates both [the object and the subject] once they have been unified.
Furthermore, reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) has the nature of internal verbalization;
and that verbalization, being independent of linguistic convention, consists of uninterrupted wonder and is like an inwardly directed pointing of the head.

It is *parā* because it is full, being the very life-force of conventional words such as "a" and so forth which consist of *māyā*, and because it serves as the foundational wall for other reflective awarenesses (*pratyavamarśa*) such as "this is blue" or "I am Caitra";
and it is *vāk* (speech) because it speaks— that is, it expresses— the universe through reflective awareness.

Therefore, by its own inherent nature (*svarasena*), as the very form of consciousness (*cidrūpatayā*), it has arisen as the embodiment of rest within its own self; it is eternally unsetting, perpetual, and simply "I" (*aham*).

This alone is said to be the supreme sovereignty, lordship, and mastery of the Supreme Self, characterized by independence from anything else. However, in the state of *paśyantī* on the level of Śrī Sadāśiva and others, even when there is merely the awakening of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) in the form of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*), which is sustained by non-recognition (*akhyāti*), there is nonetheless a resting within the sense of "I" itself; thus, it is both supreme and non-supreme.
Furthermore, regarding the firm establishment of this very state of "thisness" (idambhāva), it belongs only to those presiding over the womb of Māyā, such as Viṣṇu, Viriñca, Indra, and others;
yet that [state] for them arises solely from the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Thus, in the ultimate sense, bliss is precisely this independence from anything else.
Sovereignty, autonomy, and consciousness;
therefore, what was said is correct.
"...therefore, he is indeed distinct from the insentient.
He demonstrates that this very point has indeed been shown even in the Pradhāna scriptures:
"That [reality] is the throbbing, the Great Being, undifferentiated by space and time;
as such, it is declared to be the essence, the Heart of the Supreme Lord. (IPK 1.5.14)
When it is asked, "Why does a jar exist here?
and "Why does a flower in the sky not exist?", those who speak reply, "For the jar manifests to me, but the other does not.
Now, if this very "jar-ness" were the manifestation itself—that is, the relation with manifestation—[then the question would be redundant].
Does that manifestation flash forth for everyone at all times, or for no one at all?
Therefore, what is the meaning of the statement "it flashes forth for me"?
It means that my own manifestation—that is, my own vibration—is designated [as such].
Vibration (*spandana*) is a slight movement;
and this very state of being "slightly formed" is that wherein even the immovable appears as moving,
for it does not differ in the slightest from the nature of Light (*prakāśa*).
It seems as if it exceeds [all things], yet it remains truly immovable, appearing as if endowed with various manifestations. Therefore it has been said:
"Śiva alone, whose nature is blissful consciousness, shines within all beings; His flow of will is unobstructed, and His powers of vision and action are ever-expanding."
Thus: "Just as one who is extremely angry, or exceedingly joyful, or reflecting 'what shall I do?', or while running, reaches a certain state—therein vibration is established. (Spa. 22)
for the sake of discerning the reality of Spanda} (Spa.
21). Thus.
And as it is said: "{The outflows of the vibration of the qualities, etc.}” (Spa.

19). Even in the world, there is the state of being characterized by vibration through the conjunction with various diversities. And existence (*sattā*) is the agency of becoming, which is autonomy (*svātantrya*) in all actions.
And she is "great" because she pervades even her own flowers and so forth;
since she herself creates space and time just as she creates blue and other qualities, she cannot be qualified by them—
for that which appears as being of equal status with something else cannot be its qualifier, just as a bracelet [is not the qualifier] of Caitra.

Furthermore, space and time do not appear as equal in rank to the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because it is impossible for them to be of equal status in the manifestation; for they appear as "this" (*idantā*), whereas that [reflective awareness] appears as "I" (*ahantā*).
Thus, by not being touched by space and time, it possesses omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and eternity (*nityatva*); yet, there is also a touching of all space and time.
"Because of its connection with that emanation," therefore, from that [emanation] as well, there is pervasiveness and eternity. As it has been said:
"The Great Being, the Great Goddess, is called the life-force of the universe.
That which is the essence—that form which is not trivial—is this very power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*).
"That which is the luminous nature of both the grasped and the grasper—this very [power] implies its distinction from non-luminosity; this has also been established in the *Śrīsāraśāstra*:
'That which is the essence of this world is that supreme power Mālinī.
By the words "this very [one]," the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the Power is shown.

And what is called the "heart" (hṛdaya) is said to be the locus of support; and according to the principle already stated, that [support] consists of consciousness for insentient things, and even for that [consciousness], its nature as manifesting subjectivity arises from Light (prakāśa).

His power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*)— this very heart, consisting of supreme mantra and having the nature of reflective awareness— is said to reside here and there within him who stands and rests in the supreme state of the universe;
for the heart of everything is indeed mantra,
and mantra is essentially reflective awareness.
And reflective discernment consists of the power of supreme speech (parāvāk-śakti).
For this very reason it has been said:
"Without them, there would be no word, no object, nor even the movement of consciousness."
Thus [it is said]:
"In that regard, those who have entered [meditative absorption] assume the state of a mother...
and so forth; such is found in the Āgamas.
In this regard, the venerable Bhartṛhari also said:
"There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
every cognition is perceived as if permeated by speech."
"If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness,
its manifestation would not be manifest; for that [manifestation] is characterized by reflective awareness."
"This very notion (saṃjñā) of those subject to saṃsāra exists both externally and internally;
for upon departing [from the body], this one is seen to be unconscious, like a piece of wood or a wall," and so forth. By this, the statement "they know" is established.

Even by the Buddhists, who assert that the validity of manifestation depends upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), this point is almost entirely accepted, because conceptual determination consists of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*). //14//

Now, one might ask: "Since this very power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) is thus consecrated within the Supreme Śiva, whose body is adorned by a multitude of countless powers, why is it so? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, He makes Himself an object of knowledge as something separate;
yet His sovereignty is not fragmented by that orientation toward the object of knowledge. (IPK 1.5.15)

The Lord, who is himself liberated through his own sovereignty due to his non-dual nature, creates the liberated soul by means of volitions such as "I am the Lord" and so forth, and causes him to engage in worldly activity.
The power of agency (kartṛtva-śakti), which is the essence of sovereignty, encompasses all powers;
and since that [agency] consists of reflective awareness (vimarśa), it is logical that its preeminence alone is primary—this is the intended meaning of the reply.
This is the nature of the word’s referent.

That the Supreme Lord, whose nature is light, makes his own self— which is unknowable because it is of the singular form of the knower— into an object of knowledge, is what is rendered possible by a firm presumptive inference (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*), since no other cause has been shown to be plausible;
and that [act] occurs precisely from that agency characterized by the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
For since this [Self] perceives itself, it shines forth as blue and so on due to its being full of the universe.
But how can such a possibility even be conceived—
that the Self makes itself an object of knowledge?
He said: There is no object of knowledge whatsoever that exists as a state external to and separate from manifestation;
the particle "tu" (but) serves for emphasis.
And the arguments regarding this have already been stated.
He also states the argument for cumulative proof:

if the object of knowledge were distinct [from the self], then that orientation toward the object of knowledge—which belongs to the Self whose nature is the knower and which is established by self-awareness—would not belong to it.
By means of that orientation toward a distinct object, a state of dependence, namely subordination to another, is brought upon this [Self].
Dependence is the opposite of independence;
and since independence— defined as the self not looking toward another— is the very nature of the self, a self that is oriented toward something external would be a non-self indeed.
Furthermore, it follows as a logical consequence that what is non-self and insentient cannot be directed toward an object of knowledge.
Therefore, by the reversal of this consequence, the following is established: being independent and directed [toward itself], it makes itself the very object of its own knowledge. //15//
Furthermore, it is not only forms such as blue and so forth that are the objects of knowledge;

rather, the connection is this: even that which is conceived—that [the Lord], having fashioned Himself by His own sovereignty while remaining entirely undivested from His nature as the agent, engages with worldly transaction through means such as meditation, worship, adoration, and instruction—that too occurs for this very reason.

Is it not contradictory that something is both "endowed with autonomy" and "created"? To this he replies: because of the autonomy of that whose nature is non-dual and whose sole form is consciousness, this is not untenable—that which indeed appears extremely difficult to accomplish within the sphere of *māyā*.
That very sovereignty which is unimpeded in the accomplishment of that [action] is again indicated by the word "sovereignty" (svātantrya).
Therefore, the phrase "by this very [fact]" is not redundant, as it refers to the nature of the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti).
Alternatively, the two verses should be connected through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the words "by this very sovereignty."
He shows an example for this point:
because this independent creation (*svatantranirmāṇa*) is not established [in common experience], like the creation of blue and so forth;
for in such cases as "the Lord (Īśvara), the Blessed One (Bhagavān), the Self (Ātmā), eternal, all-pervading, independent," [it is merely a designation] of the subject (*pramātṛ*).
That object of cognition, which is to be worshipped, is non-different from the one who worships or the one who meditates.
And since that which is to be meditated upon appears, it is therefore a creation,
and not without a Lord;
for in this way, there is indeed a Lord.
If [the Lord] were not the sovereign (anīśvara), there would be an equivalence between [mundane] conceptualization, meditation, and so forth;
however, this is not the case, as a difference in their results is observed.

Therefore, by means of the power of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), the Supreme Lord manifests both of these objects of knowledge—which consist respectively in the manifestation of the absence of autonomy and the manifestation of being endowed with autonomy—as His very own nature.
Thus, it is that very [nature] which is the primary cause. //16//
Now, surely the determination of an entity’s existence depends upon manifestation,

and since that manifestation has reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as its essence, it is logical to say that when there is no difference in reflective awareness, "that is indeed this. Furthermore, in conceptual constructions such as "the Lord" or "the Self," there is a reflective awareness of the created object as "this-ness" (*idantā*).
But autonomy consists in the nature of the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa);
thus, if that which is created lacks that nature, how could it be called autonomous?
To resolve this, he says:
Because this [Self], which is not of the nature of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), possesses no distinction such as the reflection "I" (ahaṃ-parāmarśa),
its manifestation exists solely through being the object of the reflection "I," just like the object denoted by a verb ending in a personal suffix (tiṅ).
The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*);
by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the reference to [terms such as] *ātman*, *īśvara*, and so forth;
and the mention of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is an illustration for any suffix that expresses action (*kriyā*).
The mention of "action" (*karman*) is an elliptical indication of the nature of power (*śakti*) which has not yet become a sentient being (*asattvabhūta*).
This is the meaning:

there is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose very nature is "I," and there is the infinite variety of reflective awarenesses such as "the Lord," "the cognizer," "the Self," "Śiva," and so forth.

Although there is indeed a mutual difference between these two forms, nevertheless, because of that very difference, the distinction suspected between this Self— which consists of the reflective awareness of "I" and is the nature of the creator— and that which consists of the objects of creation, namely the locus of the reflective awareness of Īśvara and so forth, is not tenable.
Since even the conceptual reflection "Lord" (īśvara) finds its rest in that reality which consists of the nature of being a knower and an agent characterized by the power of ruling (īśana),
and since this quality of being a knower and so forth is sovereignty over knowledge and action, the state of not looking toward another, and the connection with uninterrupted knowledge;
And the uninterrupted state of "I know" and "I act," which rests upon the "I-sense" (asmadartha), is precisely the fact that this creation of the Lord, the Self, is to be contemplated as "I.
Alternatively, the ablative case in "sṛṣṭeḥ" (from the creation) expresses cause;
for it is from this Lord that even in the volitions of the Lord and so forth, there is a creation of that which is alone fit to be referred to as "I."
The *kṛtya* suffixes are used in the sense of the worthy (*arha*).

For example, the powers such as action, agent, conjunction, and option— whose ultimate reality consists of the mental reflections determined by the respective employment of *tiṅ*, third-case endings, and particles like *ca*— are expressed by words such as "cooking," "agent," "conjunction," and "option," even though they have been brought into the state of being [grammatical] entities (*sattvabhāva*).
In such fundamental reflections as "Caitra cooks" or "by Caitra," they find their rest;
otherwise, those [meanings] would not be perceived at all.
It is the same here as well.
This is what is meant: "reflection" (parāmarśa) is the locus of rest, and that is exclusively ultimate and absolute; and it is precisely of the nature of "I."

However, as for that state of repose in the middle which is like the foot of a tree on the way to a village, its being "created" in relation to that [ultimate state] is stated; what contradiction is there in this?

By this, the fact that even blue and other objects consist of the Self (*ātman*) is established: for even when there is a middle-level reflective awareness such as "this is blue," one ultimately reposes in the root reflective awareness as "I" alone.
Even in the thought "I know this blue," the reality is simply "I am manifest."
As it has been said, beginning with "of this [which is] 'this'," etc.:

the deluded person, however, through the very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of blue and so forth, falsely imagines satisfaction regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and the like; thus, it was stated that blue and so forth are devoid of autonomy. But in the case of the Self (*ātman*) and so forth, even the deluded person does not falsely imagine the completion of cognition or causal efficiency without resting in the fundamental reflective awareness that is their root; therefore, even in its manifestation, the Self does not relinquish its autonomy.
It has been stated. //17//

By the power of Māyā, that very [consciousness] of the All-pervasive Lord, when its sphere of objects becomes differentiated, is designated by such names as knowledge, volition, and determination. (IPK 1.5.18)
That which appears despite being logically untenable is called "māyā";
therefore, the entire range of appearances that is distinct from the Light is māyā,
and within that, the sovereignty of the very nature of consciousness (cittattva) is the power of māyā.
That which is to be cognized (saṃvedya) by her is differentiated from the cognizer and from one another;

that which is to be cognized by the group of instruments—which, through the power of Māyā, is differentiated from the cognizer and from the object of cognition—is itself the sphere of experience. Being such that its place of rest is therein, that very consciousness, whose nature is reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa), is the Supreme Speech (parāvāk) and is called knowledge (jñāna).
It is called "volition" (saṃkalpa) and "determination" (adhyavasāya); by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," doubt, memory, and so forth are also meant.
For instance: consciousness (*saṃvit*) as such, when constrained by a sense organ that perceives clearly and by an external object that is manifest, is *jñāna* (cognition).
When constrained by the mind (*manas*) and an object that is not manifest, it is *saṃkalpa* (volition).

And when constrained by the intellect (*buddhi*) and an object that possesses the quality of being an object (*viṣayatva*) to its ultimate extent, it is *adhyavasāya*, which is to say, ascertainment (*niścaya*).

Furthermore, the apparent difference between the object and the external and internal organs is untenable because they are non-different from its light; rather, it is manifested as the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*). Thus, while there is a resting place in difference, this is not a case of difference merging into non-difference, as is the case with [the categories of] Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and so forth.

Consequently, cognition, volition, and the rest are said to be the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) of that reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), which maintains a continuous awareness of itself and whose own nature remains undestroyed in its non-difference.
Doubt and the rest are distinct, as is the variety of blue and other colors; thus, everything remains unimpaired. //18//
Now, one might object: let the nature of reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) belong to the powers of consciousness such as volition and memory, which are conceptual in nature;
but how can it apply to that power of direct perception (anubhava), which is characterized by immediate intuition and is non-conceptual (nirvikalpa)?
For reflective awareness consists in the application of specific linguistic expressions,
and the application of specific linguistic expressions depends upon the recollection of conventions;
and that [recollection] depends upon the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Thinking that even this [consciousness] is of such a nature, [the author] says the following in order to dispel the confusion of others as to how there can be a connection with verbal expression at the very first moment:
"Even at the moment of direct perception, there exists reflective awareness (vimarśa); otherwise, how could it be so?"
Running and so forth would be possible [in such a state], devoid of reconnection.
In this context, consciousness possesses an inherent connection with verbal expression, such as the pointing out of a finger and so forth;
otherwise, when a child's initial linguistic activity is observed, no acquisition of meaning (vyutpatti) could ever occur.
For it is through a succession of non-conceptual cognitions that the child hears that word.
Then, one perceives that object before oneself,
and subsequently perceives that ground devoid of it; through such worldly transactions as "Bring the jar" or "Take away the jar," how could the thought "This is its meaning" flash in the mind—
that "this is a jar"?
"Bring this," "Take this"—
for this meaning indeed has its life-force in such syntactical connection (*yojanā*).
And *yojanā* (synthesis) is the operation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Here, for the ignorant person, due to the recollection of conventions experienced in previous births, [the object] appears as "thus" (*evam*).

Nevertheless, because at the time of the convention that word was apprehended as an object through the mode of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*), it has fallen away from its distinctness; appearing thus, it comes to rest within the body of consciousness and becomes the signifier (*vācaka*).
Thus it occurs:
if that which appears as the very nature of consciousness shines forth, then it must consist of verbal expression (*abhilāpamaya*) itself.
Just as knowledge appears as consisting of pleasure even though the object lacks the nature of pleasure, so too let it be that the object—form and so forth—is not essentially verbal expression.
Nevertheless, consciousness will manifest as having that very nature.
In this view, however, because even the object consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it is in reality nothing but consisting of linguistic expression (*abhilāpa*).

Even states such as stillness (*staimitya*)—if they do not consist of reflective awareness—then their occurrence is in truth merely a matter of oath, since the activity of the subject, which is essentially conceptual, does not arise therein.
Furthermore, there would be no recollection;
for if a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were to arise as a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) regarding an object such as form, what else could it be?
There would be no such thing as "stagnation" (*staimitya*), which consists in the withdrawal of all thought.
Thus, even in that case, there is an internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*);
for all things endure being denoted by the entire range of words,
and therein a specific application of words is made.

For instance: the innate reflective awareness of an infant before him—whether as "I" without interruption or as "this" with interruption—is immediately followed by the superimposition of the word "white" or "cow";
through repeated practice, even that [word] becomes identical with the cognizer.
And following that, there is another convention such as "this is white" or "this is an ox"— such is the nature of convention.
Therefore, there is a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) in direct perception.
This is the intended meaning of the word "also" (*api*):
here, direct perception is in fact nothing other than the culmination of the activity of conceptualization (*vikalpana*), such as "I see."
For even the opponent maintains that conceptualization (vikalpa) is the function (vyāpāra) of perception; and it is not logical for a function to be distinct from that which possesses it,
since it is indeed of the very nature of that [perception].
Or, let it be granted that direct realization has a nature lasting for only a single moment; even in that case, there is reflective awareness (vimarśa),
and this is necessarily so.
How otherwise?
If he were not that [self], then while moving swiftly with the intention of reaching a single goal and rapidly reciting the names of trees, [he would not do so].
And while reciting the mantra-text rapidly,
one should not proceed [only] with what is desired;
one should utter it or cause it to be recited.

For instance: in that [first] place, there is the cognition [of it], the desire to step forward (*ācikramiṣā*), the stepping forward (*ākramaṇa*), the cognition of having stepped upon it, the consideration of another purpose, the desire to leave (*tityakṣā*), and the connection with another place;

even in that case, how could the attainment of the desired place occur without such a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) consisting of the forms of joining and disjoining, beginning with the "desire to step forward" and so on?
This should be understood to apply similarly to rapid grasping, recitation, and so forth.
In that regard, there is specifically the application of the sequence of places of articulation (*sthāna*), organs of production (*karaṇa*), and so forth.

And because no subsequent coarse conceptual construction (*sthūla-vikalpa*) is perceived therein, it is for that very reason characterized by rapidity; thus, one must cultivate the subtle reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) consisting of the creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of sound.
For the cultivation of sound (*śabdabhāvanā*), when being expanded from its condensed state, becomes a gross conceptual construction (*sthūlo vikalpa*).

For example, the expansion of the thought "this" is "pot," "white," and so forth; and the expansion of that [concept] is "that which has the form of a broad base and belly," "that which possesses the quality (*guṇa*) associated with the universal (*jāti*) of whiteness," and so on.
Because of the reading "dhāvu" in the sense of "purification of movement," the root *dhāv* occurs in the sense of rapid motion by virtue of its own inherent power. //19//
Let it be that such a subtle reflection enters into the very body of light;
however, where conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is manifest in its grossness, there the word appears distinctly, just like the blue object itself— as "this is blue."
How could that [reflective awareness] be non-different from the nature of light?
For reflective awareness is the very essence of sound,
and you maintain that even here, in the state of duality characterized by Māyā, it remains non-different from light.
Anticipating the question, "How is this to be understood?", he says:
"This determination that 'this is a jar' is the power of the Supreme Lord, which appears like the Self, transcending name and form; however, it does not appear as 'this-ness' (idantā). (IPK 1.5.20)
By whom was this said: that the gross word "jar" is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose very nature is the life-force of manifestation?

For even that gross word appears as something distinct from its object, just like the object itself. That supreme power of the Lord, which consists of reflective awareness and is like the Self, is the faculty of ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*), which perceives those two—the word and the object characterized by name and form—as being of one and the same nature in the form "this is that."

It shines as "I" in its undivided state, and never at any time does it shine as "this" in a divided state. If it were to appear in a divided state, it would be established in something other than itself; consequently, there would have to be another act of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and for that too the same would apply—thus, due to infinite regress, the manifestation of the blue object itself would not occur, because it would lack a foundation.
Therefore, every act of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is indeed inseparable from the Light (*prakāśa*).
[The term] "adhyavasā" [is derived] according to *Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.3.106: *ātaścopasarge*.
Thus, that which ends in aṅ is feminine. //20//

Now, if it is the case that the entire complex of cognitions is established solely as "I," then there is no contact with the plane of the object of knowledge (*vedya-bhūmi*); and on the plane of the object of knowledge, there is a connection with space and time, but not in the aspect of the knower (*vedaka*).

If there is an absence of connection with space and time, how could this sequential nature observed in cognitions—both in relation to space and in relation to the factors such as the subject (*pramātṛ*)—be possible?
And in the absence of sequence, there would, in reality, be nothing but unity.
Then, in order to pacify the doubt as to how that which was stated—that "the Supreme Lord possesses knowledge, memory, and so forth"—could be sustained, he concludes what was previously said:
"Only due to the influence of different objects of cognition, space, and time, do knowledge, memory, determination, and so forth appear as sequential. (IPK 1.5.21)
It is true that the essence of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) is indeed without succession;

however, there exists space—consisting of distance, proximity, extension, and non-extension—which is produced by the differentiation of forms belonging to those objects of knowledge (*vedya*) that appear as distinct due to the power of its own energies (*svaśakti*);
and there exists time—consisting of slowness, speed, sequence, and so forth—which is produced by the differentiation of actions.

Following after those two and supported by their mere shadow, the [successive] acts of cognition, recollection, and determination appear as if they were parts of themselves, even though they are partless;
and the appearance of succession is produced by the appearing parts relative to one another and relative to their own parts.

Although it is temporal succession alone that clearly appears within cognitions, and not spatial succession, nevertheless, for one who is deluded, the perception of a mountain appears as if extended and the perception of a jujube fruit appears as if subtle; thus, spatial succession is also shown.

Therefore, because there is an appearance of accepting a succession residing in the object of cognition, even though succession appears, it is not ultimately real, since that which appears is for the sake of another.
Therefore, it is rightly said that "knowledge and the rest are the powers (śakti) of this Blessed One.
By the verse beginning with "by the power of māyā, [the Lord]," the manifold variety of the forms of knowledge is demonstrated.
However, the distinction here is that there is a variety of places and times. Thus all is auspicious. //21//

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Power of Knowledge," in the first section on Knowledge of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
[He perceives] entities whose wealth is non-difference from His own Self, through the chisel of their exclusion (*apohana*).
"Another [aspect] is Śiva, who by his own will creates manifold forms; we praise him.

Thus, the power of memory (*smṛti-śakti*) and the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) have been described. Now, the power of exclusion (*apohana-śakti*), which sustains both of those, is explained at length in eleven verses, beginning with "The reflective awareness of 'I' which is of the nature of light... and ending with "in every living being that has been established."

In that regard, by means of the first verse, it is indicated that non-conceptuality (*avikalpa*) is the distinguishing feature in the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). Then, by means of the next verse, it is stated that when the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃpratyavamarśa*) is pure, the operation of exclusion (*apohana*) is impossible.
Finally, by means of the subsequent verse, it is shown that its occurrence is possible only within one's own direct perception (*svadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, by means of two [verses], the conceptual nature of the impure self-reflective awareness "I" is established;
then, by means of one verse, the conceptual nature of subsequent synthesis (*anusandhāna*) is also established;
and finally, by means of one verse, it is shown that the creative power of the Supreme Lord consists precisely in such forms as this subsequent synthesis and so forth.
Then, with one verse, the existence of the manifestation of objects within the primordial conscious Self (cidātman) is withdrawn;

then, with two verses, the manifold variety of that very manifestation of objects in experience, memory, and so forth is described; and its description is shown to be useful for the recognition of one's own Self as the nature of the Lord (īśvara), which is the subject at hand—this is stated in the [final] verse.
Such is the intended meaning of this daily lesson (*āhnika*).
Now, the meaning of the text itself is being explained. This has been stated: [The text follows...]
"...the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the manifestation [is its] own-being.
In this context, reflective awareness is indeed conjoined with a word whose nature is expression;
and because of that conjunction, the state of being conceptual (*vikalparūpatva*) follows even for the pure Supreme Lord.
Anticipating the objection that this is not accepted because [the self] is established as being essentially of the nature of the transmigratory state (*saṃsāra*), he says:
"That reflective awareness which is *ahaṃ* (I), though its essence is light and its body is speech, is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
For that is said to be a conceptual construction which, while being a certainty, implies a duality. (IPK 1.6.1)

The self of light— which is the nature of pure consciousness, unpolluted by contact with the body and so forth, which constitutes life, whose essence is its own being, which is devoid of interruption, which is conceived as internal, and which consists in resting in the sovereignty of not looking toward any other source— is the reflective awareness "I"; this does not constitute a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
He shows the seed for the suspicion that [speech] might be conceptual by saying "even though its body is speech" (*vāgvapur api*).

By the word "speech" (*vāk*), he refers to that which is distinct from the sound (*śabda*)—which is the form of the object and is grasped by the ear—and which, appearing internally, is an expression (*abhilāpa*) whose nature is verbalization (*śabdana*) and which enters into the form of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa-āveśin*): it "speaks" (*vakti*) the object through its own superimposition (*svādhyāsena*), by means of the intention (*abhisaṃdhānena*) that "this is that."
If it has speech as its body, why is it not conceptual construction?
He says: For it does not possess the defining characteristic of conceptual construction.
For instance: *vikalpa* (conceptual construction) is the conceptualization (*kalpa*) of that which is suspected to be manifold by means of excluding other possibilities (*anyavyavacchedana*).
And this "manifoldness" occurs when there is no exclusion of the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the possibility of non-fire in the case of fire;
thus, it implies a duality consisting of both fire and non-fire.
Therefore, in conceptual construction, that [the object] must necessarily be ascertained as such, and the other [the non-object] must be excluded. And in that case,
there would indeed be an appearance of two distinct things, namely a jar and a non-jar.
Just as in the case of light, there is no manifestation of anything else that is distinct from it.

For when a jar is perceived, even though it is not a jar, that which has the nature of a cloth or other objects—possessing the habit of occupying a location considered suitable for a jar, brought forth by its own causes, and capable of generating cognition—is possible at that very place where the jar stands;
thus, because both the jar and the non-jar are possible within the field of appearance, superimposition (*samāropa*) finds scope.

Since there is a function of exclusion (*apohana*) characterized by negation regarding the non-jar once superimposition has occurred, the conceptual nature of the certainty "this is a jar" is sustained by that [exclusion].
The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).

That which is possible in the place of this so-called "manifest" (*prakāśa*) does not, for its part, possess the nature of the unmanifest (*aprakāśa*); for possibility occurs only between things of equal status.

Furthermore, that which is to be accomplished by the manifest has never been seen to belong to the unmanifest. And it is precisely through the force of the attribution of possibility that its state of being unmanifest would be dismantled.

Therefore, there is no manifestation at all of another distinct entity that is non-luminous by nature, which would be of an equal status to light and incapable of sustaining the operation of differentiation consisting of exclusion (*apohana*). In the absence of such an entity, what could be excluded?
Even if it were to appear, its very nature would be that of luminosity.
Furthermore, there is no difference in the nature, location, or time of Light such that a second Light could be excluded from the first.

For this reason—since it is so—and because exclusion is impossible due to the absence of duality, and because there is an absence of the nature of conceptual construction (vikalpa), the reflective awareness "I" within pure consciousness, whose essence is self-awareness, is indeed not a conceptual construction. //2//
Now, when a jar is seen in its fully established form, how can a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that depends upon that perception effect the negation of the non-jar?
For the name "non-jar" has certainly not been grasped by anyone;
and furthermore, how could the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a non-jar be awakened when a jar is being perceived?

True; thus the Śākyas may be questioned, but not we, because this conceptual construction "this is a jar" is said to be the ascertainment of that [object] through the mere exclusion of what is not that, by means of a manifestation that possesses both that and its opposite. (IPK 1.6.3)

Here, the so-called cognizer (*pramātā*) has been shown to be distinct from the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), independent within acts of cognition, and the agent by virtue of exercising the power of conjunction, disjunction, and so forth.

Furthermore, it has been stated that within this cognizer exists the manifestation of all objects; although his body is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), he also functions in coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those objects, according to the analogy of a city reflected in a mirror.

And thus the cognizer experiences—that is, resorts to—that manifestation as the appearance of a jar (*ghaṭābhāsa*) and that which is not its manifestation as the appearance of a non-jar (*aghaṭābhāsa*). In that state of non-conceptualization, this jar, whose nature is consciousness, is like consciousness itself: it has the universe as its body and is full.

And since no linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) pertains to that [non-existence], by negating the operation of illusion (*māyā*), it also negates even a real entity (*bhāva*). Thus, the exclusion (*apohana*) of things such as a cloth from the nature of a jar is performed in the form of a negation.

Relying precisely upon that exclusion (*vyapohana*), the ascertainment of that jar is said to be "the jar alone," because the meaning of the particle "alone" (*eva*) consists in the negation of other possible objects;
this very [ascertainment] is "delimitation" (*pariccheda*), because it is like the carving out [of wood] by cutting it off from all sides.

The word "hi" (for) [indicates]: since this is so, therefore it is logical that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) implies a duality. Thus, the two entities mentioned in the preceding verse are stated as the reasons in sequence;
because conceptual construction is thus, "I"—the pure reflective awareness—is not a conceptual construction. This is the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*) across the three verses.

The Śākyas also have stated that this operation belongs to the knower alone, as they say "the single [cognition] called reflective awareness" while using such terms as "the cognizer" and "himself. But how can that [operation] be established by them?—let this matter rest for now. //3//

One might object: "In that case, why would even the reflective awareness 'I' not take on the nature of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since it involves the exclusion (*apoha*) of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as a jar, which is of a non-I nature? With this intention, he says:
"That which, having abandoned the true nature of consciousness (*cittattva*) through *māyā*, appears as if distinct..."
Whether in the body, in the intellect, or in the vital breath, it is imagined as if in space.
The reflective awareness "I" as the subject [of cognition] arises from the exclusion of others;
it is indeed a conceptual construction (vikalpa) produced by the manifestation of its opposite.
The reflective awareness of "I" is twofold: the pure and the illusory (māyīya).
Among these, the pure is that which occurs in pure consciousness alone, which is non-different from the universe, or in the Self which is translucent yet suffused with the reflection of the universe.
The impure, however, is that which occurs in the form of objects of knowledge, such as the body and so forth.

In that case, within a pure reflective awareness (*ahaṃpratyavamarśa*), no counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) exists that could be excluded (*apohitavya*); for even objects such as a jar, having light as their essence, are not counter-correlatives and thus cannot be excluded.
Therefore, in the absence of anything to be excluded, how can there be the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalparūpatā*) therein?

On the other hand, an impure [awareness]—occurring with respect to the body and so forth, which are of the nature of the object of knowledge (*vedya*)—is indeed a conceptual construction, because it arises through the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of other bodies or jars and the like. This is the meaning of the sentence.

As for the literal meaning: having set aside—that is, having rendered secondary by means of rejection—the reality of consciousness (*cittattva*), which consists of pure luminosity even though it exists, one forms the conceit that "I am indeed the body and so forth" with respect to the differentiated body and the like, and "I am the knower" with respect to objects of knowledge such as blue.
This reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of "I am gross" and so on is nothing but conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
But it is not merely pure reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).

The reason for this is as follows: there is the manifestation of a "counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*)—namely, another [entity] such as the body and so forth, or a jar and so forth—which is of equal status and opposed by way of mutual exclusion; that which is characterized as a superimposition (*samāropa*), from which [reflective awareness] is animated by the negation of that [other].
The reflective awareness "I" arises as: "I am stout, not thin, nor am I a jar or the like."
The very rejection of that which is of the nature of pure light is the cause of the differentiation of the body and so forth;

however, when that [light] is rejected, the cause is the power of Māyā, which consists in the Lord’s sovereignty and takes the form of the desire to conceal His own Self, resulting in the non-manifestation of non-duality and appearing as delusion.

Furthermore, the rejection of the conscious nature belongs precisely to the body and so forth—which, while not having abandoned their status as objects of knowledge, appear as distinct entities—and it is the mere conceit of being a subject (*pramātṛtva-abhimāna*) based on the fact that such distinction is devoid of logical justification.

And likewise, the Cārvākas, who abide on the level of identifying with the body, declare that the body alone is primary, stating: "The person is the body characterized by consciousness," because women, children, and the ignorant have such a conviction. Even more discerning than them, [others] consider the body to be unstable due to the power of transformation arising from being cooked [by digestion] and so forth; they perceive that the body undergoes hundreds of mutations without the presiding influence of the vital force (*prāṇaśakti*).
Some scholars of the Upaniṣads consider the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—which is subject to hunger and thirst—to be the Self (*ātman*).

Even more refined in their discernment, those such as the followers of Kaṇāda, seeing that the vital breath is also impermanent and thus unfit for the role of the underlying substrate of reflection, declare the intellect (*buddhi*) alone—which is the locus of knowledge, pleasure, and so forth—to be the Self.

Others, however, considering even that intellect to be inferior because it becomes an object of cognition during the state of yoga, maintain that the Self is that which is of an unperceivable nature and exists beyond the stages [of the evolutes].

Certain proponents of the doctrine of the Void-Brahman (śūnyabrahmavādins), such as the Sāṃkhyas and others, claim that there is a certain form of reality—the principle of the subject—which is entirely devoid of the aggregate of all objects of knowledge; because it is empty, it is like the sky, yet it does not have the nature of the physical space of the great elements (mahābhūta-ākāśa).

However, even within that object of knowledge there is another void, and within that yet another void; as long as there is differentiation, conceptual construction (kalpanā) does not cease. For this reason, he says: "in the imagined" (kalpite).

And there is no infinite regress, because everything is manifest by the power of the manifestation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and not by virtue of the body and so forth; for through that [ultimate reality], the body is merely a matter of conceit as the subject (*pramātṛ*),
while the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) is the void, consisting of nothing but contraction.

Just as the absence of a jar is the ground itself, so too the very essence of consciousness (cittattva)— when permeated by the shadow of the limited, knowable portion— is what appears as the intellect, vital breath, body, and so forth.
These very specific stages are described in the scriptures as "waking" and so on, or as "stationed in the body" (piṇḍastha) and so on, for yogins ascending higher and higher.
And the refutation [of that objection] will be explained:
"This very *cit-tattva* (the principle of consciousness), consisting of agency and empowered by *kalā*,
exists as a limited attribute of the insentient [principles] such as the void (*śūnya*)."
Thus, it is established: the reflective awareness "I am impure" is nothing but a conceptual construction (vikalpa). //5//

Moreover, this notion of "I" (ahaṃ-pratyaya) is twofold, being of two kinds: that which consists of mere experience and that which is of the nature of synthesis. It is pure and twofold: as "I am Śiva" in the self of Śiva, and as "I am this" in the self of Sadāśiva. It is also impure, as in "I am gross."
I who was fat am now thin; I was a child, then a youth.
The "Elder" and the thought "I am he" constitute the two types of impurity.
Regarding that, it has been stated that in the case of purity, the nature of conceptual construction is simply non-abiding.
It has been established that when experience is impure, it possesses the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

However, one might suspect that even in an impure state, because non-difference flashes forth through its nature as a synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*), it could be considered non-conceptual. To dispel such delusion, he says:
"In the case of an occasional manifestation, there occurs a synthesis with previous manifestations and so forth."
Conceptual construction is said to arise from mental conditioning; that [conditioning] also occurs when there is an appearance of difference.
The phrase "in the body" and so forth continues [from the previous context].

That which occurs occasionally—meaning that which arises at certain times—is the manifestation of the body and so forth, which possess specific spatial, temporal, and formal characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
In that regard, the "conjunction" with a prior manifestation refers to the synthesis: "I who was a child am now a youth," based on the manifestation of the bodies of childhood and so on.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is a mental conjunction with a future manifestation yet to come, such as "I shall become an elder";
that conjunction is entirely conceptualization (*kalpanā*), which is nothing other than discursive thought (*vikalpa*), and not pure reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).

Here, the qualification regarding the body and so forth is intended to show their status as causes— because even at that time, the appearance of difference in the body and so forth remains uninterrupted.

For if one were to perform the synthesis "I am this" while perceiving that very body and so forth as being entirely full and devoid of limitation, then how could this stage be called the level of Sadāśiva by way of being a state of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), since that synthesis occurs precisely when there is no interruption?

If it is asked how there can be a connection even when [the body] is broken, he says: "By means of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*," which means by virtue of memory arising from the awakening of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) produced by previous experiences;
that is to say, the connection occurs through the strength or weakness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Because of the gradations of knowledge, bliss, and so forth in the intellect (*buddhi*),
and because of the association with expansion and non-expansion in the void (*śūnya*),
this too is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
In this way, even in the synthesis of a jar and so forth—such as "this very jar is that one"—it must be understood as conceptual (vikalpa).

However, because the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) shines intensely like a flash of lightning within these planes of synthesis, they are accepted as the primary means for the initial stage of cultivating the supreme state (parapada).

Furthermore, it is not the case that the body and so forth are merely objects of cognition for a preceding subject, such that the object of cognition would not appear when the subject is unmanifest, nor that its manifestation would not occur without a prior manifestation.
He too would not [be manifest] without the manifestation of another cognizer, and thus there would be an infinite regress;
