rather, demonstrating that the manifestation of the universe is indeed pure manifestation itself, he shows— by the reasoning already stated— that the Lord is always inseparable from the powers of emission and the rest.
Thus, even in the realm of worldly transaction, the Lord, entering the body and so forth,
may by His will manifest externally the very mass of objects that are already shining within.
That which was previously shown regarding the body, the intellect, and so forth, is established in this way. How?

If, in the sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—the realm of *māyā*—the Lord himself, whose ultimate reality is Light, by his own will and through the power of *māyā*, enters even the body, vital breath, and so on, manifesting his own nature primarily as body, breath, and the rest.
Within the pure consciousness alone,
the multitude of objects— which shines in the form of "I"— is made to appear externally as "this" by His will alone; therefore, this is logically established,
for otherwise there would be an infinite regress.
The word *liṅ* refers to the logical reason (*hetu*).
The words *api* and *eva* have been displaced in their order;
that which has been stated thus far [is as follows].
The word "tad" means for that reason;
thus, it has arisen in the form that will be described hereafter— what is that?

It is indeed conceived that when the Lord, during the course of mutual worldly transactions— such as buying, selling, observing, or explaining— causes the bodies, vital breaths, and so forth belonging to Caitra, Maitra, and others to appear externally as a single manifestation, while they remain internally manifest and have not abandoned their internal luminosity; this is what has occurred.
Thus, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility.
By this [suffix], unity with this or that subject is created at this time,
and unity with another subject is withdrawn.
A state of persistence is established within the mere form of the jar and so forth;
concealment is imposed by the closing off of its full nature;
and grace is bestowed by granting the fullness of the manifestation of unity within that very appearance.

Therefore, the Lord’s engagement with the fivefold cosmic activity (*pañcakṛtya*) is not only during the great emanations, maintenances, dissolutions, manifestations of wrath, and the bestowals of grace such as initiation and knowledge; rather, it occurs constantly even within ordinary worldly experience. As it has been said:
“[The Lord] whose constant diversion is emanation, who always dwells in the bliss of maintenance...”
"Salutation to the Lord, who is ever satiated by devouring the three worlds.
Thus:
"At every moment, without resting, [he devours] the triple world with hundreds of mental constructions."
"Even while conceptualizing, a certain one remains non-conceptual and unborn"—and so forth. Likewise:
"When you manifest within yourself the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*)," and so on.
And also: "Because of manifestation... //7//

In this case, the appearance of the non-existence of an internal object is already established; therefore, what is the use of investigating another cause? This is the subject matter under discussion, and the logical proof for its establishment has been stated.

"Without that [reflective awareness], there would be no reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) consisting of volition"; thus, having established the nature of reflective awareness, conceptualization, and so forth as a necessary consequence, he concludes by establishing the subject matter at hand in order to settle the minds of his students: @-----
Thus, whether in memory, or in conceptualization, or even in cognition intent upon exclusion (apohana), it is certain that an internal appearance remains present. (IPK 1.6.8)
The Supreme Lord alone is the nature of light, because even in the state of the conceit of being a subject [limited] by the body and so forth, he remains in reality the true subject;

for this reason, the following is established: in memory, in conceptual thought whose life is exclusion (*apohana*), and in the cognition of direct experience, the internal manifestation remains indeed resting within the Light.

There is no doubt whatsoever on this point: for if the body and so forth were indeed the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*), then the statement that "the jar and so forth are within the body, the vital breath, the intellect, or the void" would be nothing at all— because the body and so forth would already exist as distinct from the jar and so forth.
But the manifestation of ultimate reality is all-enduring; thus, the universe is contained within it—this is established without effort. //8//

Now, one might object: "If the external manifestation of the class of internal appearances exists everywhere, then what is the difference between that manifestation and [the manifestation] in memory and so forth?
For this difference is certainly not unperceived, since the flash of clarity, lack of clarity, and so on, cannot be denied. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But in knowledge, whose nature is the external manifestation [of the internal], there is an innate [difference]."
But that which exists in the form of a prior experience persists in acts such as recollection.

When experiential knowledge (*anubhavajñāna*) manifests externally what is internally manifest as "this is blue," the appearance of its own internal state arises naturally from its inherent freedom (*svātantrya*), and not through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by another cognition, as is the case with memory and so forth. In memory, in creative imagination (*utprekṣaṇa*), and in the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) that follows perception, the internal manifestation of blue and so on— which is to be determined as being external— is not of its own nature, but rather is born from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a previous experience.
In this regard, what is called *saṃskāra* is the persistence of an experience even at a later time;

therefore, because that persisting experience is permeated by the manifestation of blue and so forth, memory and other such states, having attained identity with it, likewise manifest in that same way.

Therefore, since the appearance [in memory] cannot possibly exist at the time of recollection, it is understood to be determined by the very time of its prior experience; thus, it is proclaimed that recollection and the like are themselves devoid of an object (*nirviṣaya*) and grasp what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhin*).
This itself constitutes "unclarity" (*asphuṭatva*);

hence, the distinction between appearances in experience, recollection, and so forth is established: clarity consists in the external manifestation of the internal multitude of appearances without any intervening separation.
But due to the intervention [of other factors], there is a lack of clarity because of the absence of simultaneity. //9//
Now, having raised the objection that all cognition other than sensory perception must, due to the intervention [of mental constructs], consist of an external appearance, he states the distinction:
"That [externalization] exists naturally in a freely wandering conceptual construction, because of the appearance of whatever form is intended within the domain of the intellect. (IPK 1.6.10)

That conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— such as a mental wish or a resolve— which does not depend upon the operation of direct perception and whose essence is distraction, moves, arises, and passes away by its own impulsion, through its own independence without requiring external instigation.
In that process, the external manifestation of blue and so forth, which consists of internal manifestation, is entirely natural (*naisargika*).
For instance, even a white elephant with two trunks consisting of a hundred rows of tusks, though never seen before,

is manifested at that very moment by that conceptual construction— though it exists internally on the plane of the cognizer and externally on the plane of the internal organ, which is of the nature of the mirror of the clear intellect. //10//
And from this investigation into the differentiation of appearances, which arose incidentally in the context of establishing the emergence of internal appearances,

he demonstrates that the primary purpose intended by the treatise— namely, the recognition of the Lord within one's own self— is established without effort, according to the principle of a *siddhānta* (established conclusion) based on the nature of its subject matter.
Therefore, because the manifestation of the intended representation occurs exactly as desired,
both cognition and action are clearly established for every living being.
Although the manifestation "the jar appears" shines forth as being indeed conjoined with the object, nevertheless that is not the jar's own nature;
rather, it is consciousness itself that shines forth in such a way, because of its attachment to the subject, as expressed in "it appears to me.
And thus, [the same applies to] the Veda...

"Everything shines after Him alone as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. Here, by the use of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), the state of incessant radiance is indicated. By the term acting as a *karmapravacanīya*, the defining relationship (*lakṣaṇātmā saṃbandhaḥ*)—consisting of the nature of the object and subject of cognition produced by the act of emanation (*nirmāṇakriyā*) fashioned through His sovereignty—is illuminated.
Merely by the power of the delineation of objects, the external appearance of succession is established.

That which has been described as *pratibhā* (intuition) is colored— that is, affected by way of being a reflection— by that sequence (*krama*) of entities, which consists of various forms such as succession and simultaneity, and which is fashioned by the power of space and time, whose nature is the aforementioned sovereignty of the Lord; it is thus permeated by that sequence, namely the temporal and spatial order.
By the passage beginning with "{merely [consciousness] whose objects of perception are distinct...}" and so forth, "this" refers to everything as having the nature of its own self-luminosity;
and because, in the ultimate sense, there is no duality due to the fact that it manifests solely as light through its inward-turned nature, it is without succession (*akrama*).

He alone is Maheśvara, whose nature is that very consciousness (*citta*) or awareness (*saṃvit*) which has no existing limitation (*anta*)— whether spatially, temporally, or in terms of its own essential form. For this very reason, within the multitude of means of knowledge (*pramāṇavarga*), which consists of the nature of cognition (*vijñāna*) directed toward external objects, there exists an internal reflective awareness (*vimarśātmā*) composed of conceptualization (*vikalpamaya*) and infinite in its modes, such as "this is this" with respect to each individual manifestation.

The aggregate of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is that wherein the subject (*pramātṛ*) is said to be one who is filled with the manifold forms of absolute freedom—such as conjunction, disjunction, and repose—and who consists of the pure reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*).
Therefore, the external manifestation of a jar is "this jar," while the internal mental construct (*vikalpa*) is "I," which assumes its prior form; the locus of repose for both of these is the "I."
Thus, this much is the complete nature of light. //1//
Right here, in order to demonstrate the logical proof, he first states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*):

"When entities become established within a single subject through the various gateways of their respective distinct cognitions, this state of being known (*jñāteya*) is logically established. (IPK 1.7.2)

Regarding the statement that "the determination of objects is grounded in consciousness," this is not established merely by resting in a consciousness that consists of a single, undifferentiated form;
rather, it is established through those various distinct cognitions which are of the nature of ascertainment and whose essence is valid knowledge (*pramā*).

These very [cognitions] are the faces, the doors, the means, and the paths. If these entities, such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, [are to be determined], they must do so through those faces which are like the currents of rivers.
Being carried along, they come to rest and find repose directly within that single great ocean of supreme consciousness which takes the form of the subject as "I"; therefore,
among these [individuals], that kinship consisting of mutual interconnection is logically established.
The state of being kinsmen (*jñāti*) is that which constitutes the ground for the application of that term, namely, that they should know one another;
and kinship (*jñāteya*) consists of the mutual support of each other's welfare and security,
and this has been shown here with the intention of demonstrating their interconnectedness.
This is to demonstrate that for insentient things, there is never at any time an inherent connection [to consciousness] by their own nature. //2//

And thus, he expresses this very point by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka): "For objects that possess spatial and temporal succession and which terminate within themselves, this [recognition] is accomplished by means of their simultaneous manifestation; otherwise, what kind of synthesis could there be? (IPK 1.7.3)
Of insentient objects, of the cognitions thereof, of the conceptualizations thereof, and of the certainties thereof— which do not abandon spatial succession and temporal succession,
yet are self-contained, meaning they are established solely in their own essential nature— ...
What is this "conjunction" (*samanvaya*)?
The meaning is that there is none at all;
for this conjunction can only be established by means of a simultaneous manifestation—a manifestation of synthesis whose nature consists in the mixing of place, time, and form—and not otherwise.
For when the streams have individually ceased to flow, the grass, shrubs, and other things being carried along by them do not maintain any continuity whatsoever.

With the intention that there is a distinction of place, time, and so forth due to their multiplicity, the word "simultaneously" (*sakṛt*) is employed with the purpose of negating that [continuity]. //3//

In this regard, raising the doubt as to what that "concomitance" (samanvaya) is, [the author] first demonstrates the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), which is more extensively pervasive: "The establishment of the causal relationship between perceptions and non-perceptions—which fall upon their respective distinct parts—is due to a single cognizer. (IPK 1.7.5)
In memory (*smṛti*), an object previously experienced appears;
in that case, this memory of the object is not a new manifestation, but rather its manifestation is precisely that prior experience.

And since that experience, being of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*), lacks the nature of an object of cognition (*jñeya*), it is not perceivable by another cognition, but is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).
And if that [object] were non-existent at the time of recollection, how could it be manifested?
Or, even if it were so [non-existent], there would still be recollection;
therefore, this is established in this way.
That which is the self-awareness of memory is itself the self-awareness of the experience;
no other means of knowledge— neither perception nor inference and so forth— applies there, as they are distinct from self-awareness.

Consequently, it is established that the very self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) which persists as a single, uninterrupted continuum for that duration is itself the state of being the subject (*pramātṛtva*). Elsewhere, it has been stated previously that the existence of the subject is proven by this reflection of memory— namely, that a rememberer cannot be other than the one who experienced [the original perception].
But now, the distinction is that it occurs through another mode, namely, by way of unification with self-awareness (svasaṃvedana). //5//
Now, one might object: "Even regarding an object that transcends direct experience, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) may indeed be valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

for invalidity arises only through the force of sublation (*bādha*), and in the absence of such sublation, how could that [invalidity] occur? Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies]: "Furthermore, this very relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists by way of the distinction between the real and the unreal."

He demonstrates in detail that the very lifeblood of all worldly transactions cannot be established without a single principle of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*): "Even the relationship of the sublated and the sublator arises among cognitions that are mutually contradictory when they are grounded in a single subject. (IPK 1.7.6)

The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is as follows: since validity consists in the absence of sublation, one must necessarily establish how even that conventional usage of "sublation" (*bādhavyavahāra*) occurs.
In this case, no such thing as the sublation of silver by mother-of-pearl is ever observed;
nor is it logical to say that the cognition of silver is sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl.
Because there is no mutual contradiction between two cognitions that are fully established and resting in their respective objects and in themselves;

for if contradiction were merely the mutual exclusion of one by the other, then, since all cognitions would thus be contradictory, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator could never be fully established within itself. This is all the more so because...
The distinction between the real and the unreal would collapse; furthermore, the negative particle (*nañ*) here should be explained according to the principle of *tantra* (elliptical repetition).
This is what is meant: if cognition perishes by itself, then what is accomplished for it by another cognition?
For it is not possible for that [subsequent cognition], being non-existent at that time, to effect the removal of the object of the former;
nor does the cognition "this is not silver," while making its own absence of silver its object, remove the object of the cognition of silver.
Furthermore, there is also the position that [the former cognition] is destroyed by another cognition.
In that case as well, since this very same path applies to all cognitions, how could it be that only some [cognition] is sublated?

However, when the cognition of silver and the cognition of mother-of-pearl both find their rest within a single self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then this [distinction between sublation and non-sublation] becomes possible;

for indeed, even among cognitions resting within the single reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*), their mode of rest is not of a single kind, but rather it is experienced precisely through its manifold variety.
For instance, in the cognitions "this is blue" and "this is a lotus," which rest upon the subject (pramātṛ), they rest by means of the appearance of mutual coloring.
In the cognitions "pot" and "cloth," they rest through mutual non-exclusion.

Or, a cognition such as "this is mother-of-pearl" or "this is not silver" effects the uprooting of the cognition "this is silver"; it does so by destroying the persistence of that [erroneous] cognition's own activity in the form of valid reflective awareness (vimarśa) within the subject.
It attains its foundation.

Thus, in the case of the relationship between cause and effect and so forth, the variety of resting points—which is impossible within the objective domain (*prameya*)—is constructed by the subject (*pramātṛ*) through his own autonomy; for that very reason, it must be said that this [variety] bestows autonomy upon the act of cognition (*pramā*).
In this way, because a firm state is established within a single subject through the relinquishing of prior cognitions, [the subject remains sovereign].
Thus, the conventional relationship between the sublated and the sublator is established;
for indeed, just like blue and other objects, that very Supreme Lord, by His absolute freedom, manifests even those linguistic conventions, and therefore they too are truly real. //6//
Here, anticipating the opponent's view which he intends to refute, [the author] says:

"Just as the cognition of a bare ground is the cognition of the absence of a jar, so too, if you claim that the cognition of mother-of-pearl is the cognition of the invalidity of the cognition of silver. (Ipk 1.7.7)
In this context, the cognition of mother-of-pearl, by cognizing its own self, cognizes its own validity as non-different from itself, according to the principle that "it determines that [object].

And since the exclusion of others is inseparable from that determination, the cognition of the invalidity of the silver-cognition— which consists in the cognition of what is not mother-of-pearl— is precisely said to be this very cognition of validity that is non-different from the cognition of the mother-of-pearl.
Nor is this a novel idea that the cognition of one thing is itself the cognition of the absence of another thing;
for it is well known that the apprehension of a bare patch of ground is indeed the apprehension of the absence of a jar.
Likewise, the very awareness of the invalidity [of a cognition] is said to be the sublation of the cognition of silver.
If it is argued that the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is thus established, we reply: "Is that [established] by virtue of the identity of the cognizer? //7//

In this context, while intending to establish the reality of the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) as a corollary, [the author] first refutes the example presented in the opponent's system:
"It is not the case that [non-existence] would be established through the cognition of a bare location by way of its being 'not a jar';
for here, there is no absence of the jar even though it is capable of being perceived. (Ipk 1.7.8)
The example that was stated is not [valid];

if one asks why, it is said: here, in the case of "there is no jar on the ground," the absence must sometimes be expressed through identity (*tādātmya*) as "the ground is not a jar," and sometimes through difference (*vyatireka*) as "there is no jar on this ground."
In that regard, this initial conventional usage is established through the knowledge of a pure ground,
wherein perceptibility is not a factor; for even the fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension does not exist for things such as *piśācas* due to the power of their own nature.

Alternatively, in the case of something such as sound, because its absence is not ascertained due to the lack of perception of another object associated with it within the same cognition—despite the completeness of the causal complex consisting of the auditory organ and so forth that would grasp it—the absence of that [sound] is also apprehended through identity, as in "the ground is not a piśāca, nor is it sound.

However, where visibility (*dṛśyatva*) is necessarily required as a qualification, this method is not applicable when one must employ the conventional usage of absence by means of exclusion (*vyatireka*). //8//
If it is asked, "Why?", we reply: "Because it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
He demonstrates this very point:
"The ground is eternally distinct [from objects], because all entities are established within their own selves."
How, then, could that cognition ever establish the non-existence of something distinct?
Even when a jar is present, the ground remains purely as it is;
for entities do not become intermingled,
and therefore even then there exists the cognition of the pure ground.
Thus, even when the jar exists, why is its absence not conventionally expressed as "there is no jar on this ground"? [The answer is:
"That cognition" refers to the cognition of the portion of the ground as distinct [from the jar];
"at some time" means in a certain state characterized by the non-proximity of the jar.
In what manner could it establish the non-existence of a broken jar, but not its non-existence at all times?
By this [reasoning], one must consider that the consequence would follow that "there is no piśāca on this ground" would also be established. //9//
Now, one might object: "In this way, worldly practice—which rests upon the absence of difference—is indeed observed in certain states without contradiction;
what, then, is the resolution for that? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] shows the method of establishing that [absence of difference], which has not been perceived by the ancients:
"But rather, for the blind man, there is a mass of light, or a touch such as warmth that is soft."
In that case, one should establish for him his own cognition as having the nature of a non-pot.
In this regard, the empirical path—that the very existence of one thing must be treated as the non-existence of another thing—must certainly not be abandoned.
In that context, the relationship of container and contained (*ādhāryādhārabhāva*) between one entity and another entity is precisely the same as that between an entity and its absence.

Consequently, when a distinct object such as a stone or a mass of light appears in visual cognition on the ground, that very object is conventionally designated as "the absence of a jar on the ground."

Or, as in the case of "there is no jar on the ground," even where there is no operation of the eye— such as when the eyes are closed or in total darkness— one perceives a surface that is soft, warm, cold, or neither warm nor cold, being devoid of the hard touch appropriate to a jar; by perceiving that very [surface], one conventionally designates it as "the absence of a jar here," [just as one does] in the case of the touch of air.
The meaning of the sentence is that [the Lord] is necessarily omnipresent;
as for the meaning of the individual words: "kiṃ tu" (but rather) is a reflection on a question arising from one's own intuition, intended to introduce one's own view.
What, then, is the correct position here? To this he says: in that case, first of all, a mass of light exists on that ground and must be known;
there is also a tactile sensation such as heat for the blind man.
That which is the self-cognition of either that mass of light or that tactile sensation—that is, the cognition of it in its own form as distinguished from other objects such as jars—is the agent.

It is possible to establish that this light and so forth possess the nature of the absence of a jar—that is, the nature of the non-existence of a jar—on that ground; this is the meaning intended here. The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used according to *Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.3.172 (*śaki liṅ ca*).

Furthermore, by hearing the subtle sound produced by the internal vibration of the vital breath, and thus having the integrity of his auditory faculty and other senses restored, he hears that very sound as being associated with a single cognition and thereby negates any other sound.
It is not that there is no other sound here;
rather, even the absence of subtle sounds is perceived by one whose auditory faculty is fixed upon the most subtle internal resonance (*antarnāda*).

Likewise, the absence of taste, smell, and touch is to be known only by one who is simultaneously experiencing the taste of the water in the mouth, the smell of the *tripuṭikā* (the root of the nose), and the tactile sensation of the body.
For there is no certainty regarding the completeness of the causes of perception without the apprehension of another object capable of entering into a single cognition;
thus, this [certainty] is absolute.

If it is argued that—since there is no suspicion of the destruction at that very moment of the experience of each respective object that has just occurred, which is produced by that [experience]—the certainty regarding the completeness of the causes of the sense-organ [itself] does not require its association with a single cognition, we say: no.
For one who desires to grasp the true nature of reality is observed to be exerting effort precisely by directing each respective sense organ toward its object. //10//
Now, one might object: even for an invisible entity such as a *piśāca*, the linguistic usage of negation would follow by way of difference (*vyatireka*) as well;
for that mass of light is different from a jar, and it is likewise different from a *piśāca* and so forth.
Anticipating this objection, he says:
Just as a piśāca might exist within the light even though it is without light,
being invisible within the interior of the earth, it cannot be refuted in any way.

Although it may be established that a mass of light is distinct from a *piśāca* and that there is light which is not of the nature of a *piśāca*, nevertheless, it is impossible to determine definitively that "there is no *piśāca* here," for even in the midst of a flood of light, a jar might be impossible to perceive due to the failure of the light to reach it when a jar is present nearby.
And from this, it is established that "there is no jar here";
however, a *piśāca* (demon) is of such a nature that, even while existing within the surface of the ground or within light, he does not destroy the density of that ground or light.
Consequently, since its presence within the light is possible, how can there be a linguistic usage of negation through exclusion (*vyatireka*)?

In this way, because the existence of taste and so forth is possible within form, there is no negation of them either. Just as it is conceivable that a *piśāca*— though not light and distinct from light— might be invisible while remaining inside the interior of the ground,
in exactly the same manner, it is indeed conceivable that it exists even within the light.

And thus, although the *piśāca* has been refuted by the path "it is other than light," it has nevertheless not been refuted in every respect; therefore, how can linguistic conventions based on its absence proceed there? This is the meaning of the verse. //11//
Having thus demonstrated, by way of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*), the true nature of the conventional usage of non-existence, he applies it to the present case:
"In this way, the cognition of mother-of-pearl would consist in the absence of the cognition of silver;
however, it could not be the indicator of the invalidity of the initial cognition of silver. (IPK 1.7.12)

Just as when one perceives light, it is said that there is an absence of a jar, yet nothing happens to the jar previously perceived; in the same way, it may be conceived that the cognition of mother-of-pearl is the absence of the cognition of silver.

Just as the cognition of a jar is the awareness of the validity of the cognition of the jar, and the absence of the cognition of a cloth is the awareness of the validity of that absence, by this much the previously occurring cognition of the cloth does not become invalid.
For all this is merely an investigation into the nature of that cognition of the jar; nothing at all has arisen from it for the sake of the other, the initial [cognition].

In this way, let the very cognition— "this is mother-of-pearl" and "this is not silver"— be manifested by its own nature as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding myself, the mother-of-pearl, and the absence of silver; but it is not [the means of knowledge] regarding the silver.
But since nothing has happened to the previous cognition of silver by that much, how could the silver that was its object be unreal? //12//

Is it not the case that by the word "this" (idam), one refers back to that very place where the cognition of silver occurred, and there now arises a valid cognition in the form "this is not silver" and "this is mother-of-pearl"?
From this, it is inferred that the prior cognition of silver was invalid;
for it is not possible for two cognitions that apprehend two contradictory objects to both be valid with respect to a single object.
Anticipating the objection that "therefore, this practice of sublation would be merely inferential," he says:
"Sublation would not occur through inference even due to the non-establishment of the locus (*dharmin*);
rather, it is logical [only] when established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and arising from a single cognizer. (IPK 1.7.13)
Not only is sublation not established through self-cognition,
it is also not established through inference,
because the locus (dharmin) is unestablished.
Because of the word "api" (also), it should be understood as applying to both the reason (*hetu*) and the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Here,

when the subject (*dharmin*) is established, the function of inference (*anumāna-vyāpāra*) is the exclusion of the non-connection of the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) by means of an established reason whose pervasion is being recollected.

And here, in the case of the previously mentioned cognition of silver as the subject (*dharmin*), the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is invalidity; therein, either the cognition of mother-of-pearl,
or the cognition "this is not silver," or the state of being made the object of that cognition— which resides in the object— would be employed as the logical reason (*hetu*).
And this is not tenable, because at that time the subject (*dharmin*), which is the cognition of the previously perceived silver, does not exist;
nor are the cognitions of mother-of-pearl and so forth its properties (*dharmas*);
and there is no establishment of the probandum from what is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*).
Therefore, the claim that "that [silver] would be the locus (dharmin) of the memory" is also incorrect.

Now, if it is being argued that "the mother-of-pearl is not the object of the cognition of silver because it is the object of the cognition of mother-of-pearl," then if this is the case, it is a proof of what is already established (siddhasādhana).
If it is argued that, in that case, the former [cognition] has its object sublated by the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of that [subsequent cognition],
then by what means is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) grasped— namely, that "wherever there is now another cognition, there was not another [cognition] previously"?
If it is said to be by another inference, [we reply:]...
Non-infinity [of regress].
By this, the following is answered: how could there be two cognitions regarding a single object?
For who could know that those two cognitions have a single object?
For it has already been stated that they indeed rest within themselves and within their own objects;
thus, there is no sublation even by means of inference,
nor is such an intervention perceived here in the cognition.
Because it manifests instantaneously through the establishment of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), for this very reason it is impossible to say, "Let there be no such thing as sublation (*bādhā*).

Having thus demonstrated the impossibility [of sublation] in the opposing view, he concludes with the statement previously promised—that the relationship of the sublated and the sublator arises because [all things] are grounded in a single cognizer (*ekapramātṛ*)—in his own view: "It is logical..."
If it is argued that she (the power of manifestation) arises from a single cognizer,
it has already been explained that he alone is the creator (*nirmātā*);

and this being established, if it is further claimed that there is an "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) for the sake of establishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), then let it be stated as you wish.
Now, everything is accomplished. //13//

Not only are these functions— namely, the causal relationship, memory, sublation, and worldly transaction— established in a single cognizer as the common transactions constituting the entire course of worldly life;

but even intermediate transactions such as buying and selling, which are "stained," as well as those such as the relationship between teacher and taught, which are "pure," are likewise so established.
These too are established solely within a single cognizer;

for all worldly transactions have their life-force in [their] coordination. Thus he demonstrates by way of conclusion: "In this manner, within the all-pervasive [consciousness], which is inlaid with the manifestations of objects that appear as utterly distinct..."
Whether stained or stainless, worldly activity is experienced.
By this method of reasoning expressed in these two verses—
consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—
and likewise by the manner of illustrating worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) stated in other verses, this too should be understood: that [the Self] is pervasive (*vibhu*), unconditioned by space and time.

Therefore, all worldly transaction is experienced as resting within that which is inlaid— meaning colored by— the manifestations of blue, pleasure, and so forth, which, though appearing utterly distinct through the power of *māyā* and whose sole life-breath is difference, exist as nothing other than [the Self] itself, like reflections; for they do not deviate from its own essential nature.

In this matter, direct experience (*anubhava*) alone is the most firm authority; for it is experienced by those intent on focused attention along with their instructions that whatever state of worldly transaction these [beings] consider to be the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), that very state is the ground of Śiva (*śivabhūmi*), whose nature is the manifestation of the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*). As it has been said:
"[... attentiveness toward the connection..."
Thus, for those who have not recognized the ultimate reality of the self, worldly activity is defiled; for others, that very same activity is stainless.
Thus all is auspicious.
14. From the beginning: //77//

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Single Substratum," in the first section on Knowledge of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, accompanied by his commentary named *Vimarśinī*, which was brought to completion by the feet of the illustrious Utpaladeva, the preeminent teacher of the venerable Māheśvara tradition. // 7 //
Now begins the eighth chapter, titled "The Definition of Maheśvaratva," within the Section on Knowledge:
We praise that Śiva, who is eternally established as the Great Lord (Maheśvara) for the perfected ones (siddhas), by virtue of the worldly activity established through self-awareness.
Having thus explained knowledge, memory, and exclusion, it has been established by this much that linguistic usage is not tenable without a single substratum for these [three]; thus,
the statement "one" (*ekaḥ*) made in the passage "{if [the object] were not internalized...}" is now fully integrated.
It has also been established that by means of the manifestation of internal appearances, the infinite forms of the universe are contained within;
furthermore, that which was referred to here as "the Great Lord" (maheśvara) must be explained as the sovereignty consisting of absolute freedom (svātantrya).
And that [consciousness] is of two kinds: having cognition as its object and having action as its object;

for in this regard, the Blessed Lord is both the knower and the agent, even though the nature of consciousness is one alone—a single, compact mass of consciousness consisting of light and self-reflection (prakāśa-vimarśa).
Nevertheless, for the sake of exposition, this division is indeed constructed upon that [foundation];

therefore, although sovereignty—which has as its object the action consisting of knowledge—is of the nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), it must nevertheless be determined within the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*) because it has that as its object.
And in this way, the meaning of the word "knower" (*jñātṛ*) becomes fully determined both from the perspective of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).
In this context, what is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the self-referential awareness of "I," which is uncontracted by the constraints of dependence on the distinctions of manifested appearances.
Among those manifestations, that very sovereignty which exists becomes the sovereignty that constitutes the domain of the power of knowledge.
[The sensory perception occurring at that moment...]
This is investigated by means of these eleven verses, beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "{......................................... since knowledge and action are pure}".
Having stated there, in one verse, that "the manifestation either depends on another manifestation or otherwise," he states in another verse that "that very manifestation is one.

Having stated in two verses that "the manifestation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is likewise determined by manifestation," he then states in two further verses in which manifestation that causal efficiency resides.
By means of one verse, [the text] establishes that internality is like the foundation for appearances variegated by other appearances;
then, by a pair of verses, it explains externality both in terms of its essential nature and its divisions;
thereafter, by one verse, there is a summary of the single substratum of the powers such as knowledge (jñāna).
By concluding the state of Maheśvara with another verse, there is an introduction to the forthcoming section on ritual action (*kriyādhikāra*); such is the summary meaning of this chapter (*āhnika*).
Now, the meaning of the verse is examined.

[Objection: If this entire worldly transaction exists solely as grounded in the Supreme Lord, then the well-known variety of its manifestations—consisting mostly of clarity and lack of clarity—would be untenable.
Anticipating the objection that "the Blessed Lord alone is indeed that by whom this [world] is enlivened,
and apart from him we perceive no inherent reality whatsoever for worldly transaction," he says: "In some cases, they depend solely upon the immediate perception of the senses at that very moment."
In other cases, however, there are appearances; but in states such as blindness or thick darkness, there are none.

There is no distinction whatsoever regarding the existence of the appearance of an object within conceptual constructions that refer to objects yet to come, those currently existing, or those that have passed. (IPK 1.8.2)

The connection between these two joined verses is as follows: by this much alone there is a distinction among appearances (*ābhāsa*), but there is never any distinction within the appearance itself regarding its own nature.
At the very moment that an appearance shines forth, it exists;

and while there is another appearance called "perceptibility" (*akṣasāmakṣya*)—namely, being directly perceived by the external senses in the form "I see"—certain appearances may be dependent upon or mixed with that [other appearance].

Where there is the conventional usage of "clarity," that is the domain of the blind—the domain of the subject situated in darkness. Furthermore, as for the other conventional usage consisting of "lack of clarity," in that case those manifestations (*ābhāsa*) are otherwise;
for indeed, for one born blind, there exists no other manifestation characterized by direct perception through the external senses.

But for one who has seen [the object] and yet has become blind and is situated in deep darkness, that [perception] does not exist at that moment; rather, he merely recollects the previous state of direct perception by means of the external sense organs. //1//
Therefore, one should not entertain the possibility that there is any distinction in the nature of the appearance of an object even among certain conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
For those conceptual constructions—whether they refer to a future thing, or have their culmination in the future, or have their culmination in the non-present, or rest upon a past thing—it is said:
"I see this blue."
I intend, I imagine, I remember.

In such cases as "I do" or "I speak," this appearance of blue is, in its own nature, neither deficient nor excessive; likewise is that which occurs in the case of yellow and so forth when one says "I see.
However, when these appearances are joined together or separated by the Lord through His sovereignty, then there arises this conventional usage of "clarity" and so on.

In the case of the manifestation "blue," when there is a mixing of manifestations such as "I perceive" through the exclusion of other manifestations like "I imagine," there occurs the conventional usage of "clarity.
In this way, the diversity of temporal conventions is established.
However, when manifestations are included within the nature of the Supreme Lord, there is no exclusion from anything, nor is there any mixing with anything. //2//

Now, one might object: "Let this be possible in the case of blue and other such objects where there is the operation of the external senses; but since that is absent in the case of pleasure and so forth, how can there be such variety? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Even in the case of pleasure and the like, and in those objects which are the causes of pleasure and so forth, although the manifestation exists, it remains as such because it has passed away. (IPK 1.8.3)
But when pleasure and so forth are intensely delineated by conceptual construction,
their state remains exactly as it was, because they are clearly perceived in that very way.

Although the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) is indeed the same whether it concerns pleasure such as a garland or sandalwood and its causes, or pain such as a snake or a thorn and its causes— whether past or future— nevertheless,
because there is a commingling through another manifestation in the form "this is past" or "this is future," and because of the manifestation [itself], one experiences [them] as "I am experiencing."

Because there is a negation [of that state], even though those [factors] are present, the cognizer does not exist in that manner as he did previously—such as thinking "I am now happy" or "I am suffering"—or as one who has acquired the collection of causes and conditions for each respective state. //3//

But when one firmly delineates those objects through conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), then—due to entering into the semblance of causes for the designation of the repeated delineation of pleasure and its causes, and due to the intermingling with other appearances—it occurs in that very manner described by us, and not otherwise;
thus it is said: "in that way."
It is possible that stability occurs through such [notions] as "I am happy";
this is appropriate because at that time, he perceives an appearance of happiness mixed with a clear manifestation.
The mention of the past is also an elliptical indication for the future. //4//

Now, what has been stated by this much? That garlands and the like, which possess external forms, are the causes of pleasure and so forth; and that pleasure and so forth, produced by external things, are the causes for the conceit "I am happy.

Consequently, in the absence of externality and in the absence of being produced by such [external things], it would not have been stated in that way; and in that case, those very things do not exist at all.
Then, having raised the objection: "How can it be said that there is no difference anywhere regarding the existence of the manifestation of objects, since existence itself is absent?", he says:

"The external state is held to be the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of manifestations of both existence and non-existence; their essence is not existence, for they are always internal and real. (IPK 1.8.5)

In this context, those appearances of existence and appearances of non-existence— such as "I have happiness here" or "I have no suffering"— do not have externality as their essence or intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
For the essence of that which is called "happiness" does not manifest with the form of being external.

For the very nature of pleasure is indeed pleasure itself; however, when externality— which is merely another manifestation— appears mixed within that manifestation of pleasure by the Lord solely through the power of His sovereignty, then it assumes the state of being an attribute (*upādhi*), a coloring factor (*uparañjaka*), or a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for it.

And thus, just as in the absence of the appearance of blue there is no change whatsoever in the appearance of the lotus in its own nature, or in the absence of the appearance of a king there is no change in the appearance of a man, so too, even in the absence of the appearance of externality, there is no fading whatsoever in the appearance of pleasure, the appearance of the absence of pain, or the appearance of a beloved in their own nature; therefore, internal appearances always persist here within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is of the nature of the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*). For the appearances of blue and the rest possess internality as well, because they arise within the internal organ.
Externality, moreover, consists in the nature of being an object of apprehension due to its appearing as distinct from the subject;
and this externality is simply the state of being externally perceptible.
And in both these states, these [objects] certainly perform causal efficiency (arthakriyā), ultimately [resulting in] knowledge having itself as its own object.

Furthermore, raising the objection as to how these [objects] would not perform some kind of causal function (*arthakriyā*) if they possess internality characterized by identity with the subject (*pramātṛtādātmya*), he says:

"Because of internality, there is unity with the subject; therefore, for these [objects], there is no causal function based on differentiation. But when they are external, that [causal function] exists due to the difference in their differentiated appearances. (IPK 1.8.6)
Regarding the phrase "in the unity of the cognizer":
because of that immediate succession caused by it,
there is no causal efficacy whatsoever for these appearances.
For that purposeful action (arthakriyā) occurs only when there is difference;
since this appearance of blue differs from the appearance of yellow and differs from the cognizer, it would perform for that cognizer a distinct purposeful action to be accomplished by itself.
But this difference does not exist at that time, because of the identity of the cognizer.
For that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is determined by the distinction between appearances;
thus, even while the appearance of the beloved remains external, when another appearance characterized by embracing disappears, she recedes into the distance;
and upon the arrival of yet another appearance, a different causal efficiency altogether—one contrary to the previous delight—is perceived.
Therefore, there is an absence of difference between appearances, because they are internal due to the unity of the cognizer; consequently, there is no causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, even the appearance of causal efficiency is merely another appearance; thus, the capacity for causal efficiency is not the true existence (*sattva*) of entities, such that their absence would imply their non-existence by way of their own nature. //6//

But surely, at the time when the manifestation of the external is being dissolved, the internal manifestation is severed due to contradiction; so how can it be said that "the manifestation of internal things is always [present]"? He resolves this:
"Insofar as they consist of consciousness, manifestations always abide within."
Because they appear through illusion as if external, this [consciousness] is also outside.

In this context, the manifestation of appearances— whether they appear as external or whether that externality is absent— always resides within the light of the subject alone; for these [appearances] consist of consciousness, otherwise they would not manifest at all, as has been stated.

But when their externality is manifested by the power of *māyā*, which consists in the sovereignty of manifesting [things] as distinct, then, depending upon that [externality], there arises this state of those things appearing both externally and internally. This internal manifestation is not a contradiction of externality; on the contrary, it serves as the very foundation for all manifestations. Therefore, how could there be a contradiction? Thus it is rightly said that "those things which are always internal possess existence. //7//

Now, [one might argue: "Causal efficiency (arthakriyā) exists only when there is externality, and that [externality] consists in being perceptible by the external senses; however, this is not possible for those things delineated by conceptual construction."
Anticipating the objection— "In that case, how could these [entities] perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*),
since a demon or similar being conjured by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is seen to produce effects such as terror?"— he says:
"This very representation (*ullekha*) within conceptual construction is also external, appearing as something distinct."
Internal proximity consists in identity with the subject; externalization, on the other hand, is indeed differentiation from that.
Even that object, such as a beloved woman or a thief, which is delineated within conceptual cognition in the form of a specific reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is also external—
not only that which is perceived externally— because it manifests as distinct from the cognizer precisely as "this."
And that state of resting as "I" alone within the cognizer is innerness;
"inner" (antara) means proximate,
and that [proximity] is relative to something else.
And since the cognizer alone is to be depended upon in all cases when no other thing to be depended upon exists, identity with the cognizer is already attained as being proximate;
therefore, that which is distinct from him is indeed external, and thus it is logical that even a mental representation possesses causal efficacy. //8//

Now, one might object: "Granted that jars and the like possess externality due to the activity of potters and others, but what causes that [externality] for that which is within the scope of the internal organ? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The manifestation of mental images, pleasure, and so forth, occurs by way of an external nature."
Just as the Lord, by His will, is the presiding form over those things born of the senses and so forth.

The manifestation of blue and other objects— which are reflections within internal conceptualization— by way of an external nature severed from the subject, occurs solely through the will of the Lord (Īśvara), who sustains internal appearances and nourishes external creation;

just as the manifestation of blue and other things by way of an external nature, when they have become objects of the eyes and so forth, is designated by the term "perceptual cognition" (*pratyakṣajñāna*).

This is what is meant: the so-called activity of the potter is, in the ultimate sense, nothing other than the will of the Lord (Īśvara) itself, extending as far as the vibration of the body manifested by that [will];
it is not some separate entity at all.

Consequently, by such a will of the Lord, even objects such as "blue" and so forth—which do not actually exist outside of the Light—are made the objects of the external senses; they appear as external and with a seemingly severed form to the imagined subject.
Likewise, what is the difference [between these and those] that have become objects of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)?

However, those consisting primarily of pleasure and pain—such as the *sthāyibhāvas* and *vyabhicāribhāvas* described by Bharata and others, including *rati*, *nirveda*, and so forth—which have become objects solely of the internal organ, appear as if they were external;

for although the *kṣetrajña* alone possesses sovereignty over volitions (*saṅkalpa*), nevertheless, because it is impossible to subordinate the ultimate reality of consciousness (*cit-paramārthatā*), that sovereignty belongs in fact to the Lord (*īśvara*) alone.
As stated by the author himself:

"Even though the stability of objects is restricted within the individual soul (jīva), which is constrained by the vital breath and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), it nevertheless resides in the Supreme Self."
"In that case, how could there be for him any constraint by means of the vital breath (prāṇa) through his own self?

Thus, where there occurs for the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), even though he is unwilling, a creation consisting of volition (saṅkalpa) whose essence is a spontaneous projection, there the activity belongs clearly to the Lord alone.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that even in the external manifestation of those things produced by volition, the will of the Supreme Lord is the cause. //9//
Now, he concludes the aforementioned unity and the sovereignty of Maheśvara:
"Without that unity, the worldly course of cognitions would not exist;
because of the unity of light, there is that oneness, and it is established that the Knower is one. (IPK 1.8.10)
He alone, by virtue of his constant nature as reflective awareness, is the Great Lord (Maheśvara);
for the pure power of knowledge and action belong solely to the God insofar as they consist of that very reflective awareness.
"That which has been established by the aforementioned passage," means "for that reason."
Without the unity of cognitions— that is, of knowledges— the entire worldly path, the course of the world, which is to say all conventional transaction, would not be possible;
yet this [worldly path] does indeed exist.
Therefore, these [cognitions] are one;
and this is not difficult to establish, since consciousness is said to be nothing other than the manifestation of the object,
which— merely by virtue of its association with the object— is directed outwardly as the manifestation of blue, distinct from others.
There is also another [manifestation], such as yellow light;
however, in ultimate reality, because light is devoid of any contraction of space, time, or form, it is indeed one alone—
thus, light is but one, resting within itself.
And it is established by logical reasoning that he alone is called the cognizer; this is now [the conclusion]. //10//
Moreover, this nature of His, characterized by luminosity, does not remain devoid of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—as if it were like a crystal—when colored by objects such as blue;

rather, its form is always being reflected upon. Thus, its nature as that which reflects consists in unconditioned reflective awareness, non-orientation toward anything else, and being a single mass of bliss.
That alone is His Maheśvaratva (the state of being the Great Lord).
For that very self-awareness (*vimarśa*), whose essence is the sense of "I," constitutes the pure, ultimate knowledge and action of the God who consists of play and the like:
luminosity (*prakāśa*) is knowledge, and within that very luminosity, the self-determining awareness is action.
And since reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) has internalized luminosity,
it is reflective awareness alone that constitutes knowledge and action in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*); however,

in the intermediate state (*parāparāvasthā*), on the level of the Lord Sadāśiva, they consist of the nature of unstruck reflective awareness (*ahatāvimarśa*) which has attained grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "this-ness" (*idantā*).
Furthermore, the distinction is that in the subsequent state, while abiding in the plane of *māyā*, there is a predominance of the sense of "this-ness" (*idambhāva*).
However, it has been stated that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone is knowledge, for without it, this [consciousness] would be insentient;
and since that very awareness is action (*kriyā*), this constitutes an introduction to the forthcoming chapter on action. May there be auspiciousness!
11. From the beginning: //89//

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of Maheśvarahood," and the first section on Knowledge in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* composed by the venerable and preeminent Māheśvara teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* written by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
Now, [begins] the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
The second chapter, titled "The Authority over Ritual Action" (Kriyādhikāra).
[Vimarśinī]

He who, in the mirror of his own expansive and clear self, reveals his supreme river of action— which is radiant with the essence of his own powers— upon the two shores of the objects of knowledge that constitute the portions of the subject, [reveals] that ground which consists of the manifold manifestations of worldly existence.
May that glorious Lord of Gaurī reveal to us the supreme Truth (ṛta).
We praise that Śiva, upon whom, having attained repose, the wondrous expansion of his playful sport displays this power of action (kriyā-śakti) to such an extreme degree.
Now, another section is commenced in order to determine the nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
Therein, by means of eight verses, [it is said]:
"For this very reason... and so forth.
By this passage,
ending with "that which is manifested," [it is shown that] in the Supreme Lord, action is ultimately devoid of succession.
And because it is joined with the manifestation of the sequence of limited transmigratory subjects, it is also established as being sequential;
for thus is the refutation of the previously stated prima facie argument stated in the verse.
Then, by means of one verse, there is a distinction between that which possesses succession and that which is without succession.
Then, by means of three verses, there is a determination of the nature of succession.
Then, by means of two verses, there is a demarcation of the respective domains of that which possesses succession and that which is without succession.

And since there is a distinction between their respective domains, it is established by this verse that, in reality, both find their final rest in one and the same place; such is the purport of this chapter.
Now, the meaning of the verse is analyzed.

In this regard, once the previously mentioned determination regarding the utility of establishing the power of knowledge has been accomplished, another object of knowledge is also established without effort; thus, he demonstrates this according to the method of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion of a topic).
Therefore, even that which was stated—that action cannot be successive for a single entity because it is one, and so forth—is refuted by the demonstration of its being a single [entity]. (IPK 2.1.1)
As for what was stated: that cognitions themselves—distinguished by the forms of experience, conceptualization, and so forth—have no substratum whatsoever;

that memory is established through mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); and that if cognition were insentient, there would be no manifestation of the object, whereas if it were sentient, it would be non-different from the reality of the Self due to the absence of spatial and temporal limitation.
That [position] has already been refuted, because the experience and so forth of distinct [entities] are untenable, as has been demonstrated at length.
Furthermore, it has also been stated that memory does not arise from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) alone;
rather, cognition is indeed non-inert and possesses an uncontracted form.
Furthermore, it has been shown that the appearance of limitation for that [consciousness] occurs by virtue of its coloring by the objects of knowledge manifested through its own sovereignty;

for this reason, not only have the objections raised against the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*) been refuted by this collection of arguments, but the criticisms concerning the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) have likewise been removed by this very same collection of arguments— this is indicated by the word "also" (*api*).
It is logical to ask: "How can a single action be successive when its substratum possesses a single nature? Thus, [it is stated]:
"In each respective case, while [the substratum] remains..."
Thus,
what was stated— that "because that which resides in two [places] possesses multiple forms"— is also refuted.
For, given this much of the prima facie argument— that "how could this single life-principle possess so many diverse natures?"—

it has been stated here that, just as in the case of a mirror whose nature is consciousness, when various appearances arise without subverting its unity, what contradiction could there possibly be? Therefore, by the power of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), this single essence of an object may [manifest] all its diverse and even contradictory natures.
First, those [factors], appearing as a sequence precisely because of their mutual opposition, accept that single substratum of action;
and from that, the occurrence of relations and so forth is also established. //1//

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that succession is the very nature of action, and since such succession does not exist in the Lord—who consists of consciousness and is devoid of the measurement of time—how could action belong to Him? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And the succession of worldly action is possible through the power of time, but it is not so for that which is eternal; rather, it belongs to the Primal Power (Prābhavī), just as it does to the Lord.
The moments that precede and follow the thought "he raises his hand" or "he lowers his hand" possess succession;
for those, such as the followers of Kaṇāda and others, for whom these very moments constitute action, that succession appears through direct perception itself.
However, there are those who maintain that there exists some transcendental [entity] which brings about the distinction in form perceived by such direct perception.

The power residing in the hand, which consists of the awakening of activity and is eternally inferable, has only its state of being prior and posterior that is inferred; thus, the sequential nature of worldly action is established and justified through a specific power of the Supreme Lord, which consists of the capacity to manifest the differentiation of temporal appearances. However, as for the eternal power of action belonging to the Lord, which is non-different from Him and untouched by time, there is not even the possibility that it possesses sequence.
Just as it is impossible for the Lord to possess sequential movement, so too it is for this [atom]. For it has been said:
"If the hand were to possess sequential movement, then the action residing within it would likewise [be sequential].
Now, one might object: "Time, by assuming various specific states, delimits an entity according to its own form; what, then, is this so-called 'time'? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Time is the movement of the sun and other [celestial bodies], or the birth of various flowers and such; or else it is cold and heat. In reality, however, it is essentially nothing but sequence (*krama*). (IPK 2.1.3)
Those appearances which are established as having a definite limit—such as the moon, the sun, and so forth; the *sahakāra*, jasmine, and *kuṭaja* trees; cold, heat, and the like;

and the intoxication and dalliance of the cuckoo—it is precisely these that constitute time, because through them undetermined activities such as walking or reading are brought to a definite conclusion, just as gold is refined by means of a crucible.
And that very specific nature of the sun and other [luminaries], when ultimately and supremely considered, is the sequence; there is no other thing called "sequence.
Furthermore, time is precisely this sequence and nothing else.
Thus, the particle *eva* (precisely/only) should be applied to both the distinct and non-distinct sequences.

Even the simultaneity of two appearances is, in relation to other appearances, nothing but succession; even the cognition of "slow" or "quick" is, due to the expansion or contraction [of time], nothing but succession within the differentiation of appearances;
and the cognition of "remoteness" or "proximity" likewise resides in that very same [differentiation] by way of clarity and so forth.

Thus, when measured in conjunction with the movement of the sun and so forth—which act as various corresponding standards of measurement—the diversity of distinctions within the appearance of Devadatta, which occupies the place of gold, is described in this way: "the day passes. //3//
Now, one might object: "In that case, let time be simply the very nature of entities;
what then is this so-called power of time? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Sequence is based on difference, and difference [itself] exists through the presence or absence of manifestation."
But regarding the existence or non-existence of appearances, it is due to the Lord who produces manifold appearances.

In this context, if time were merely a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the four fingers, being of the nature of clay, would have to exist at different times. Therefore, sequence is produced by that difference— consisting in the presence of the appearance of redness and the absence of the appearance of a distinct mass of light— which is itself animated by the presence and absence of appearances.
The Self is the nature of time;
furthermore, it has been demonstrated in detail that the appearance and disappearance of manifestations are not produced by external causes.

Thus, the very Self, whose essence is consciousness, who is the sovereign and powerful lord in the creation of the diversity of manifestations within His own volitions and so forth, is self-known; from Him alone do those two [appearance and disappearance] arise.

For he, manifesting appearances such as blue and so forth within himself, manifests them with an immeasurable variety; for instance— the appearance of red, the appearance of a jar, the appearance of height, and the appearance of solidity— [he manifests] the appearance of a jar and the appearance of a cloth through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and [he manifests] their mutual distinction through the non-appearance of one in the other.
Within one's own self, however, there is no emergence of succession because the manifestation is of a single flavor;

but when it manifests the autumnal appearance as entirely empty by means of the winter appearance, and the winter appearance by means of the autumnal appearance, then succession, which is the nature of time, arises.
Thus, this power of the Lord, which manifests the diversity of existents in such a manner, is called the power of time (kāla-śakti). //4//
He clarifies precisely the capacity for producing variegated appearances:
"By means of the variety of forms, this Lord causes the succession of space to appear;
and by means of the manifestation of the variety of actions, He causes the succession of time to appear as well. (IPK 2.1.5)
The "own form" (*svarūpa*) of an object is its configuration (*mūrti*); the diversity or differentiation of that [form] is as follows: for example, "house" is one specific configuration.
The courtyard is one thing, the marketplace is another, and the temple is yet another.

A garden is one thing, and a forest is another; therefore, from that which is manifested as manifoldness, the Blessed One causes to appear a sequence of spatial forms— such as being distant or near, extensive or non-extensive— and so forth.
However, when—by the power of the illumination of intense recognition—the realization arises that "this very thing is the hand," there is no difference in the body's form;
yet, since various distinct forms appear within that single essential nature, those various forms are called "simultaneous actions" (asahabhavatkriyā) due to their mutual contradiction.

The manifoldness of these actions, consisting of both limited and unlimited aspects, manifests as the very form of time (krama) through the process of unification, appearing according to one’s inclination by means of the accomplishment of results and other such factors.
Nor should it be argued: "How can that which has a single nature have another, different form?
For there is no such entity whatsoever that could be conceptualized in this way;
rather, it is consciousness itself that appears in such a manner.
Furthermore, its very manifestation is its sovereignty;
for no contradiction whatsoever prevails regarding manifestation,
since that [contradiction] arises solely from the manifestation of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
For the very absence of such manifestation is the essence of contradiction;
this has been shown by the word "api" (also) and by the word "īśvara" (Lord). //5//
But surely, in this way, the sequence of space and time must arise solely from the objects of manifestation;
and the subject is non-manifest,
for he does not manifest as anything at all.
Since everything shines forth from him,
how then could those two [past and future] exist in the subject?
Yet they are indeed perceived as "I did not exist," "I am," and "I shall be."

"I stay in the house, in the forest, or in a temple"— and furthermore, for one who is himself devoid of the sequence of space and time, what is distant and what is near, what is present, what is past, and what is future? Thus, even regarding objects, a sequence based on the subject (the knower) is not logical.
And even though these [objects] are independent of a cognizer, there exists within themselves such things as distance or pastness;
in order to establish this, he says:
"In all cases, even when there is a difference in manifestation, it would be characterized by a sequence of time."
The appearance of emptiness and so forth is intermittent; it does not manifest simultaneously with the manifesting subject.
Spatial sequence also appears among objects for the limited subject;
however, for the unlimited one, objects appear as full within their own self by means of their own self, just like the self itself.

Regarding all things that possess both singular and manifold forms, that which is the source (*ākara*) of the temporal sequence (*krama*)— which is the very nature of time— is explained as the basis for their arising;
he considers that the distinction between the presence and absence of a manifestation arises from the void (*śūnya*), vital breath (*prāṇa*), intellect (*buddhi*), body (*deha*), and so forth.
For that [object], such as emptiness and so forth, has its light severed; indeed, its manifestation is not its own inherent nature because it is insentient like blue and other objects,
but rather its manifestation is the radiance of consciousness.
When that [power] is absent in him—
just as in the case of a sleeping person whose body has fallen into the course of worldly existence, wherein the vital breaths and so forth are empty— then his manifestation is severed.
Thus, there exists a temporal sequence produced by the presence or absence of appearances, such as:
"I existed in the past in the form of the appearance of a child's body," and "I am [now] in the form of the appearance of a youth's body."

And because that cognizer, due to the incomplete immersion into the sense of "I," is precisely characterized by an overflowing temporal succession, he manifests temporal succession even within objective entities [bhāva], such as:
"I who was a child—along with that, the manifestation of the tree was also present.
However, according to this formulation—"that which shines forth all at once"—the cognizer, whose nature is consciousness (saṃvidrūpa), is one whose manifestation is uninterrupted.
The succession of time belongs to him within his own self,
nor does it belong to the multitude of objects to be known in relation to that [self],
for those [objects] shine forth therein as non-different [from him].

In this way, even spatial sequence appears within the self of that which is limited and of a delimited nature—ranging from the void (*śūnya*) to the body—as "I am standing here. And in relation to itself, among objects as well, that which exists with a limitation of conjunction relative to oneself is "near," while the other is "far. However, for the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), which is immeasurable and devoid of any limit in its essential nature, all objects appear by virtue of its own self as the "I-sense" (*ahaṃbhāva*); therefore, they are full—that is, their essential nature and extent are undelimited.
Since his own Self is exactly such [as it appears], this is a *samuccayopamā* (cumulative simile). As it has been said:
"For this is without before or after in terms of form and action; everything is complete in every respect.

In connection with the discussion of action (*kriyā*), the sequence of time (*kālakrama*) was introduced as a contextual example, and in connection with that, the sequence of space (*deśakrama*) has been described here.
Since it was stated previously that "the illustration (dṛṣṭānta) should be mentioned first," it is logical to mention the sequence of space at the beginning when describing variety;

however, in the conclusion, the sequence of time pertaining to the subject matter (prākaraṇika) is mentioned first, while the sequence of space, which is incidental (prāsaṅgika), follows afterwards. //6; 7//

Now, one might object: "If this is so, then since there is no succession of time, and since action depends upon such succession, it follows that there is no action whatsoever in the Blessed Lord, who is the eternal subject. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But that power of manifestation belongs likewise to the knowing Lord;
for in this way, the distinction between the knower and the knowable is made to appear. (IPK 2.1.8)

In this context, it will be concluded in another section that, in reality, for the Supreme Lord, action is indeed Will itself— consisting of the uninterrupted self-reflection of His own nature characterized by unimpeded freedom, and having the form of non-orientation toward anything else; thus, Will alone is causality, agency, and action.
Even for Caitra, Maitra, and others, that very internal desire which consists in "I cook" is itself the action;
and thus, even when there is a connection with many movements such as placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth, this [sense] "I cook" is not interrupted.
That which is the form of the desire "I cook" appears precisely as the nature of such movement.

In that regard, however, there is no sequence whatsoever in reality. Thus, even for the Lord, in His sovereign manifestation, such reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) consisting of will—as "I shine," "I pulsate," "I am aware"—is essentially nothing more than the "I" itself; therein, there is no sequence at all.
And this very point is expressed by the sentence, "May the sequence of the variety of subjects and objects thus manifest," for even here there is no sequence whatsoever;
rather, that which is of the nature of will— such as "I cook"— appears as having assumed a sequential form, having reached the state of vibration (spandana) extending as far as the body.
