Then the will of the Lord, which culminates in the distinction between subject and object, appears as conjoined with that sequence, just as the surface of a mirror is conjoined with the sequence of the flow of a wide, surging river; yet in this case, the mirror itself does not possess such a will.

But that [power] belongs to the Supreme Lord; thus, in both ways, His power of action consists of the capacity to produce action in the form of succession and the connection with the coloring (uparāga) of action in the form of succession.
The same should be stated regarding spatial succession;
however, in that case, it is called His power of consciousness (cicchakti) by others.
But here, the essential meaning is that this very [power] is accepted as the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

As for the literal meaning: "thus" (*tathā*) refers to the differentiation of the cognizer—the subject (*pramātṛ*) such as the void (*śūnya*) and so forth—which is characterized by a distinction of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) that effects spatial succession, and by a distinction of action (*kriyā-bheda*) that effects temporal succession, [as well as] the mutual differentiation from one another and from the object of cognition (*jñeya*).
In this way, that jar and so forth, as well as the knower, are manifested by the Blessed One;
that manifestation is the Lord’s power of emanation (*nirmāṇa-śakti*) and his power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and not merely the activity of the void (*śūnya*) and so on.

Furthermore, because that wise one perceives incessantly the diversity of distinctions between the constructed varieties of the knower, the known, and action, it flashes forth precisely therein; for this reason also, he possesses that power of action.

Therefore, because there is no interruption in its manifestation, even if—due to the absence of succession—there might, from the perspective of gross observation, arise a doubt regarding the impossibility of its activity, nevertheless, its power of action is established in this way; such is the connection.
Thus all is auspicious. (8) [Total: 97]

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Power of Action," in the *Kriyādhikāra* of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* written by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. 1.
The Second Chapter on Ritual Action:
We praise Śiva, the knower of the reality of mantra, who establishes both contradiction and non-contradiction, as well as difference and non-difference, by his own will alone. (1)
As it was stated that the Blessed One possesses the power of emanation because his capacity is unimpeded,

that very point is now being established by means of supporting the entire collection of categories— such as action, relation, generality, and so forth— which are untenable according to the views of those who propound external objects.
{Action, relation, generality...}
The daily lesson is introduced by these seven verses, beginning with "ityādi" and ending with "{....................................... tena na bhrāntirīdṛśī}".

Therein, by the first verse, which functions as a sutra, he demonstrates that even though action and so forth— possessing both unitary and manifold forms— are logically untenable within the externalist (bāhya) doctrine due to the contradiction of superimposing incompatible properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa), their nature must nevertheless be necessarily established.
By the second [verse], the logical justification for this is indicated.

By the third [verse], it is stated that although these are to be known through non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-saṃvedana*), their form is clearly manifest precisely at the time of conceptualization (*vikalpaka*).
By the fourth and fifth [verses], the distinction between objects based on whether they possess a single or manifold nature is investigated.
By the sixth [verse], the essential nature of action, agent, and so forth—which are accepted as being related as indicated by the *Prahāṇaka-sūtra*—is explained.
The seventh [point] is the application of purposeful action; this is the summary.

Now, if it is thus, then that which is emanated by the power of manifestation (*nirmāṇa-śakti*), which consists of appearing, is nothing other than its very manifestation—that is the emanation, not anything else.
And that [cognition] exists even in the case of a double moon and the like, in the case of blue and the like,
and even in the case of the action, universal, relation, and so forth residing in blue and the like.

Then, one might ask: "How could conventional usage regarding things of this sort—such as 'the unreal is real' or 'conventional truth'—be consistent, given that there is no difference in their being non-existent? Anticipating this objection, [the author] states the following, asserting first that the unreality of actions and so forth is well-established, and indicating that even in this manner, the unreality of double moons and the like is demonstrated: [The text continues: ...he says: "Just as the moon is not truly two, nor is it truly one, because its nature is not established as either; likewise, all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent. This means: just as the moon is not truly two, because its dual nature is not established, nor is it truly one, because its singular nature is not established; in the same way, all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent. Just as the moon is not truly two, nor is it truly one, because it lacks the nature of both, so too all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, because they lack intrinsic nature. The cognitions of action, relation, generality, substance, space,
and time are considered real, based on both stability and utility, and they have single as well as multiple substrata.

Apart from the reality of consciousness (*cittattva*), whatever notion of action arises regarding the agent, the object, the instrument, and so forth—such as "Caitra cooks," "the rice grains soften," or "the fuel burns"—its substratum and objective support (*ālambana*) is the referent Caitra and the like, which possesses both a single and a manifold form.

To explain: although Caitra’s body there is differentiated by various places, times, and forms, and thus possesses a manifold nature, it nevertheless appears without abandoning its unitary form, such that one perceives, "this is that very same person."
Furthermore, that very action, which possesses both unitary and manifold forms, is ultimately real because it appears in exactly that way;

whereas a double moon, although appearing in such a manner, is unreal because at a later time its stability—which consists in the persistence of the operation of valid cognition—is uprooted by the realization that "the double moon does not exist.
In this case, however, the reflective awareness "Caitra is moving" is experienced as persisting and is not uprooted by anything.
And although the double moon and such may be useful for pleasure or agitation,
nevertheless, one who has the conceit of seeing a double moon does not conceive of such causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) therein; rather,
he conceives of that which is to be performed by a single moon, such as the removal of cataracts and so forth.
Because it is exactly like that [other] one, one does not determine a twofold causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) therein,
nor is it employed for such [efficiency].

In the case of movement (*brajyā*), however, whatever attainment of a village one determines upon, its application (*upayoga*) is complete within that [attainment]; thus, due to stability and application, there is a cognition whose object is the reality of action in both unitary and manifold forms.
This should be stated likewise for the [categories] beginning with relation (*saṃbandha*) and ending with time (*kāla*); he will clarify this in the subsequent verses. //1//
Now, one might object: "Unity and multiplicity are mutually contradictory;
how could they both exist in a single entity?
Therefore, this method of uprooting stability is produced by a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In that regard, there is one internal reality which, having attained the state of being perceivable by the senses,
reaches multiplicity through [differences of] place, time, and intrinsic nature.
In this case, when Caitra is seen moving, the cognition "this one does not move" never arises—unlike [the negation] "this is not silver.

Even regarding a double moon, there occurs a subverting cognition: "This is not a double moon; due to ophthalmia, my eyes are impaired, and thus I perceive it so. As for what was said—"How can that which is one become many?"—[that objection is refuted].

To this it is replied: how can that which is here a cause become a non-cause? If it is argued that "it is so because of a difference in the object," then why has this opportunity been granted for the claim that "this is not contradictory when there is a difference in the object"?

If you say "because of consciousness" (*saṃvedana*), then why is it not accepted that in cases such as "it moves," we have already established consciousness itself as the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?
Furthermore, it is not impossible to state here that there is also a distinction of objects;
for instance: when there is no commingling with another manifestation, there is merely that single manifestation.

Precisely because of this, due to its lack of dependence on anything else and its being internal, it is internal (*āntara*). As such, it persists as a mere manifestation of that nature, being cognizable by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is suited to grasping such a mere manifestation.
And because it does not deviate from its own essential nature, and because it is capable of expanding through the conjunction with other manifestations, reality is perceived as one;
that very same reality appears as "here" or "there" through the manifestation of space.
Through the appearance of time, [an object] is perceived as "now" or "then";
through the appearance of its own nature, as "thin," "thick," and so forth;
and through their combination, as "manifold"—all this is cognized when there is perceptibility by the external senses. Likewise,
According to the principle stated [in the verse]: "{...of the Lord who abides within the self...}", the entire universe alone is the one reality that is without interval;
that very same [reality] is the object of perception by both types of senses for one who exists with intervals [of differentiation].

Thus, according to the view of the reality of the relationship between cause and effect as will be explained, multiplicity exists when [an object] is perceivable by the senses due to the mixing of appearances such as place and so forth.
Unity, however, exists when there is no mixing with other appearances— that is, when it is perceivable solely by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and consists of pure consciousness (cinmātratā).

Furthermore, multiplicity occurs when there is a mixture with another appearance, when there is perceptibility by both instruments [of cognition], and when there is an appearance of something distinct from consciousness;
thus, the distinction of objects is clear.
And its being such [i.e., multiple] arises solely through the power of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), just as in the case of causes and non-causes, or material causes and auxiliary causes.
Now, if [you argue] that this—such as "cause" and "non-cause"—is merely a designation, then here too, "one" and "many" are merely conventional designations;
even "blue," "yellow," "non-conceptual," and "conceptual" are all merely conventional designations within the realm of *māyā*. Thus, everything is the same.
Therefore, the contradiction between unity and multiplicity is not a subverting factor; this very point has been expressed by the word "eva" (only).
In that regard, among those [categories] such as action and so forth, that which is the internal reality is one.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: that very [entity], having attained the state of being perceivable by the senses, reaches a state of multiplicity due to differences in location and so forth;
"therein" means while its reality remains established, or else, between those two—oneness and multiplicity—the construction is either "oneness is thus" or "multiplicity is thus. //2//

But if a distinction between objects is thus admitted, then when one appears, the many do not appear, and when the many appear, the one does not appear; so how could an object possess both a unitary and a manifold nature?
For instance, Caitra, who occupies various locations, is perceived by the external sense organ;

however, they say that the non-conceptual operation born of the external sense organ has no capacity to mix multiple appearances, because it arises through the power of a proximate object and is devoid of deliberation.

Furthermore, even by means of mental conceptualization (*vikalpa*), such an object is not touched at all. Therefore, by what cognition could an object be grasped as having both a single and a manifold nature?
Thus, in order to dispel the delusions of others, he says:

"Taking those two as its object, the mind, acting as a subsequent reflective awareness, performs the conceptualizations of action and so forth, which consist of the activity of the subject. (IPK 2.2.3)

It was established previously that here, within the *Jñānāmālā*, the subject (*pramātṛ*), whose nature is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), is like the internal thread and constitutes the very life-force;
furthermore, it has been determined that he is autonomous (*svatantra*).
Moreover, he is Śiva by nature, possessing a pure essence.
In the state of *māyā*, however, the bound soul (*paśu*) possesses a contracted nature; thus,
at the occasion of the mind's manifestation, its unfolding becomes clearly manifest on the plane of conceptualization (*vikalpa*),
because the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara arise within non-conceptual sensory perception (*nirvikalpaka*).
The operation of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) belongs to that which is not outside of non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpabodha*).

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), producing a subsequent conceptual determination (*vyavasāya*)—which is of the nature of certainty and is denoted by the term "after-cognition" (*anuvyavasāya*)—brings about these conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the connection with action and so forth.
And those conceptual constructions take as their object that pair consisting of unity and plurality.
For it has been stated that what appears within conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) is not a real entity, since "the very state of being manifest is what constitutes reality.

Furthermore, apart from the nature of manifestation itself, it is not logical for a conceptual construction to possess any other operation designated by such names as "superimposition" (*āropa*), "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*), or "conceit" (*abhimāna*).
Therefore, statements such as "they superimpose the external upon the non-external" are devoid of any objective basis.
And this has been stated in the passage: "If the determination [of the object] were an error... and so forth.
Now, the opponent might say: "How could conceptual construction touch upon that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is to be illuminated by sensory cognition?"

It would be so—if conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were independent; however, it is an operation of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), and the cognizer consists of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) culminating in a prior experience. And this very impression (*saṃskāra*) of the prior experience is that which remains even at the time of the operation of conceptualization, not relinquishing its nature as that prior experience.

Therefore, as long as the prior experience consists in the manifestation of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), conceptualization—which is the operation of the reality of the subject that has attained identity with that prior experience—has that very [specific characteristic] as its object;
for this reason, it was stated by the Teacher: "This very [conceptualization] is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the prior experience belonging to the subject."
"Even at the time of exclusion (apohana), that prior experience remains.

Therefore, it is established that the very activity of the cognizer—which consists in the synthesis of unity and plurality—is the subject under discussion; and it is the mind alone that performs such conceptual constructions regarding action and so forth, having as their objects single or multiple entities, as indicated by the introductory statement.

Although the appearance of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth occurs even in non-conceptual [cognition], as in the case of the mere appearance of a jar and the like, nevertheless, at that time, the universal and so forth are not manifest. This is because, when two related entities arise as mutual qualifiers (*uparañjaka*), there is no abandonment of the succession of successive moments, nor is there any acceptance of a collection of parts (*avayavakadambaka*).

Because categories such as the general property (*sāmānya*), relation (*saṃbandha*), action (*kriyā*), substance (*dravya*), direction (*dik*), and so forth, manifest in ultimate reality through the apprehension of the negated and the negator,

it is established that universals and the like— possessing both unitary and manifold forms— are objects grasped by mental conceptualization (*mānasavikalpa*). And thus, conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*) is the conceptualizing intellect.
On account of that, let it be called conventional truth; however, since it is merely a mode of truth itself, it is not unreal like a double moon or similar illusions. //3//
And therein lies this sequence for entering into consciousness: that this entire expansion is the unfolding of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) itself;
even there, the relationship (*sambandha*) alone is the fundamental basis. For instance, that which appears as one among similar things is the universal (*sāmānya*).
That which is the extension (*vaitatya*) of Devadatta is action (*kriyā*); that which is the unity or extension of parts in space is the whole (*avayavī*);
and having taken this as a limit, such notions as "this is thus from that" or "this is to the east of that" constitute direction (*dik*).
This expansion of action exists either through coexistence or non-coexistence; this is time, such as the present and so forth.

For as long as the form of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) shines as something following upon [the root], everything beyond that is merely a relation (*saṃbandha*). Thus, even for the factors of action (*kāraka*), their nature is nothing but relation; it is only in certain cases that this relation admits of another designation or a complex grammatical construction.

Just as for those things possessing horns and so forth, the relationship [of inherence] is capable of sustaining the single designation "cows," wherein the linguistic usage of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so on occurs;
yet, when the knot of other designations is severed, it is simply the expression of the relationship itself.

For this very reason, that which consists of the measures of *diṣṭi*, *prastha*, and *pala*—whether in the form of measurement (*parimāṇa*), weighing (*unmāna*), or contained therein—as well as minuteness, largeness, and so forth, along with number and separateness (*pṛthaktva*), all of that is merely the unfolding of the relationship itself.
Even those who considered universals (*sāmānya*) and the like to be distinct entities admitted that inherence (*samavāya*) exists therein as their very life-force;
and for some, inherence is of the nature of a relation or is supported by it, as they say:
"The relation supports that power called inherence."
Thus,
whatever is a causal factor (kāraka) is also dependent upon action; and that action, in turn, relies upon Time as its sovereign lord.
He too, by means of activity, brings forth the relation that constitutes the essence of all things; thus, this manifold course of worldly affairs is entirely dependent upon relation.
As the Teacher himself has said:
"The [world] is established through all objects accompanied by relations whose nature is both difference and non-difference."
"I bow to that Śiva, whose manner of conducting the affairs of the world proceeds according to his own will.
Therefore, in order to define the very relationship first, he says:
When entities, which are distinct appearances resting within their own self,
are joined with a unity consisting of mutual interpenetration within a single cognizer, they become the locus for the cognition of relation.
When the king and the man, standing on the outside as separate entities, attain unity upon the ground of the subject (*pramātṛ*) which is fully realized in its own singular self-nature—
yet this is not a mere unity, for that would entail the dissolution of their distinction—

but rather a state consisting of the mutual interpenetration of their forms, characterized by simultaneously mounting the swing of the two poles of difference and non-difference as they sink and emerge, which is of the nature of a continuous synthesis (*anvaya*).
Then, those two alone become the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition of the relation, as in "the king's man.

For instance, when the king, though previously apprehended by the mind, is not satisfied by resting within his own self, he then achieves his purpose by entering into a connection with the person through another form;
and the person likewise does so.

And this very fusion of forms (*rūpaśleṣa*), which consists in the abiding of both [subject and object] in that way within the conscious self (*cidātman*) and is grounded in the consciousness previously attained, rests in absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) because of the immersion of even greater consciousness; thus, it manifests therein as that very reality where even the ultimate principle of the person (*puruṣaparamārtha*) has been completely transcended.
Thus, there is multiplicity externally, but internally there is unity through the mutual blending of their forms; such is the nature of the relationship. //4//
Conceptual constructions take as their objective support both the uniformity of universals and substances even externally, as well as the distinction between the individual and its parts.
Those conceptual constructions which grasp a universal (*jāti*)— which itself appears as a manifest form—
not only take as their objects an internal unity (as in the case of a relation) and an external multiplicity; rather,

they also lead to the taking as an object both the plurality characterized by the difference between individual instances (*vyakti*) externally, and the unity consisting in the continuous thread (*anusyūtatā*) of that [universal] externally.

For in the manifestation "cows," individual external entities appear as distinct, which accounts for the plural number; and a recurring form also appears among them, because there is a continuous reference to the meaning of a single nominal stem.

And since both of these are designated by the finger as being "outside," their mere externality remains even while they are included within the manifestation of ultimate reality; thus, in that case, neither difference nor non-difference constitutes a flaw, just as in the case of the perception of a variegated [color].
By this, the contradiction regarding redness and non-redness even in a substance has been countered;
however, internal unity exists everywhere in that very same way through the medium of relation.
Thus, those conceptual constructions which grasp the composite substance appearing as "a jar" are not merely—

Just as in the case of a relationship, [the mind] grasps through the internal and external forms that which has both a single and multiple object; for even externally, it accepts what is one as having a nature free from joints or bonds, and what is divided by way of parts characterized as distinct portions—as in the case of "a jar," which appears as a single, dense mass free from joints, yet also as an extended form. //5//
The coordination of the factors of action (kārakas) has as its object the deliberation regarding the activity;
the cognition of direction and so forth is supported by the relation between the limit and that which possesses the limit.

The mutual correspondence that is observed among the factors of action (*kārakas*), which are the substrata of powers such as agency (*kartṛtva*), and among substances— just as, for example, there is a mutual relation between the knower (*mātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*meya*), and the means of knowledge (*māna*)—
is caused solely by the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the residual [elements] such as the action consisting of the internalized act of knowing (*pramā*).
For here, no direct positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of an entity is perceived apart from the intervening reflective awareness of the means of valid cognition (*pramā*).
The meaning of "object" (*viṣaya*) here consists in being restricted to that [entity] alone, which is based on its nature as a positive existence (*bhāva-rūpatā*).
Furthermore, even the connection of the potencies of the causal factors (*kāraka-śakti*) with their own substrates is caused by the reflective awareness of the action (*kriyā-parāmarśa*).
Since there is a direct connection between substances, powers, and action, it is this very Blessed Action that manifests such a relationship.

That form which is perceived— situated between two entities that are externally apprehended as distinct (such as "this is prior to that" or "this is far from that")— and which consists of an awareness of difference preceded by non-difference and resting ultimately in non-difference, is called *diś* (direction).

For in this context, the consideration of the specific parts such as the faces of the two [persons], the determination of their being face-to-face or turned away from one another, and the apprehension of their conjunction, their being conjoined with others, or the smallness of such conjunctions, are all useful.

As for the consideration of time, when it takes the form of "prior," "subsequent," and so on, there is an investigation into birth, duration, smallness, and so forth; and when it takes the form of "long" or "quick," as in "he will cook," "he cooks," or "he cooked," there is the [consideration] of a particular result—whether potential, manifest, or clearly past—which consists of other actions such as the movement of one's own consciousness, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or the activity of the sun.
And just as the apprehension of boiled rice and so forth is employed [as a cognition],
so too in the case of number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, and the rest, it is precisely the nature of a relation that must be expressed;
in every respect, this is the summary.

Where, due to a lack of satisfaction through the repose of the manifestation of an object within itself, there is a non-finality of its own nature because of a longing for repose in the reflective awareness of another manifestation, in that case there is indeed the nature of a relation; and even there, let there be yet another relation in dependence upon other entities,
as they consider inherence (*samavāya*) to exist in cases such as number.
Furthermore, even if there were an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), it would not constitute a fault, just like the infinite succession of creations in preceding and succeeding kalpas;
for there is no loss whatsoever in the manifestation of a prior relation that occurs without the creation of a subsequent relation, such that one could suspect a damage to the root. //6//
Having thus explained the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which consists in becoming the intimate bond of numerous relations that vitalize the entire course of worldly life,
he says the following in order to determine its stability and utility, as previously indicated:
"In this very way, the accomplishment of the object occurs for the mother who seeks purposeful action."
Therefore, because it possesses the nature of both difference and non-difference, such a [cognition] is not an error.
In this context, the existence of entities does not consist in a relation with "existence" (sattā),
because that would entail the faults of non-pervasion and infinite regress;
nor does it consist in causal efficiency (arthakriyā), because that is a distinct entity.
That capacity to produce an effect does not exist at all times, because its manifestation is not observed [at all times]; for it has been said:
"The causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of objects is also not innate...

Since that capacity to produce an effect is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which consist of perception and non-perception, if it were itself imperceptible, then the effect as well would necessarily be imperceptible.

Its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākaraṇayogyatva*) cannot be determined at the time of deciding whether it is real or unreal, because everything [in that state] lacks manifestation; furthermore, since all of this would be like a "man's horn" due to its non-appearance, and because seeking further causal efficiency leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Thus, the very state of manifestation— consisting of the undestroyed vibration of such an appropriate reflective awareness— is the existence of an entity;
and since this exists for relations and the like, which possess a nature of both difference and non-difference,
their reality is indeed beyond all doubt.
Nevertheless, if another should persist in questioning: "In this world, people for the most part seek purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and designate 'truth' to that which accomplishes it;
does such [purposeful action] exist in the case of relations and so forth?"—then his heart is comforted by this:
If you do not object, then in every transaction whatsoever— even where a cognition of a relation and so forth does not explicitly arise— it is exactly the same; thus,
the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) occurs through that very object which possesses both difference and non-difference by way of its relational nature and so on,
but never at any time does any causal efficiency occur through that which rests solely within its own self-nature.
For instance, from the recollection of pleasure arises desire;
in this sequence, all worldly activity proceeds such that only that which has been experienced as a manifestation of pleasure is desired, and not something else that has not been experienced.
Only that which has been experienced is desired, and not something else that has not been experienced.

If that very thing is obtained, one is satisfied thinking, "What was desired has been attained. Now, if it is indeed that very thing, then why is it desired? Because it has already been obtained. Or, if it is not that very thing, then how can it be sought? Because it is unknown. Therefore, this situation occurs thus: it is both that very thing and not that very thing; it is both that and not that.
The same should be said regarding the means of happiness.
As it was stated by the Teacher himself:
"When there is a desire for a desired object, one either reflects upon that desired object itself, or upon that which brings about the desired object."
Nor is the unseen [force] desired, for heaven too is desired as a place for the enjoyment of the unseen.

"Once seen, it perishes along with the very act of seeing"—thus its existence is questioned; "it is dissolved through identity with the seer," and so forth. And thus, within this [consciousness] whose nature is manifestation, even another manifestation that is not [directly] perceived enters into it by way of being a universal relation.

Otherwise, there would be no worldly transaction whatsoever; therefore, if this worldly transaction—which is useful for all places, times, conditions, and persons—is not real, we do not know the reality of anything else.
Thus, one should not be deluded by thinking that there is no error here. May there be auspiciousness! (7) [Total from beginning: 104]

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Contemplation of Difference and Non-difference," in the *Kriyādhikāra* of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* written by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. // 2 //
The third chapter in the Section on Action.

We praise that Śiva, whose faces look upon the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when they enter into the act of knowing, as they proceed by the sequence of their own inherent power toward the object of knowledge (*prameya*). (1)

Thus, in the course of defining the expansion of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), the reality of the categories beginning with generality (*sāmānya*) has been established preceded by an analysis of their relations.
Now, however, the very reality of relation itself must be elucidated as a single, unified whole.
And that, in the ultimate sense, is of only two kinds: the state of the signified and the signifier (*jñāpya-jñāpakatā*), and the state of cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇatā*).

In that regard, within the former [section], which serves as the locus for investigating the relationship between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the objects of knowledge (*meya*), everything previously stated and all that is yet to be said is dependent upon it—since it is well-established in various places that "the establishment of an entity depends on the means of knowledge.

Thus, because it is necessary for the support of the subject matter at hand and because it constitutes the very nature of their connection, one must necessarily investigate the status of the means of knowledge and so forth; to delineate this, [the author says]:
"This is such-and-such... and so on.
Beginning with "ityādi" and ending with "{.............................
īśādivyavahāraḥ pravartyate //}", another chapter (āhnika) is commenced by means of seventeen verses.
Therein, by means of two verses, the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is established;

thereafter, in order to determine the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), it is shown that the operation of the means of knowledge pertains to each individual appearance (*pratyābhāsa*), and not to a restriction to a single reality consisting of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)— this being demonstrated through the power of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*),
which establishes the arrangement of appearances.

Thus it is stated in ten verses; following that, the nature of false cognition is described in one verse, and the establishment of the nature of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), although relevant to the present context, sets aside the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*).

This is demonstrated by the verse beginning with "ambya ghaṭate," which states that this entire differentiation of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), their results (*tatphala*), and objects of knowledge (*prameya*), exists only when there is a knower (*pramātṛ*) of the nature already described;
therefore, he cannot himself be an object of knowledge (*prameya*), such that a further operation of a means of knowledge would be possible even in this regard.
The intended meaning of the three verses is this: in this context, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its result only the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
As it was stated: "Cognitions such as those of action, relation, and so forth, are not of the nature of error."

To determine that very point, he first restates the well-known nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*): "That by virtue of which a thing is established as being 'this' or 'of such a kind' is the means of valid cognition; and that [means] is also a new arising of its own manifestation. (IPK 2.3.1)

Thus, that cognition whose nature consists of internal reflection is an uncontradicted means of knowledge regarding a real object that is the referent of a single designation, even though it is undivided by space, time, and other such factors.

By virtue of which—namely, by its power—the entity, such as blue or pleasure, is established; that is to say, it does not transcend a fixed limit of manifestation, such that "this is such-and-such" in its own nature and "it is characterized by such attributes" through its connection with qualities like permanence or impermanence; thus it is established that this is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the world.
And this must be investigated by a discerning person: here, the nature of an object does not remain established by its own power alone, because it is insentient;
for how could there be an appearance such as "blue appears to me" or "to Caitra"?
Therefore, it remains established through the power of another.
If it were something else that is insentient, then that would be like one blind man taking hold of another blind man by the hand;
therefore, this [object] must be distinct from consciousness.

If that [distinct object] were also pure and devoid of distinctions, then it could not be the cause for the determination of blue alone, because it would be the same with respect to yellow and other colors as well.
Thus, being a manifestation characterized by being tinged with blue, oriented toward blue, and having the nature of the light of blue, it establishes the blue;
for its very nature as that light is what constitutes its status as the establisher of that [blue].
And if that light of the blue were non-distinct [from it],...
That [manifestation] would belong to the yellow as well, because there is no difference in its identity with the *cittattva* (the essence of consciousness) which is of the nature of light;
therefore, that manifestation belongs to the blue which has been differentiated from it.
And if the blue is thus capable of appearing as distinct from that, then that manifestation itself must be differentiated from the great Light.
Because it would follow that there is no distinction between that [object], such as blue, and the Great Light (mahāprakāśa) if it were not distinct from it,
and because the Great Light does not tolerate any distinction whatsoever,
it must necessarily manifest contraction within itself.
That which constitutes the life-force of the contraction of consciousness and objects, taking the form of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), is called "the void" (*śūnya*).
Furthermore, the very manifestation of this contraction is the emergence of the subject belonging to *māyā*.
Thus, through the single power of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-śakti*), there occurs, in reality, the unfolding of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

Therefore, for that limited subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*)— who consists of the assumption of contraction through the acceptance of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the void, intellect, vital breath, and body, and who is inward-turned consciousness throughout infinite time— as long as that manifestation accepted as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) possesses the nature of being directed toward an object of knowledge (*prameya*),
so long must it also be created as having various different forms moment by moment, because the object of knowledge is characterized by a fusion with the manifestations of place, time, and form.

As it has been said: "The ever-new arising" (*abhinavodaya*). "Ever-new" (*abhinava*) means not stained even by the fading that comes from lingering for a moment; thus, it is said to be an "ever-newly arising.

If even such [consciousness] were not connected to the subject of *māyā*, then the thought "this blue appearance belongs to me" would not exist, nor would there be the thought "this yellow appearance belongs to me" for whoever possesses it.

And there exists this self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) which is uncontradicted in all respects; thus, that manifestation appearing as "self"—which arises ever anew due to its orientation toward ever-new objects of knowledge—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it effects valid cognition (*pramā*). If it is asked, "What is that?"—it is of the nature of the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). If [this is objected]: The translation of the provided text is as follows: "And there exists this self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) which is uncontradicted in all respects; thus, that manifestation appearing as 'self'—which arises ever anew due to its orientation toward ever-new objects of knowledge—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it effects valid cognition (*pramā*). If it is asked, 'What is that?'—it is of the nature of the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*)."
He says: "That very manifestation whose nature is consciousness is the cognition; it is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is the connection [of the words]. [Objection:
But in this way, a synonymy would be stated, and not the status of being a fruit.
He replies: "In that case, by virtue of its outward orientation and its nature as light, it is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."

However, that very consciousness which was previously established as having the nature of inward-turned self-reflection (*vimarśa*), when it is merely contracted by the state of objects through its own essential nature, is the fruit. For instance, just as "I am a hero" and "I am victorious" are established by one who possesses discernment as cause and effect within a single substratum— since "because I am a hero, therefore I am victorious"— so too is this case.

Thus, since there is the manifestation of blue, there is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that "this is blue"; therefore, even though they possess a single form, there exists the relation of cause and effect, as it has been said:
"Because of that [cause], that [effect] is established...

Furthermore, in this context, the fruit is nothing other than the very nature of the operation (*vyāpāra*), and the operation is established as being non-different in form from that which is operating or that which is being operated upon.

Thus— there is non-difference between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*). And since this [non-difference] occurs through the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and since both the means of knowledge and reflective awareness have their life in speech (*śabda*),
and speech functions toward a single manifestation alone that is untouched by other manifestations such as space and time—
as in "jar" or "red"— [there is indeed non-difference].

Therefore, because the appearances of space and time—which are inclined toward imparting their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa)—are not mixed together, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) operates upon the appearance that functions as a universal (sāmānya).
For even the appearance "this" refers merely to the manifestation of an object situated in front, unmixed with other appearances;
thus it has been stated by the venerable Ācāryapāda himself:

"Even when this [object] is present before one, the reflective awareness that 'this is determined' arises solely through the universal of 'this-ness' (idantā) which is common to all entities. Therefore,
the object is nothing but a mere appearance.

The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), however, is a distinct manifestation (*ābhāsāntaram*) that consists in the appearance of co-referentiality with that [particular] manifestation; it is indeed another [manifestation], and for it there is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, as will be explained later, among those manifestations that are mixed together, a [cognition] that grasps what has already been grasped is not a means of valid cognition.

According to the method we have stated, since determination (adhyavasāya)— which is animated by words— rests upon individual manifestations (pratyābhāsa), one who asserts that its validity (prāmāṇya) is dependent upon those [manifestations] must accept that validity resides solely in the individual manifestations;
so let it be, what is the use of this intermediate step?

Now, if reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), does it not then exist even in the case of a double moon? Not so; for that [reflective awareness] exists in such a way because, through the connection with latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it persists—its activity unextirpated—and remains stable until it reaches the attainment of the desired object capable of causal efficiency. However, if it admits of being extirpated in the interim, then it is not such a reflective awareness.
This reflection did not exist even previously— since it was already eradicated by that single inward-turned form—
and here, one's own consciousness is the witness;
for at that very moment, the non-reflection of the reflection that had previously occurred is experienced as "this is not silver."
And this has been stated in the investigation of sublation (*bādhavicāra*), and it will also be stated [in the section on] "the single reflective awareness of silver" (*rajataikavimarśa*).

In this regard, such being the case, even with respect to the double moon, as long as one desires to produce wonder in others— which is considered a purposeful action for the sake of seeing a previously unknown object— one’s prior perception of the "double moon" is uprooted by hearing the words of other people, leaving one helpless under the sway of contempt, derision, grief, and so forth.
One conceives the reflective awareness "this" precisely through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Now, one might ask: in a case where one does not seek causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), how can there be the conventional usage of sublation (*bādha*) or non-sublation?
Let it be so—what is lost for us? For activity (*pravṛtti*) does not always proceed solely on the basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

What then? It is because of doubt alone, or because of the superiority of the object, or even due to the gradation of desire—as is seen in the case of agriculture and the like, or in engaging in theft and such acts where the visible retribution is certain or merely probable;
therefore, an intensity of desire is the cause for people's engagement in action.
And that [cognition], having arisen, attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it is not uprooted by any sublation (*anummūlitapramitika*),

whereas in other cases, being otherwise, it is a misconception (*viparyaya*). Thus, because the distinction between the valid and the invalid has been practiced by him since birth— or even from hundreds of previous births— he perceives their specific nature as distinct at the very first moment of appearance, just like [the difference between] a gem and silver.
For there is indeed, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), a distinction in that [cognition] produced by differences in its causes and so forth;

and consequently, when one considers a certain suffering to be limited and bearable, one is not driven here and there by an excessive grasping for an object. Thus, being afraid of non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*), when one acts upon a cognition whose validity has been ascertained—whether toward something unseen or even toward something seen—one is not deceived.

Thus, he is called one who acts with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārī*); by him, the nature of worldly means of valid cognition (*laukika-pramāṇa*) has been restated in order to dispel the suspicion of invalidity arising from delusion even regarding the knowledge of general relations and so forth.
For this very reason, the world has not been burdened here with detailed classifications, definitions, and critical examinations.

Whatever possesses uncontradicted stability— and for that very reason, possesses uninterrupted continuity— is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) provided it results from inquiry, consists of consciousness, is directed toward an object of knowledge, and finds its rest in the nature of the cognizer.
And this is indeed beyond dispute in the case of sensory perception, the experience of pleasure and so forth, and the knowledge of yogis.
This is because [consciousness] rests directly and primarily within the manifestation that constitutes the object of cognition (*prameya*).

However, a cognition born of inference is the apprehension of one manifestation from another manifestation—whether that other manifestation be of the nature of an effect or of its own essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, the necessity of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and the necessity of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between a thing and another must be understood as depending solely upon the power of the Lord’s necessity (*niyati-śakti*), and not otherwise.

Therefore, inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only to the extent that necessity (*niyati*) is known regarding a particular place or time. However, scripture (*āgama*), which consists of words in another name, is more firmly established and has the nature of non-deliberation; it is the very internal activity of the Lord, whose essence is consciousness, and is like the very life-force of perception and the other means of knowledge. Thus, whatever is clearly ascertained by it is exactly so.
"This poison does not kill me; I am indeed Garuḍa.

In that regard, however, the collection of words (*śabdarāśi*) which conforms to such a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of sound is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the Vedas, the Siddhāntas, and so forth.
Or even another [tradition], such as the scriptures of the Buddhists or the Jains;
for by that [scripture], a certain proclamation is raised: "I, performing the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, am one who will go to heaven"; "I, being initiated, am one who shall not return again";
or "I, being compassionate, am one who will go to the state of a Buddha."
When the thought arises, "I am capable of enduring intense afflictions and shall attain the state of an Arhat," no misconception arises therein,
because tomorrow he will indeed be fit for its practice.
However, because another person lacks the nature of firm conviction, such a verbal expression consisting of deliberation is simply not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
But if this were so, it would follow that the very same scripture is a means of valid cognition for one person and not for another;
and this is not tenable, because a means of valid cognition is impartial.
"You are ignorant of the way things appear to consciousness;
nevertheless, you are not to be disregarded. What is the meaning of this statement: 'A means of valid cognition is impartial'?"
Is it that the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of blue belonging to one person makes blue manifest to everyone, or does the cognition of smoke [make fire manifest to all]?

And as for the traditional scripture (*āgama*) consisting of a prophetic instruction (*siddhādeśa*), such as "You have obtained a treasure this morning by this method," is that a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for everyone,
or is it something for someone at some time?

Likewise, here too, that which is called *āgama*— a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of verbalization in the form of firm deliberation— is for everyone a means of knowledge because it causes the object to be understood in its entirety (*ā-samantāt*).
In this regard, just as light, the sense organs, and so forth, are non-means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) when they associate with false cognition and thus lack the nature of valid knowledge,
yet this does not entail any partiality on the part of perception (*pratyakṣa*), which consists of right cognition.

Likewise, that very word such as "Jyotiṣṭoma" and so forth, even while acting as an auxiliary to a pseudo-scripture— which is not a valid means of knowledge because it consists of a lack of firm discernment on the part of Śūdras and others— nevertheless possesses validity in its utility for the true scriptural word characterized by firm discernment; thus, it is not subject to the fault of being refuted by the fallacy of *pallapāta* (vain babbling).

For every scripture indeed effects an inquiry that is strictly constrained by specific objects of knowledge, place, time, auxiliary factors, and so forth—whether its nature be affirmative or negative.
Therefore, in the verse beginning with "prasiddhi," it was stated: "where" and "when."
Therefore, the venerable Bhartṛhari, the author of the Nyāyabhāṣya, and others maintain that perception and scripture are the sublaters of inference;
consequently, once the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is known, the entire nature of the means of valid cognition becomes known— what is the use of specific definitions?

As for the one who states that its definition is non-contradictoriness (*avisamvādakatva*), even he, by asserting that the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in being a "conveyor" (*prāpaka*), being an "instigator" (*pravartaka*), or being the "indicator of an object capable of attainment and suitable for activity," has not stated any essential nature (*svarūpa*) that rests within the cognition accepted as a means of valid cognition;
and since that [essential nature] is established by this very definition, it is thereby accomplished.
Otherwise, that [speech] would consist merely of facial contortions, shaking the head, wringing the fingers, and so forth;
therefore, enough with this elaboration. //2//
Now, regarding what was stated— that cognition has a single denotation as its object—
if that single denotation operates only upon the external particular (svalakṣaṇa), then how can it be said that there is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for every appearance?

Dispelling the doubt that the appearance of the mixture [of the object and its cognition] might be the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), he speaks in order to define, from the perspective of ultimate reality, that which is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "Even with respect to a single object, the appearance varies according to one's inclination, according to one's need, and according to one's training, once it has been established through synthesis. (IPK 2.3.3)
Although the object perceived externally as "a jar" appears to be a single entity, it is not merely that much; rather, it also admits of being analyzed separately—
whether by independent analysis, according to one's specific interest, or by relying on what was previously established.
In that regard, when an analysis is conducted in these three ways, the manifestations appear as distinct entities.
Now, if this is so, how can there be a single *svalakṣaṇa* (particular)? It is said:
although those manifestations appear separately, the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which serves as their vitalizing principle sometimes rests within each individual manifestation.

Then there is the grasping of both higher and lower universals (*sāmānya*); however, when at another time there is a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose life-force is their synthesis—determining "this is such-and-such" here by establishing a relationship of primary and secondary importance—then that is the single particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The word "also" (*api*) has a different syntactical position; for even though there is only one object—the singular reality consisting of the particular which is established through synthesis and the reflective awareness of its integration—the "inclination" (*ruci*) is autonomy (*svātantrya*).

Without overstepping the state of being driven by the desire for purposeful action (*arthitva*) and the reliance upon the linguistic usage of elders (*vyutpatti*), the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) indeed undergoes differentiation. //3//
To demonstrate how this is so, he says:
"Just as appearances—such as those of a tall, round, upright person, smoke, or camphor—are differentiated by their qualities, even though they do not differ in terms of space and time. (IPK 2.3.4)
In the same way, the distinct appearances such as a real jar, a substance, gold, or brilliance—which produce different effects—are the referents of words. (IPK 2.3.5)

In this regard, even with respect to a single individual essence of a person (puruṣa-svalakṣaṇa), which is well-known as being conscious, one might at times contemplate its extension over a vast space— that is, its very length— which is also found in trees; or its state of having no joints or connections— that is, its roundness— which is possible even in stones.
Or, "uprightness" (*ūrdhvatā*) may consist in the act of ascending toward the upper direction, which is a quality belonging even to a pillar;
or "manhood" (*puruṣatva*) may consist in the capacity for independent states such as going and coming, which is common to other men as well.
For instance, by means of an independent will in the form of desire, one might act exactly as has been described.
"Because of the mind's tendency toward distraction, that [notion] arises spontaneously.
Alternatively, one might make a distinction while seeking an object whose causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is characterized by concealment, even though that object pervades an extensive space;

or one might make such a distinction when desiring to instruct, or when wishing to explain to someone who is learning, what kind of thing is called "long" (*dīrgha*) according to the usage of the elders.
Thus, in this way, there is a distinction among the manifestations (*ābhāsa*) therein.
However, the single particular characteristic (*ekasvalakṣaṇa*) [is established] because it comes to rest within a single manifestation of space and a single manifestation of time.

For it is precisely the manifestations of space and time—which function in close proximity to the negation of pervasiveness and permanence that are the causes of the nature of the universal—that bestow the nature of the particular.
In this same manner, other appearances such as "Brahmin" and so forth, which are like the appearance of "manhood," are also to be analyzed.
Thus, for now, the most well-known distinction of appearances here is due to its being the locus of many properties common to both the insentient and the sentient;
by this example, even in the case of smoke, well-known distinctions of appearance—such as "smokeness," "being sandalwood-smoke," and "originating from white sandalwood"—are to be differentiated.
By means of a well-known example, even that part which is not yet established— namely, the jar— possesses a differentiation of its appearing parts (*ābhāsabhāgabheda*).

For instance, when one perceives a jar while undergoing what is like a "shattering of the heart" at the thought, "Nothing exists here at all," one perceives only the appearance of existence (*sattvābhāsa*) in the form "this exists," while disregarding other appearances even by name.
Likewise, one seeking water perceives the appearance of a jar; one seeking an object capable of being independently carried here or there perceives the appearance of a substance;
and one seeking its value and so forth perceives the appearance of gold.
One who desires what is charming [seeks] the appearance of brilliance;
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," it should be understood that one who desires a more firm state of being seeks the appearance of firmness.
In this same manner, the application should also be made for taste (*ruci*) and proficiency (*vyutpatti*).
Thus, these various manifestations (*ābhāsa*) alone constitute the real object (*vastu*), because the essence of being a real object consists precisely in its appearing as such.
Furthermore, even that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the very life-breath of manifestation, pertains to each individual manifestation;
for verbal expression, whose nature is internal discourse (*abhijalpa*) and which resembles the life-force of consciousness, finds its rest in each individual manifestation.
For example: "the jar exists," "it is red," and so forth.

Even the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is restricted to each individual manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because by means of the manifestation of existence (*sad-ābhāsa*), there is merely the accomplishment of the avoidance of the heart's [fear of] destruction.

In that regard, whatever dependence there is upon another manifestation for the sake of accomplishing a causal efficiency—such as the manifestation of a vessel for the sake of the causal efficiency produced by the manifestation of fire—is due to the fact that even that other manifestation is necessarily concomitant with that primary manifestation.
Because of dependence [on cognition].

Thus, by whichever means an object is investigated, it is established that it consists of mere appearance, because it appears in that very way, because it is so determined through reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), and because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

In this way, although an object is in fact one, the author has described it in three ways—namely, as "long," "circle," "smoke," and "existent jar"—according to the varying degrees of its being more or less well-known or unknown. //5//
Now, one might object: "If every manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*) were itself a real entity (*vastu*), then a single pot-essence would not be a real entity. Anticipating this, he says:

"Furthermore, because of the difference in manifestations, the restricted causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of objects [is established] through their appearance as co-referential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), even though they are non-different. (IPK 2.3.6)

Regarding the mixed form of appearances (*ābhāsa*), there must necessarily be one appearance that functions as the primary locus of rest for the other appearances; this is their common substratum (*samānam adhikaraṇam*).

The relation they have with that [primary appearance] is "grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyam*). The manifestation characterized by this—namely, the light directed toward the object (*arthonmukhaḥ prakāśaḥ*) and the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) consisting of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ-anta*) which enlivens it—is such that all of it is necessarily restricted to resting within a single appearance.

Therefore, that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which constitutes the essence of the sentence— taking the form of an examination of the sentence-meaning such as "here, now, this jar exists"— completely subsumes that appearance of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For that reason, those things which are non-different,

having attained the state of a single specific characteristic (*ekasvalakṣaṇa*) while not abandoning their own individual natures, possess another, distinct, collective causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, when there is a distinction between manifestation (*ābhāsa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), other [entities] are determined as having a form consisting of each one alone; in this Sūtra, by the two words "manifestation" (*ābhāsa*) and "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) must also be understood as being implied.
The word "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) indicates a distinction and should be applied to both [terms], like the eye of a crow (*kākākṣivat*).
By means of the plural number, it is stated that even though there is unity, the abandonment of the distinction in their own nature (*svarūpa*) does not occur.

And in that case, when there is an appearance of unity, if the dependent nature (*paratantra*) exists as a distinctness among appearances, then, by virtue of being colored by individual manifestations of a similar form, it possesses the nature of an ultimate universal (*sāmānya*).

However, for a pure appearance of a jar, its status as a universal exists merely through the capacity for independent reflective awareness (*svatantraparāmarśa*), not in reality—for every category other than substance has as its essence dependence on something else. Likewise, it is also true that "the jar is one," because it is established as such through the power of appearance, reflective awareness, and causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). //6//
Is it not the case that causal efficiency does not arise from a single [manifestation] alone,
but rather that a collection of causal efficiencies arises from a collection of manifestations;
and even if these manifestations are distinct, they nevertheless coalesce in order to perform a single causal efficiency?
Then, it refutes the objection: "What is the limit of their number?

with the following verse: "Just as the lights of separate lamps [merge] in the ocean, or as streams [flow into it], so too the cognition of unity arises from appearances that are not contradictory, having a single purpose. (IPK 2.3.7)

Those rays of light belonging to a lamp, which exist separately and were incapable of performing a specific causal function characterized by the capacity for extremely subtle perception, perform that very same function once they have merged within a single dwelling; yet, in that case, there is no collection of distinct causal functions.

And just as waters fallen into the ocean perform the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of initiating far more numerous waves, so too a golden jar— whether red or otherwise— is seen merely upon sight to perform the purposeful activity characterized by intense joy, such as being suitable for bringing water to wash the head of a Śiva-liṅga;
thus, its capacity for purposeful activity is indeed established.
Furthermore, what is the limit regarding the mixing of appearances (*ābhāsa*)?
To this it is said: only those appearances that are non-contradictory (*avirodha*) are mixed;
for instance, the appearance of form (*rūpābhāsa*) does not mix with the appearance of wind (*mārutābhāsa*), because of their contradiction.
And that [consciousness] too is brought forth by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*).

Just as a single cognition of unity is produced by means of those individual lamp-lights which relate to one thing in the ocean, or by that which relates to the currents of rivers; likewise, regarding those appearances—such as a jar, red color, gold, and so forth—which are not mutually contradictory, that which relates to them...

The connection is as follows: that single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the cause of the cognition of unity regarding its effects. It is accepted that through this cognition of unity, there occurs a manifestation, a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). //7//

Now, one might raise the objection that since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) comes to rest with each individual appearance, the cognition of fire would be a valid cognition only in the appearance of fire, and the cognition of smoke only in the mere appearance of smoke; likewise, the manifestation of the causal relation would apply only to that much.
Consequently, even the appearance of smoke might deviate from the appearance of fire, leading to a multitude of other logical fallacies. To dispel this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, within the undifferentiated fire and so forth, there is the causal relation and heat."
The nature of being the referent of this or that word is considered to be derived solely from valid cognition.
In this regard— on the view that "the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) comes to rest with each individual manifestation (pratyābhāsam)," there is no defect whatsoever; for instance,
although the manifestation of fire is indistinct [from others], it remains unmixed with manifestations such as those of space and time.

Because its nature consists solely of the universal (sāmānya), nevertheless, that very manifestation enters the path of certainty established by the means of valid cognition only after having assimilated as many manifestations as are inseparably linked to it and determined by the Blessed One’s power of necessity (niyati-śakti).

Consequently, the manifestation of fire [enters this state] through the manifestation of being an effect of fuel, the manifestation of being a cause of smoke, and the manifestation of having heat as its intrinsic nature.
And an essential, non-deviating rule, when perceived, is perceived as such everywhere and at all times—
because it is one and the same.
Even that nature which is non-essential, being dependent upon human conventions and the like, [is likewise perceived].
For example—such as being denotable by the word "fire," or being capable of producing the cognition of a jar, and so forth—all of these are determined from a single perception alone.

For that cognizer, this manifestation of fire is perceived through either its artificial or its other form as being inseparable from other manifestations; thus, it is perceived as existing in all places and times.
Thus, in this regard, what is the need for another means of valid cognition?

Since a word may be assigned any meaning at will by human convention—such as saying that "this appearance" refers to an object with a blazing and radiant form—it follows that the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) alone is the refuge in all cases.

What is meant by this is that whether something is artificial or otherwise, whenever the appearance of an entity manifests as being inseparable from another appearance, there the power of necessity alone is the ultimate [determinant].

That [manifestation], however, is of the nature of *niyati* (necessity) over an extended period of time—whether it appears as the effect of fuel, the cause of smoke, or the nature of heat; the distinction is that for a very short duration, it appears as the denotation of words such as "fire" and so forth.
Consequently, by depending upon the power of *niyati*, even the manifestation of smoke does not deviate from the manifestation of fire, and thus there is no error whatsoever.
The state of being an effect, the state of being a cause, heat, and the denotation of each respective word— that is, being the referent of those specific words—
and by the inclusion of the term "etcetera," [the states of] being devoid of smell and taste, possessing conjunction with the upward direction, and being opposed to water:
such a self-nature or essence in fire and so forth is known from a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)— that is to say, it is cognized.

"Non-interruption" (aviccheda) is this convention regarding poetry, but not regarding a formal treatise; even if the second and third quarters [of a verse] are combined as one whole, there is no fault.

The use of the suffix indicating separation (*pṛthagbhāva*) is intended to indicate a distinction between categories based on whether they depend or do not depend on another entity, and based on being produced or unproduced. //8//
Thus, the determination of the intrinsic nature of entities is performed by a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that rests upon each individual manifestation; furthermore,

the mutual inseparability (*nāntarīyakatva*) of those manifestations, as appropriate, is ascertained by a single form of consciousness whose inward-turned nature animates the preceding collection of cognitions regarding the objects manifested through those various means of valid cognition.

And that [synthetic awareness] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) insofar as it consists of the synthesis of a mere appearance of unity; however, with respect to the appearances being synthesized, it is not a means of valid cognition because it apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitvāt*); in that case, each individual [appearance] is itself the prior means of valid cognition.

To demonstrate the manner in which bodily activity—which is distinct from the operation of the mind that establishes the intrinsic nature of entities—is useful as an object of valid cognition, he says: "But for one who desires [an object], there may be an immediate activity directed toward a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is distinct from other perceptions such as those of place and so forth... (IPK 2.3.9)

External causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) first pertains to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); and regarding this particularity, the internal factor is precisely the conjunction with the appearances of space and time. Even there, the specific form is nothing at all without reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

However, by means of reflective awareness, it comes to rest within the subject; and because the subject, whose sole nature is consciousness, is a unity due to the non-connection with space and time, it indeed abandons its specific form.
Thus, in every case, non-duality is the ultimate reality.
Nevertheless, that which is the cause of the manifestation of specific form is precisely the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord;
this is called the power of *māyā*.

In that regard, for one who desires a particular purposeful action to be accomplished through a specific [object], the activity of speech, mind, and body directed toward that object—which possesses its own specific characteristics and specific form—at that very moment, occurs in space.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there are many other perceptions—such as those occurring at a specific time, regarding a different nature, or in the subsequent reflection upon that [object]—which arise when there is a distinct difference as the cause; it does not happen otherwise.

That activity does not proceed from each individual means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) alone, but rather from the collection (*samūha*) of the means of knowledge. Furthermore, for the opponent, such a state of being a collection is not tenable.
But for us, that [consciousness] is understood as consisting of repose in a single self-awareness;
as was stated previously:
"If it were not internalized... (IPK 2.3.7).
In this context, this very [process] is the application of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and it is called the "reasoning that applies" (*yojikā yukti*).
It is like the reasoning [involved in preparing] substances such as perfumes.
The intended meaning is that activity proceeds from the very collection of perceptions themselves.
Even in the case of perceptions regarding space and so forth, there is a connection— either by way of the synthesis of the appearance of space and so on,
or by way of that which is the internal, undivided particular (svalakṣaṇa) within the cognizer (pramātṛ).

Alternatively, the construction may be understood as follows: "Activity occurs when the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) has become differentiated by other appearances—such as place and so forth—which are perceived by other means of direct perception.

In this case as well, following the same method used for determining the multiplicity of objects of cognition (prameya), the collection of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is stated to be the cause.
Now, is the collection of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) useful only for activity that is based on perception? No, he says:
"Also from inference. (IPK 2.3.9)

Activity does not proceed solely from perception—namely, from the collection of means of knowledge consisting of the various distinctions of perceived objects such as place and so forth—but likewise also from inference.

This occurs when there is the mere appearance of smoke and the mere appearance of fire, given that smoke is invariably concomitant with the appearance of fire; and when there are other perceptions regarding the appearance of a mountain, and separately, regarding the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) concerning what was grasped therein, in the form "fire is here."

The connection is as follows: inference is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and it is precisely from that collection [of cognitions] that the activity of one who desires an object occurs at that time. //9//
Thus, the determination of difference and non-difference arises solely through the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);
for that indeed is the manifestation of the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord Śiva, whose nature is consciousness.
Consequently, even that which is asserted by others—that there is no difference in the object regardless of whether it is distant or near—is thereby established.
But it is not otherwise in any way— this is what is being determined.
[This occurs] through the remoteness or proximity of objects, and by way of their being beyond perception or directly perceived.
Whether by external or internal defects, or otherwise, [the manifestation] is affected by faults.

Even for those whose appearances and shadows are distinct, their unity is not precluded by virtue of a primary manifestation known as a single unifying reflective awareness (ekapratyavamarśa). (IPK 2.3.11)
For one who establishes [reality] based on mere appearance (*pratibhāsa*) alone, how can there be no difference between objects that are distant and those that are near,

given that appearance itself differs in some way according to whether it is complete or incomplete, obscured or unobscured, and so forth? But surely, even in the case of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there is likewise a differentiation for each individual appearance?
True; nevertheless, that supreme reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) itself is this very category of object (*padārtha*), consisting in the form of a single unifying recognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*).
By means of that which is like its vitalizing principle, there occurs the manifestation—that is, the unfolding—on all sides of the primary appearance, the appearance of the state of a single form.
For even within that single unifying recognition, there exists an appearance of unity that is appropriate to it.
Because manifestation (*ābhāsa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) are inseparable from one another,
the oneness of the primary manifestation remains unimpeded.
That which is inferred is precisely that which is perceived.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: for those things whose secondary manifestations (*avabhāsa*) consist of appearances that are differentiated by their own nature (*svabhāva*) in the form of being either perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) or imperceptible (*parokṣa*), there is unity through the primary manifestation, which is animated by a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*).
This is the unity of appearances that are differentiated as external or internal, such as: "That very thing which was seen, that same thing I now delineate internally as 'I'."
Due to defects in the manifestors—such as lamps, light, and so forth—the appearances [of objects] become unified;
for instance, one thinks: "That very same red lotus which was seen as blue by the lamp, I now see as red by the rays of the sun.
