Furthermore, by another manner—such as through a deficiency of the sense organs or by being positioned on one side facing [the object]—those whose shadows of appearance are distinct [are nevertheless perceived as one].

Even for those [individuals], on account of the power of the nature of manifestation which conforms to the primary reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), there is indeed unity; thus it is established. // 10 // 11 //
Now, one might object: "Let it be that the same object exists whether at a distance or nearby, since it is equally useful in the respect of the causal efficiency determined by the cognizer;

but how can this apply to the distinction between external and internal? For there is no application of an internal object to a causal efficiency as determined by the cognizer. To dispel this delusion, he says:
Even the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of objects is innate and not determined by the will of a Lord;
for that [efficiency] is fixed by Him, and thus its non-activity could not be anything other than [the absence of] activity. (IPK 2.3.12)

In this context, regarding the phrase "the state of performing an action" (*kāryakaraṇatā*), that purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) which was enumerated in between— just like the essential nature itself—
is not something that constitutes the innate nature of the object.
For that capacity to act is indeed determined by the will of God (Īśvara) regarding both the coming into being and the non-coming into being [of things].

Since this [capacity] is not the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of the entity, one should not suspect a change in the entity's state due to its non-production; for a change would be possible only through a difference in intrinsic nature, and the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva) is not the intrinsic nature [of the entity].
This has been stated [previously] and will be stated many times more;

and the essential nature [of consciousness] is indeed one alone, by virtue of the power of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), even with respect to what is external, internal, and so forth. //12//

Now, if the determination of difference and non-difference among objects arises solely from the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), then all talk of delusion has now ceased in the three worlds;
for even in the case of mother-of-pearl, it would follow that it is truly silver, since it is being reflected upon as "this is silver.
Consequently, in the absence of delusion, sublation (*bādhā*) would be impossible; so for what purpose was it said that "cognition is uncontradicted with respect to the object" (IPK 2.3.2)?
He dispels the doubt that "if there is no deviation (vyabhicāra), then nothing would be excluded by the qualification 'unsublated' (abādhitā)" by stating:
"Even when there is a single cognition of silver, there is no actual state of being silver in the mother-of-pearl."
Because there is no contradiction regarding the location of the substrate, the sky remains otherwise even in the case of the double moon.

"This is silver, stable, common to all subjects, and capable of causal efficiency"—in this [cognition], there is no falsity whatsoever regarding the "this" aspect, the "silver" aspects, or the aspect of their synthesis, by virtue of the power of the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of those manifestations. However, at a later time, there will arise a reflective awareness: "This is not silver; it is not a stable reality, nor is it accessible to other subjects, nor does it perform the desired function."

Thus, that which is to be reflected upon by that [subsequent] reflection must indeed possess a form appropriate to the time of the preceding reflection; yet, at that very time of the preceding reflection, it is not reflected upon as such, for there must be something to be reflected upon.

For in that very context, the subsequent reflective awareness is "this was not silver," and not a reflective awareness of "this is not" at this present moment, like [the thought of] a flash of lightning that has already arisen and vanished.
Therefore, as long as that which ought to be manifested in its complete form up to the limit of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is not so manifested,

this non-manifestation (*akhyāti*), consisting in incomplete manifestation, is itself the essence of error. By virtue of that, let other forms of manifestation— such as the manifestation of the non-existent (*asat-khyāti*), the contrary (*viparīta-khyāti*), or the inexpressible (*anirvacanīya-khyāti*)— also be spoken of.
But is not even the cognition of real silver an incomplete manifestation (*apūrṇakhyāti*)? What follows from that?
This: therefore, everything is an error (*bhrānti*).
Thus he would come, saying:
"By good fortune, the vision of the Venerable One shall be opened;
for the entire realm of illusion is indeed delusion."
Even there, however, this other delusion is said to be like a dream within a dream, or like a pustule upon a boil,
because even the reflective awareness (vimarśa) that is appropriate for persistence lacks stability.
And therefore, there is no delusion whatsoever regarding the appearances of "this-ness" (idantā) and so forth as distinct [from the self].

However, regarding the objective aspect (mekanāṃśa), the eradication of the persistence of reflective awareness (vimarśa) is carried out by the subverting cognition starting from the very moment that reflective awareness arises;
thus, it is established that the state of error resides precisely there.

Although there is a single reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) regarding silver together with the mother-of-pearl, nevertheless, that state which was conferred upon the silver by the cognition "this is silver" with respect to the mother-of-pearl does not [belong to it],
because the locus of the mother-of-pearl— which is of the nature of a limiting condition (*upādhi*)— colors itself with the reflection of silver, thinking "silver is here."
Because of its lack of correspondence;
"correspondence" (saṃvādana) is the manifestation through the persistence of correct reflection, and here the root *vad* has the sense of "manifestation"—
it is because of the absence of that [correspondence] as the cause.
Granted, let this be the case with the silver in mother-of-pearl;
however, in the cognition of two moons, where there is the appearance "two moons," no convergence with anything—such as with the mother-of-pearl—is manifested, wherein a sublation could occur;
and as for the aspect of the single manifestation, there is no sublation there either.
This has been stated by you yourself.
Who says this—that there is no conjunction with anything?
For if that were so, how could there be an appearance characterized by its own specific nature (*svālakṣaṇya*) and restricted to a particular place and time?
Even there, in conjunction with space and time, there exists an appearance of their fusion, wherein the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that seeks to persist is obstructed;
likewise, in the case of the appearances of duality and the moon, one must speak of the cessation of the persistence of reflective awareness within the appearance of their fusion.
This is what he says: "even in the case of the two-fold moon."
It is not only in the case of silver;
"the sky" is a particular location. "Otherwise" means that which was examined as being occupied by two moons is not so [in reality].
"—thus, by means of the subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), the persistence of the previous reflective awareness is uprooted.
In this way, manifestation and their unification are animated by necessity; this alone is the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
These very things will be explained as the *tattvas* in the *Āgama*.
"Entity," "reality," and "object of cognition" are synonyms.
Likewise, that which appears as hardness is earth;
that which appears as red is form and fire.
The appearance of cohesion is *rajas*,
while the structural arrangement is of the nature of *niyati*;
for *niyati* is indeed restriction (*niyama*).
And that is the vital breath of non-existence (abhāvaprāṇa); moreover,
the very manifestation of non-existence appearing as the manifoldness of the earth-manifestation is its form with a broad base and belly,
and the appearance of duality is māyā.
Following that, the appearance of the light of truth is the Śiva-tattva;
let this suffice for now, as it will be addressed further on.

In every respect, therefore, regarding this object of knowledge (*prameya*), the Blessed Lord alone possesses sovereignty over both its differentiation and non-differentiation; and the very perception of the difference or non-difference of appearances residing in a jar is the means that must be relied upon for entering into the ultimate vision of non-duality (*advaya*). This conventional usage, moreover, is not in contradiction with the penetration into the essential nature of the Supreme Lord.
Thus it has been established. //13//
Clarifying this very point, he demonstrates that the establishment of all objects of knowledge depends solely upon the Supreme Lord:
"Difference [is established] by means of qualities such as sound, and non-difference by means of universals and the like."
In this way, the existence of all entities is established within a single cognizer.
In this world, regarding an object that appears as both continuous and discrete, by which of these two forms could it not be called real? For there is no sublation (bādhaka) in either case.

Indeed, if there were a sublation of one of the two from the perspective of reality, then upon its arising, that very part would dissolve like a flash of lightning, incapable of re-emerging; but such is not the case.

Therefore, those who consider the contradiction between difference and non-difference to be irresolvable maintain that both are of the nature of ignorance (avidyā) and thus indeterminable (anirvācya).
Furthermore, those who assert that things are merely conventional because they are attached to appearances have deceived both themselves and others.
However, both [subject and object] shine as resting within consciousness due to the sovereignty of consciousness.

For this is established by the self-awareness of everyone, even down to an animal: that even water and fire, when brought into unity by resting within the interior of consciousness, are not contradictory.
Therefore it has been said:
"For this very reason, [there is] the delineation of whatever is intended...

(IPK 1.6.11). And thus, the distinction that arises from qualities (*guṇa*)—which are intended as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—whether by means of sound and so forth, or even by means of a staff and so forth;
Whether by virtue of genus, similarity, or the non-apprehension of difference—
that non-difference of entities which has been established according to the method thus described, starting from [the section on] "the connection with action" (2.2.1)— is as follows:

This [phenomenon] is possible only when there exists the Lord, designated by the term *Śiva*, who dwells exclusively within our hearts, and whose sovereignty is suited to the manifold and innumerable array of diverse activities—such as the conjunction and disjunction of all cognitions and means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) within a single cognizer; it is not otherwise.

Furthermore, since the qualifiers themselves are the differentiators, what is the use of other ultimate particulars (*viśeṣas*)? This is that very atom which, at the time of the commencement of a jar characterized by such-and-such a location and so forth, was the constituent of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) formed subsequently during the process of aggregation.
He has been encountered before;
this is that very self who, in the past, in the abode of heaven, thus embraced this celestial nymph.

Thus, by this much alone, the appearance of difference regarding atoms, the self, and so forth, is established for the omniscient ones among the yogis; enough with this digression. It is established, therefore, that the reality of the object of knowledge, which consists of both difference and non-difference, attains freedom from doubt through its repose in the single subject. //14//

Now, if this cognizer is indeed of such a nature, then one should strive to present the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) precisely there, and not the object of cognition (*prameya*), as it is said: "For effort directed toward the primary [goal] is fruitful.
Anticipating this objection, the Teacher reminds us of the very object of cognition that was introduced at the outset. To explain:
"Who, being of non-inert nature, could effect either a negation or an establishment?

(IPK 1.1.2). Thus, only that reality which is now fit to be sustained once the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the nature of the Supreme Lord have been known—such indeed is the means of knowledge; for how could such a means of knowledge function toward a Blessed One who is of such a nature?
To clarify this, he says:
"In the Supreme Lord, who is ultimately real, who is untouched by contradictory states, and who is like a perfectly level wall for the painting of the manifold variety of the universe. (Ipk 2.3.15)
But when the subject is the primordial one, whose form is eternally manifest, what new manifestation could there be as a means of knowledge for that which partakes in all cognition? (IPK 2.3.16)

It has been stated that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the ever-new manifestation directed toward the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which is grounded in the limited subject (*parimitapramātṛ*).
In that regard, what utility or even possibility could there be for a means of knowledge within the Light, whose nature is pure luminosity and which is already established?

And thus, since the subject is already established, the means of knowledge bestows upon the object of knowledge an unprecedented establishment consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is contained within the luminosity grounded in that [subject].
And for a knower who is himself unestablished, how could there be an established connection?
For the manifold variety of the universe shines forth within the Supreme Lord, whose sole nature is Light, just as a painting appears upon a wall.

If blue, yellow, and so forth were perceived as entirely separate from one another, then—while resting within their own respective selves—the cognitions regarding each other's objects would be like those of the dull-witted, the blind, and the deaf; they would be restricted solely to their own particular objects.

And since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise in accordance with that [perception], they are likewise [of that nature]; thus, how could there be a cognition that "this is a painting"? However, in the case of a single surface such as a wall—which is devoid of actual depressions and elevations, yet possesses divisions of depression and elevation demarcated by lines—the appearance of a painting, such as "this woman has a deep navel and elevated breasts," is indeed logical.
In the same way, the emergence of differentiation, which consists of manifold variety, occurs by virtue of being grounded in the single wall of light;
thus, he declares the self-luminosity of the wall of light, which never departs from the apprehension of the differences between entities.
In that regard, what is the need for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) concerning that which is self-luminous?
Now, if it is argued that its manifestation did not previously exist,
then it would follow that it does not exist at all, because its nature consists solely of manifestation;
yet it is not the case that this [consciousness] does not exist.
Thus, contact is established through non-existence,
for that alone is real from the perspective of ultimate truth,
because of the very existence of light.

And because it is impossible for that which exists to have the nature of non-existence. Now, if it is argued: "His status as Lord (Īśvara) is not yet cognized, but will be cognized"—that too is not correct; for if he does not manifest as a cognizer (pramātṛ), of whom could this [status] be predicated?
If it shines forth, then subjectivity itself is lordship;
thus he says: "In the Lord, the subject, whose form is eternally manifest.
It is called *vigraha* because it is specifically grasped (*viśeṣeṇa gṛhyate*); that is, its unique, uncommon essential nature.

Precisely because its nature is independent luminosity, there is no temporal convention here involving entry into non-existence, since that would entail contact with non-existence; thus it is stated in the *Purāṇa*: "It does not exist here. What is the proof for this?
For what purpose is there a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and what is the utility of that means of valid cognition therein? Thus [it is asked].
And in that regard, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? The meaning is that nothing at all is established by logical reasoning.

For a so-called means of valid cognition becomes a *pramāṇa* only when, in the form of a novel manifestation, it effects a repose characterized as valid knowledge (*pramiti*) within the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
And the cognizer is one whose manifestation is uninterrupted; he enjoys all acts of valid knowledge within himself in his inward-turned nature.

Therefore, how can there be a novel manifestation therein, and where could its cognition find rest? Consequently, let it be said that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) resides only in a subject who is essentially nothing more than the body, the vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void.
And even there, it may apply to the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*), but by no means to the aspect of consciousness (*saṃvid-aṃśa*).

Even in that case, since [consciousness] is contracted precisely because it is oriented toward an object, let self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) be called the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its connection to the true subject who is free from contraction within the manifestation of the new [object].

Even for the Buddhist, that [self-awareness] must be accepted as being connected to an imagined subject in the form "this is my cognition," but there is nothing whatsoever by means of a means of knowledge regarding the ultimate subject.
And this has been stated by me myself:
"Everyone feels ashamed within themselves at the thought, 'I have been made an object of cognition';
how then could the Great Lord endure being made an object of cognition?

Now, if it is the case that there is neither utility nor logical possibility for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the Blessed One, for what purpose is there a treatise (*śāstra*) concerning him?
For that [treatise] is indeed a means of valid cognition; for a treatise consists of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
And in that regard, the ultimate truth consists precisely in the reality of the sixteen categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As for what is criticized by the Buddhists regarding the five-membered syllogism and so forth, that is merely due to their dogmatic attachment;
for when the sixteen categories are properly examined, the opponent is correctly led to an understanding of what is to be established.
And by the passage beginning with "the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful," [it is shown that] what is the purpose for another?
For that [teaching] is for the sake of another's comprehension.
And that [inference] is for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*);
therein lies the utility of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the other members.

Thus, in the ultimate sense, the entire treatise—which brings about the complete understanding of another—is *parārthānumāna*. This was determined by Akṣapāda, the creator of the system of logic (*nyāya*), as distinct from mere scripture (*āgama*).
Thus, even here, he says [the following] in order to remind [us] of what was previously stated: "But [this occurs] through the power of delusion" (Ipk 1.1.3).
"In this case, it has never occurred before; it is solely due to the power of ignorance."
Through the manifestation of power, the conventional usage of [the lords] Īśa and the others is set in motion.

In this regard, the supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord consists precisely in this: the accomplishment of things that are exceedingly difficult to achieve and impossible for those in our current state as limited, animal-like subjects (*paśu*).
What, then, could be more difficult than this:
that while the Light manifests in its own undivided nature, there nevertheless appears the manifestation of a negation of that very manifestation?

Therefore, that supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord—which consists in not manifesting [the world] as it truly is, but rather manifesting it in the form of a bound soul (paśu), namely, the emergence of the subjective aspect and through that, the manifestation of the objective aspect—is called the Blessed One’s power of Māyā. As it has been said: "Māyā is known as the deluder..."

Thus, from such sovereignty—which consists of the power of *māyā*—there arises a state of delusion, which is the destruction of full consciousness. This refers to the fullness of one’s own nature, which is filled with the manifestation of the universe clearly pulsing forth from the emergence of the vibration of Will; as well as to sovereignty, which consists of the powers of memory and so forth.

Due to the contraction and deficiency of space and time, there occurs a conceit that what is manifest is not manifest, despite its being a reality whose sovereignty and eternity are effortlessly established;
by virtue of— that is, through the power of— that [conceit],
[the state] was previously not set forth in the Lord, the subject, whose nature was described in the two preceding verses, as being [identical with] Īśvara and so forth.

Let people carry on their worldly discourse by means of that very [notion] already mentioned—such as fullness and so forth—which indeed appears as "I am," and which is of the nature: "He is full, all-pervading, independent, and eternal.
Let them thus engage in such conventional usage.

By this treatise— which consists of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) aimed at accomplishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which reveals the powers of will, knowledge, and action, and which takes the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)— the performance of those [powers] is carried out for those who set that transaction in motion. The two *ṇic* suffixes [in the words *pravartayatām* and *pravartyate*] signify "causing to act" and "being set in motion," respectively.
The word "only" (kevalam) means that nothing new is being created,
nor is anything that is not actually manifesting being made manifest;
rather, what is removed is the misconception that something which is already manifesting is not manifesting.
For indeed, the very withdrawal from that [identification] is the attainment of supreme lordship, which is liberation; the non-withdrawal from it is transmigratory existence (saṃsāra);
for both of these have as their essence nothing more than mere mental conceit.
Both of these, moreover, are indeed the manifestation of the Blessed One himself.

This is what is meant: just as the delusion of a terrified person—who, while his own self is manifesting, thinks out of ignorance "I have been carried away"—is dispelled [by being asked], "Who indeed are you? [so too is the delusion of the world dispelled].
If it is argued that "he has such clothing and such a face," [the teacher] replies by repeatedly stating, "See, that exists in abundance elsewhere," yet nothing new has been created for him.
Likewise, the delusion of the worldly person— who, while perceiving the Self, falsely identifies with it through delusion, thinking "I am not the Lord," and so forth— is dispelled.
For he who is endowed with sovereignty over knowledge and action is the Lord (īśvara), as is well known in the Siddhāntas, Purāṇas, and other texts; and such you are.
Alternatively, he upon whom something depends is the lord thereof, just as a king is the lord within his own realm.
And likewise, since the entire universe resides in you,
the designation "Lordship" has no other cause;
this is the pervasion (vyāpti).
Indeed, whatever appears as conjoined with something is filled by that, like a treasure-chest with jewels; and the universe is conjoined with You.
Thus, whatever appears within someone, that person is pervasive over that extent, like a casket containing jewels.
And within you, whose nature is consciousness, resides the entire universe—from the earth up to Sadāśiva—as described in the systematic exposition of the scriptures.

That which arises and dissolves while something else remains present must pervade its preceding and succeeding parts, just as a sprout exists upon the ground; and so too does the universe exist within you, whose nature is light.

In this way, other phenomena as well— even by the thousands— established through scripture and other means, should be applied accordingly. Thus, when delusion has been dispelled, even though the body and so forth persist merely due to its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), for one who has known the reality of a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), there remains only the conceit of "self" regarding the body and so forth preceded by the conceit of "non-self," while the conceit of "non-self" remains manifest regarding jars and the like.
Just as one who perceives a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) does not experience delusion regarding its true nature, so it is for one who has recognized the true nature of the Self.
When the body—having reached its end through the process of departure—has ceased to exist, there is nothing but the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratā*).

However, by the power of the cultivation of practice (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*) taught in the Śiva-scriptures, one who, having firmly entered into the immersion of the state of the Supreme Lord within the very body, a jar, or other objects, perceives [the Divine], experiences the emergence of the qualities that are portions of the Supreme Lord's sovereignty right here in this body.
But this is not actual fullness;
for when the limitation of the very life-force of embodied existence dissolves, one attains the state of being the universal self as it truly is.
However, for one who maintains the conceit of non-establishment even regarding the collection of reasons used to accomplish worldly transaction, [this is not the case].
Even in that case, his delusion must be removed by means of conventional linguistic instruments alone;
however, for one in whom it does not depart in any way,
that is simply a state of stupidity resulting from the power of the Lord’s creative energy (īśvara-śakti).
Because that [impression] also enters the path of the ear, its recovery of its own nature will necessarily occur at some point through the ripening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, what was stated by the two verses beginning with "kartari" (IPK 1.1.2) has been further refined and re-examined by the three verses beginning with "viśvavaicitrya" (IPK 1.5.1).
Such, then, is the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How, then, could it be established in the case of the Blessed One who is of such a nature?
Therefore, what was stated at the beginning of the treatise is now justified by means of this alternative formulation. Thus all is auspicious. (17) [Total: 120]

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Means of Knowledge, its Fruit, and the Object of Knowledge," in the *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, within the section on Action (*kriyādhikāra*).
In the section on Action, the fourth daily lesson:
We praise that Śiva, the Agent who, manifesting all entities within the stainless mirror of his own self, creates the wondrous relationship between cause and effect.

Having established the true nature of the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*jñāpya-jñāpakabhāva*) by way of its primary connection with the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), another chapter (*āhnika*) is commenced with twenty-one verses in order to establish the true nature of the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
This begins with the words "And this... and concludes with "Thus, will alone is causality, agency, and action."

In this regard, by means of one verse, the author introduces his own position that the very relationship of agent and object (*kartṛ-karmabhāva*) is the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Thereafter, with three verses, the causality of the insentient (*jaḍa*) is refuted.
Then, with six verses, the causality of consciousness alone, in the form of agency,
is established. Following that, as a corollary, it is stated in three verses that the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) must necessarily be relied upon in inference.
Therefore, even the ultimate reality of cause and effect as taught by the followers of Sugata relies upon our own position;
otherwise, it would be nothing at all—
thus [it is stated] in three verses.
Even the relation of cause and effect demonstrated by the Sāṃkhya is not tenable if the agency of the conscious principle, as stated by us, is not accepted—
thus [it is concluded] with three [verses].
Even for one who possesses volition, this [creation] is not possible if there is a lack of sovereignty;
such is the summary meaning of the phrase "by both.
Now, the text itself shall be explained.
Having thus established, by way of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), that the Blessed One possesses the nature of the single subject (*pramātṛ*) as that which must be conventionally designated,
[the author] says the following to show that the nature of the agent (*kartṛ-rūpatā*) is also established from that very same source without effort:
And because he possesses infinite power, he causes these entities to appear in this way by the force of his will; this is his activity, which is his creative agency. (IPK 2.4.1)
The word *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

This very same primordial subject (*pramātā*) manifests these very entities—those manifestations (*ābhāsas*) that have been manifested before—in an uninterrupted continuity. How so? By the power and efficacy of the Will, which is non-different from the Lord, non-conceptual in form, and devoid of succession. Where, then, were those entities situated prior to this?
He said: "Because of its infinite power.
For all things exist as His very power, having their own nature as His own essence; as it was said: "{Of Him who is non-different and abiding in Himself...}" (Ipk 1.5.10).
In this context: that which is this manifestation and that which is the will, that is action;
it is the creative agency of this Blessed Lord. //1//
But surely a sprout is seen arising from a seed, and no conscious agent is observed entering into this process; so how can this have been stated?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"But that power does not belong to the insentient; for existence arises from non-existence.
Therefore, the nature of cause and effect consists precisely in the status of agent and object. (IPK 2.4.3)
Whether it be existent,
non-existent, both, neither, or the inexpressible—
it is contradicted by its own words; so what is the use of this?
If a jar were non-existent, then its very nature of non-existence would be its ultimate reality; how then could it admit existence, which is contrary to its own nature?
For even by a hundred prostrations at one's feet, blue does not tolerate yellowness within itself.
If the pot already exists, then what else is requested beyond the staff, the wheel, and the string?
Even such qualities as manifestation, being an object of perception, and clarity must be considered in terms of their nature as either existent or non-existent.
"Surely, then, one should remain silent";
[the author] says that even this is not correct: "And yet, it is said... (Ipk 2.4.3).
This means that this matter must necessarily be accomplished. //3//
And thus, he shows how this is logically established: "In the world, the relationship of cause and effect belongs to that which revolves internally;
its perceptibility by both types of sense organs occurs due to the power of a certain [internal] factor. (IPK 2.4.4)

Within the heart of the Potter (Kumbhakāra), because it is the object of the inner mind, there is that very state of being both cause and effect, wherein the world— which, even previously, existed as a single essence within one's own self-consciousness and which manifests through its vibration as a variety consisting of both difference and non-difference— is made manifest as the object of perception by both the internal and external organs.
This indeed is the nature of cause and effect.
The mention of "both" is illustrative;
that is to say, for whatever [object], to whatever extent its full purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) reaches completion.
The "creation" (*nirmāṇa*) of pleasure and so forth consists precisely in making them objects of cognition solely by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Nor does this [consciousness] reside in the potter, who is like a body devoid of life, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and intellect,
because he too is insentient. Therefore,
consciousness alone manifests the universe within itself through the variety of its powers.
"Of that certain one" refers to what was previously mentioned, meaning: of Him whose majesty is inconceivable and beyond questioning.
Nor should it be said that being perceivable by both types of sense organs is either existent or non-existent;
for this is the ultimate truth here: just as in the reflection of a jar or other object being fashioned by a potter within a mirror, the power of appearing in such a way belongs to the mirror alone.

Likewise, in the perception of a dream, although there is consciousness, nevertheless, by the very power of that [consciousness], the conceit arises: "By this [consciousness], this external object is made manifest in a clear form.
In the same way, when a jar exists in the hands of a potter along with the staff, wheel, and so forth, by the very power of that [consciousness] alone, the conceit arises.
"Just as this was done by me,
this was done by him;
it has throbbed in my heart."

"It has flashed forth in his heart"—in this regard, since the conceit of agency is utterly remote in the case of insentient things such as clay and the like, agency is established as being the very nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*).
Now, one might object: "Let this [agency] be manifested simply as a positive entity; why is it stated here that it is perceivable by two types of sense organs?"
By this, it has been clearly stated that form is capable of purposeful action;
thus, what contradiction is there? //4//
And by this investigation, the nature of action under discussion is also established;
thus he shows:
"In this way, that very single action has a sequential existence both internally and externally."
It has been established that a single [entity] alone is capable of sustaining both aspects.

Regarding the phrase "this very [consciousness]": that which was previously criticized on the grounds that its existence is untenable both in terms of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its substratum (*āśraya*), has now been established through logical demonstration.
For, beginning from the internal nature of consciousness itself and extending outward to the range of the senses, its state consists in manifestation (*ābhāsanā*).
For that very reason, [the sequence] is established as being successive through its embrace with the object of knowledge (*vedya*), which is of the nature of action (*karman*);
and it is also unitary because of the identity consisting in the single locus of both agent and object.
And that single locus, by virtue of its nature as consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpatva*), sustains both the internal and external forms through its transparency and autonomy. //5//
Now, one might object: "Let this be so in the case of a jar and the like;
but in cases such as the seed and the sprout, where no entry of consciousness is observed, why is it that the sprout does not become the effect of the seed alone?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That which is internal with respect to something else is its external effect;
thus, the dual state of being external or internal is described in relation to the subject. (IPK 2.4.6)
Therefore, the Mother alone is the cause; and while abiding as a twofold manifestation, she alone remains as the effect. Thus, the activity of the One is proclaimed.
Emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is the external manifestation of that which appears internally, precisely without abandoning its internal form.

Consequently, whatever object is said to be "internal" in relation to something else, that very object becomes fit for externalization—that is, it is capable of being made external—as a mere transformation of its internal form.

Since all entities that appear internally are relative to the cognizer whose nature is consciousness, they appear as external only in relation to him; therefore, it is logical that their manifestation as external occurs through that very [cognizer].
And therefore, the cognizer alone is the cause, not the insentient;
for the word "hi" (indeed) has the sense of "because.
Since that cognizer exists as the cause of the twofold manifestation—internal and external—the two manifestations, which depend upon him, would be impossible without him.
Therefore, agency—the state of being a creator—is manifested as an established form for a single cognizing subject alone, and not in any way for that which is insentient. //7//
This very point is confirmed:

"For this very reason, even in the case of a sprout, the Supreme Lord is accepted as the cause; otherwise, the causality of other factors such as the seed and so forth would not be logically tenable. (IPK 2.4.8)
Since the creator is thus indeed consciousness itself, for this very reason the Naiyāyikas and others have accepted the Supreme Lord—who possesses intellect—as the cause of the sprout and so forth.
Now, one might object: they have accepted His status as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) by way of atoms and other factors that arise through a sequence of action, disjunction, and so on.

However, it has been stated that through a succession of initiations by its own constituent parts, which are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), even things other than that Lord— such as seeds, soil, and water— possess causality. True, it has been so stated, but that [causality] is not logically tenable.
Because, according to the reasoning already stated, an insentient entity cannot function as a cause;
therefore, it is the Lord alone who, through association with the appearances of seed, soil, and water, manifests in the form of a sprout—this much is the ultimate truth here. //8//
Anticipating the opponent’s delusion—asking, "What is contradicted by postulating an intelligent cause distinct from the observed seeds and so forth?"—he says, in order to dispel it:
"For indeed, this potter, through a specific arrangement of his own power, would produce a jar by means of a sequence of refinements upon that particular clay and other materials. (IPK 2.4.9)
For thus, by beginning with an illustration (*tathā hi*), he confirms that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed of such a nature:
"Inert causes perform their effects only when impelled by a conscious agent."
If clay and the other factors were to produce the effect by their mere proximity, what role would the potter have here?

If it is argued that they produce it through a succession of stages such as the cart, the mound, and so forth, and that this succession depends upon the potter, then our point is proven: even in the production of the cart, those [factors] require the instigation of a conscious agent.
Inert causes are never capable of producing an effect without being impelled by a conscious agent;
for if they were, then even clay and other such materials would [produce effects on their own]—
this is an absolute certainty.
And therefore, the essential nature [of things] is this: whatever is insentient yet performs an action depends upon a sentient agent, just like clay and so forth, as well as seeds and the like.
For the fact that an insentient entity performs an action is necessarily accompanied by a cause because it occurs only occasionally;
and no other cause for this is possible, as none is perceived.
Thus, if one were not to take the impulsion of a conscious being as the cause, it would follow—contrary to the pervading rule—that the action is causeless.
And that is not tenable,
because it would follow by the same logic even in the case of clay and so forth;
thus, the pervasion (vyāpti) is established.
And for this reason, O Kumbhaka-deva, the Lord is present there.

This very point he states: "By means of the arrangement consisting of the form of the Lord, whatever refinement there is of the clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth—that is, the kneading of the clay [is performed]."
The straightness of the pole,
the turning of the wheel, and so forth;
that sequence which constitutes their commencement, consisting of forms such as the palanquin and the funeral mound.
Therefore, he necessarily produces the jar, and not otherwise; the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes this necessity.

Furthermore, if one does not become angry [at this], then even the potter, by virtue of the very sovereignty consisting in his nature as the independent Self of the universe, acts through the manifestation of his own power called "necessity" (*niyati*), which is demonstrated in dependence upon the preparation of the clay and other materials.
[The Lord] would produce [them];
otherwise, how could insentient things like clay conform to the will of the potter? Or why would even threads not heed the desire to produce a cloth?
This very point has been stated by this same Sūtra with the words "for thus.
[Objection: But if it were so, the potter would have no status as an agent, and thus the established order of dharma and adharma would collapse.
If you accept this through both reason and scripture, then it is exactly so;

nevertheless, even in the midst of all other emanations, this too was created by the Supreme Lord himself: namely, that unshakable conceit of false agency held by that potter-animal, which is like a debtor’s conceit of indebtedness toward his guarantor.

If, however, it is argued that this very desire of the Lord is such that "let no such conceit arise in him," then he is not a creator at all. This too has been stated by the author of the Sūtras with the words "tathā hi" (for thus).

Even for a potter, the deliberation consisting of inquiry— such as "Shall I produce a jar through the sequence of processing clay and so forth, or shall I not produce it?"— which aims at determining one side or the other,
arises from a state belonging to the Lord alone, characterized by the various concealment of his own nature and the manifestation of reality.
Thus, the suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of inquiry.
Therefore, in reality, the Lord alone is the agent everywhere,
and since I am He, I am not a limited agent.
Rather, it is established that one must, in every way, fix this much in one's heart: "The agent exists everywhere. //9//
It is observed that this conscious being possesses sovereignty alone, which unfolds everywhere and brings even insentient things to the state of its own self;
for it has been said that insentient things lack the capacity to manifest other objects.
He confirms this by means of an illustration well-known to all disputants:
"Even for yogins, that [pot and so forth] arises from earth and seed even without [those causes], by the power of their will; it performs its respective stable, purposeful actions. (IPK 2.4.10)
If that which is commonly known as a cause— such as clay and so forth, impelled by volition—
and that which is independent of such [volition], such as seeds and so forth, which produce jars and sprouts respectively,
were the only causes in an ultimate sense, then how could the birth of a jar, a sprout, or the like occur through the mere will of a yogi in the absence of those [material causes]?
Because it would follow that [the effect] is causeless, or else because it would follow that those [causes, such as clay or seeds] are not causes at all.
Now, if it is argued: "Those jars, sprouts, and so forth produced from clay, seeds, and the like are one thing entirely, while those produced by the will of a yogi and so forth are quite another."
Thus it is said;
even there, you are being awakened: first of all, non-difference [of the object] arises from the non-difference of reflective awareness—this has already been stated previously.
In that case as well, the yogi indeed possesses unimpeded will;
and his will is such that he thinks, "Let there be a jar which is capable of performing the manifold purposeful actions (arthakriyā) arising from a pot made of clay and other materials.
This is what he says: "A jar or similar object is produced with a form that is a cause for, and conforms to, the performance of various stable purposeful actions"—thus it is said.
As for those who say: "The production of a jar or similar object does not occur without its material cause (upādāna);

however, a yogi, perceiving atoms by means of his will, brings them into conjunction," they should be addressed as follows: If indeed the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva), established through positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka) and scripture (āgama), is not subverted even in the case of yogis, [then your claim is untenable].
Thus, it captivates your hearts; so what is the use of grasping at atoms?

If not, then for a jar there are potsherds, and for a body its own constituent parts; and their respective well-known worldly causes alone are sufficient, which cannot tolerate any other state of being even as much as a blade of grass or a sesame seed.
Thus, in the case of a jar, [the causes] such as clay, staff, and wheel,
and in the case of the body, [the causes] such as the union of male and female— both being required— the arising of the body and so forth is indeed difficult to justify; rather,
it is consciousness itself that becomes such and such [a thing].

The Blessed One, the Great God of abundant splendor, possesses the sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) that consists in both following and transcending necessity (*niyati*). In this regard, his sovereignty over the worldly, well-known relation of cause and effect is one of following necessity; however, for him who honors the transcendence of that [necessity], it pertains to the supramundane realm, which is well-known among those who are like yogis.
Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever;
and this much is indeed the case in the world.

But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that very [Reality] manifests as the nature of the fivefold expansion of activities, such as the creation of the universe in both sequential and non-sequential forms.
For it is the established doctrine that consciousness manifests objects like reflections in the mirror of its own self.
As the former teacher said:
"They extend [the universe] without a collection of material causes, indeed upon no wall at all."
Salutations to that wielder of the trident, who is praiseworthy for his artistic skill and who is the wondrous painting of the universe.
Thus [it is said] in verse 9 of the *Stavacintāmaṇi*.

Now, if effects are produced that possess the same mode of operation as those specific effects [of a cause], even by transgressing the well-known causes, then the discourse of inference is shattered. For instance, one might object: "How can one thing be invariably related to another elsewhere? Anticipating this, those who consider themselves more authoritative have accepted identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) as the grounds for such invariable relation.
For an entity cannot be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*),
nor can it possess a differentiated intrinsic nature, because [in that case] there would be a distinction [of the entity] due to the distinction of its intrinsic natures;
furthermore, since those two types of intrinsic nature do not exist as distinct modes (*paryāyaśas*), it would follow that the entity is devoid of intrinsic nature.
The same should be stated regarding an effect that is either causeless or has a different cause;
in both cases, however, the determination is made solely by the cause.
For it is from its own cause alone that a *śiṃśapā* tree is born as one whose nature is invariably concomitant with being a tree.
Furthermore, by its own cause, fire has the nature of producing smoke;
therefore, if the relationship between cause and effect were now to transgress necessity (*niyati*), all of this would fall apart.
For, by the will of a yogin, even a *śiṃśapā* tree could come to have the nature of a non-tree.
But in the case of smoke, a double effort is required;
for otherwise, the causal complex consisting of fire and so forth produced by the yogi’s will might not produce smoke,
or the yogi’s will might produce smoke without fire.
Thinking that, on these grounds, there would be no inference, yet such [inference] exists in the world, he says:

When the existence of a yogic emanation has been ascertained by another means of valid cognition, [the probans] is either an effect or an essential nature; for it arises from that very [cause], being rooted in origination.

The will of a yogin also produces an effect that is in every respect exactly like that [original], and does not produce an effect that differs even slightly in terms of taste, potency, and so forth— according to the analogy of a scorpion produced from cow-dung and other such sources.
It is precisely for this reason that it has been stated that an effect, such as smoke, serves as a logical reason (*hetu*) for inferring fire and the like,
or that a specific nature, such as being a *śiṃśapā* tree, serves as a logical reason for inferring being a tree.
If, even in the case of inference through other means of knowledge, one must necessarily rely upon such factors as practice in previous lives and worldly renown—
and since these constitute the seeds for the wisdom derived from scripture and inference—
Patañjali stated that these fall within the scope of *ṛtambharā* [wisdom].
Furthermore, other rationalists have postulated the existence of a perception resembling the direct perception of yogis for the sake of grasping all objects.
However, we place no reliance on conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*),
for our subject matter is the very nature of God (*īśvara-svarūpa*).
And that [consciousness] is indeed self-luminous;
it has been stated more than once that it is not obstructed even when the object of cognition is obstructed.
Now, one might ask: what need is there for further reflection regarding the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*)?

He says: "The very cause from which the production of a *śiṃśapā* tree—which does not deviate from the nature of being a tree—arises, from that alone is born its essential nature (*svabhāva*) which is invariably concomitant with existence.
And therefore:
"The cognition of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which depend on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), [is derived] from taste (*rasa*)."
"By means of inferring the properties of the cause, as in the case of the transformation of smoke and fuel"—
this is the principle of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
But is it not observed that scorpions and the like have multiple causes, such as insects, cow dung, and so forth?
However, as for the distinction regarding taste, potency, and so forth,
that is another matter altogether;
indeed, even the smoke produced by fire can be admitted to be [of such a nature].
But how could there be any possibility of error regarding intrinsic nature? For no authoritative person would admit that what is blue is ever non-blue simply by the will of a yogi.
It is said:
here, indeed, there are two kinds of essential-nature reasons (*svabhāvahetu*): that in which the relation of cause and effect is internally implicit, and its opposite;
for example, "this mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke."
"This [sound] is impermanent because it is produced.
Regarding this, since the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is the very foundation of the first [reason], what need is there to say anything about it?
However, the other [reason] is now examined.

If, first of all, the nature (*svabhāva*) of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) consists in its dependence upon a cause, how could the nature of impermanence (*anityatva*)—which consists in the state of coming into existence delimited by non-existence—be its nature? This is because their appearances (*ābhāsa*) differ. If, however, there were no difference in appearance, then once the cause is established, the probandum would already be established;
at most, only conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) would be proven.
According to the logical principle, "This is a tree because it is a *taru*," worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which consists of cognition and verbal designation, is indeed an effect.
And in that regard, the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) has been accepted even by you;
therefore, in all cases of essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāva-hetu*), there is merely the establishment of conventional usage, apart from a difference in appearance.
For in such cases, the "semblance of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāsa*) is not something additional, precisely because it consists of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
This same principle applies to exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*),
and this is precisely the path for universals (*sāmānya*).

Therefore, according to the previously stated method, the appearance of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the appearance of a *śiṃśapā* and the appearance of a tree is necessarily established by the power of the cause.
Therefore, this essential nature (*svabhāva*) is rooted precisely in the relationship between cause and effect;
for that very reason, it should be understood as stated in general terms: "Every essential nature as a logical reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is born from a root of origination.
And the appearances themselves are the real entity (*vastu*).
And this has already been established previously.

Consequently, when a single *śiṃśapā* tree is being produced, since other entities possessing branches and so forth are not produced, there is not even the name of the intended probandum—the appearance of a "tree" as a universal; thus, this is indeed possible.

As for that specific tree-ness which is of one and the same form as that [tree], it is indeed nothing other than *śiṃśapā*-ness, and since that is already established, it is not something to be proven;
this [tree-ness] is dependent upon its cause.
Thus, even when there is the appearance [of permanence], there would be no appearance of impermanence;

likewise, even in the absence of causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*), there would be an absence of the appearance of momentariness. Therefore, all essential reasons (*svabhāvahetu*) depend solely upon necessity (*niyati*) and not otherwise—this is the definitive conclusion. //11//
But surely, in the doctrine that reality consists of appearances (*ābhāsa*), fire that does not appear is non-existent;
how then can smoke be produced by that which does not appear?
And consequently, how can there be an inference of fire, the cause, from smoke?
Anticipating this doubt, he says in order to reassure [the reader]:

"Furthermore, from the single manifestation of fire belonging to each respective cognizer, there may arise a new manifestation of smoke and so forth, even though [the fire] is imperceptible. (IPK 2.4.12)
First of all, in the kitchen, the causal relationship between the appearance of fire and the appearance of smoke was apprehended once through the power of perception and non-perception.

In that regard, according to the view of the Vijñānavādins, since the appearance is different in each individual continuum— meaning that the causal relationship is apprehended only between appearances belonging to the same [mental] continuum and not between those belonging to different continua, because the occurrences within other continua are not experienced.

Consequently, in that case, there would be no inference— such as the certainty [of the existence] of a fire-manifestation residing in the mental continuum of another cognizer, such as a worm or an omniscient being, from a smoke-manifestation occurring within one's own continuum.

However, in this [Trika] system, at the stage of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti), for all those cognizers whose presence is possible in that location, this single smoke-manifestation and fire-manifestation are [experienced] just as they are in the external [dualist] systems.
It has been stated that their unity with the Supreme Lord was created to that extent;
therefore, by abandoning the distinctions of one's own and others' mental continuums, the mere appearance of smoke is the effect of the mere appearance of fire.

Thus, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been grasped, one again perceives on the mountain that which appears as smoke; having remembered the pervasion—that this too arises solely from what appears as fire—one infers: "On this mountain, there is what appears as fire.

To this extent, having unified with other subjects of cognition regarding that specific appearance of smoke, one unifies with other subjects of cognition within the general aspect of the appearance of fire—which is accompanied by its imperceptible portion and distinguished from other specific appearances—until such a point is reached.

The word "again" (*bhūyaḥ*) refers to having grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, whatever appearance of smoke arises again—and by the inclusion of the term "etcetera," appearances of sprouts and so forth are also included—that appearance too is "new" (*nūtana*) or unprecedented, and not merely "fresh" (*apratyagra*) like the smoke produced from previous smoke.

And that [new appearance] can arise only from a sovereign [cause], such as an unperceived appearance of fire or an appearance of a seed; it is capable of being born from that alone, and not from anything else.
The optative suffix *liṅ* expresses possibility (*śaki*).
And that manifestation is one and the same among those various subjects;
for if it were manifold, this would not be tenable—this is the intended meaning.

And since that single dominant [cause], appearing as fire, is the cause of the appearance of smoke, therefore the appearance of smoke is the non-deviant effect and the logical mark (*liṅga*) of this very appearance of fire, provided it is certain that it was not produced by a yogin.
For this reason, that [fire] is inferred from its effect; for it is imperceptible precisely because it is a dominant [cause]. //12//

Now, one might object: "In that case, would there not also arise an inference of the appearance of fire from the appearance of smoke that has emerged after having remained for a long time within the interval of a cowherd's water-clock?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The effect is an infallible mark (*liṅga*) for another cognizer."
The appearance of that [object] arises from the appearance of that very [consciousness] itself, which is the supreme sovereign.

The meaning of the remainder of the argument is as follows: how could an appearance of fire (*vahnyābhāsa*), which is not its cause, be inferred from an appearance of smoke (*dhūmābhāsa*) that is distinct from the former, belonging to another cognizer, and being imperceptible (*parokṣa*) due to its nature as a dominant condition (*adhipati-rūpa*)?
For those who are skilled indeed perceive this distinction.

With the intention that "the mastery of this subject matter, which is useful for the most common forms of inference-based linguistic usage, must be achieved through diligent effort," that which was indicated by the term "new" has been made clear by way of its exclusion [of what is not new]. //13//
But if it is accepted that the appearance of smoke [arises] from the appearance of fire, then how is it that what was stated— that agency belongs to consciousness alone—
is maintained?
For instance, one might object: "Since it is observed that when the seed exists, the sprout comes to be—just like smoke [arising] from fire—how can this [principle] be an object of disregard?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The relation of cause and effect, expressed as 'this being present, that exists'..."
That [causality] also is not possible for those who are dull-witted and devoid of [the understanding of] dependence.
First of all, a single entity cannot constitute the relationship of cause and effect;
nor can two entities existing simultaneously—such as a jar and a cloth—be of the nature of cause and effect;
and even those occurring sequentially cannot have an indefinite order, such as the cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth.
Even though there is a fixed sequence, the effect does not exist prior [to the cause] and the cause does not exist at a later time; rather,
the cause is that which necessarily precedes, and the effect is that which necessarily follows—
such is the view of the opponent.

In that case, if priority and posteriority do not exceed the essential nature [of the entities], then those two states are merely "that" and "that"—and thus there is no sense of conjunction (ca) either, since conjunction itself consists in mutual dependence; for it would simply be "that" and "that.

Now, if priority means being the cause of existence and posteriority means being the effect of existence, then the existence of the seed which causes the sprout must rest in the sprout, bringing the sprout's inclusion within itself.
In the absence of the sprout, there would be mere agency; yet even that is nothing, because it depends upon something else.
The same should be said regarding the existence of the object to be employed.
Thus, not only is the mere existence of an entity [as the cause] untenable, but positions such as these are also not logically consistent.

Even that nature of cause and effect, which consists in the state of having existence as its object of application through the case-ending used in the sense of "as long as this exists," is not tenable; it is not possible according to valid means of knowledge for insentient things, for here their very life depends on mutual dependence, and that is not possible for insentient things. //14//
If it is asked how so, it is said:

For this meaning of the locative case is not even postulated for those who are established solely in their own self and devoid of synthetic reflection, even with respect to the state of existence or non-existence. (IPK 2.4.15)
Inert things (jaḍa), it is said, are incapable of synthesizing one another's forms;
the state of being a synthesis of one another is pervaded by consciousness (caitanya), which is the opposite of inertness;
and this synthesis, as well as dependence, is the very nature of consciousness itself.
In other cases, however, it is used figuratively.
Therefore, because it lacks continuity, how could an insentient entity—whose body is contracted by the satisfaction of resting solely within its own self—extend itself into another?
Consequently, whether the seed exists while the sprout does not, or conversely, or if both exist, or if both do not exist; [in all such cases, the same difficulty follows].
Moreover, whether one [of the two] is denotable and the other is non-denotable,
or both are denotable, or both are non-denotable, in any case, the mere meaning of the nominal stem remains unqualified by any other property, such as conjunction and so forth.
Because that entire [universe], being of the nature of dependence, rests within consciousness. //15//
Since dependence is not possible for that which is insentient,

for this very reason the meaning of the case-endings— which consists of the relationship between action and its factors— is logically established as a connection of entities based solely upon the knowing subject.

The very meaning of the seventh case-ending—or indeed of any other—as characterized by the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva), is precisely what constitutes the "conjunction" (samanvaya) of entities; it is nothing else, such as some abstract or "dry" relation.
And that [conjunction] is only possible if the two entities find their rest within the independent nature of consciousness (cidrūpa);
otherwise, it is not possible in any way whatsoever.
For even when this [object] is dealt with by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it does not prove to be grounded in a real entity (*vastu*);
for conceptual construction, whose very life-breath is the pursuit of a real entity, occurs only by following upon direct experience (*anubhava*),
and such [experience] is absent here, because [the object] does not originate from a real entity.
For experience follows the object,
and the object is said to reside within itself;
therefore, when the seed exists, the sprout arises.

And [in the case of the inference] "when there is fire, there is smoke," all of this is logical only when there is repose in the subject as the independent consciousness-natured perceiver, and not otherwise. //16//
Now, if dependence— characterized by the existence of the prompted and the prompter— is not tenable when [the self] is restricted solely to its own nature,
then it is certainly possible in the view of the Sāṃkhyas, who maintain the identity of cause and effect;
so what is the point of supporting a doctrine of an agent consisting of the unfolding of consciousness?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "If cause and effect were mutually identical in nature, they would indeed be one; for if there were difference, there could never be the nature of each other. (IPK 2.4.17)

If the sprout were the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the seed, then the sprout alone would exist and the seed would not exist at all, or else there would be a reversal [of their identities]. What, then, would be the cause and what the effect? Or, if the seed is one thing and the sprout is another—
In that case, there would be no mutual identity;
for difference and non-difference, when directed toward a single object at one and the same time, are indeed contradictory. //17//

But even so, the seed, appearing as a variety such as the sprout and so forth, is perceived without contradiction by those possessing long-continued reflection as having a nature that is indeed uninterrupted, like a flowing stream.
And thus, when asked, "Where has the seed gone?", speakers reply:
It does not exist anywhere in the form of a sprout, nor is it the case that "this sprout has become the sprout.

In this way, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), having become everything from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the earth, and having expanded until it has attained the nature of an infinite succession of creations and dissolutions, [remains as such].
"Thus, cognition grasps [the object] as a whole;
however, the conceptualization of the relationship between cause and effect, arising from the force of attachment to parts, is essentially nothing but a dissection of that very entity.
Anticipating this objection, he says:
The differentiation of the single self and action following the sequence of time would likewise exist only as agency itself, as it transforms accordingly through that [action].

In this context, the far-sighted [author] establishes— by relying on recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) rooted in any one of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception, inference, or scripture— that it is precisely this equilibrium of pleasure, pain, and delusion that has become the universe by assuming an infinite variety of states of imbalance.

In this regard, by the power of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), that which is of a single nature and a single essence—its differentiation, its state of having various distinct forms, is precisely what is called "action" (*kriyā*). This is because it is followed by a sequence characterized by time;
for those things, possessing distinct natures, do not appear simultaneously.
Action is defined precisely as having a sequential nature (pūrvāparībhūtarūpa).
Since action is thus, by that very manner— namely, through the specific characteristic of action belonging to the primary cause and so forth— there would be agency itself,
and not merely a dry state of being a cause.

For this reason—that is, because [Prakṛti] enters into the activity characterized by transformation, which consists in the constant appearance of the *krimikā* (the individual soul) in various ways such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth—it abandons, relinquishes, and sets aside one form while following another; thus, through that primary cause consisting of the predominance of a third form being brought into existence, [the transformation of] Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) and the rest occurs. //18//
But surely, by this much it has been established that the Pradhāna possesses the nature of an agent with respect to the activity of transformation; what is the fault here?
For its lack of agency is not intended [by us] as it is for the Puruṣa.
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"And such [a state] is not possible for that which is insentient, because of the contradiction between difference and non-difference;
however, it is logical in the case of the single conscious Self, due to the differentiation of its manifestations. (IPK 2.4.19)

Thus, that which was stated— that the subject (*dharmin*), whose nature is undivided, possesses the agency of the act of transformation characterized by its sovereignty over the intermingling of various constantly flowing attributes— is not tenable for the *pradhāna* and the like, because they are insentient (*jaḍa*).

For that which is called "insentient" has a fixed nature, falls within the domain of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and must be established as distinct through a difference in form, like blue, yellow, and so forth.
Furthermore, because it possesses existence as a single entity, it is non-different, like the color blue;
however, that very same intrinsic nature cannot be both different and non-different, because affirmation and negation are contradictory in a single locus at one time.
Rather, some intrinsic nature is different, while another is non-different.
If this is argued,
then there would be two intrinsic natures for a single intrinsic nature,
and this is not logical.

"Thus, the distinction between difference and non-difference is severed in all things," according to this principle. In this way, for that which is insentient (*jaḍa*), which has fallen into the category of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) because it possesses a form delimited on all sides by being established as "this is [it]," this differentiation of intrinsic nature is not possible when there is unity.

However, that which does not fall into the state of being an object of knowledge, but rather whose ultimate nature is light by virtue of its conscious form (*cidrūpatā*), and which is transparent with consciousness as its sole intrinsic nature (*cidekasvabhāva*), [is different].
In that regard, it is perceived as having the nature of both difference and non-difference;

for, through experience alone, the body of a clear object such as a mirror—which remains undivided in its own essential nature—is seen to assume a form intermingled with thousands of appearances such as mountains and elephants.
Nor does this occur in the manner of silver or a double moon, which exist by way of concealing the true nature of mother-of-pearl or the single moon.
Likewise, mountains and the like appear in a mirror.
For when the mirror appears in such a way, its very nature as a mirror is all the more revealed—due to the conceit that "this mirror is stainless" and "this mirror is excellent.
Indeed, the external mountain does not actually transfer into it, for that would entail the consequence of its abandoning its own location.
Nor does it appear behind him, because that would entail the consequence of not being reflected in the mirror;
nor in the middle, because there is no possibility of entry into that which is by nature dense, solid, and resistant;
nor behind, because it is not seen there and appears only from a distance.
Nor do the visual rays, having fallen upon it and rebounding back, perceive only the mountain;
for both the original image and its reflection are observed within the appearance of the mirror situated on the side of the mountain.
Therefore, this is the majesty of purity: that there is both a fusion with infinite manifestations and yet a state of unity.

And just as for one standing upon a mountain peak, there is the simultaneous appearance of thousands of cities and objects within a single act of perception, so too is agency established as belonging to consciousness alone; for it is possible for that which is non-differentiated to admit the penetration of differentiation through the penetration of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). //19//

Now, one might object: "In that case, let consciousness itself, being of the nature of Brahman, assume this manifold variety of the universe; what is the use of postulating a Lord (Īśvara)? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Even though there is a single reality of consciousness, there can be no action between two things differentiated by their appearances without the reflective awareness of oneness characterized by the desire to act. (IPK 2.4.20)

If it is argued that the unity of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) is real, whereas this diversity arises from the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā*), then it must be asked: whose is this affliction of ignorance?
This does not cohere, for how can Brahman, whose sole nature is knowledge (*vidyā*), possess the nature of ignorance?
And there exists no other entity in reality, such as a living soul (jīva) and so forth, for whom this ignorance might belong.
If it is argued that "this ignorance is indefinable (anirvācya)," [we reply:]...
We do not know to what it is indescribable;
yet it shines forth by its own nature.
Nor is it inexpressible— what does this mean?
It is not tenable through reasoning.
If this is argued, what indeed could be called a "reason" that subverts direct experience (*saṃveda*),

and what other "inconsistency" (*anupapatti*) could there be for that which is manifesting? For it is Brahman itself, in its very nature as existence (*sadrūpa*), that shines forth undifferentiated in non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka*).
If it is argued that "this distinction arises from the power of conceptual construction (vikalpa)," then whose activity is this so-called conceptual construction?
If it belongs to Brahman, then there is no other [agent] in connection with ignorance; moreover,
that which is free from conceptual construction is the truth, while that which is characterized by conceptual construction is unreal.
Thus, how can there be a distinction [between them], given that their state of appearing is indistinguishable?
If it is argued that "even though difference appears, it is sublated,"...
Non-difference is likewise [negated] in this way,
because it is sublated by the manifestation of difference;
for sublation is nothing other than the arising of a contrary cognition.
Furthermore, even negation (*bādha*) is real precisely because it appears, not for any other reason;
thus, how can difference (*bheda*), which also appears, be ignorance (*avidyā*)?

If you argue that this non-difference is based on the authority of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*), disregarding the fact of its appearance—then scripture itself is essentially of the nature of difference, as are the distinctions between the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Thus, this is nothing at all.
Therefore, even if one accepts the reality of the oneness of consciousness (*cidekatva*), an action characterized by agency—which consists in the entry into diverse forms—is not possible;
however, if there is freedom (*svātantrya*) whose very nature is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), then everything becomes possible.

For *parāmarśa* (reflective awareness) is indeed a desire in the form of a wish to act (*cikīrṣā*); and within that [desire], everything that is to be manifested exists as non-differentiated—thus it has been said: "Of the Lord who is established in his own self... (Ipk 1.5.10).

In this context, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) manifests the universe— which is His own essential nature, whose true form is reality, whose ultimate essence is the nature of light, and which exists as nothing other than non-different from uninterrupted light— as a differentiation precisely through that very ultimate essence of light. This very capacity of His to perform what is extremely difficult to accomplish is called His sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).
In the phrase "of the two [aspects] differentiated by manifestation," the genitive case denotes a general relationship dependent on an action;
it is subsequently divided as appropriate.
The two manifestations—insentient and sentient—are differentiated by their manifestation.
The jar and so forth are inert and thus of the nature of the object, while the reflection of consciousness is of the nature of the agent;
[if this were the case], there would be no action belonging to these two, nor could one possess the state of being acted upon while the other possesses agency.

Without the reflective awareness of non-difference with respect to that which is to be manifested in the form of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), how could this single action be the inherent nature of two distinct entities?

Since the relationship of cause and effect is under discussion, the agent and the object have been mentioned; however, other factors of action (*kāraka*) as well must participate in the unity of a single agent. Otherwise, if the multitude of factors such as the instrument were ultimately distinct, how could that [action] be non-different?

Or rather: [the objection is that] the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) regarding two things—insentient and sentient—which are distinct even through their manifestation, consists in the state of being desired for one and the state of being the desirer for the other; this cannot exist without the reflective awareness of unity (*ekatva-parāmarśa*).

Or else: it is without that reflective awareness in the form of "I am this," which is the essence of the desire to act and whose nature is a resting in oneness regarding those two things distinct in their manifestation.
Or rather: how could there be an action characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) without a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*) of two things that appear as distinct?
Thus, the genitive case is used in relation to the action, the desire to act, or the reflective awareness; and because it is always dependent [on these], a compound is formed. //20//
He summarizes this as follows:
