"In this way, for one who desires to abide in the form of the world appearing as jars, cloths, and so forth, his very will is the cause, the agency, and the action. (IPK 2.4.21)
Just as an insentient thing possesses neither causality nor agency, so too does a sentient being who is not the Lord;
by this very mode of reasoning, it follows that the very desire to act which belongs to one who intends thus, when it reaches its external limit, is designated as "action" (kriyā).
That alone is agency and that alone is causality; there is nothing else whatsoever.

Therefore, the meaning of the statement "the jar remains" is as follows: the Lord, who is Light, remains—not because He is unable to assume that form [of the jar], but because, out of His sovereignty, He freely accepts the state of remaining while desiring to remain in the form of the jar.
Thus, it is He who remains.

That which is called the world has the form of appearances such as jars and cloths; he who, being independent, desires to abide as that very world— through its own nature, in such a way, and in each of those various forms consisting of the thousandfold activities and the modifications of existence such as birth and persistence belonging to that world—
his very desire for such a manifold form, expressed as "thus" (*evam*), is itself his action (*kriyā*).
— such is the connection.
Therefore, the Blessed Maheśvara alone is the creator of the universe; — may there be auspiciousness! //21//

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Reality of Cause and Effect," in the *Kriyādhikāra* of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* written by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
And this second chapter, titled "The Section on Ritual Action," is complete. // 2 //
The First Daily Lesson in the Section on Tradition (*Āgama*).
[Vimarśinī]:
Having reached whom, the entire multitude of the oceans of traditions attains fullness and the state of having achieved its purpose;
I have [crossed] that ocean of the supreme scripture, which contains the essence of the multitude of jewels of contemplation on the Śāmbhava reality, by means of the boat of [this work].
We praise that Śiva, within whom shines the wheel of principles (tattva-cakra) born from the earth up to the noble beginning of the illustrious Sadāśiva.
Thus, the nature of knowledge and action has been determined at length through these two sections.
Now this must be stated: it was just mentioned that what is called "action" (kriyā) is characterized by the manifestation of all objects;
but what are those "all objects"?
In this regard, objects—characterized as either insentient or sentient—are essentially of the nature of manifestations, and they are subsumed under the form of action.
For direct perception does not operate everywhere for one who perceives through illusion;
inference is likewise [restricted],
for it is not possible to grasp the logical mark (liṅga), its pervasion (vyāpti), and so forth, with respect to every single thing that exists.

But why should scripture— which has as its ultimate reality the supreme *vimarśa* of Maheśvara, whose nature is undivided light— not see [all things]? Therefore, with the intention of making the determination of categories (padārtha) according to that scripture accessible to the heart of the subject who has attained the state of the transcendent knower (*pramātṛ*) by taking the entire universe as his object of knowledge, the Teacher begins the third chapter, the "Chapter on Scripture" (*Āgamādhikāra*).

In this regard, by means of eleven verses beginning with "Thus, the internal and external activity" (*evam antarbahirvṛttiḥ*) and ending with "due to the non-difference between the gross and the subtle" (*sthūlasūkṣmatvābhedataḥ*), [the author] demonstrates that which is established by scripture— the reality extending from Śiva down to the earth— which consists of the nature of each individual manifestation and is designated as "the universal" (*sāmānya*) in other philosophical systems;

and through its connection with grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), this entire manifestation of the body, worlds, and so forth, preceded by the array of infinite particular manifestations of specific characteristics.

The purport of this chapter is to demonstrate that the entire collection of principles (*tattvagrāma*), established by the scriptures of the Supreme Lord and understood through reasoning, exists within each individual.

In doing so, while connecting the transition between sections (*adhikārasaṃgati*) and concluding the refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he speaks as follows in order to reveal the very nature of the Śiva-principle:
"Thus, action (*kriyā*), which functions internally and externally, follows the sequence of time."
In that state, knowledge and action are mutually inseparable, just as they are in the case of a mother.
Thus it is said: because the relationship of cause and effect as described in other systems of philosophy—which is established upon the nature of insentient matter—is in no way tenable;

rather, it is the very nature of consciousness (*cit-rūpa*) itself, existing as a manifestation through its own essence which is the ultimate reality of light (*prakāśa-paramārtha*), both internally and externally, that—by projecting the sequence of time—is designated as "action" (*kriyā*).
This [action] is a property belonging to that very subject (*pramātṛ*), whose body is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Thus it is.
Therefore, knowledge and action are inseparable;
knowledge is enlivened by reflective awareness (vimarśa), and reflective awareness itself is action.
And for one devoid of the power of knowledge, there can be no application of action.

Thus, that which consists of the inseparable nature of knowledge and action, which through the medium of action is capable of reflecting hundreds of emanations and withdrawals contained within the entire mass of principles (*tattva*), and which appears in such a manner during its instruction, contemplation, and so forth—though in reality it is without appearance—is said to be the *Śivatattva*. //1//

If the Śiva-principle is indeed of such a nature, then since this entire universe is not distinct from it, what other principle could there be? Furthermore, when all principles rest within the single reality of consciousness, how could there be a temporal sequence among them, given the non-difference of space and time? This is so.
However, due to the predominance of the internal state, the principle called Sādākhya arises first;
but when there is a predominance of external existence, the principle of Parameśvara follows after.

Although the reality of Śiva (śivatattva) is indeed one alone, nevertheless, its very sovereignty displays within itself a differentiation of forms, as it were, by means of reflection. This very diversity of form is the succession of space and time; for it consists of the manifold variety of the powers of manifestation and action.

Then, when there is the manifestation of the intensification of that intermediate state which is of the nature of knowledge, there is the *sādākhya* (the "ever-so-called"), which exists within the *sadākhya*.
From this point on, the designation "existent" (*sat*) arises; and this reality is the signified object of the *sadākhya*, which consists of the word-form *Sadāśiva*.
In the instruction on the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) and so forth, that which is first appropriate is the *tattva* called Sādākhya.

When the external manifestation, consisting of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), exists in a state of transcendence (*paratva*) through the emergence of an intensified appearance (*udrikābhāsa*), there is the *tattva* named Īśvara, which belongs to the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*) and is denoted by the term "Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*).
And that is the subsequent appropriate manifestation of the unmanifest (sādākhya).
This is what is meant:
here, its state is its reality (tattva).

Thus, that which appears as one and undivided, serving as the cause for the grouping of diverse categories, is *tattva* (the principle). For example, mountains, trees, cities, and so forth, as well as rivers, lakes, oceans, and so forth, possess the common nature of being earth or water. Consequently, the category of pure consciousness known as the Mantramaheśvaras— [The text continues: ...is also such a *tattva*. Furthermore, the various categories of impure consciousness, beginning with the individual souls (*paśu*), are likewise grouped together by means of their common characteristic of being insentient (*jaḍatva*). Therefore, it is established that the Lord is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*) because He is the cause of the grouping of all these diverse categories. In His first creation, that cycle of objective entities—which is to be known solely by our internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is predominantly indistinct, and which is like a painting just begun—shines forth in such a manner;
and likewise at the time of withdrawal, it appears as something of the same nature, consisting almost entirely of reflections due to its orientation toward dissolution.
That specific state of consciousness belonging to that group of pure spirits, which consists in such a flow toward that mass of objective entities, is the *Sadāśiva-tattva*.

However, for the mass of consciousness whose form is Mantreśvara and the rest, the universe—manifested as a reflection corresponding to the collection of objects that have entered the path of our external senses—shines forth.
That such a manifestation occurs for him is the *Īśvara-tattva*.

As for the venerable Lord Sadāśiva and the venerable Lord Īśvara, who exist in the form of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) and the meditator (*upāsya*), they should be understood as distinct from [the *Īśvara-tattva*] and equal to Brahmā and Viṣṇu; one must not be deluded by the similarity of their names.
As some have said: "Why are even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra not included among the categories of reality? //2//
He also shows another set of names for these two principles here: "Īśvara is the external unfolding (unmeṣa), and Sadāśiva is the internal withdrawal (nimeṣa)."
And there is grammatical coreferentiality between the cognition of "Being" (sat-vidyā) and the cognition "I am this" (aham-idam-dhī).
In the statement, "The unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of which is the arising of the world," it is the *īśvara-tattva* itself that is expressed by the word "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*),
for the unfolding of the universe is its manifestation as something distinct and external.
Nimeṣaṇa (closing) is the bringing about of non-manifestness and the intensification of the form of non-greatness;
thus, Nimeṣa is the Sadāśiva-tattva,
because it is the dissolution of the world.

This vibration (*spanda*) of the Supreme Lord is pure, characterized by the attainment of a different form that has not yet fully developed, because it possesses a manifest nature through its quality of slight movement.
For, in the ultimate sense, these powers of the Supreme Lord constitute the entire collection of principles (*tattva*);

however, one particular power, by encompassing many other powers within itself due to its proximity, becomes the object of worship, just as the nature of "pot-ness" is the object of perception for a pot.
Another [power] is dependent on others, established solely in its own nature, and remote, like the existence (*sattā*) of a jar;
likewise, the powers of closing and opening the eyes are Sadāśiva and Īśvara, and their presiding deities are also named accordingly.
Now, he explains the *vidyā-tattva*, which is the instrument residing in those two presiding deities:

When the Light rests in itself alone, that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) characterized by resting in the self-luminosity of one's own nature, not directed toward anything else, is called "I" (*so'ham*); whereas that which is directed toward another is called "this" (*idam*).
And that [consciousness], in the ultimate sense, comes to rest in its own self-luminosity, which is by nature not oriented toward anything else.

Among these, the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the first state is the *śiva-tattva*; in the second, it is the state of a *vidyeśvara*. However, in the middle state, the reflective awareness in which "I" and "this" are held in equilibrium like the pans of a scale is the Lord Sadāśiva and the venerable Lord Īśvara.
However, there is a distinction between the states of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*) based on whether it is turbid or non-turbid.
Regarding these two cognitions—“I” and “this”—their having separate substrata within the illusory subject consists in "I" residing in the grasper and "this" in the grasped.
When, by means of dispelling that [duality], there occurs a unification within a single substrate—a manifestation in the form of a relationship—that is true, pure *vidyā*.

The [power] residing in the subject of Māyā is indeed other than that which arises from impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*). In that regard, when [the subject] causes the "this" (*idam*)-aspect to manifest within that very locus which is the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—the locus of the "I" (*aham*)—then, because of its lack of clarity, there is the state of Sadāśiva, expressed as "I am this" (*ahamidam*).

However, when the "this"-aspect has become clear in the locus and one infuses the reflective awareness of the "I"-aspect (*aham-aṃśa-vimarśa*) into it, then there is the state of Īśvara, expressed as "This is I" (*idamaham*).
— Thus is the division. //3//
Now, one might ask: why is this called "pure knowledge" (*śuddhavidyā*)? To this he says:

"For those things that have attained the state of 'this-ness' (*idambhāva*) and have entered the plane of the knowable, [pure knowledge is so called] because their essence is consciousness and because they are perceived according to reality. (IPK 3.1.4)
Avalokana is initial observation, vedana is knowledge,
which consists in accordance with reality and conformity to the object;
its purity is non-erroneousness.

For those entities that have reached the state of being known— that is, those that have been accepted and are thus endowed with the appropriate reflective awareness in the form "this is so"— consciousness alone, whose nature is light, is the essential reality; and this light is the "I," whose essence is self-referential awareness (*vimarśa*).
Therefore, because the notion "I am happy" is firmly rooted precisely in that which is their ultimate reality, it consists of pure sensation (śuddha-vedanā). //4//
The two principles are distinguished from the two deities in the form of the presiding subjects;
this is demonstrated through the method of scriptural discourse.
Herein, the "inferiority" of entities consists in their appearing as non-self.
Indeed, that is the state of both the supreme and the non-supreme, due to the concealment of otherness by the sense of "I."

"Priority" (*paratā*) is the state of being prior, independent of anything else, expressed as "I"; "posteriority" (*aparatva*) is the state of being subsequent, characterized by incompleteness and dependence on another, expressed as "this.
Furthermore, regarding these two principles, because entities—which possess both turbid and non-turbid forms—touch upon both aspects, they are termed "prior-posterior" (*parāpara*).

The state established in the nature of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is the essence of the reality (*tattva*), consisting of the objects of knowledge perceived by pure subjects such as the Mantreśvaras who illuminate that [reality]. That state of consciousness which is established in that [reality] is Pure Knowledge (*vidyā*); its status as the presiding subject over those [pure] subjects is the nature of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva and Īśvara. This is the summary. //5//
Thus, according to the view of some, Śuddhavidyā is that which has as its primary function the manifestation of that aspect which veils the "I" (ahaṃ).
Others, however,
maintain that Śuddhavidyā is that which has as its primary function the manifestation of that very aspect of "this-ness" (idaṃ-bhāga) which is to be veiled.

Otherwise, by what could this "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) be illumined? For māyā is absent there; or, if it were present, there would be the undesirable consequence of its sprouting [into a real entity].
Therefore, because she illumines this "this-ness" while remaining incapable of allowing it to sprout, she is pure (śuddhā). And because she is an illumination, she is called Vidya.
Precisely because it has not yet fully emerged as the power of illusion (*māyākalpā*), this Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) was taught by the venerable teachers of the *Raurava* and other scriptures;
thus he says:
"That very notion of duality regarding objects which belongs even to the agent whose nature is consciousness..."
Others say that Vidyā is like the power of Māyā, just as the Vidyeśvaras [are]. (Ipk 3.1.6)
When the subject of Māyā, whose nature consists of the void and so forth, has not yet emerged,

and while the subject and agent remains pure consciousness alone, that sovereignty which— despite all entities being of the single nature of consciousness— consists in the manifestation of difference by way of their appearing as non-conscious, is Śuddhavidyā; it is similar to the power of Māyā.
Because differentiation is manifested in the objective portion (*vedyabhāga*),
yet it is not merely illusion (*māyā*),
since there is no error even in the pure consciousness portion (*cinmātrabhāga*) of the subject (*grāhaka*).
In whatever manner the venerable Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta, exist,

they indeed possess the state of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) grasped as pure consciousness alone; yet, by their own nature, they perceive objects of knowledge (vedya) as distinct, just like the Lord (īśvara) of the dualists.

Thus, in the subject—which is in part of the nature of consciousness and is of the nature of ultimate reality—there exists the power of Śuddhavidyā, which has the capacity to remove the misconception regarding the object, for the Vidyeśvaras. //6//
Others say: the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara consists in the manifestation of non-manifested duality for the Blessed Lord Maheśvara.
In that state, when duality is indistinct, the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) of Īśvara is active; when it is distinct, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is active.
However, when the two-fold rooted perversion of the grasped and the grasper occurs, that is the power of *māyā*, and it resides in the limited subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*). On the other hand,

even while the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the perversions regarding both the grasper and the grasped have not yet ceased, that manifestation of the ultimate reality of things which occurs in non-limited subjects such as yogins and men of knowledge is the operation of the power of *vidyā*.
This he demonstrates:
"The power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) is that which manifests the state of the bound (paśu-bhāva) for that [Lord] whose nature is sovereignty... (IPK 3.1.7).

When the state of being a bound soul (*paśubhāva*)— characterized by the single flavor of error, the condition of being bound by fetters (*pāśanīyatva*), lack of autonomy, and the distinction between the seen,

the seer, and the act of seeing— has arisen, nevertheless, that power of the Supreme Lord which illuminates this aforementioned sovereignty [attained] through the force of the previously stated reasoning—
that by virtue of which some, having honored those reasonings, become perfected ones with their hearts satisfied— that is the power of knowledge (*vidyāśakti*).
This very position, though seen in the *Ṣaḍardhasāra* and other works, wins over the heart of this teacher,
because he does not mention "others. And since the *māyātattva* is being defined immediately following this [point], he says:
Furthermore, there is that which is called Māyā, which effects concealment.

Furthermore, the power of *māyā*, by maintaining a firmly rooted conceit of subjectivity within non-conscious entities such as the void (*śūnya*), and by causing one to conceive of even those things consisting of consciousness as being distinct [from oneself], completely conceals its own true nature;
that deluding power veils it. Here, "concealment" (*tirodhāna*) is not to be understood as a form of dissolution (*vilayana*).

That which is counted among the five duties in the scriptures—even for one who has been initiated—is indeed an obscuration (āvaraṇa), consisting primarily of the disparagement of the Guru, the mantra, and so forth. //7//
It clarifies that concealment consists in obscuration:
when difference appears as having a single flavor, when the non-self is perceived through the sense of "I," and when either the void or the body is cognized, the power of Māyā unfolds.

In deep sleep, at the time of cosmic dissolution, or during the meditative absorption of non-existence (*abhāva-samādhi*), that which is empty, resembling the sky, devoid of self-nature, and characterized by the absence of any object of knowledge, is perceived as the "I" through the sense of self; or, in states such as inhaling and exhaling, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself, augmented by fire, or the intellect (*buddhi*)— which resembles a clear reservoir of water and possesses the reflections of objects of knowledge— is identified internally as "I know," "I am suffering," and so forth, during states such as reflection.
Indeed, it is the body itself—composed primarily of earth—which appears as the "I" or as the self in states such as "I am emaciated.
And all this, from the void onwards, is in reality nothing but the essence of pure consciousness; it is only through *māyā* that it is manifested as having an insentient form.

Yet, while being exactly of such a nature, it has been made the locus for the persistent attachment to the form of consciousness as "I," resulting in an unquiet state of inertia. This is the unsurpassed power of the Supreme Lord, consisting in the non-obstruction of the accomplishment of such an exceedingly difficult task.
The phrase "the power of Māyā... thus unfolds" indicates that even external forms—such as sons, wealth, and wives—are reckoned as objects of the persistent attachment to the sense of "I. //8//

Now, one might object: "If that which is non-conscious in nature, such as the void (*śūnya*) and so forth, is the non-self (*anātman*), yet when it is clung to as the self (*ātman*), it becomes precisely conscious in nature;
therefore, it would possess the very qualities of pure sovereignty, such as omniscience and omnipotence.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And that cognizer who is [perceived as] empty and so forth with respect to an object of cognition that is distinct [from him], being himself an object of cognition,
is enveloped by the pentad beginning with time.

There might be a conjunction of sovereignty and dharma for the void (śūnya) and so forth, if—even while being attached to the notion of "I"—it were to abandon the state of being an object of knowledge (*meyatā*).
For if that were the case, even its status as an object of cognition would not appear as something distinct from blue and other such objects.
However, as for that which is called the cognizer (*pramātā*), such as the void and so forth—

As long as the cognizer remains [engaged] with an object of cognition such as "blue," which is intended to be distinct from his own nature, for that long he himself is indeed a cognizer only insofar as he has become an object of cognition.
For an object of cognition is delimited precisely because it is being cognized;
thus, its distinction is established only in relation to another such object of cognition.
But the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) is not like this, because it is unlimited (*aparimitatvāt*).

That which constitutes the limitedness of the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*)—namely, emptiness and so forth—is precisely the pentad beginning with time. For instance, time, manifesting as the subject (*pramātṛ*) by weaving together succession, subsequently extends itself even toward the object (*prameya*) in accordance with that [subject].

When one reflects upon the self in the form of the body as if it were sequential— thinking, "I who was thin am now fat, and I shall become even fatter"— it manifests a sequence of elemental forms within the objects of cognition that accompany that reflection. Of this insentient [self] beginning with the void, *vidyā*— which consists in the unfolding of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjhatva*)— discriminates the mass of objects, such as blue or pleasure, as they are reflected in the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*).
The *kalā* manifests the effect as consisting in the reinforcement of limited agency, such that one thinks:
"I know something;
I do something."

And here, even though the aspect of "some-ness" (kiñcitva) is common to both, why is this [particular thing] alone "some-thing"?— it is in response to this point that *rāga* (attachment), consisting of a form of intense clinging (*abhiṣvaṅga*), operates within the subject (*pramātṛ*) and toward the object of knowledge (*prameya*) such as the body and so forth, appearing as if it were the attribution of qualities (*guṇa*) and the like.
Nor is this merely the absence of detachment (*avairāgya*) residing in the intellect (*buddhi*).
For even in the case of an old man toward a young woman, that physical passion (sthūla) might not exist,
yet attachment (rāga) certainly does;
furthermore, such attachment is observed even among the eight qualities of the intellect (buddhi).

"Why is there attachment precisely to this [object]?"— this very matter is regulated by *niyati* (fate). Thus, interwoven with *kalā*, *vidyā*, *kāla*, *rāga*, and *niyati*, and having had the entirety of his sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) stripped away by *māyā*,
this limited subject (*mita-pramātā*) shines forth once again as merely a portion situated within the mass of all those [powers] that have been restored to him.
"Now, knowing this little, performing this, and being attached to this very thing, I am he"— thus [one thinks].
And sometimes even a difference in the objects of these [cognitions] occurs.
Just as elsewhere, even one who is attached is made to act otherwise by necessity;
and these [categories] appear as being attached precisely to the subject (*pramātṛ*),
thus they are the powers (*śakti*) of that very [subject], distinct for each individual subject.
However, occasionally they may even become unified through the will of the Lord (*īśvara*), as in the case of watching actors or wrestlers;
for these [individuals] possess no life of their own apart from the will of the Lord—this has been stated repeatedly and will be stated again. //9//
Regarding what was stated as "the knower [is established] through the negative inference (vyatirekin) concerning this object of knowledge," he demonstrates that object of knowledge there:
"The object of knowledge is twenty-three-fold, consisting of effects and instruments."
Its single primordial cause, Pradhāna, is of an undifferentiated nature.

That which consists of the twenty-three-fold group of effects and instruments, and that which is their fundamental cause—the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) characterized by the non-differentiation of all effects and instruments—all that is the object of knowledge (*meyam*).
This is the connection [of the terms].

For for the yogis, the mantra-deities, their lords, and so forth, everything is indeed an object of knowledge, because they possess the power to master the elements, the subtle potentials (*tanmātras*), the instruments, and the *pradhāna*.
Even for those transmigrating beings, the objects of knowledge are indeed limited to what is established through the methods of inference, scripture, and so forth;
such is the extent of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
Time and the other categories, though they are objects of knowledge, are nonetheless bound up within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself.

Thus, because they are of the nature of the power of the subject (*pramātṛśakti*), they are not counted here as objects of knowledge (*prameya*) at this juncture, when discussing objects of knowledge distinct from the subject of Māyā. For in reality, even this subject here is indeed an object of knowledge; however, being made into a subject, he is said here to be one whose state of being an object has been concealed. //10//
Now, having raised the doubt as to what among these twenty-three is the effect (kārya) and what is the instrument (karaṇa), he says:
"And here, the series of external and internal instruments is thirteenfold."
And the category of effects is tenfold, according to the distinction between gross and subtle.

The employment of the instruments (karaṇa) precedes that of the knower; herein, first of all, are the thirteen instruments. Among them, the intellect (buddhi) consists merely of the general form of determination (avasāya), while the ego (ahaṃkāra) consists of the conceit of being the grasper and the grasped.
The mind (*manas*) is the cause of volition (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth; thus, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is threefold.

The five sensory organs (*buddhīndriya*)—namely, hearing (*śrotra*), [touch, sight, taste, and smell]—are useful for the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of sound and other objects.
skin,
eye, tongue.
Smell, and so forth.
As for the objects of action, there are five organs of action which are useful therein;
for instance, there is the pair consisting of relinquishing and grasping.
The external objects are those [perceived] therein; the hand, the anus, and the foot are the instruments (*karaṇa*).
That by which this very [internal] end is performed within the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*).
The *upastha* (organ of generation) is that which serves the function of rest through the pacification of its agitation.
Furthermore, the organs of action (*karmendriya*), which consist of specific forms of egoity (*ahaṅkāra*), pervade the entire body.
Therefore, just as one who has had his hand cut off takes hold with his arms and grasps with his very palm, so it is with the others.
Merely because it is the locus for obtaining those various distinct and complete functions, its substratum is said to be in the form of the five fingers;
thus, there are thirteen instruments (*karaṇa*).
And although these are effects (*kārya*), they are designated as "instruments" by virtue of their unique instrumental nature.
The gross effect consists of earth, water, and fire.
Wind, ether— these are the five elements.
The subtle form of these very [elements] is odor, taste, and...
Form, touch, sound, and so forth;
therein, space and the other elements each possess a single quality.
Or [the view that] each [subsequent stage] possesses an increment of one quality— such are the differences of opinion; they have not been analyzed here because they are of no practical utility.
In that context, the gross [form] is differentiated yet leads to the inference of the undifferentiated;
thus, the commencement with the gross form has been stated.

Here, the manifestations of earth and the other elements, having become intermingled and attained the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of jars and so forth, are approached by the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
Perceived by the sense organs,
conceptualized and determined as desired by the internal organ,
and discerned by knowledge;
The intended meaning is that [the objects], colored by the aesthetic emotions (kalā) and so forth, come to rest within the subject (pramātṛ).
And this has been determined by me in detail in such works as the *Tantrāloka-sāra*, which are primarily devoted to that [subject];
thus, because it would be of no use here, it has not been elaborated upon—may there be auspiciousness! //11//

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Principles" (*tattvanirūpaṇa*), in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta, within the section on Revelation (*āgamādhikāra*). //1//
The second chapter in the section on Tradition (*āgama*).
[Vimarśinī]:
Although its own nature is undivided, it possesses a manifold conceptualization of the subject (*mātṛ*).
We praise that Śiva who expands within the wheel of one's own heart-lotus.

Thus, once the aggregate of the categories (*tattvarāśi*) has been determined, another chapter is introduced with twenty verses beginning with "In this mere state of being the subject" (*tatraitanmātṛtāmātre*) and ending with "the supreme [consciousness] whose nature is the universe of the pervasive breath" (*vyānaviśvātmakaḥ paraḥ*), in order to determine in detail the principle of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*), which— though mentioned as being included within the aforementioned [categories]— is primarily what remains to be determined.
For it is thus: in this scripture, the recognition of the true nature of the knower (*pramātṛ*) is taught.

For he, knowing his own nature as that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted, and entering his own self—which is the supreme object of attainment and the very nature of Śiva—without distinction, becomes liberated even while living.
In that regard, by means of a verse, the nature of the triad beginning with Brahmā is [described].
The differentiation of the cognizer is treated in seven verses;
the nature of immersion (*samāveśa*) in two verses; and the states of the cognizer, such as deep sleep and so forth, in five verses.
By means of this triad, he determines the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted among them;
such is the purport of this chapter (āhnika). Now, the meaning of the text itself is being examined.
In that state, when there is the abiding solely in the condition of being the Mother (Mātṛkā), Rudra is the presiding deity;
when the expansion of distinct objects of knowledge occurs, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are established.

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): when this very nature of reality—which is established by scripture and supported by reasoning—is thus present, that which consists of the state of the subject (*pramātṛtā*) enveloped by the pentad beginning with time (*kāla*), becomes pure in that state called withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), wherein the entire range of objects of cognition (*prameyajāta*) has been reabsorbed. In that state, [the Goddess] possesses the status of the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛdevatātva*) by bringing about that state for her own circle of worshippers who have attained immersion in the meditation upon that state, through the accomplishment of her own orientation toward them.
And the one who is to be worshipped is the venerable Lord Rudra himself,

the Blessed One, whose third eye is opened by the touch of the nature of the subject— which, even within the sphere of Māyā, is the form of the middle light, free from the sun and moon, day and night, and the dharmas and adharma consisting of prāṇa and apāna.
But Viṣṇu is the presiding deity over the expansion of the divided object of knowledge, characterized by the continuous flow of its succession.

For this very reason, because those two consist of the expansion of the object of cognition (*prameya*)—having the nature of manifestation in the form "this is blue"—and because they lack the entry into the state of the subject (*pramātṛ*) as "I," there is no opening of a third eye.
*Devatā* is simply *daivata*.
*Prasara* means origination and continuity. //1//
He now defines the division of that which was described as mere subjectivity (mātṛtāmātra), as well as its various designations according to scripture:
"This cognizer (pramātā), blinded by Māyā, is a transmigrating being bound by karma; when his sovereignty is made manifest by Vidyā, he is called 'liberated,' a mass of consciousness. (IPK 3.2.2)
The subject is called the Lord (pati) with respect to those entities that are his own body;
through Māyā, he becomes the bound soul (paśu), divided from them and defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth.
Blinded and deluded by *māyā*,

and therefore imagining that actions are the binders of his own self, this subject— such as the one consisting of the void (*śūnya*) and so forth— is enveloped by time and other factors and transmigrates; for this reason, he is a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*).
For even the body, by persisting in its similarity of essential form throughout childhood, youth, and so forth, seems to transmigrate;
whereas the intellect and other faculties indeed undergo transmigration even into another birth.
But for one whose divine nature has been brought to the state of recognition by knowledge—that is, by the power of manifesting its own essential form—[transmigration ceases].

Therefore, one who considers even the body and the entire universe to be nothing but consciousness—and for whom, precisely because of that, the nature of reality is pure, dense consciousness (cid-ghana) devoid of any admixture with non-conscious forms—is fit to be designated as "liberated" while the body still persists, due to the absence of the bond of rebirth. But once the body has fallen away, he is Śiva, a single mass of density; so who is liberated, and from what?
However, by way of conventional usage based on past states and in relation to other subjects, there is the designation "Śiva is liberated.
And he who is liberated, perceiving objects as his own limbs, cognizes them; thus, he is their master.
Because he bestows his own essential nature, which is the supreme reality, he is taught in the scripture as the "Lord" (*pati*) and the "Protector.

When [the Self] perceives the distinctions created by the power of *māyā* as being truly separate from itself, it is then bound by those very objects of cognition, which take the form of fetters; thus it is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*).
For indeed, it is solely due to the mass of objects of knowledge that there arise in this [Self] the afflictions such as ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the desire for self-preservation.

Actions consist of dharma, adharma, and so forth; by the word "and so forth," the latent impressions (vāsanā) consisting of intention are included; and maturation (vipāka) consists of the experience of the fruit.
Thus, turbidity is of infinite varieties;
because he is bound by these, he is called a *paśu* (bound soul). //3//
"That which is this very form of the bound soul (paśu) is itself the threefold impurity (mala) in the scriptures," he says:
"The loss of autonomy of consciousness, and the lack of consciousness regarding autonomy—this twofold atomic impurity (āṇavamala) arises from the forfeiture of one's own true nature. (Ipk 3.2.4)

In this very [state], the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is called *māyā*, which bestows birth and experience; while the *kārma* [bond] resides in the ignorant agent. All three of these arise solely through the power of *māyā*. (IPK 3.2.5)
In this context, the essential nature of consciousness (*cittattva*) consists of the forms of the knower and the agent;
its "seizure" is what is called the *āṇava* impurity, by which this [consciousness] becomes a limited individual (*aṇu*).
In that regard, the contraction of its own nature is what constitutes limitation (*saṃkoca*).

When that [Self] abides in its nature as consciousness, there occurs either the closing up or the reversal of another essential nature characterized by agency (*kartṛtva*), which consists of autonomy (*svātantrya*).
Thus, in both cases, *āṇava-mala* is one and the same, consisting in the loss of one's own true nature.
"In this very state" means: when *āṇava-mala* has occurred in its two forms as a contraction of one's own nature, the manifestation of that which is divided is merely designated by the name *māyīya*.
The three impurities (*mala*) are also of the nature of *māyā*, because they are produced by *māyā*.

Among these, when there is the manifestation of objects as distinct from the self—such as the body and so forth, which are of the nature of the non-awakened agent—the impurity of action (*kārma-mala*) arises in the form of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).
From this [impurity] come birth and experience, and that [birth and experience] has a fixed limit.
Thus, it is stated that karma has birth, lifespan, and experience as its fruits. // 4-5 //

Now, in order to clarify the nature of these impurities by defining their distinct objects, he first states the object of the principle "the loss of autonomy of consciousness": "Even though they consist of pure consciousness, those who do not possess supreme agency have been created by the Lord as distinct from Himself due to the loss of their agency. (IPK 3.2.6)

Those for whom pure consciousness alone is the ultimate reality—and not that supreme freedom, which consists of bliss through resting in one's own self and is characterized by the sense of "I"—have been created by the Supreme Lord as distinct from His own self. The reason for this is: because of the absence (atyaya) of agency, which is characterized by supreme sovereignty.
The remaining intention [of the author] is that the Supreme Lord, however, possesses the nature of consciousness inseparable from supreme sovereignty. //6//

One might object: "Granted that they are distinct from the Supreme Lord due to this reason, how can there be mutual difference among them? For their nature as consciousness, as well as their lack of distinction in space and time resulting from their pervasiveness and eternity, are identical.
And if there is no mutual difference, how can they be 'created' and why is the plural number used [in the term 'they']?
He dispels this doubt.
Even though they are identical in their single characteristic of pure consciousness, they possess mutual differentiation;
likewise, through the diversity of the Lord's will, they are known as the Vijñānakevalas.

For here, indeed, it has been stated more than once that it is the Supreme Lord alone, whose power is unimpeded everywhere, who becomes this or that while desiring to manifest Himself as such; there is no other whatsoever that exists in the ultimate sense.

And thus, although there is a unity among them—since they have all transcended the state of the subject (pramātṛpada) beginning from the body and ending with the void, and possess a common set of attributes such as consciousness, eternity, and omnipresence—there is nevertheless mutual difference between them.
And these are called *vijñānakevalas* in the scripture. Among them, the *vijñānakevala* is joined with only one impurity (*mala*).
In such passages, "consciousness" refers to that which has the nature of cognition, consisting solely of form devoid of autonomy. //7//

Having thus stated that the portion [of the verse] concerning "the loss of autonomy for consciousness" pertains to the *vijñānākala*, he clarifies this other aspect—namely, "the lack of consciousness even regarding autonomy"—by demonstrating its subject matter:
"But the *pralayākalas* are agents whose nature is the non-consciousness of the void (*śūnya*) and so forth;
they possess the *kārma* impurity (*mala*), while the *māyīya* [impurity] is [only] conceptualized for them. (IPK 3.2.8)

In the void, because it is insentient and devoid of the nature of cognition, or likewise in the vital breath or the intellect—those for whom agency arises through the connection with the wonder of "I-ness" are rendered into dissolution; they become "without parts," meaning they are devoid of the instruments and effects characterized by the principle of *kalā*, and are of the nature of non-cognition.
For they are made such until the limit of dissolution, but in subsequent time, they indeed become connected with effects and instruments once again.

Since for them there exists not only the aforementioned impurity (mala), but also the impurity of action (kārma) consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and having the nature of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*);
if this were so, then for them there would also be the manifestation of distinct objects of cognition.
True; [this applies] in the state of deep sleep when there is sensation (*savedya*), but it does not occur when there is no sensation (*apavedya*);
therefore, the *māyīya* impurity is posited for them as having a restricted objective domain.
For instance: some rest in the void and other [levels], rendered inert by deep sleep, abiding in the state of dreamless sleep (suṣupta) where there is no object of knowledge;

others, however, being established in the intellect and so forth, are joined with the perception of distinct objects of knowledge consisting of the general residues of pleasure and pain, and are thus merged in the state of dreamless sleep accompanied by an object of knowledge (savedya-sauṣupta).
Yet, the nature of being dissociated from the body and organs—which constitute the causal and instrumental apparatus—is common to all, characterized as it is by the state of the *pralayākala*. //8//
Thus, this aspect— that even autonomy possesses a state of non-awareness— has been clarified;
and incidentally, the domain of the *kārmamala* has been shown,
as well as the occasional nature (*pākṣikatva*) of the *māyāmala*.
Now, however, it is shown that even though the two impurities of *āṇava* and *kārmika* are absent, one remains pure yet still an object of the impurity called *māyīya*:
"Even for those who possess consciousness and enjoy agency, when the *kārmika* impurity has perished..."
Those whose objects of experience and enjoyments are distinct possess the impurity of Māyā; they are the Vidyeśvaras.

Those who perceive pure consciousness alone as their own self, and who, through the emergence of wonder (*camatkāra*), act as agents— thereby becoming all-knowing and all-doing— are the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*). However,

that which appears to them as an object of knowledge (*vedya*) and as an effect (*kārya*)— namely, the body, the instruments [of sense], the worlds, and so forth— is, despite being distinct from them like the cloth from the weaver, nonetheless [non-different].
Thus, there exists for the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśvaras) a connection with impurity known as Māyā. //9//
Now, in order to show the object common to all three impurities simultaneously, he says:
"For all beings, including the gods and others, there are three kinds of impurity. Even among those, the karmic impurity alone is the primary cause of saṃsāra. (IPK 3.2.10)
In this context, the Vidyēśvaras and Vijñānākalas are not "bhavins" (beings subject to rebirth), because they have transcended the path ending with Māyā;
even the Pralayākalas are for a certain time without existence as bhavins.

However, those fourteen classes of beings enumerated in the scriptures, ranging from the gods down to immobile objects, who revolve within the sphere of the Māyā-tattva—they are all bhavins, that is, transmigrating souls.
And among those three, all three impurities (mala) function simultaneously.
Now, among these three impurities, which one brings about their transmigration?
He says: even there, when all three are present, the karmic impurity (kārma-mala) is primarily the cause of transmigration by coming together [with the others]. As it has been said:
"From karma, however, arise bodies, objects, and organs. Thus, the very connection with the body, organs, and objects— whether present or future—
occurring continuously in an uninterrupted series, is called *saṃsāra* (transmigration).

Although the impurities of *āṇava* and *māyā* are not the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), nevertheless, in the absence of *kārmamala*, those two are devoid of the power to bring about the various states such as the body and so forth within the *vijñānākala* and other levels; thus, it is primarily *kārmamala* alone that is reckoned in various scriptures as the cause of transmigratory existence.
Therefore, once that [impurity] has been exhausted, the placement of the steps for non-transmigration has indeed been granted;
with this intention, the scriptures such as the Sāṃkhya, Purāṇas, and Mahābhārata teach with great effort precisely the abandonment of the conceit of karmic bondage.
Thus, regarding the three impurities (*mala*), there are three varieties each consisting of one type, three consisting of two types, and one consisting of three types.
Thus, seven subjects arise;
and so it is stated in the scripture:
"The seven [subjects], beginning with Śiva and ending with Sakala, are possessors of power."

Thus it has been stated. Even therein, there is an infinite variety of modes due to internal subdivisions, the distinction between the subordinate and the primary, and the distinctions between option, combination, and so forth. //10//
And he shows that there are two types of transmigrating beings due to the emergence and disappearance of these three impurities:
"This very essence of consciousness (cittattva), consisting of agency, is empowered by *kalā*."
That which possesses the nature of the acid, such as emptiness and so forth, exists as a measured quality.

The primacy of agency and of consciousness belonging to the cognizing self (cidātman) within the void and other qualities [of the elements] constitutes knowledge; its characteristic is absorption into that. (IPK 3.2.12)

And this [is what is meant]: that consciousness of the thirty gods and other transmigrating beings—which consists of agency because the aspect of pure awareness is submerged due to the predominance of the aspect of agency—is the reality of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). This reality is empowered and vitalized by the principle called *kalā*, which is essentially a power of the Supreme Lord; though it was suppressed by impurity (*mala*), it has now been awakened.
It belongs to the illusory subject (māyā-pramātṛ), which extends from the void (śūnya) up to the body;

it exists as a subordinate quality (guṇatva), that is, as non-primary, because it is limited (mita) due to being submerged in the portion of the objects of knowledge (prameya)—ranging from the void down to the body—which have attained the state of "this-ness" (idantā). Thus, it is an object of knowledge (prameya).
He who is fair-complexioned, he who is happy,
he who is thirsty—
"I am he who is devoid of all forms"— thus indeed does this state of "this-ness" (idantā), wherein the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) has been internalized, manifest for those in transmigratory existence.
This very state of transmigratory existence consists of the forms of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

But when, according to the aforementioned direction of the Guru’s instruction and so forth, that very *ahaṃbhāva* (I-consciousness), by virtue of its nature as autonomy, performs the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) within itself of attributes such as pervasiveness and eternity,

and thereby remains as if emerging from the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) such as the void (*śūnya*), then that is the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*). Furthermore, when the entire range from the void to the bodily elements is permeated by the *ahaṃbhāva*— which is inseparable from such eternally sovereign power (*nityaiśvarya*) whose majesty has been thus reflected upon— by means of a union with the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*), [that too is the same state].
Then, in this fourth state (*turyadaśā*), even that [the subject] seems to abandon the status of being an object of cognition.
This twofold state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*) is called "immersion" (*samāveśa*) in the scriptures;
for in each case, complete immersion is indeed the primary factor.
However, there are other instructions for the sake of achieving that [state], as it is sung in the Gītā: "Those who, having fixed their minds on Me... (Gītā 12.2).
Thus [it is said], and also [the passage beginning] "Now, in order to cause the mind to enter" (Gītā 12.9),

and so forth. Furthermore, the very sprouts of this immersion (*samāveśa*)— such as the praise, prostration, worship, meditation, and absorption (*samādhi*) offered to the Supreme Lord— are animated by the cultivation of a state of total surrender toward that portion of the subject which consists of the well-known body and its adjuncts.
The elaborations of action;
as it is also sung:
"If you are unable even to practice [meditation], be intent upon My work" (Gītā 12.10).
Thus, at the fall of the body, the Supreme Lord alone remains as the single essence; who, then, could enter where, and how?
This is what he says: furthermore, that which is the primacy of agency is inseparable from the subordinate status of the void and the other [principles].

And when that insentient nature has become subordinate, there is also the "unawareness" of sovereignty; thus, by the rejection of the operation of impurity (*mala*), even that supreme aspect of consciousness which was characterized by awareness but had been suppressed by impurity now attains primacy through its emergence.
And that which constitutes the primacy of agency is this very state of emergence.
This very knowledge is [defined as] such because it is the antidote to the impurity consisting of ignorance;
this is the primary characteristic of immersion (samāveśa), by virtue of which the Lord, even while remaining in the body, is described in the scriptures as "liberated. //12//
Now, one might object: "In that case, let the state consisting of the Lord's immersion be of the nature of the Fourth (turya) and Beyond-the-Fourth (tadatīta);
but how can there be a distinction between the states of deep sleep, dream, and waking for the bound soul (paśu), as stated in the Āgamas?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] first explains the very nature of deep sleep through three verses.

In that which is empty—being the self wherein intellect and the rest are absent, the locus of "I-ness" and agency, and consisting merely of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of indistinct forms—there is the emptiness of the object of knowledge (*jñeyaśūnyatā*). (IPK 3.2.13)
The internal function of the senses is considered to be that which impels the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth;
it is called "life" (jīvana), or else it is the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) within the vital breath, consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka). (IPK 3.2.14)

When one remains in that state alone, it is called the state of deep sleep, which is like cosmic dissolution; it may be accompanied by an object of awareness or devoid of it, and may be joined with or free from the impurity of *māyā*. (IPK 3.2.15)

In this context, the reality of consciousness (cittattva), concealing its own essential nature, manifests as the object of knowledge—whether as the intellect and so forth up to the body, or as jars and the like.
This is all a single display of its own sovereignty;
there is no real succession or duality here.
Even there, however, sequence and differentiation appear by virtue of its own autonomy.

This being the case, when that portion which constitutes the concealment of the true nature (*svarūpa*) of consciousness comes to rest— either because it does not arise again, or because it has been destroyed, or because it is disregarded, as in the case of dissolution, sleep, meditative absorption, or fainting— it remains unmixed with the subsequent portions.

In that very state, the locus of agency (*kartṛtā*), which consists of the form of "I-ness," becomes joined with a pure latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—an indistinct reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that, being formless, has not yet reached the level of an object of knowledge (*vedya*).

At that time, although that very state involves a fusion with a very clear reflective awareness whose object is the intellect and so forth (which are the things to be negated), yet which does not depend on even a trace of the reflective awareness "not this" (*na iti*), it nevertheless possesses a negandum by virtue of the inevitable connection with what is to be negated; thus, like the thought "I am nothing," it accepts a negandum in the form of a general category.
For this very reason, that which has rendered the objects of knowledge (jñeya) as mere residual impressions (saṃskāraśeṣīkṛta) is called "void" (śūnya).
In such a state, which consists of the non-existence of everything from the intellect (buddhi) down to the body and blue objects, "voidness" (śūnyatva) is predicated;
for therein the voidness of the objects of knowledge consists in their being of the nature of non-existence and remaining only as residual impressions.
For this alone is non-existence everywhere, and not the destruction of existing things in their entirety.
In that very void subject (*pramātṛ*), there resides an impelling power within the wheel of vital airs (*vāyu-cakra*) consisting of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*.
And that [power] is the internal function of the two categories—the groups of the cognitive and active senses—which constitute the manifestation of *vidyā* and *kalā* respectively.

For the external function of these two consists of the perception of sound and so forth, the manifestation of sound, and the striking of the locations [of articulation], and so on. As it has been said:
"The function of the common organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with *prāṇa*" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 29).
Thus, in the void alone, the egoity (*ahaṃtā*), supported by the wheel of the senses, constitutes life.

Thus, that living being (*jīva*) transmigrates as nothing other than emptiness. Or, if life is that very internal common vitality consisting of the powers of the senses— which is denoted by the word "prāṇa" and consists of the impelling force of the specific vital airs such as *prāṇa*— and which, when superimposed [upon the self] as "I," constitutes living,
then the *prāṇa* itself is the transmigrating living being.
That very [self] is empty; and the vital breaths (prāṇas), denoted by the term "puryaṣṭaka" (the eightfold city),

consist of the pentad beginning with prāṇa, the group of sense organs, the collection of action organs, and the intellect (dhī) which is of the nature of determination, from which [the world] is manifested.

"Others [hold that] the five *tanmātras*, mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*) [are the constituents]; [thus] mind, ego, and intellect [arise] in the form of the emergence of the *tanmātras*" (Spa.
And saying, "Earth, water, fire... (Gītā 7.4),
they maintain that the repose within the pure state of that which is of both natures— the *puryaṣṭaka*— is precisely to that extent.

When that [state] exists, that which is characterized by awakening from the deep sleep of egoity (*ahaṃtā*), being both of the nature of existence (*bhāvarūpa*) and of the nature of action (*kriyāsvabhāva*), is the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*).

For the subject (*pramātā*) is asleep due to impurity (*mala*), yet as if not asleep due to his limited agency (*kalā*); here, upon the immersion of those two, he is "well-asleep" (*suṣupta*), and its state or activity is thus called *sauṣupta*.
In that state of empty deep sleep (*śūnya-sauṣupta*), there is nothing whatsoever cognizable as distinct [from the self];
thus, due to the absence of the impurity called *māyīya*, it is "incognizable" (*apavedya*).
However, in the case of the vital-breath deep sleep (*prāṇa-sauṣupta*), because of the presence of pleasure, pain, and so forth produced by touch, the impurity known as *māyā* exists.
Thus, that [state] is accompanied by sensation (*savedya*).
In this way, dissolution (*pralaya*) should also be understood as being like the two types of deep sleep— the intense and the non-intense—
except that it is characterized by the destruction of the body and so forth and the non-arising [of new ones], and it lasts for an exceedingly long time.
Deep sleep (*suṣupta*), however, is characterized by disregard for the body and so forth, and it lasts for a short duration—
this is the distinction.
Even therein, there is sleep caused by fatigue.
Fainting is caused by an imbalance of the bodily elements (dhātu-doṣa); intoxication, insanity, and so forth are caused by substances;
and meditative absorption (samādhi) is caused by independence.
Such are the internal subdivisions.
However, some maintain that the form of meditative absorption (samādhi) is "with experience" (savedya), while the other is "without experience" (apavedya). //15//
Now, one might object: "In that case, let the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) be indeed devoid of clearly perceived objects;
but what is the difference between the states of dreaming and waking, both of which involve the manifestation of clearly perceived objects?
Anticipating this doubt, he explains the distinction with two verses.

Even though it lies within the path of the mind alone, because of the delusion that it is an object of the senses, the creation of phenomena with a vivid appearance is considered the state of dreaming. (IPK 3.2.16)
That common creation which, by being within the range of all the senses, exists as something external and stable, belongs to all subjects; that is the waking state. (IPK 3.2.17)
The external sense organs, such as the eyeballs and so forth, are observed to be closed when one is asleep; yet, while they are closed, no activity of grasping external objects is seen in them.

Therefore, it is the Supreme Lord alone who creates forms, touches, and other entities within the pure path of the mind, making them capable of appearing with a clear form suitable for perception by the senses.
But it is not by even a slight degree, because only that which is undesirable is seen, and even that which is desirable [is seen] only through connection with another place, time, and so forth.
Precisely because it exists solely within the mind, this creation is not common to other subjects.
As for the appearance there of being an object of the external senses and being common to other subjects,
although it appears as such for as long as it shines, [it remains essentially mental].
Nevertheless, for one who has subsequently awakened,
because of the reflective awareness that "it was not so," that form appears as being without foundation;
thus, it is an error.
For the certainty is this: those other subjects and their respective sense organs that appear in a dream are non-different from those very same entities existing at the time of waking.
And since it is not so at the time of awakening,
the persistence of that certainty is indeed sublated;
therefore, both are said to be erroneous.
Instability is indeed nothing other than being erroneous.
Thus, by the very fact of not being an object of the sense faculties, its uniqueness (asādhāraṇatva) is implied; and by error itself, instability [is likewise implied].
Thus,
it was not shown even at the occasion of defining the attribute that is the counter-correlate of waking;
such a creation, because it exists for the bound soul (paśu) during the time of dreaming, is the "dream-state," meaning it is the object during the time of sleep.
The state of being a subject (*pramātṛtva*) for an object that has become thus is what is meant by the "dream state" of the bound soul (*paśu*).
The mention of the "senses" (*akṣa*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the ten external sense organs.
However, where the object of the external senses appears as ultimate reality—common to all subjects and accompanied by a continuous determination free from sublation—[it is the waking state].

Therefore, that [perception] which is the stability of the object for the bound soul (paśu) is "creation" (sṛṣṭi); the state of being a subject (pramātṛtva) regarding that object is the waking state (jāgara)—this is the meaning.
And as long as the persistence of the certainty [of that object] shines forth, so long is there waking.
And in the midst of that, because the persistence of certainty is uprooted, there is "dream"—
since objects consist essentially of manifestation,
even within a long dream, that wherein another dream occurs is, in relation to that [longer dream], indeed waking.
Or even that which is considered waking may, due to the persistence of certainty over a very long period of time, be regarded as nothing but a dream in comparison to another waking state. //17//
By demonstrating that these three states are to be abandoned, [the text] indicates that from the fourth state (*turya*) onwards they are to be accepted:

"This triad is to be abandoned because of the predominance of the agency inherent in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest; for it is through this that one is joined with pleasure, pain, and so forth, primarily by way of their loss or increase. (IPK 3.2.18)
In that which this cognizer perceives as the affliction consisting of rejection, appropriation, the desire for them, effort, and so forth, that very thing appears to him as something to be abandoned;
and this [cognition] is produced precisely through the variety of his connection with pleasure and pain.

And this occurs in these three states; for when that body consisting of consciousness—which is a single mass of bliss characterized by resting in one's own self with no orientation toward anything else and whose nature is agency—attains the state of being a subordinate quality within the levels of the void, the *puryaṣṭaka*, the body, and so forth, which possess breath and the like; [then it manifests as such].
Then, when that [consciousness] has become subordinate, the predominance of the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth manifests.
Thus, to the extent that there is a loss of that which is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), to that same extent there is an accumulation of suffering;
and to the extent that it emerges even slightly, to that same extent there is an accumulation of happiness.
For instance: at the time of hunger, suffering arises from the predominance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone;
upon satiety, pleasure is logical because that [breath] has subsided and the "I-sense" (*ahaṃtā*) has become predominant.
In the same way, regarding the massaging or non-massaging of one who is fatigued, one should understand it as the predominance or non-predominance of the body.
But for one who knows the reality of immersion (*samāveśa*), there is simply no arising of suffering at that time. As it has been said:
"Since even a weak person, having taken hold of it, proceeds to action;
likewise, one who is extremely hungry can cover over his hunger. (Sp. 48)
Thus, when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth are predominant and agency is subordinate, the connection with hundreds of varieties of pleasure and pain becomes a ground of exertion.
Therefore, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there exists both the predominance of the vital breath and the like, as well as the subordination of agency;
consequently, these three [states] alone are to be abandoned.

However, due to the unfolding of the predominance of agency (*kartṛtā*), beginning from the state of the Fourth (*turya*) and extending to the state beyond the Fourth (*turyātīta*) which consists of its stabilization, there arises a desire to acquire—that is, a lack of independence and exhaustion—until that cessation [is achieved] through the attainment of a nature that is a mass of bliss of a single flavor;
such is the intended meaning. //18//

Now, an objection is raised: "Has it not been stated that the predominance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth is the cause for being abandoned? If that is the case, then since they are absent in the fourth state (*turya*) and beyond, it would be impossible to emerge from absorption (*samāveśa*) when one is in those states.
He dispels this doubt with two verses:
"The vital breath consisting of *prāṇa* and *apāna* exists individually in both the sleeping and waking states."
The state called *samāna*, whose nature is the cutting off of that [breath], exists in deep sleep, like the equinoxes.
Moving through the middle and upwards, it is called udāna; moving through the fourth state, it consists of fire.
It is Vijñānākala, the Lord of Mantras, and as vyāna, it is the supreme, whose nature is the universe. (IPK 3.2.20)
"Prāṇa" refers to that state of the one whose nature is consciousness, which consists of the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) and has the nature of life;
it is, first of all, of the nature of a general vibration.

Consisting essentially in the imposition of the autonomy of "I-ness," which effects the animation of the insentient body, the vital breaths, and so forth, it is composed of the reflective awareness of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). That very [state], through its specific forms such as prāṇa, apāna, and the rest, assumes a fivefold nature.
It partakes [of both]; therein, moving slightly upward and falling slightly downward in the form of inhalation and exhalation, it gradually manifests the specific qualities of *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
These two specific qualities are indeed manifest during the waking state, because [the breath], having issued forth from the body, comes to rest upon the objects of the senses.

Even beyond that, [the two] rest within the body or within the objects of cognition such as memory; for the existence of both prāṇa and apāna is very clear there. Even in dream, those two certainly exist.
For even while one is sleeping, the two vital breaths—prāṇa and apāna—which consist of exhalation and inhalation, are clearly perceived by another;
and because it is itself experienced through its own awareness, the state consisting of rejection and appropriation is indeed felt.
Therefore, in the waking state, the act of breathing consists of these two specific forms of prāṇa and apāna.
Likewise, there is dream;
"dream" (svapna) is that which is slept (supta), but when that very state becomes more fully developed, it is called a dream.
Then the cognizer is in deep sleep;
this is his state of deep sleep (sauṣupta-pada).
Both of these [states] assume the vital-breath-related form known as "samāna" (the equalizing).
In the state of *savedya-suṣupta* (sensationless deep sleep), although the movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths is still perceived,
nevertheless, that rest which occurs between them in the abode of the heart, in the region devoid of the senses— that alone is primarily *suṣupta*. Therein,

the cessation and rest of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* for some time is the very nature of the process of equalizing the entire range of *rasa* (flavors/energies) and so forth throughout the upward, downward, and transverse directions.

Precisely because it grants the expansion of the heart-lotus, the *samāna* wind effects the digestion of what has been eaten and drunk; due to its temporary equilibrium and cessation between the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds—which take the form of day and night—it is like the time of the equinox (*viṣuvat*).
It is so called because it "deserves" (*arhati*) the state of being pervasive (*viṣu*), that is, equalization.
Thus it is said.

The suffix *vati* is applied by the rule *tadarham* (Pāṇini 5.1.117). Furthermore, the indeclinability (*avyayatva*) of *vati* when used in the sense of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is established by usage, as seen in such expressions as *uddhato nivataḥ*;
for this is logically proven, not merely a matter of explicit scriptural injunction.

It impels (*suvati*) or urges on incessantly the distinction (*viśeṣa*) characterized by the increase and decrease of day and night; thus, by virtue of the suffix *śatṛ*, it is called *viṣuvat*. And in that *viṣuvat*, there exists the state of the breath (*prāṇa*) and the downward breath (*apāna*), which are being severed, in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
For it has been stated more than once that this very state is a cessation, but not a destruction in its entirety;
and therefore, the state of being a seed for both abandonment and acquisition exists in deep sleep.

And at this stage, the entire class of bound souls (paśu), ending with the *pralayākala*, [is transformed]. However, when that movement of vital breath (*prāṇana*), causing the left and right paths to become desolate, flows upward in its central form, then that flow—

performing a dissolution characterized by the bestowal of the essence of non-duality upon all duality, like the melting of congealed clarified butter— is the function of the *udāna* breath, beginning from the *vijñānākala* up to Sadāśiva.
And that state consists of the fourfold [tattvas];
for above Māyā lie the Vijñānākalas—
it is from that point onward that the dissolution of duality proceeds.

When duality has dissolved—in its form as the pervasion of the body, which consists of the collection of all objects of knowledge, the categories of reality (tattva), the elements (bhūta), and the worlds (bhuvana)—the activity of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti) takes the form of the pervasive breath (vyāna). This is permeated by the Supreme Śiva, who is the soul of the universe, and takes the form of the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
Thus, the vital breath itself is the subject (pramātā), existing in the forms of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
such is the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
He is the *vijñānākala* and he is the *mantra* with respect to the categories (*varga*);
and he is the *īśa*, who has the form of Sadāśiva and Īśvara—this is the *udāna*.
This is what is meant:

Although vital breath (*prāṇana*) exists even in the states of the Fourth (*turya*) and Beyond-the-Fourth (*tadatīta*), for otherwise neither the state of being alive nor emergence from samādhi would be possible;
nevertheless, because these two stages primarily consist of resting in non-duality through the withdrawal of all distinctions, they are devoid of the variety of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Thus, by virtue of consisting of supreme bliss—the nature of which is resting in one's own self as a single, undivided mass—they are solely to be embraced.

However, in states such as deep sleep, because there exists a differentiation consisting of the manifestation of indistinct objects of knowledge—which is of the nature of latent impressions—and the manifestation of distinct objects of knowledge, there is a variety of pleasure, pain, and so forth; thus, [this state] is indeed to be abandoned.
Therefore, it is rightly said that "this triad is to be abandoned," and so on.

Furthermore, it is shown by this that the Blessed One, whose body is the universe, exists precisely as the forms of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna, while his nature is that of Śiva—the state of the groups beginning with the sakala, pralayākala, and vijñānākala, which consist of the emergence, entry, and dissolution of all things. As it has been said:
"The universe consists of thirty-six principles; these are the powers of Śambhu, beginning with prāṇa."
Thus //20// From the beginning, [verse] 171.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of the Subject," in the *Āgamādhikāra* of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. // 2 //
And this third chapter on the scriptural authority is complete. // 3 //
The First Chapter in the Section on the Compendium of Reality (*Tattvasaṅgraha*) [Vimarśinī]:
[To Him who] possesses the non-differentiation of the infinite variety of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and so forth;
"We praise that Śiva who manifests Himself to His devotees.
Thus, having extensively determined the nature of the Self— which is the form of Maheśvara established through self-awareness, reasoning, and scripture— by means of the three sections [of this work],
[the author] now seeks to instill that very same reality into the minds of his disciples by means of eighteen verses summarizing the meaning of the scriptures.

He demonstrates that [the Lord] is indeed the very self of all living beings with one chapter, beginning with "svātmaiva sarvajantūnām" and ending with "utpalenopapāditā. In that [chapter], he describes the ultimate nature in one verse; the nature of bondage from the perspective of the reality of the subject and object of cognition in nine verses; and the reality of liberation, which consists of recognition, in seven verses.
He shows the conclusion with a verse—
this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Now, the meaning of the text itself is being examined.
One's own self alone is the one Great Lord of all living beings;
it is I, whose form is the universe, nourished by the unbroken awareness that "this is I. (IPK 4.1)
In this world, insentient objects appear as if submerged within consciousness;
for the reflective awareness of the insentient, expressed as "this," ultimately rests within the reflective awareness of pure consciousness, expressed as "I.
Consequently, insentient things are devoid of self, whereas living beings alone are sentient and possess a self.
And for them, Maheśvara alone is their own self; he alone is Maheśvara and no other whatsoever.
Because his nature is consciousness (*saṃvit*), and there is no distinction whatsoever in consciousness by way of space, time, or essential form.
Granted that the body, vital breaths, and so forth may be differentiated,
they nevertheless belong to the category of the insentient and are entirely immersed in consciousness;
thus, there is only the single conscious Self who, by its own sovereignty, manifests the manifoldness of the universe within itself.

Then Maheśvara, having internalized this state of "thisness" (*idantā*), becomes full of the *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (the reflective awareness of "I") which consists in resting within his own self while turned away from the *parā* (the supreme) level;

for this very reason, omniscience and omnipotence are not to be achieved by him through effort, since just as the states of being a knower and a doer belong to a single Self with respect to the objects of the various faculties of cognition and action, so too do they belong to Him with respect to the thousands of Rudras and individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) who stand in the place of those faculties.
Whatever knowledge arises from the aggregate of objects, and whatever is its instrument, both reside in the single Self that is Consciousness. //1//
Now, one might object: "If this Self is indeed one alone, in the form of Maheśvara, then what is bondage for which there is this effort toward liberation?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In that regard, within the portion of 'this' created by Himself, [the Self exists] as the subject through the intellect and so forth."
By him, that state which is the object of the grasping of egoity has been brought to its conclusion.

In this regard, while Maheśvara abides thus within his own self—that very mirror of one's own self consisting of the nature of light—the Supreme Lord, by his own sovereignty, first brings forth through that same [light] a contracted "this-aspect" (*idambhāga*).
