Within that, this object of knowledge (*vedya*) consisting of intellect, vital breath, and body—which is known as "this"—is appropriately the perceiver (*grāhaka*) of the object of knowledge distinct from the intellect and so forth; yet, because it lacks the power to overcome the state of being "this," it possesses only a contrived and incomplete sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*).
That which appears through conceptual determination shines forth as "I am Devadatta" or "I am Caitra. //2//
Granted that this may be so,
even then, whose is the bondage?
For who else exists apart from the Lord?
To refute this, he says:
"That [individual] is considered to be many, consisting of a lack of recognition of his own true nature.
In that regard, within creation, there is activity and bliss; experience consists of the nature of suffering and pleasure. (IPK 4.3)

True; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no bondage whatsoever. It is simply that when [the Lord], out of His own unsurpassed sovereignty (*svātantrya*), manifests Himself as contracted, then that very non-recognition (*aparijñāna*) of His own full nature—which consists in a lack of reflective awareness (*aparāmarśa*) despite its being manifest—is the cause under discussion. That person whose essence is merely the non-manifestation of fullness (*pūrṇatvākhyātimātratattva*) is thus called "Puruṣa."
For this very reason, he is manifold due to the assumption of contraction through the particularities of each respective body, vital breath, and intellect.
And that person, as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), experiences the connection characterized by enjoyment (*bhoga*).
Furthermore, what is called "enjoyment" for him consists of the two—action and bliss—which are superimposed upon it.
Action performed through conceptualization is suffering,
for *rajas*— being of the nature of illumination, non-illumination, and restlessness— is said to be suffering; whereas *sattva*, being of the nature of illumination, is happiness.
Darkness, however, is of the nature of non-luminosity; it is a state of rest in the middle, corresponding to dissolution. //3//
Now, what is excluded and what is included by the phrase "in creation"? To this he says:

"The knowledge and action of the Lord which exist toward entities that are the forms of His own limbs—these two, with Māyā as the third, constitute the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* of the bound soul (*paśu*). (IPK 4.4)

The light (*prakāśa*) and the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that exist everywhere as the very nature of the Lord of universal form (*viśvarūpa-bhagavat*) are indeed His knowledge and action; these rest solely upon the reflective awareness of His own dual nature, which is the ultimate reality of Sadāśiva and Īśvara expressed as "I am this. That is the Lord’s power of *māyā*.
These three powers are innate to the Lord and are uncreated.
But when the true nature [of the Self] is not recognized, knowledge and action occur with respect to distinct entities;
pure difference alone is devoid of light (prakāśa) and self-reflection (vimarśa).

Thus, for the bound soul (paśu), there is light, light-and-non-light, and non-light, which correspond respectively to the qualities of goodness, passion, and darkness (sattva, rajas, tamas), characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion, and whose nature consists of illumination, activity, and restriction. //4//

But if this is so, then just as the powers of knowledge, action, and māyā are said to be non-different from the Supreme Lord, in the same way, the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* [should be non-different] from the bound soul (*paśu*).
It follows that they would be distinct [from the self], and yet those [qualities] are counted as being included within masculinity;
how can this be?
Thus he pacifies the doubt:
"The state of being a power (śaktitva) is not predicated of the possessor of power (śāktimat) when it exists as something distinct [from the powers];
for these qualities undergo transformation into the form of instruments and effects. (IPK 4.5)
This would indeed be true if there were no apprehension of difference; however, this very difference is what is being investigated.
And in that regard, the *puruṣa* has as its essential nature pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which is contracted.
Its nature as manifestation and so forth, which has objects as its domain, is not innate, because that would entail [such manifestation] at all times;
rather, it is produced by connection with another.
And therefore, since these qualities such as *sattva* and the rest exist as distinct from that animal (the subject), which is suspected of possessing those powers—
Therefore, the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are not described as being distinct [from the qualities], but rather, because they are instruments (*upakaraṇa*), they are called qualities (*guṇa*).
Now, why are they described as distinct from the *puruṣa*?

It is said: here, this group of thirteen instruments and the ten products, which consist of the transformations of pleasure, pain, and delusion, are experienced as having the very nature of pleasure and so forth.

Thus, if pleasure, pain, and delusion—which function through identity with the categories of instruments and effects—were to share in an identity that pervades the *puruṣa*, then the *puruṣa* would become composed of the entire creation up to its effects and instruments, and the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāma*) would be refuted. Therefore, it follows that the *puruṣa* is omniform (*viśvarūpa*) by virtue of his power of sovereignty;
and thus, no *puruṣa* whatsoever is merely the Lord (*īśvara*).

Therefore, it is established that in an investigation into the true nature of the person (puruṣa), which consists of non-recognition, the qualities such as sattva and the others are indeed distinct. //5//
But how can knowledge and the other [qualities] take the form of *sattva* and so forth with respect to the bound soul (*paśu*)? To this he says:
"Sattva is the bliss and activity of the Lord; its absence is that same [quality] in the bound soul.
That which consists of both is passion (*rajas*), which is suffering, being a concretion of *sattva* and *tamas*. (IPK 4.6)
In this context, the Protector—whose nature is self-luminous—is characterized by the manifold manifestations of the universe through the processes of emanation and so forth.

That existence (*sattā*) of the Lord of the Universe, which is his agency of becoming (*bhavanakartṛtā*) and consists of the form of radiance (*sphurattā*), was previously explained in the passage: "That radiance is the Great Existence" (*Ipv 1.5.14*).

Because it is inseparable from the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the Light, that very [existence], being of the nature of the wonder (*camatkāra*) consisting of reflective awareness, is called the Power of Action (*kriyāśakti*).
And because it consists in resting within one's own self through the abandonment of orientation toward the other, that very state is bliss;
thus, in this way, the Lord possesses all these forms precisely by virtue of being the conscious self (*cidātman*).
For the bound soul (*paśu*), however, existence and its absence, as well as bliss and its absence, exist because his nature is contracted.
Therefore, that which possesses the portion of existence and bliss, whose function is luminosity and happiness, is *sattva*;
that which is its absence, whose nature is obscuration and delusion, is *tamas*.
And although these two, *sattva* and *tamas*, exist in mutual exclusion like blue and non-blue, they nevertheless stand in the relationship of cause and effect.

Even by that [quality], with respect to the substrate (*dharmin*) which is the object of a single unifying cognition, it appears as mutually intermingled—according to the analogy of the variegated color of a butterfly consisting of both blue and non-blue;
therefore, this dual nature of a mixed essence is the *rajas* quality.
For this very reason, because *sattva* and *tamas*, whose natures are respectively luminous and non-luminous, abide here in conjunction, there is the state of suffering (*duḥkhatva*).
For bliss is indeed a single, undivided manifestation (*prakāśa*) of one's beloved son and so forth; delusion (*moha*) is likewise a single, undivided non-manifestation.
As for that which is a manifestation in some way—such as the form of a body afflicted by disease, which is undesirable—[it is not bliss].
And how it is in some way unmanifest is as follows: that very state of suffering [is understood] by virtue of its being associated with the desired quality of having abandoned disease;
and this alone is the essence of the sequence of prior and posterior, which is the ultimate reality of action (*kriyā*).
In this regard, however, there is no state of being neither [of the two].
Because that [non-existence] does not enter into any cognition whatsoever—whether its form be imagined (*kalpita*) or non-imagined (*akalpita*).
For instance: first, blue appears in a cognition whose form is non-imagined;

however, even though the absence of blue is a mere nothingness (*tuccha*), it is nonetheless imagined by conceptual construction (*kalpanā-kalpita*), and because it appears [in cognition], it is for the time being both conventional and ultimate reality.
Let it be granted that something "blue-and-not-blue" might appear due to the commingling of both [blue and not-blue];
however, as for that which is of neither form, if it is not made an object by a non-conceptualized cognition of blue, then it would follow the conceptualized cognition of "not-blue.
On the other hand, if it does not enter into that conceptualized cognition and is instead made an object by a non-conceptualized [cognition], then it must be simply blue.
Thus, the fourth quality does not belong to the bound soul (paśu).
Furthermore, the word "api" is used in the sense of "even," [indicating that] for the bound soul,
that existence is its very essence (sattva).
The connection is as follows: darkness (*tamas*) is the absence of that [light], and passion (*rajas*) consists of both [light and darkness]. //6//
Thus, the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*), consisting of the Lord and the bound soul (*pati* and *paśu*), has been briefly determined.

Now, in order to determine the reality of the object (*prameyatattva*), [the author] says the following regarding the Lord (*pati*) to establish that this is indeed the reality of the object: "Those [objects] which arise from the Lord’s non-conventional awareness of 'this-ness' (*idantā-parāmarśa*)..."
These appear as mixed, as distinct, and likewise as variegated.
It has been stated here that objects are, in fact, nothing but appearances;
and these are sometimes mixed together through the unity of reflective awareness when they take on the form of particulars.
Sometimes these [entities] are perceived as entirely unmixed when they possess a generic form;

yet even these objects, though possessing both natures, must be made the object of a non-generic, non-constructed "thisness" (*idambhāva*)—which consists of an innate awareness and is like the pointing of a finger—not only for a newborn infant, but for the Lord (*īśvara*) as well.
In that way, by means of that mode of being both general and particular, they manifest with manifold variety.
For their "manifoldness" (citratva) consists in this: that both their state of mixture and their state of non-mixture shine simultaneously, resting within a single I-ness (ahantā).

Thus, in the state of the Lord (īśvara), as a necessary concomitant of the emergence of objective phenomena (bhāva), the void—which takes the form of the contraction of consciousness and consists merely of the meaning of the negative particle uncolored by any object to be negated—shines by the very light of the manifestation of consciousness; it brings forth a non-conventional "this-ness" (idantā) in the form of the negation of I-ness. //7//
Thus far, such is the nature of the object of knowledge regarding the Lord (pati) who has the form of Īśvara;
but as for the Blessed One Paramaśiva, how could even the discourse concerning an object of knowledge arise?
For it is precisely the capacity to give rise to the discourse concerning objects of knowledge that constitutes the state of Sadāśiva-Īśvara of the Blessed One.
Therefore, [the author] now dispels the doubt as to what the status of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is with respect to the bound soul (*paśu*) by means of three verses:
"But those objects which appear as distinct must be postulated [as belonging] to the inner self (*pratyagātman*)."
[This occurs] within the range of memory, imagination, and so forth, by means of various distinct designations.
His creation is unique, subsisting upon the creation of the Lord; yet this very creation, though appearing real due to ignorance, is in truth the power of the Lord, being of His own nature.

By means of the activity of conceptualization—which takes the form of various phonemes and consists of the vital breath (prāṇa) that is immobile for the sake of obstructing its own repose— [the Self is bound]. (IPK 4.10)
This highlights a distinction:
whereas for the inner self (pratyagātman), objects exist as such in the form of cognizable entities,
they do not exist in the manner described for the Lord (Īśvara).

"Divided" means that those objects whose manifestations are differentiated by being either mixed or unmixed— those objects which consist of both the particular and the universal— are to be postulated, that is, they must be conceptually constructed, from the perspective of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is an unconfused self-awareness for each individual and consists of the unmixed light of "I" (*ahaṃprakāśa*).

In accordance with the respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of each individual, objects are employed as various pleasures, pains, and so forth, through memory, imagination, volition, and other forms of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
This has been stated at length: for the Lord (*īśvara*), objects are made the domain of pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) independently of conceptualization;
for the bound soul (*paśu*), however, those same objects become established within a conceptualization characterized by mutual exclusion (*apohana*) and the impulse to reject.
"Because it is useful for worldly transactions such as rejection and acquisition.

Now, if the object is conceptualized only to the extent that it is [already] non-conceptualized, then what is the distinction regarding the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) as being either the Lord (*pati*) or the bound soul (*paśu*)?
It is said: "Of that... [referring to the following].
The creation performed by the individual subject (*paśu*) exists above those objects created by the Lord;
therefore, subsisting upon that creation of the Lord, it is unique, restricted to each individual subject.
For example, that which is created by someone with the thought "this is pleasing" belongs to him alone at that time, and not to anyone else.
Now, if even an animal possesses the power of creation, is it not then simply the Lord? True, it is indeed the Lord.
But if this is so, why does the creation not become common [to all]?
This would be so if he were fully aware of his own power;
however, while that power remains unknown to him, the activity of conceptualization—the capacity for conceptualizing—arises precisely while he is under the sway of another.
But surely, by whom is that [capacity] aroused in him?

He said: The power of the Lord—which consists of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) by virtue of being the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), or which consists of the circle of deities such as Brahmā and others whose purpose is to obstruct His supreme sovereignty characterized by repose in His own nature—is variegated through the diversity of those various phonemes beginning with *ka*.
Through that [power], the activity of conceptualization belonging to that bound soul (*paśu*) is flickering, because it lacks stability in any single object.

Through that activity of conceptualization, which is permeated by the diversity of mental constructs such as "this is a friend" or "this is an enemy," there occurs the unique creation of the bound soul (*paśu*), whose very nature is that of the Lord (*īśvara*).
{The five-faced, four-tusked elephant is held in the sky.}
Thus, even in the state of mixture, there is the creation of conceptual construction (vikalpa);

since [the individual] subsists upon those manifestations created by the Lord, it is said that the entire animal creation is a creation of cognition that subsists upon the creation of the Lord. //10//

Now, if this emanation belonging to the bound soul (*paśu*) is of the nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), then what would the emanation of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī sṛṣṭi*) do for the bound soul?
This is determined as follows:
"The emanation of the Lord is both common and otherwise, because it is clearly manifest."
Through the abandonment of conceptual construction and one-pointedness of mind, one gradually attains the state of lordship.
The divine creation (*aiśvara-sarga*) is twofold:
common, such as jars and the like, and uncommon, such as the double moon and so forth, which is described otherwise;
and its general characteristic is what is called "clear manifestation" (*spaṣṭāvabhāsana*).

When this very creation, through the process of abandoning conceptualization, becomes the object of non-conceptual apprehension alone, and by relying on one-pointedness toward a clearly manifest object, it reaches the state of the reflective awareness of sovereignty as "I am this," then— by way of avoiding the opening and closing of the eyes directed toward the internal object— the gradual intensity of practice destroys the beast-like nature of the bound soul (paśu) and reveals its true lordship (īśvaratva).

Furthermore, even this "fettered" (pāśava) creation of conceptual construction (vikalpasarga) which has been described— if it is thoroughly known by the power of the Lord (īśaśakti) as being "otherwise," that is, through the reversal of its previously mentioned form— then it becomes entirely common [to all], like the conceptual constructions of nourishment, malevolent rites, pacification, and so forth, for one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) has been cultivated through the application of mantras. //11//

Thus, by the gradual reduction of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), liberation has been shown to be one's own realization (*svapratyaya*) characterized by the direct perception of the universal self (*viśvātmaka-sākṣātkāra*), occurring when the non-conceptual form becomes internalized;
now, he shows that same [liberation] even in the absence of the reduction of conceptual construction:
"For one who fully understands: 'All this is my own manifestation.'"
Even amidst the proliferation of conceptual constructions, the Great Lordship of the Universal Self remains.

For that which is called the innermost Self (pratyagātman) is not some other limited being (paśu) such as "I"; rather, it is the Supreme (para), who is a single mass of light consisting of the grasped and the grasper; He alone is "I," and "I" am indeed He—there is no other whatsoever.
Therefore, even the creation of conceptual constructs is my own power, characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).
When such a realization has become firm, one is liberated while still living, even if conceptual thought has not yet been entirely exhausted. As it has been said:
"Even doubt should not be suspected; this state of being free from doubt is manifest."
Thus [ends the twelfth].

But surely, in this case, what is the difference between the bound and the liberated with respect to the object of knowledge (*prameya*)? It is said: The object of knowledge is common [to all], yet the liberated one perceives it as non-different from his own self, just like Maheśvara; whereas the bound one, on the other hand, perceives it as possessing absolute difference. (IPK 4.13)

The liberated one identifies as his very self that which consists of the form of "I-consciousness" (ahamiti), which presides over the entire range of subjects from the venerable Lord Sadāśiva down to the level of a worm; and consequently,
what is an object of knowledge for the universe is also an object of knowledge for him, and what is an object of knowledge for him is also an object of knowledge for the universe.
And this object of knowledge (*prameya*) is a limb of my very self, and other objects of knowledge are likewise;
by this sequence, the object of knowledge is non-distinct from one another and from the entire class of subjects (*pramātṛ*).
Thus, everything attains the state of being an object of reflective awareness (*parāmarśapada*), whose essence is resting in the non-duality of a single flavor.
For the bound soul, however, all of this is the reverse;
thus, due to the differentiation of the single flavor, he does not find rest in this [state]. //13//

Now, one might object: "The account of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) has been examined in relation to Sadāśiva, Īśvara, the stage of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), and the bound subject (*paśupramātṛ*);
but how does this apply to Paramaśiva?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In every respect, however, Śiva is filled with the infinite flood of principles merged within him; he is a mass of consciousness and bliss, whose form is the supreme syllable.
Indeed, in the Blessed One, the illustrious Supreme Śiva, there is no body whatsoever that is an object of cognition (*prameya*),
because the flood of reality (*tattvaugha*) is dissolved therein by resting entirely within the state of pure consciousness alone.

Consequently, that state is a single, unified mass characterized by the wonder of one's own self, which consists of an unartificial, innate self-reflection through the bliss of resting within one’s own nature as the essence of consciousness.

Possessing a form that is uninterrupted in its nature through the supreme immutable (paramākṣara), she is designated as the embodied consort of the Blessed One who consists of the universe; she is the unconditioned, unsurpassed abode, eternally pure, transcending all things, and beyond the discourse of objects of knowledge. //14//
Thus, he states the result of that reality which was described through the fourfold qualification:
"Knowing his own self, as well as right knowledge and action, in this way, and seeing them as they are desired, one knows and acts. (Ipk 4.15)

"Thus" means: knowing the Self as having the form of the Lord (Īśvara), and knowing that His knowledge and action consist solely in His sovereignty which is non-different from Himself—one reflects that "this Self is of such a nature, and not as shown by the followers of Kaṇāda and others;

and thus knowledge and action are not anything separate from Him. One who is intent on the practice of immersion (samāveśa) perceives that whatever he desires, he knows and accomplishes with this very body.
But one who is not intent on that [worldly life], while still possessing a body, is liberated while living (jīvanmukta); upon the fall of the body, he is indeed the Supreme Lord. //15//
Although this meaning is established through one's own realization, the instruction of the lineage of gurus must be stated as its corroborative support,
for the vision of the scripture has indeed been shown by means of the section on traditional authority (āgama).
Thus, this [meaning] becomes firmly established through the guru, through the scripture, and from oneself.
With this intention, he demonstrates the lineage of the gurus: "Thus has this new path, easy to practice, been revealed by me, just as it was taught by the great gurus in the Śivadṛṣṭi-śāstra."
Therefore, one who places their foot here, having realized their own agency as the creator of the world and constantly entering that state consisting of Śiva-nature, attains perfection.

In the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise, our supreme preceptor, the venerable Śrī Somānanda, stated that this [system]— being Abhinava’s, contained within all the secret scriptures, and previously unknown due to its being concealed— is nevertheless easily accomplished because it is devoid of even a fraction of the painful exertion involved in external and internal rituals, breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth;
that very system has now been brought here into clarity by removing the suspicion of the stains of opposing doctrines.
Since this matter is established through the scriptures, the teacher, and one's own conviction, therefore—

resting the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) upon this very ground of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and having contemplated the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) characterized by universal agency within oneself—
one reflects with firmness; at that time, by that mere act of reflective awareness, one becomes the Lord Śiva himself, liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
As it has been said by the venerable Parameṣṭhin:
"Once Śiva-nature, which resides in all things, is known through firm realization,
there is no further task to be accomplished by means of ritual instruments or even by meditative cultivation."
"Once gold is known, what is the use of further cultivation (*bhāvanā*), practice (*karaṇa*), and so forth?
In every respect, its reality is as firm as that of one's father, mother, and the like.

(Śivadṛṣṭi). Having contemplated this, if he enters incessantly into either one or both of those [states] which are other than the body, vital breath, and intellect, he immerses everything right there.
He continuously attains various such manifestations, culminating in the Great Manifestation. //16//
Now, if the entity called the "self" is indeed that very thing, then there would be no distinction between its recognition and non-recognition;
for is there not a necessity for the seed to be recognized?
It is said in reply: there are two kinds of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
The external [recognition] consists of sprouts and so forth, while that whose essence is the wonder of resting within the subject takes the form of joy and so on.
Of these, the former truly does not require recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

The second [type of recognition], however, necessarily depends upon that [first]. And here, the recognition of the Lord (īśvarapratyabhijñāna) is indispensable, for it consists of the functional efficacy (arthakriyā) characterized by the manifestation of both higher and lower accomplishments, which has as its essence the wonder of "I am Maheśvara," and is composed of the yoga of the splendors of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).

Now, one might object: "Has not purposeful activity, whose essence consists in resting within the subject, been seen to be impossible without recognition (pratyabhijñāna), yet seen to be possible when it exists?
Where, then, has this been observed? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Just as the beloved of a slender woman, though standing near her, is not recognized as such because he is indistinguishable from other people due to their various entreaties and thus cannot provide pleasure;
so too is the Lord of the Universe, for this world does not perceive His own Self despite its inherent excellence.
This recognition of her has arisen so that she may no longer be content with her own former splendor.
When a passionate woman, her affection intensified by hearing of the hero’s virtues, desires nothing more than the sight of him,

remaining day and night with a heart beyond her control, performing prayers to the gods, dispatching female messengers, and reporting her own condition through Madalekhā, she stands with the slender vine of her body wasted away by separation.

Then, by the power of that very vow, when her beloved standing nearby was beheld unexpectedly, although the sight of her beloved was accomplished— yet it did not fill her heart, for she perceived him through various extraordinary qualities that had reached the stage of being scrutinized and reduced to the commonality of all people.

Likewise, although the Lord of All (Viśveśvara) is constantly manifest within one’s own self, that manifestation does not bestow fullness upon the heart; for that Self, too, has not been seized by the supreme state of sovereignty characterized by the unimpeded power of omniscience, agency, and so forth— thus its condition becomes identical to that of a jar or other objects which are merely appearing.
But when, through the words of a messenger, through signs of her characteristics, or through other means, one touches those excellences by making them penetrate the heart,
then at that very moment one attains a certain plenitude according to the maxim of the "wondrously blossoming flower";
yet, in the savor of the repeated practice of enjoyment, one also finds intervals of rest.

In the same way, when through the word of the Guru or through the recognition of the powers characterized by knowledge and action, there arises within the Self an internal realization of the excellence of supreme sovereignty, then that very state, characterized as such, is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which consists of fullness; however, when one takes delight in the practice of immersion (*samāveśa*), the attainment of supernatural powers (*vibhūti*) occurs—thus, for him, it is precisely this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that bestows both the higher and lower accomplishments. //17//

This treatise, which is beneficial to all and yields great fruit, is concluded by mentioning the name of his father in order to inspire people to engage with it; for such engagement arises through a conviction characterized by the confidence produced by remembering its excellence, which is established both by its well-known lineage and by the renown of its title.
For the sake of the effortless accomplishment [of liberation] for people, this *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* has been established by Utpaladeva, the son of Udayākara. (IPK 4.18)
"Of any living being whatsoever"—here there is no consideration of caste or other such factors; thus, its universal beneficence is stated.
"So that supreme and non-supreme accomplishment may be achieved without effort"—thus, its great fruitfulness is shown.
"The illustrious Utpaladeva, son of Udayākara and our supreme teacher, composed this treatise"—this is stated by way of his renown.
People proceed [toward liberation]—thus, by means of this instigation, he (the Lord) becomes a benefactor; such is the designation of both names.
This [teaching], brought to the heart through hundreds of logical arguments, is "this" (iyam). May there be auspiciousness. (18) [Total from the beginning: 190]
This concise and unerring commentary (*vṛtti*) on the *Pratyabhijñā*, which investigates the meaning of the aphorisms, has been composed by Abhinavagupta.
Through this, the meanings of sentences, means of knowledge, words, principles, and the true scriptures attain their utility for one's own self via this treatise.
Except for the sun alone, no other here is capable of employing both the terrestrial juices and those consisting of water for the nourishment of crops.
"What can be said of that deluded person who, without knowing himself, desires to discern another?
To him, when asked 'Who are you?', what answer can he give?

Thus ends the chapter on the Compendium of Principles (*tattvasaṅgraha*) in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, together with the commentary named *Vimarśinī* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta.
The venerable *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* is completed.
